questions.stem: The carbon content of MILD STEEL is about:
questions.solution:
**About 0.15 to 0.25 per cent.**

**The carbon content of the ferrous materials:**

| Material | Carbon content | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **WROUGHT IRON** | **Below 0.25 %, and practically 0.05-0.15 %** | **Very ductile, fibrous, forgeable; almost obsolete** |
| **MILD (low carbon) STEEL** | **0.15 to 0.25 %** ← | **DUCTILE, weldable, tough — the structural steel** |
| **Medium carbon steel** | **0.25 to 0.6 %** | Stronger, less ductile; shafts, rails |
| **HIGH carbon (hard) steel** | **0.6 to 1.5 %** | **HARD and BRITTLE; tools, springs, cutting edges** |
| **CAST IRON** | **2.5 to 4.5 %** | **Very hard, brittle, EXCELLENT in compression and weak in tension** ← |

> **Every option offered is a real carbon range from that table, so the material named in the stem must be matched.**

> **Option (b) 0.6-0.8 % is HIGH CARBON steel and option (d) 2.5-4.5 % is CAST IRON — both real values for other materials.**

> **The boundary worth fixing is 2 PER CENT: below it the material is STEEL, above it CAST IRON. That single division separates a weldable, ductile structural material from a brittle casting material.**

**Why carbon content governs everything about the material:**

> **Carbon dissolved in iron forms hard, brittle IRON CARBIDE (cementite), dispersed through the softer ferrite matrix.**

> **So MORE CARBON means MORE cementite, and the properties follow directly:**

| As carbon INCREASES | Effect |
|---|---|
| **STRENGTH and HARDNESS** | **RISE** |
| **DUCTILITY and TOUGHNESS** | **FALL** ← |
| **WELDABILITY** | **FALLS sharply — above about 0.3 % special precautions are needed** ← |
| **Ability to be HARDENED by quenching** | **RISES — low carbon steel cannot be hardened usefully** |
| **Melting point** | Falls |
| **Machinability** | Peaks at medium carbon |

> **The WELDABILITY consequence is the one that matters most in construction: mild steel is the structural material precisely BECAUSE its low carbon lets it be welded without preheating or special electrodes.**

> **A higher-carbon steel welded without precautions forms brittle martensite in the heat-affected zone and cracks — which is why the structural grades are specified with a maximum carbon content and a carbon EQUIVALENT limit.**

> **So the low carbon content is not a limitation of mild steel but the property that makes it useful.**

**Why CAST IRON behaves so differently, since it is the extreme case:**

| Property | Cast iron | Mild steel |
|---|---|---|
| **Compressive strength** | **VERY HIGH — 600-800 MPa** | 250 MPa |
| **Tensile strength** | **LOW — 100-200 MPa, and unreliable** ← | **410 MPa, reliable** |
| **Ductility** | **NONE — it fails without warning** ← | **Excellent — 15-20 % elongation** |
| **Weldable?** | **Poorly, and only with special procedures** | **YES** |
| **Castable into complex shapes** | **EXCELLENT — the reason it is used** ← | Poor |
| **Vibration damping** | **Good — the graphite absorbs energy** | Poor |

> **So cast iron is used where COMPLEX SHAPES and COMPRESSION are wanted and tension is not — pipes under internal pressure being the classic case, since a pipe's hoop stress is carried in tension and cast iron pipes are accordingly made thick.**

> **Its lack of ductility is the decisive limitation: a cast iron member gives NO WARNING before failure, which is why it was abandoned for structural framing after a series of nineteenth-century collapses.**

> **DUCTILE (spheroidal graphite) IRON was developed to address exactly that: by treating the melt so the graphite forms spheres rather than flakes, the material retains cast iron's castability and gains substantial ductility — which is why modern water mains are ductile iron rather than grey cast iron.**

**The structural steel grades, since mild steel is where the syllabus concentrates:**

| Grade | Yield strength | Ultimate strength | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fe 410 (E250) — mild steel** | **250 MPa** | **410 MPa** | **Structural sections, plates** ← |
| **Fe 250 — mild steel reinforcement** | **250 MPa** | — | **Plain round bars; largely superseded** |
| **Fe 415 (HYSD)** | **415 MPa** | — | **Reinforcement — the common grade** |
| **Fe 500 (HYSD/TMT)** | **500 MPa** | — | Reinforcement |
| **Fe 550** | 550 MPa | — | Reinforcement, less ductile |

> **Note the potential confusion in the first two rows: "Fe 410" for STRUCTURAL steel is named for its ULTIMATE strength (410 MPa) with a yield of 250, while "Fe 415" for REINFORCEMENT is named for its YIELD strength.**

> **So Fe 410 structural steel and Fe 415 reinforcement are entirely different materials with confusingly similar designations, and the numbers refer to different properties.**

> **That is a genuine trap in the codes' nomenclature, and the way to keep it straight is to remember that REINFORCEMENT grades are named for their YIELD strength — which is what the design uses through 0.87 f_y.**

**And how HIGH-YIELD reinforcement achieves its strength, since it is not by carbon:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **COLD WORKING (cold twisted deformed, CTD)** | **Twisting and stretching work-hardens the bar; raises the yield and REDUCES the ductility. Largely superseded** |
| **THERMO-MECHANICAL TREATMENT (TMT)** | **Quenching the surface then letting the hot core temper it — giving a HARD surface and a DUCTILE core** ← the modern method |
| **Micro-alloying** | Small additions of vanadium, niobium |

> **The TMT process is worth understanding because it explains why modern reinforcement is both strong and ductile, which cold working could not achieve:**

> **The bar leaves the rolling mill hot and is quenched briefly, hardening a thin surface layer while the core stays hot.**

> **The core's retained heat then TEMPERS that hardened surface from within, and the core itself cools slowly and remains ductile.**

> **The result is a composite bar — hard, strong surface over a tough core — that has a high yield strength AND good elongation AND remains weldable, which cold-twisted bars did not.**

> **It also has better corrosion resistance and better performance in fire, and it is cheaper to produce — which is why TMT displaced CTD entirely within a decade.**

examTip.trick: **Mild steel 0.15-0.25 %.** The whole ladder: wrought iron below 0.25, mild 0.15-0.25, medium 0.25-0.6, high carbon 0.6-1.5, CAST IRON 2.5-4.5 %.
examTip.trap: **Every option is a real carbon range for another material** — 0.6-0.8 % is high carbon steel, 2.5-4.5 % is cast iron. The boundary at 2 % separates STEEL from CAST IRON.
examTip.mnemonic: **Low carbon is why mild steel is WELDABLE** — above about 0.3 % the heat-affected zone forms brittle martensite and cracks. And note the nomenclature trap: Fe 410 structural steel is named for its ULTIMATE strength, Fe 415 reinforcement for its YIELD.

questions.stem: The constituent of a paint that gives it its colour and opacity, and forms the body of the film, is the:
questions.solution:
**The BASE.**

**The constituents of a paint and what each does:**

| Constituent | Function | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **BASE** | **Gives BODY, OPACITY and the principal colour; the main solid** ← | **White lead, zinc oxide, TITANIUM DIOXIDE, red lead, iron oxide, lithopone** |
| **VEHICLE (binder, medium)** | **CARRIES the base, and on drying forms the continuous FILM that binds everything and adheres to the surface** ← | **Linseed oil, alkyd resin, acrylic emulsion, epoxy** |
| **THINNER (solvent, diluent)** | **Reduces the VISCOSITY so the paint can be applied; EVAPORATES entirely and forms no part of the dry film** ← | **Turpentine, mineral spirit, water (in emulsions)** |
| **DRIER (catalyst)** | **ACCELERATES the oxidation and hardening of the vehicle** | **Compounds of lead, cobalt, manganese** |
| **PIGMENT / extender** | **Modifies the COLOUR and the properties; extenders add bulk cheaply** | Chrome yellow, ultramarine; chalk, barytes |
| **Plasticiser** | Keeps the film flexible | — |

> **So the BASE is the solid that makes the paint OPAQUE — it is what hides the surface beneath — and the VEHICLE is what makes it a coherent, adherent film.**

> **Option (a) VEHICLE is the designed distractor because both the base and the vehicle are essential and permanent parts of the dry film, and their roles are easily interchanged.**

> **The distinction: the BASE is a SOLID POWDER that provides opacity; the VEHICLE is a LIQUID that dries to a film.**

> **And option (b) THINNER is distinguished absolutely by the fact that it is NOT PRESENT in the dry film at all — it evaporates, which is why a paint's covering power is computed on its solids content and not its volume.**

**Why TITANIUM DIOXIDE displaced WHITE LEAD — a case worth knowing:**

| | **White lead (basic lead carbonate)** | **Titanium dioxide** |
|---|---|---|
| **Opacity (hiding power)** | Good | **EXCELLENT — the highest of any white pigment** ← |
| **Toxicity** | **HIGHLY TOXIC — lead poisoning, particularly of children** ← | **Inert and non-toxic** |
| **Durability** | Good; chalks on exposure | Excellent |
| **Status** | **BANNED or severely restricted in most countries for domestic paint** | **The standard white pigment** |

> **The lead paint hazard is worth stating plainly because it is a real public-health matter that a civil engineer may encounter: old paint layers in buildings under renovation contain lead, and disturbing them by sanding or burning releases it as dust or fume.**

> **So the removal of old paint in a refurbishment is a controlled operation, not a preparatory nuisance — and specifying lead-free paint for new work is now universal rather than a preference.**

**What a paint must do, since the constituents are chosen to achieve it:**

| Requirement of a good paint | Note |
|---|---|
| **ADHERE firmly to the surface** | The vehicle's job, and the surface preparation's |
| **Be OPAQUE — hide the surface in few coats** | **The base's job** ← |
| **Form a TOUGH, DURABLE, WEATHER-RESISTANT film** | The vehicle |
| **Spread easily and level without brush marks** | The thinner and the rheology |
| **Dry in a reasonable time** | The drier |
| **Retain its colour, and not chalk, crack or peel** | Pigment and vehicle quality |
| **Be economical in covering power** | Solids content |

> **The commonest CAUSE of paint failure is none of those, however — it is SURFACE PREPARATION:**

| Failure | Usual cause |
|---|---|
| **PEELING or FLAKING** | **Painting over a damp, dusty, greasy or chalky surface — no adhesion** ← |
| **BLISTERING** | **MOISTURE behind the film, driven out by the sun** ← |
| **CRACKING and alligatoring** | A hard coat over a soft one; too thick a film |
| **CHALKING** | **Degradation of the vehicle by ultraviolet light, leaving loose pigment** |
| **SAPONIFICATION** | **An oil-based paint on fresh ALKALINE plaster or concrete — the alkali attacks the oil** ← |
| **EFFLORESCENCE showing through** | Salts from the masonry |
| **Loss of gloss, discolouration** | Weathering |

> **The SAPONIFICATION failure is the one specific to building work and it explains a firm rule: an OIL-BASED paint must not be applied to fresh cement plaster or concrete.**

> **Fresh cement is strongly ALKALINE, and alkali reacts with the oil in the vehicle to form a soap — so the film softens, becomes sticky and fails.**

> **The remedies are to WAIT until the plaster has carbonated and dried (commonly quoted as 4 to 8 weeks), to apply an alkali-resistant PRIMER, or to use an alkali-resistant paint such as an acrylic emulsion or a cement paint.**

> **Which is why emulsion paints are used on new masonry and oil paints on woodwork and metal — a division that looks like habit and rests on chemistry.**

**The related coatings, since the terms are often confused:**

| Coating | Composition | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **PAINT** | **Base (pigment) + vehicle + thinner + drier** | **OPAQUE** ← |
| **VARNISH** | **Resin + vehicle (oil or spirit), NO pigment** | **TRANSPARENT — shows the grain beneath** ← |
| **DISTEMPER** | **Whiting (chalk) + water + glue size, with pigment** | **Cheap, water-based, POOR durability; washes off** |
| **ENAMEL** | Paint with a varnish vehicle | Hard, glossy, durable |
| **LACQUER** | Resin in a volatile solvent | Dries by evaporation alone; very fast |
| **CEMENT paint** | White cement + pigment + accelerator | For exterior masonry; alkali-proof by nature |
| **PRIMER** | High-adhesion, often with an inhibitive pigment | **The FIRST coat — bonds and seals** |

> **The PAINT against VARNISH distinction is simply the presence of a PIGMENT: a varnish is a paint without its base, and it is therefore transparent.**

> **So a varnish protects and displays the surface, and a paint protects and conceals it — which determines their uses on timber, where the grain is usually wanted.**

> **And the PRIMER's role deserves its note: it is formulated for ADHESION and for sealing rather than for appearance or durability, and the finishing coats rely on it entirely.**

> **A finish applied over an inadequate primer will fail however good the finish is, which is the same principle as the tack coat in bituminous work and the prime coat before it.**

examTip.trick: **BASE = the solid powder giving OPACITY and body. VEHICLE = the liquid that dries to a FILM and adheres. THINNER = evaporates and is absent from the dry film.**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) vehicle is the close distractor** — both base and vehicle remain in the dry film. The base is a solid pigment; the vehicle is the binder.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never put an OIL-based paint on fresh cement plaster** — the alkali saponifies the oil and the film fails. Use an alkali-resistant primer or an acrylic emulsion. And a VARNISH is simply a paint without its base, hence transparent.

questions.stem: As per IS 269, the minimum FINENESS of ordinary Portland cement, expressed as specific surface, is:
questions.solution:
**225 m²/kg.**

**The fineness requirements by cement type:**

| Cement | Minimum specific surface |
|---|---|
| **ORDINARY Portland cement (OPC), all grades** | **225 m²/kg** ← |
| **RAPID HARDENING cement** | **325 m²/kg** ← |
| **Portland POZZOLANA cement (PPC)** | **300 m²/kg** |
| **Portland SLAG cement (PSC)** | **225 m²/kg** |
| **LOW HEAT cement** | **320 m²/kg** |
| **Sulphate resisting cement** | 225 m²/kg |

> **Options (c) 320 and (d) 400 m²/kg are near the low-heat and rapid-hardening requirements — both real values for other cements, which is what makes them the designed distractors.**

> **Note the interesting case of LOW HEAT cement at 320 m²/kg: it is required to be FINER than OPC even though it must generate LESS heat.**

> **That looks contradictory and is not: low heat cement achieves its slow heat evolution through its COMPOSITION (less C₃S and C₃A, more C₂S), and the extra fineness compensates for the slow-reacting C₂S so that adequate strength is eventually reached.**

> **So the composition controls the heat and the fineness recovers some of the strength — which is a good illustration of two parameters being adjusted in opposite directions to reach a particular combination of properties.**

**How fineness is measured — two quite different methods:**

| Method | Measures | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **SIEVE method (90 μm sieve)** | **The RESIDUE retained** | **A PERCENTAGE — not more than 10 % for OPC** ← |
| **BLAINE AIR PERMEABILITY method** | **The rate at which air permeates a compacted bed of cement** | **A SPECIFIC SURFACE in m²/kg** ← |
| **Wagner turbidimeter** | Sedimentation rate | Specific surface |

> **The SIEVE method is quick and crude: it tells you only how much cement is COARSER than 90 μm, and says nothing about the distribution below that size — where nearly all the cement is and where the reactivity lies.**

> **The BLAINE method measures the total SURFACE AREA per unit mass, which is the quantity that actually governs the hydration rate — since hydration proceeds from the surface of each grain inward.**

> **So the Blaine value is the meaningful measure and the specification is expressed in it, with the sieve residue retained as a supplementary check.**

**Why fineness matters so much — the effects of grinding finer:**

| Effect of INCREASED fineness | Note |
|---|---|
| **FASTER hydration and higher EARLY strength** | **More surface exposed to water at once** ← |
| **Better WORKABILITY and cohesion; less bleeding** | The fine particles hold water |
| **Greater strength at all ages, up to a point** | More complete hydration |
| **HIGHER heat of hydration, evolved FASTER** | **A hazard in mass concrete — thermal cracking** ← |
| **Greater SHRINKAGE** | More water demand, finer pore structure |
| **Greater susceptibility to DETERIORATION in storage** | **A fine cement absorbs atmospheric moisture faster and goes stale sooner** ← |
| **Higher GRINDING COST** | Grinding energy rises steeply with fineness |

> **So fineness has an OPTIMUM rather than a target, and the specification sets a MINIMUM because inadequate fineness gives slow, incomplete hydration and low strength.**

> **The upper bound is set by economics and by the heat and shrinkage consequences rather than by a code limit — which is why a specification gives a minimum fineness and no maximum.**

> **The STORAGE point is practically important: a finely ground cement exposed to humid air hydrates on its surface and forms lumps, losing strength progressively.**

| Storage period | Approximate strength loss |
|---|---|
| **3 months** | **About 20 %** |
| **6 months** | **About 30 %** |
| **12 months** | **About 40 %** ← |

> **Which is why cement is stored on a raised platform, away from external walls, in stacks of not more than 10 bags, with the OLDEST used FIRST — and why a bag that has hardened into lumps that cannot be broken by hand is rejected rather than used.**

> **In Nepal's monsoon humidity those precautions are not formalities: cement left on a damp floor for a month can be substantially deteriorated.**

**The other IS 269 requirements, since they are examined as a set:**

| Property | Requirement for OPC 43 grade |
|---|---|
| **FINENESS (specific surface)** | **≥ 225 m²/kg** ← |
| **Fineness (90 μm sieve residue)** | **≤ 10 %** |
| **INITIAL setting time** | **≥ 30 minutes** |
| **FINAL setting time** | **≤ 600 minutes (10 hours)** |
| **SOUNDNESS, Le Chatelier expansion** | **≤ 10 mm** |
| **Soundness, autoclave expansion** | **≤ 0.8 %** |
| **Compressive strength, 3 days** | **≥ 23 MPa** |
| **Compressive strength, 7 days** | **≥ 33 MPa** |
| **Compressive strength, 28 days** | **≥ 43 MPa** |
| **Consistency (for setting-time tests)** | The water content giving a standard penetration |

> **The GRADE DESIGNATIONS follow directly from the last row but one: OPC 33, 43 and 53 grade are named for their MINIMUM 28-DAY COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH in MPa.**

> **That is a rare instance of an entirely transparent naming convention, and knowing it makes the grades self-explanatory.**

> **And note that a 53-grade cement is not simply "better": its higher early strength comes with more heat and more shrinkage, so a 43-grade cement is often preferable for mass concrete or where thermal cracking is a concern.**

> **Using the highest available grade as a matter of course is therefore not always the right decision — the grade should match the application, exactly as the cement TYPE should.**

examTip.trick: **OPC minimum fineness 225 m²/kg by the Blaine method; rapid hardening 325; PPC 300; low heat 320.**
examTip.trap: **LOW HEAT cement must be FINER (320) than OPC** — its low heat comes from its COMPOSITION (less C₃S and C₃A), and the extra fineness recovers the strength that slow-reacting C₂S would lose.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fineness has an OPTIMUM: finer means faster strength AND more heat, more shrinkage and faster staling in storage.** Hence a MINIMUM in the code and no maximum. And cement loses about 20 % of its strength in 3 months' storage, 40 % in a year.

questions.stem: The minimum percentage elongation specified for Fe 415 grade reinforcing steel is:
questions.solution:
**14.5 per cent.**

**The elongation requirements by reinforcement grade:**

| Grade | Minimum yield / 0.2 % proof stress | Minimum ELONGATION |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250 (mild steel)** | **250 MPa** | **20 to 23 %** |
| **Fe 415** | **415 MPa** | **14.5 %** ← |
| **Fe 500** | **500 MPa** | **12 %** |
| **Fe 550** | **550 MPa** | **10 %** |
| **Fe 600** | **600 MPa** | **10 %** |

> **Every option offered is a real elongation requirement for another grade, so the grade named in the stem must be matched.**

> **And the pattern is the essential fact: THE HIGHER THE STRENGTH, THE LOWER THE PERMITTED ELONGATION.**

**Why strength and ductility trade against each other:**

> **The mechanisms that raise a steel's yield strength — cold working, quenching, alloying — all operate by IMPEDING THE MOVEMENT OF DISLOCATIONS through the crystal lattice.**

> **But plastic deformation IS the movement of dislocations. So anything that makes the steel stronger necessarily makes it less able to deform.**

> **That is a fundamental trade and not a defect of manufacture: strength and ductility are obtained from the same property in opposite directions.**

> **Which is why the codes specify BOTH a minimum strength and a minimum elongation — the second prevents the first from being achieved at the expense of ductility.**

**Why DUCTILITY matters so much in reinforced concrete — three distinct reasons:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **WARNING before failure** | **A ductile beam sags, cracks widely and deflects visibly before collapsing — occupants can leave** ← |
| **MOMENT REDISTRIBUTION in continuous members** | **A yielding section sheds moment to its neighbours, so the structure does not fail when one section reaches its capacity** ← |
| **SEISMIC energy dissipation** | **The whole basis of earthquake design: the structure survives by DEFORMING inelastically, absorbing energy** ← |
| **Tolerance of settlement and imposed deformation** | The structure accommodates rather than cracks |
| **BENDABILITY on site** | **Bars must be bent cold around a mandrel without cracking** ← |

> **The SEISMIC reason is why the elongation requirement is not a formality in Nepal: the entire logic of the response reduction factor R rests on the structure's ability to deform inelastically without losing capacity.**

> **A frame detailed as a special moment-resisting frame and given R = 5 is being credited with a ductility that its reinforcement must actually possess — and steel with inadequate elongation cannot deliver it.**

> **So the elongation specification is what makes the seismic design assumption true, and reinforcement failing it invalidates the whole calculation.**

> **That is why IS 13920 goes further and requires the steel used in ductile frames to satisfy additional criteria, including a minimum ratio of ultimate to yield strength.**

**The UTS-to-YIELD ratio, which is the less obvious ductility requirement:**

> **IS 1786 requires the ultimate tensile strength to exceed the actual yield strength by a stated margin — for Fe 415, the UTS must be at least 10 per cent above the actual 0.2 % proof stress.**

> **And IS 13920 requires, for earthquake-resistant construction, that the actual yield strength not exceed the specified value by more than 20 per cent.**

> **Both requirements protect the same thing, and the reason is worth understanding:**

| If the steel is STRONGER than specified | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **The beam's actual moment capacity exceeds the design value** | **So the beam does NOT yield when intended** ← |
| **The load path then overloads the COLUMNS and the JOINTS instead** | **Which were designed on the assumption that the beam would yield first** ← |
| **A brittle column or joint failure may precede the ductile beam failure** | **The capacity-design hierarchy is INVERTED** ← |

> **So reinforcement that is TOO STRONG is a genuine hazard in a seismic frame, which is counter-intuitive and important.**

> **CAPACITY DESIGN works by ensuring that the DUCTILE mechanism (beam hinging) occurs before the BRITTLE ones (column failure, joint failure, shear failure) — the strong-column-weak-beam principle.**

> **That hierarchy depends on knowing the beam's actual capacity, and steel of unpredictable overstrength destroys it.**

> **Hence the upper limit on yield strength, which appears at first sight to prohibit a better material and in fact protects the design's logic.**

**The other requirements for reinforcement, as an acceptance set:**

| Requirement | Fe 415 |
|---|---|
| **Yield / 0.2 % proof stress** | **≥ 415 MPa** |
| **ELONGATION on a gauge length of 5.65√A** | **≥ 14.5 %** ← |
| **UTS** | **≥ 10 % above the actual yield stress, and ≥ 485 MPa** |
| **BEND test** | **Bent through 180° round a mandrel without cracking** ← |
| **RE-BEND test** | **Bent 135°, aged at 100 °C for 30 minutes, then bent back to 157.5° — no cracking** ← |
| **Chemical composition — carbon, sulphur, phosphorus limits** | Carbon ≤ 0.30 %, S ≤ 0.06 %, P ≤ 0.06 % |
| **Mass per metre and tolerance** | ± 5 % on individual bars |
| **Rib geometry** | Defined by the standard |

> **The RE-BEND test deserves explanation because its purpose is not obvious: it tests for STRAIN AGE EMBRITTLEMENT.**

> **A bar bent, then heated, then bent back reproduces what happens to a bar that is bent on site, left in the sun or in a hot structure, and later disturbed or straightened.**

> **Some steels become brittle after such treatment and crack at the bend — and a cracked bend in a stirrup or a bent-up bar is a defect exactly where the stress is concentrated.**

> **So the re-bend test simulates a real site sequence and rejects steel that would fail under it, which makes it a well-designed test rather than an arbitrary one.**

> **And the practical rule that follows: BARS ONCE BENT SHOULD NOT BE STRAIGHTENED AND RE-BENT, and a bar bent to the wrong dimension should be cut out rather than reworked.**

examTip.trick: **Fe 415 needs 14.5 % elongation. The pattern: Fe 250 gets 20-23 %, Fe 415 14.5 %, Fe 500 12 %, Fe 550 10 %** — higher strength, lower permitted elongation.
examTip.trap: **Every option is a real requirement for another grade.** And the trade is fundamental: everything that raises yield strength impedes dislocation movement, which is what plastic deformation IS.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reinforcement that is TOO STRONG is a seismic hazard** — the beam then does not yield when intended and the load overloads the columns and joints instead, inverting the capacity-design hierarchy. Hence an UPPER limit on yield strength in IS 13920.

questions.stem: The horizontal member provided across the top of a door or window opening to carry the load of the wall above is called a:
questions.solution:
**A LINTEL.**

**The parts of an opening in a wall:**

| Part | Position and function |
|---|---|
| **LINTEL** | **The horizontal member ACROSS THE TOP, carrying the wall above** ← |
| **SILL** | **The horizontal member at the BOTTOM of a WINDOW opening** ← |
| **JAMB** | **The VERTICAL SIDE face of the opening — the full thickness of the wall** ← |
| **REVEAL** | **The part of the jamb NOT covered by the frame — the exposed vertical face** ← |
| **Threshold** | The bottom member of a DOOR opening |
| **Soffit** | The underside of the lintel |
| **Head** | The top of the opening generally |
| **Arch** | A curved alternative to a lintel |

> **Every option offered is a genuine part of an opening, so the option set is a test of the terminology rather than of any principle.**

> **The distinctions worth fixing: LINTEL at the top, SILL at the bottom, JAMB at the sides, REVEAL the exposed part of the jamb.**

**Why a lintel is necessary — the load it carries:**

> **Masonry above an opening has nothing beneath it. Without a lintel it would fall — or, in practice, would form a rough natural arch and crack.**

> **The lintel spans the opening and carries that load to the masonry on each side.**

> **The load it must carry is NOT the full height of wall above it, however, and that is worth understanding:**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **ARCHING ACTION in the masonry above** | **Bonded masonry above an opening tends to arch over it, transferring load to the sides and RELIEVING the lintel** ← |
| **The load is therefore taken as a TRIANGLE or a limited height of wall** | **Commonly a triangle at 60°, or a height equal to the span** |
| **BUT a load applied CLOSE above the lintel is carried fully** | A beam or slab bearing just above it |
| **AND the arching requires the masonry on each side to resist the thrust** | **An opening near a corner or another opening cannot arch** ← |

> **The last row is the practical qualification: arching action requires ABUTMENTS, so an opening close to the end of a wall, close to a corner, or close to another opening cannot develop it — and its lintel must carry the full load.**

> **That is why openings near corners are a structural weak point and why codes require a minimum length of wall between an opening and a corner, particularly in seismic design.**

**The types of lintel, since the choice is a real one:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **REINFORCED CONCRETE** | **The standard — any span, any load, and it can be cast integrally with a band** ← |
| **Timber** | Traditional; liable to decay, fire and insect attack |
| **Stone** | **Strong in compression and WEAK IN BENDING — cracks on short spans; traditional and risky** ← |
| **Brick lintel** | Only for small spans and light loads |
| **Steel (joists or angles)** | Long spans, or where depth is limited |
| **RELIEVING ARCH above a lintel** | **A brick arch built over the lintel to divert the load past it** ← |

> **The STONE lintel deserves its warning: a stone slab spanning an opening is loaded in BENDING, and stone's tensile strength is very low.**

> **Traditional buildings throughout the Himalaya use stone lintels, and a cracked stone lintel is one of the commonest defects seen — a crack at midspan, on the soffit, exactly where the flexural tension is greatest.**

> **So a stone lintel is safe only over a short span with a light load, and a cracked one must be relieved or replaced rather than merely pointed.**

> **The RELIEVING ARCH is the traditional answer to that problem and it is elegant: a brick or stone arch built above the lintel carries the wall load to the abutments, and the lintel then carries only the small triangle of masonry between itself and the arch.**

**The SEISMIC significance of the lintel level, which is why this matters in Nepal:**

> **In masonry construction, the LINTEL BAND is one of the mandatory earthquake-resistant features:**

| Band | Level | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **PLINTH band** | At plinth level | Ties the walls at the base; resists differential settlement |
| **SILL band** | At window sill level | **Reduces the free height of the pier between openings** |
| **LINTEL band** | **Continuous at lintel level, around ALL walls** | **THE MOST IMPORTANT — ties the walls together at the top of the openings and acts as a horizontal ring beam** ← |
| **ROOF / eaves band** | At roof level | Ties the wall tops; distributes the roof load |
| **GABLE band** | Along the gable slope | Ties the gable triangle |
| **VERTICAL reinforcement** | At corners, junctions and jamb sides of openings | Resists out-of-plane bending |

> **The LINTEL BAND is a CONTINUOUS reinforced concrete band running around every wall at lintel level, not merely individual lintels over the openings — and that distinction is the whole point.**

> **Individual lintels carry the wall above each opening. A continuous BAND ties the entire building into a box, so that the walls act together rather than as separate panels each free to fall outward.**

> **Unreinforced masonry's characteristic earthquake failure is exactly that: the walls separate at the corners and fall outward individually, and the roof drops.**

> **A lintel band prevents it by giving the masonry the TENSILE CONTINUITY it inherently lacks — which returns to the point made earlier about masonry's zero tensile strength.**

> **So the band is the single most effective earthquake-safety measure available for Nepal's most common building type, and it costs a small fraction of the building.**

> **A builder who casts individual lintels over the openings and omits the continuous band has provided the structural function and missed the seismic one — and the difference is invisible once the wall is plastered.**

examTip.trick: **LINTEL at the top, SILL at the bottom of a window, JAMB the side face, REVEAL the exposed part of the jamb.** All four options are genuine parts of an opening.
examTip.trap: **A lintel does not carry the full height of wall above it** — bonded masonry ARCHES over the opening. But arching needs ABUTMENTS, so an opening near a corner or another opening cannot arch, and its lintel carries everything.
examTip.mnemonic: **The seismic LINTEL BAND is CONTINUOUS around every wall — not individual lintels over the openings.** Individual lintels do the structural job and miss the seismic one, and the difference is invisible once plastered. It is the best value in masonry earthquake safety.

questions.stem: In a pitched roof, the inclined member that runs from the ridge to the eaves and directly carries the roof covering is the:
questions.solution:
**The COMMON RAFTER.**

**The members of a pitched roof and what each does:**

| Member | Position | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **COMMON RAFTER** | **Inclined, from the RIDGE down to the EAVES** | **Carries the battens or sheeting, and hence the roof covering** ← |
| **RIDGE (ridge piece, ridge board)** | **The HORIZONTAL member at the APEX** | **The rafters from both slopes bear against it** ← |
| **PURLIN** | **HORIZONTAL, part way up the slope, spanning between trusses or walls** | **SUPPORTS the rafters at intermediate points, reducing their span** ← |
| **WALL PLATE** | **Horizontal, bedded on TOP OF THE WALL** | **Receives the feet of the rafters and DISTRIBUTES their load to the wall** ← |
| **Hip rafter** | Along a hip (an external corner of two slopes) | — |
| **Valley rafter** | Along a valley (an internal corner) | — |
| **Jack rafter** | A shortened rafter meeting a hip or valley | — |
| **Batten** | Small members across the rafters | Carry tiles or sheeting |
| **Eaves board / fascia** | At the rafter feet | Finishes the eaves; carries the gutter |

> **All four options are genuine roof members, so the question is one of function and position.**

> **The confusion to guard against is RAFTER against PURLIN, and the distinction is their DIRECTION:**

> **A RAFTER runs UP THE SLOPE, from eaves to ridge.**

> **A PURLIN runs HORIZONTALLY ACROSS the slope, supporting the rafters.**

> **So they are perpendicular to one another, and the purlin carries the rafters while the rafters carry the covering.**

**The LOAD PATH in a pitched roof, which is what the members exist to form:**

| Step | Member |
|---|---|
| **1. The roof covering (tiles, sheets)** | Rests on battens or directly on purlins |
| **2. BATTENS** | Span between rafters |
| **3. COMMON RAFTERS** | **Span from the ridge to the eaves, or between purlins** ← |
| **4. PURLINS** | **Span between trusses or gable walls, supporting the rafters** |
| **5. TRUSSES (or the walls)** | Span between supports |
| **6. WALL PLATE** | **Spreads the load onto the wall** |
| **7. WALLS and foundations** | Carry it to the ground |

> **Tracing that path is the reliable way to answer any question about which member does what: each member spans between the supports provided by the next member down the chain.**

> **And it explains the purlin's purpose precisely: without purlins, a rafter must span the full slope length from eaves to ridge, which for a large roof requires a deep section. Purlins reduce that span, allowing lighter rafters.**

**The TRUSS, since it is the element that makes large spans possible:**

> **A pitched roof over a wide span cannot be carried by rafters alone, because the rafters' thrust would push the walls apart.**

> **A TRUSS resolves it by adding a horizontal TIE:**

| Truss member | Force | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Principal RAFTER** | **COMPRESSION** | The sloping top chord |
| **TIE BEAM (main tie)** | **TENSION** | **Ties the rafter feet together, absorbing the outward thrust so the walls receive only a VERTICAL load** ← |
| **KING POST or QUEEN POSTS** | **TENSION** | **Supports the tie beam at midspan, hanging from the apex** ← |
| **STRUTS** | **COMPRESSION** | Support the principal rafters at intermediate points |

> **The TIE BEAM is the member that defines a truss, and the KING POST's action is worth stating because it is counter-intuitive:**

> **A king post looks like a column holding up the ridge, and it is in fact a TENSION member HANGING the tie beam from the apex.**

> **The tie beam sags under its own weight and any ceiling load, and the king post prevents that sag by hanging it from the point where the two principal rafters meet.**

> **So the load travels UP the king post and out along the rafters — which is why a king post can be a slender member or even an iron rod, and why cutting one "because it carries nothing" would let the tie beam sag and the roof spread.**

> **That is the same lesson as the zero-force member in a truss: a member's appearance does not indicate its function.**

**The truss types by span, since the choice follows from it:**

| Truss | Suitable span |
|---|---|
| **Simple couple / couple close** | **Up to about 3.5 m — rafters and a tie only** |
| **Collar beam truss** | **Up to about 5 m** |
| **KING POST truss** | **5 to 8 m** ← one central post |
| **QUEEN POST truss** | **8 to 12 m** ← two posts, allowing a longer tie |
| **Mansard, truncated** | 12 m and more; gives usable roof space |
| **Steel trusses — Fink, Howe, Pratt** | **Any span; the standard for industrial roofs** |
| **North light truss** | **For factories — the glazed vertical face faces north for even daylight** ← |

> **The NORTH LIGHT truss deserves a note because its shape is determined entirely by a non-structural requirement: the roof is asymmetric, with a steep glazed face oriented NORTH (in the northern hemisphere).**

> **North light is INDIRECT and therefore EVEN and free of glare and solar heat gain, which suits a factory floor or a drawing office where uniform illumination matters.**

> **So the structural form follows a lighting requirement — a good instance of a building's function shaping its structure rather than the reverse.**

**And the seismic and wind considerations for a roof, since they are the modern concerns:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **WIND UPLIFT** | **A light pitched roof is lifted, not pressed down — the fixings must resist TENSION continuously to the foundation** ← |
| **The wall plate must be ANCHORED to the wall** | **Holding-down bolts or straps into the seismic band** ← |
| **A light roof is a SEISMIC ADVANTAGE** | **Less mass at the top means less inertial force** ← |
| **The roof must be TIED to the walls to act as a diaphragm** | Otherwise the walls act independently |
| **Gable walls need a gable band and bracing** | **A free-standing gable triangle is the classic earthquake failure** ← |

> **The GABLE WALL failure is worth naming because it is so common and so avoidable: the triangular gable above the eaves level has no wall returning at right angles to support it, so it stands as a free cantilever and falls outward.**

> **The remedies are a GABLE BAND following the slope, vertical reinforcement, and tying the gable to the roof structure — all inexpensive, and all frequently omitted.**

> **In Nepali masonry construction the collapsed gable is among the most frequently photographed forms of earthquake damage, and it is a detailing failure rather than a design one.**

examTip.trick: **A RAFTER runs UP the slope (eaves to ridge); a PURLIN runs HORIZONTALLY ACROSS it, supporting the rafters.** They are perpendicular, and the purlin reduces the rafter's span.
examTip.trap: **Trace the LOAD PATH to answer any such question:** covering → battens → rafters → purlins → trusses → wall plate → walls. Each member spans between the supports the next one provides.
examTip.mnemonic: **A KING POST is a TENSION member hanging the tie beam from the apex, not a column holding the ridge up.** And a light roof needs HOLDING DOWN against wind uplift — continuously to the foundation — while being a seismic advantage for its low mass.

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a triangular section of base b and height h, about its BASE, is:
questions.solution:
**b h³ / 12.**

**The triangle's two principal moments of inertia:**

| Axis | Moment of inertia |
|---|---|
| **About the BASE** | **b h³ / 12** ← |
| **About the CENTROIDAL axis (parallel to the base)** | **b h³ / 36** |

> **Option (b) bh³/36 is the CENTROIDAL value, which makes it the designed distractor — the two are constantly interchanged.**

> **And note the RATIO: the base value is THREE TIMES the centroidal value (1/12 against 1/36).**

**Confirming the pair with the PARALLEL AXIS THEOREM — the check that settles it:**

> **I_base = I_centroid + A d²**

| Quantity | Value for a triangle |
|---|---|
| **A** | **b h / 2** |
| **d — distance from the centroid to the base** | **h / 3** |
| **A d²** | **(bh/2)(h/3)² = (bh/2)(h²/9) = b h³/18** |

> **So:  I_base = bh³/36 + bh³/18 = bh³/36 + 2bh³/36 = 3bh³/36 = b h³/12** ✓

> **The two values are therefore consistent, and the theorem generates either from the other — so only ONE needs to be remembered.**

> **That is the reliable way through this whole family of questions: remember the CENTROIDAL value, and use I = I_G + Ad² for any other axis.**

**The comparison with a rectangle, which is instructive:**

| Section | About the CENTROIDAL axis | About the BASE | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE b × d** | **b d³/12** | **b d³/3** | **4 ×** |
| **TRIANGLE b × h** | **b h³/36** | **b h³/12** | **3 ×** |

> **Note that options (a) and (d) in this question are the rectangle's two values — bh³/12 happens to be the rectangle's CENTROIDAL value AND the triangle's BASE value, and bh³/3 is the rectangle's base value.**

> **So the coefficient 1/12 belongs to two different situations, which is precisely why these questions are confusing and why the parallel axis check is worth making.**

> **The RATIO difference (4 for a rectangle, 3 for a triangle) arises from where the centroid sits: at d/2 for a rectangle and at h/3 for a triangle.**

**The standard section properties, as a working set:**

| Section | Area | I about the centroidal axis | Centroid location |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE b × d** | **b d** | **b d³/12** | **d/2 from the base** |
| **TRIANGLE b × h** | **b h/2** | **b h³/36** | **h/3 from the base** ← |
| **CIRCLE, diameter D** | **π D²/4** | **π D⁴/64** | **Centre** |
| **SEMICIRCLE, diameter D** | **π D²/8** | **0.11 R⁴ approximately** | **4R/3π from the diameter** |
| **Quarter circle** | **π R²/4** | — | **4R/3π from each straight edge** |
| **Hollow circle, D and d** | **π(D²−d²)/4** | **π(D⁴−d⁴)/64** | Centre |

> **The 4R/3π ≈ 0.424 R for a semicircle's centroid is worth having, since composite sections built from a rectangle and a semicircular end are common.**

**The DIMENSIONAL CHECK, which catches every error in this topic:**

| Quantity | Dimensions |
|---|---|
| **Area** | **L²** |
| **First moment of area (A ȳ)** | **L³** |
| **MOMENT OF INERTIA (second moment)** | **L⁴** ← |
| **Section modulus (I/y)** | **L³** |
| **Radius of gyration (√(I/A))** | **L¹** |

> **Every option in this question has the dimensions of L⁴ (b × h³), so the dimensional check does not discriminate here — but it catches a great many errors in related questions, and it costs nothing.**

> **The check that DOES discriminate here is the parallel axis theorem, and the practical rule is: whenever two coefficients are offered for the same section, verify which is which by computing Ad².**

**Why the moment of inertia matters — what it governs:**

| Application | Role of I |
|---|---|
| **BENDING stress** | **σ = M y / I — a larger I means lower stress** ← |
| **DEFLECTION** | **δ ∝ 1/(E I) — a larger I means a stiffer member** ← |
| **BUCKLING** | **P_cr = π²EI/L_e² — a larger I means a higher buckling load** |
| **TORSION of a circular shaft** | **Through the POLAR moment J = I_x + I_y** |
| **Radius of gyration, hence slenderness** | **r = √(I/A)** |

> **So I appears in stress, in deflection and in buckling — three of the four things a member must be checked for — which is why it is the most-used section property after the area.**

> **And the reason it goes as the CUBE of the depth is worth restating: material far from the neutral axis contributes as the square of its distance (through the y² in the integral), and there is proportionally more of it in a deeper section.**

> **Hence the recurring practical conclusion: DEPTH is what makes a beam strong and stiff, and an I-section exists to place material where the y² is largest.**

**Where a TRIANGULAR section actually arises, since it can seem academic:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A trapezoidal or triangular retaining wall or dam section** | **Analysed as composite triangles and rectangles** ← |
| **The stress distribution under an eccentrically loaded footing** | **A triangular pressure diagram when the eccentricity exceeds B/6** ← |
| **Timber sections cut from a log, and roof members** | — |
| **Gusset plates and bracket connections** | — |
| **The compression zone of a beam with a sloping face** | — |

> **The ECCENTRIC FOOTING case is the one met most often: when the load's eccentricity exceeds B/6, the pressure at the heel becomes zero and the distribution is TRIANGULAR rather than trapezoidal.**

> **Beyond that eccentricity, part of the base would be in TENSION — which soil cannot provide — so contact is lost and the pressure redistributes over a reduced width.**

> **That is the origin of the MIDDLE-THIRD RULE: keeping the resultant within the middle third of the base (e ≤ B/6) ensures the whole base remains in compression.**

> **So a geometric property of the triangle underlies one of the most-used rules in foundation and retaining wall design — which is a good reason to know the triangle's properties properly.**

examTip.trick: **Triangle: bh³/36 about the CENTROID, bh³/12 about the BASE — a factor of THREE.** Remember only the centroidal value and generate the other with I = I_G + Ad².
examTip.trap: **bh³/12 is BOTH the triangle's BASE value and the RECTANGLE'S CENTROIDAL value** — which is exactly why these coefficients are confused. Check with Ad²: (bh/2)(h/3)² = bh³/18, and bh³/36 + bh³/18 = bh³/12 ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **The centroid sits at h/3 for a triangle and d/2 for a rectangle**, which is why their base-to-centroid ratios are 3 and 4. And the triangle matters practically: an eccentric footing's pressure goes TRIANGULAR beyond e = B/6, which is the middle-third rule.

questions.stem: The pair of perpendicular axes about which the PRODUCT OF INERTIA of a section is zero are called the:
questions.solution:
**The PRINCIPAL AXES.**

**The definition and its significance:**

> **The PRODUCT OF INERTIA is  I_xy = ∫ x y dA**

> **Unlike I_x and I_y, which are always POSITIVE, the product of inertia can be positive, negative or ZERO.**

> **The PRINCIPAL AXES are the particular pair of perpendicular axes about which I_xy = 0 — and about those axes the moments of inertia take their MAXIMUM and MINIMUM values.**

| Property of the principal axes | Note |
|---|---|
| **I_xy = 0** | **The defining condition** ← |
| **I about one principal axis is the MAXIMUM for that section** | **I_max** |
| **I about the other is the MINIMUM** | **I_min** ← |
| **They are mutually PERPENDICULAR** | — |
| **Any AXIS OF SYMMETRY is automatically a principal axis** | **The most useful practical consequence** ← |

**Why an axis of symmetry is automatically principal — worth understanding:**

> **If a section is symmetrical about the y axis, then for every element at (+x, y) there is an identical element at (−x, y).**

> **Their contributions to I_xy = ∫xy dA are (+xy) and (−xy), which CANCEL.**

> **So the integral over the whole section is zero, and the axes are principal.**

> **That is why the properties of symmetrical sections — rectangles, circles, I-sections, channels about their axis of symmetry — are so much simpler: their centroidal axes are already principal, and no rotation is needed.**

> **And it identifies exactly when the complication arises: for an UNSYMMETRICAL section, such as an ANGLE or a Z-section, the centroidal axes are NOT principal, and the principal axes are inclined.**

**Why this matters in practice — UNSYMMETRICAL BENDING:**

> **A beam bends about a PRINCIPAL AXIS. If the load is applied in a plane that is not a principal plane, the beam does NOT bend in the plane of the load:**

| Section | Behaviour under a vertical load |
|---|---|
| **Symmetrical (I-section, rectangle) loaded through the axis of symmetry** | **Bends in the plane of the load — the ordinary case** |
| **ANGLE section loaded vertically** | **DEFLECTS SIDEWAYS AS WELL, because the principal axes are inclined to the vertical** ← |

> **So a steel ANGLE used as a purlin or a lintel and loaded vertically deflects both downward and sideways, and bends about both its principal axes.**

> **That is UNSYMMETRICAL BENDING, and it must be analysed by resolving the load into components along the two PRINCIPAL axes, computing the bending about each, and superposing the stresses:**

> **σ = M_u v / I_u + M_v u / I_v**, where u and v are the principal axes.

> **A single-angle member analysed as though it bent about its geometric axes is under-designed, sometimes substantially — which is why angle purlins are either used in pairs, restrained by sag rods, or designed explicitly for unsymmetrical bending.**

> **And it is why a single angle in a truss carrying a load off its axis is a notoriously awkward member: it is eccentrically loaded and unsymmetrically bent at once.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real and different set of axes:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **(a) NEUTRAL axes** | **The axis in a bent section along which the BENDING STRESS is ZERO. For pure bending it passes through the centroid — and for an unsymmetrical section under unsymmetrical bending it is INCLINED and is NOT a principal axis** ← |
| **(b) CENTROIDAL axes** | **Axes THROUGH THE CENTROID — any pair of them. They are principal ONLY if the section is symmetrical about one of them** ← |
| **(c) Polar axis** | **The axis PERPENDICULAR to the plane of the section, about which the POLAR moment J is taken** |
| **(d) PRINCIPAL axes** | ✓ |

> **Option (b) is the closest and the most instructive: the principal axes DO pass through the centroid (for the purposes of bending), so every principal axis is centroidal — but not every centroidal axis is principal.**

> **The set of centroidal axes is infinite (any line through the centroid), and exactly one perpendicular PAIR of them is principal.**

> **So the terms are related as a general class and a particular member of it, which is why they are confused.**

**Locating the principal axes, since the calculation is sometimes required:**

> **tan 2θ = 2 I_xy / (I_y − I_x)**

> **and the principal moments are:**

> **I_max, I_min = (I_x + I_y)/2 ± √[((I_x − I_y)/2)² + I_xy²]**

> **Those expressions should look familiar — they are EXACTLY the forms of the principal STRESS equations:**

| Principal STRESSES | Principal MOMENTS OF INERTIA |
|---|---|
| **σ₁,₂ = (σ_x+σ_y)/2 ± √[((σ_x−σ_y)/2)² + τ²]** | **I_max,min = (I_x+I_y)/2 ± √[((I_x−I_y)/2)² + I_xy²]** |
| **tan 2θ = 2τ/(σ_x−σ_y)** | **tan 2θ = 2I_xy/(I_y−I_x)** |

> **The correspondence is exact, with the PRODUCT OF INERTIA playing the part of the SHEAR STRESS.**

> **So there is a MOHR'S CIRCLE FOR MOMENTS OF INERTIA, constructed and read in precisely the same way as the stress circle — with I_x and I_y on the horizontal axis and I_xy on the vertical.**

> **That is a genuinely useful realisation: anyone who can read a Mohr circle for stress can read one for moments of inertia without learning anything new, and the two topics are one piece of mathematics applied twice.**

> **The reason for the correspondence is that both quantities are second-order TENSORS, and every second-order tensor in two dimensions transforms in the same way under a rotation of axes.**

> **Which is why the same circle, the same principal directions and the same maximum-minimum structure appear in stress, in strain and in moments of inertia — three subjects that look unrelated and share their entire mathematical machinery.**

examTip.trick: **PRINCIPAL AXES are where I_xy = 0, and there I takes its MAXIMUM and MINIMUM values.** Any AXIS OF SYMMETRY is automatically principal — because symmetric elements' xy contributions cancel.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the near miss: every principal axis is centroidal, but not every centroidal axis is principal.** The centroidal axes are infinite in number; exactly one perpendicular pair is principal.
examTip.mnemonic: **An ANGLE section loaded vertically deflects SIDEWAYS too**, because its principal axes are inclined — that is unsymmetrical bending, and ignoring it under-designs the member. And the principal-inertia equations are IDENTICAL in form to the principal-stress ones, with I_xy playing the part of τ.

questions.stem: Contour lines of different elevations can cross one another only in the case of:
questions.solution:
**An OVERHANGING CLIFF.**

**Why crossing normally cannot occur:**

> **A contour joins points of EQUAL elevation. If two contours of DIFFERENT elevations crossed, the point of crossing would have TWO different elevations at once — which is impossible for ordinary ground.**

> **An OVERHANG is the exception, because the ground surface at that point genuinely has two elevations: the rock face above and the recessed face beneath it.**

> **So the crossing represents a real physical condition rather than a drafting error — and it is conventionally shown with the concealed portion of the lower contour DASHED.**

> **Option (a) a VERTICAL CLIFF is the designed distractor and the distinction is exact: at a vertical cliff the contours COINCIDE (fall on top of one another) but do NOT CROSS.**

> **A vertical face has all its elevations at the same plan position, so the contours are superimposed; an overhang has them in reversed order, so they cross.**

**The characteristics of contour lines, as the examinable set:**

| Characteristic | Note |
|---|---|
| **Every contour CLOSES on itself**, within the map or beyond its edge | **A contour cannot simply end** ← |
| **Contours NEVER CROSS**, except at an overhang | ← this question |
| **Contours COINCIDE only at a vertical cliff** | ← |
| **CLOSE contours mean a STEEP slope; widely spaced means gentle** | **The most-used property** ← |
| **EQUALLY SPACED contours mean a UNIFORM slope** | — |
| **A series of closed contours with the HIGHEST innermost is a HILL** | — |
| **A series of closed contours with the LOWEST innermost is a DEPRESSION or a pond** | **Distinguished by the values, not the shape** ← |
| **Contours cross a RIDGE line and a VALLEY line at RIGHT ANGLES** | ← |
| **A V pointing UPHILL is a VALLEY; a V or U pointing DOWNHILL is a RIDGE** | **The single most useful reading rule** ← |
| **A contour cannot split into two** | — |

> **The V-SHAPE rule is the one used constantly in reading a map and it is worth being certain of:**

> **A stream cuts a valley, and the contours crossing it are deflected UPSTREAM — so the V points UPHILL, toward the higher ground.**

> **A ridge pushes the contours DOWNHILL, so the V or U points DOWNHILL, away from the high ground.**

> **The physical reasoning is that a contour must stay at its own elevation, so where the ground dips into a valley the contour must travel up the valley to remain at that height — hence the upstream V.**

> **And the practical use: a watercourse can be identified on a contour map with no blue line drawn, simply by following the series of Vs pointing uphill.**

**The HILL against DEPRESSION distinction, since it is a real trap:**

> **Both appear as a set of concentric closed contours, and they are distinguished ONLY BY THE VALUES:**

| Feature | Innermost contour |
|---|---|
| **HILL / summit** | **The HIGHEST value** |
| **DEPRESSION / hollow / pond** | **The LOWEST value** ← |

> **So a contour map without values on the lines is ambiguous, and that is why contour values must be written — conventionally on the UPHILL side of the line, or in a break in it, and oriented to be read from the south or the east.**

> **Depressions are sometimes marked with HACHURES (short ticks pointing inward, downslope) to remove the ambiguity at a glance.**

**The SADDLE — option (d), and worth knowing since it is a distinct feature:**

> **A SADDLE (col, pass) is the low point on a ridge BETWEEN two summits — and it is a high point along the valley crossing that ridge.**

> **On a contour map it appears as an hourglass or figure-of-eight pattern: two sets of contours approaching each other from opposite sides.**

> **Its practical importance is considerable: A SADDLE IS WHERE A ROAD OR A CANAL CROSSES A RIDGE, because it is the lowest crossing point available.**

> **So identifying saddles on a contour map is the first step in a hill road reconnaissance, and every pass on a mountain road is a saddle.**

> **In Nepal that is not a minor observation: the alignment of every hill road is determined largely by which saddles it can reach and at what elevation, and a route is selected between saddles rather than between towns.**

**CONTOUR INTERVAL, since it is the parameter to be chosen:**

| Factor | Effect on the interval chosen |
|---|---|
| **SCALE of the map** | **A LARGE scale (1:1000) permits a SMALL interval; a small scale needs a larger one** ← |
| **NATURE of the ground** | **FLAT ground needs a SMALL interval to show anything; steep ground needs a LARGE one or the lines merge** ← |
| **PURPOSE of the survey** | **Earthwork computation needs fine detail; a location survey needs less** ← |
| **Time and funds available** | A smaller interval costs proportionally more |

> **Typical values:**

| Purpose and terrain | Contour interval |
|---|---|
| **Building sites, detailed design, flat ground** | **0.2 to 0.5 m** |
| **Location surveys, undulating ground** | **1 to 2 m** |
| **Reconnaissance, hilly ground** | **5 to 10 m** |
| **Mountainous terrain, small-scale mapping** | **10 to 50 m or more** |

> **And a useful rule of thumb: contour interval in metres ≈ 25 / (number of centimetres per kilometre on the map), or simply the interval such that the contours are legible without merging.**

> **The interval must be CONSTANT across a map — a map with a varying interval cannot be read for slope, since the spacing no longer indicates the gradient.**

> **Where the terrain range is too great for one interval, the practice is to draw INTERMEDIATE contours (dashed) in the flat areas rather than to change the interval — preserving the slope-from-spacing property that makes the map useful.**

examTip.trick: **An OVERHANG is the only case where contours CROSS** — the ground there genuinely has two elevations. At a VERTICAL cliff they COINCIDE but do not cross, which is option (a)'s distinction.
examTip.trap: **A HILL and a DEPRESSION look identical — concentric closed contours — and differ only in whether the innermost value is highest or lowest.** Which is why contour values must always be written.
examTip.mnemonic: **A V pointing UPHILL is a VALLEY; pointing DOWNHILL is a RIDGE** — because a contour must travel up a valley to stay at its own elevation. And a SADDLE is where a road or canal crosses a ridge, which is why Nepali hill alignments are chosen between saddles.

questions.stem: For a PRELIMINARY or approximate estimate of a building, the method most commonly used is the:
questions.solution:
**The PLINTH AREA method.**

**How it works:**

> **Estimated cost = PLINTH AREA × the plinth area RATE**

> **The PLINTH AREA is the built-up area measured at floor level, taken to the EXTERNAL dimensions of the walls, and INCLUDING the wall thickness.**

> **The plinth area RATE is derived from the actual cost of a recently completed building of similar type, specification and locality, divided by its plinth area.**

> **So the method transfers a known cost per square metre from a completed building to a proposed one — which is why its accuracy depends entirely on the similarity of the two.**

**What is INCLUDED and EXCLUDED from the plinth area — the measurement rules:**

| Included | Excluded |
|---|---|
| **The area covered by WALLS, including their thickness** | **Open courtyards, terraces and open verandas** |
| **Internal shafts for sanitary and services, up to 2 m²** | **Areas of shafts exceeding 2 m²** |
| **Lift and stair wells at each floor** | **Cornices, chajjas and architectural bands** |
| **Porches and covered verandas** | **Open balconies (or taken at a reduced rate)** |
| **Rooms, corridors, kitchens, toilets** | External steps and ramps |

> **The rules matter because the same building measured two ways can differ by several per cent, and the RATE derived from one convention must be applied with the same convention.**

> **A rate derived by including balconies and applied to an area measured excluding them will understate the cost systematically — which is the commonest way this method goes wrong.**

**The approximate estimating methods, in order of refinement:**

| Method | Basis | Accuracy | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PLINTH AREA method** | **Cost per m² of plinth area** | **± 10-15 %** | **The standard preliminary method for buildings** ← |
| **CUBE (cubical content) method** | **Cost per m³ of the building's volume, plinth area × height** | **Slightly better where storey heights vary** ← | Buildings of unusual height |
| **Unit BASE (service unit) method** | **Cost per functional unit — per bed for a hospital, per pupil for a school, per seat for a cinema** ← | Rough | **Very early planning; budget setting** |
| **Bay method** | Cost per structural bay | Rough | Repetitive structures — factories, sheds |
| **Approximate quantities method** | **Cost from a few principal quantities (concrete, brickwork, steel) at composite rates** | **± 5-10 % — the most accurate approximate method** ← | Where more confidence is needed |
| **Cost comparison with a similar completed project** | Adjusted for time, location and specification | Varies | Sanity check |

> **The CUBE method is worth distinguishing from the plinth area method because it addresses a real defect in the latter:**

> **The plinth area method takes no account of HEIGHT. A warehouse with 8 m clear height and an office with 3 m storeys have the same plinth area and quite different costs.**

> **The cube method multiplies the plinth area by the height, so it captures that difference — and it is accordingly preferred where the storey height departs from the norm on which the rate was derived.**

> **The UNIT BASE method deserves its note because it operates at an even earlier stage: before any drawing exists, a hospital's cost can be estimated from the number of beds, using a rate per bed from comparable projects.**

> **That is how a budget is set before a design is commissioned, and its accuracy is poor — but it is the only method available when the only known quantity is the requirement.**

**The DETAILED estimate — option (a) — and why it is not a preliminary method:**

| | **PRELIMINARY (approximate) estimate** | **DETAILED estimate** |
|---|---|---|
| **Based on** | **A rate per unit of area, volume or function** | **MEASURED QUANTITIES of every item, at analysed rates** ← |
| **Requires** | **Only the size and type of the building** | **COMPLETE drawings and specifications** ← |
| **Effort** | **Hours** | **Days to weeks** |
| **Accuracy** | **± 10-15 %** | **± 5 %** |
| **Purpose** | **Administrative approval; budget provision; feasibility** ← | **Technical sanction; tendering; the bill of quantities** ← |

> **The distinction is one of PURPOSE as much as of method: a preliminary estimate exists to decide WHETHER to proceed, and a detailed estimate to decide WHAT TO PAY.**

> **So a preliminary estimate that took as long as a detailed one would be pointless, and its acknowledged imprecision is the price of being available before the design exists.**

**The other kinds of estimate, since options (b) and (d) name two of them:**

| Estimate | When prepared |
|---|---|
| **PRELIMINARY (abstract, approximate)** | **Before design — for administrative approval** ← |
| **PLINTH AREA / cube / unit** | The methods for the above |
| **DETAILED estimate** | **After the drawings — for technical sanction and tendering** |
| **REVISED estimate** | **When the sanctioned estimate is EXCEEDED by more than a stated percentage (commonly 5 %), or the scope changes materially — a fresh estimate for the SAME work** ← |
| **SUPPLEMENTARY estimate** | **For ADDITIONAL work found necessary while the original work is in progress — a separate estimate for EXTRA work** ← |
| **Complete estimate** | Includes all ancillary costs — land, fees, services |
| **Annual repair / maintenance estimate** | For upkeep |
| **Extension and improvement estimate** | For additions to an existing asset |

> **The REVISED against SUPPLEMENTARY distinction is the one this option set tests and it is worth stating precisely:**

> **A REVISED estimate is for the SAME WORK at a HIGHER COST — the scope has not changed, the money has run short.**

> **A SUPPLEMENTARY estimate is for ADDITIONAL WORK — new scope, discovered or decided during execution.**

> **So the question "has the work changed?" separates them: if the work is the same and the figure is wrong, revise; if the work has grown, supplement.**

> **Both require fresh sanction, and both are administrative safeguards against a project's cost growing without authority — which is why they are defined so carefully in public works procedure.**

**And the components of a complete estimate, since the construction cost is only part of it:**

| Component | Typical allowance |
|---|---|
| **Cost of WORKS, from the estimate** | The base |
| **CONTINGENCIES** | **3 to 5 %** |
| **Work-charged ESTABLISHMENT (supervision)** | **1.5 to 2 %** |
| **Tools and plant (T&P)** | 1 to 1.5 % |
| **Design and consultancy FEES** | Where applicable |
| **LAND acquisition and compensation** | **Can dominate in an urban project** ← |
| **Services — water, power, sewer connections** | Frequently underestimated |
| **Price ESCALATION over the construction period** | **Significant on a multi-year project** ← |
| **Taxes and duties** | As applicable |

> **The PRICE ESCALATION allowance is the one most often omitted from a preliminary estimate and most often responsible for a revised estimate later: an estimate prepared at today's rates for a project to be built over three years will be exceeded by inflation alone.**

> **So a preliminary estimate should state the PRICE LEVEL at which it was prepared, and an escalation provision should be shown separately — which makes the later revision a foreseen adjustment rather than an apparent overrun.**

examTip.trick: **PLINTH AREA × plinth area rate**, the rate taken from a similar completed building. Accuracy ± 10-15 %, and it needs only the size and type — no drawings.
examTip.trap: **REVISED = the SAME work at a higher cost; SUPPLEMENTARY = ADDITIONAL work found necessary during execution.** Ask "has the scope changed?" to separate them.
examTip.mnemonic: **The plinth area method ignores HEIGHT** — a warehouse and an office of equal area cost differently — which is what the CUBE method fixes. And always state the PRICE LEVEL of a preliminary estimate: inflation alone will otherwise force a revised one.

questions.stem: A sand has a maximum void ratio of 0.90, a minimum void ratio of 0.50 and an in-situ void ratio of 0.70. Its relative density is:
questions.solution:
**50 per cent.**

**The relative density (density index):**

> **D_r = (e_max − e) / (e_max − e_min) × 100**

**The computation:**

> **D_r = (0.90 − 0.70) / (0.90 − 0.50) × 100**

> **= 0.20 / 0.40 × 100**

> **= 50 %** ✓

> **The in-situ void ratio sits exactly midway between the loosest and densest states, so the relative density is 50 per cent — which is the check that confirms the arithmetic.**

**What the formula expresses and why the subtraction runs that way:**

> **Relative density measures WHERE the soil's in-situ state lies on the scale between its LOOSEST and DENSEST possible packings.**

| In-situ condition | e | D_r |
|---|---|---|
| **LOOSEST possible** | **e = e_max = 0.90** | **0 %** |
| **Midway** | **e = 0.70** | **50 %** ← |
| **DENSEST possible** | **e = e_min = 0.50** | **100 %** |

> **Note that the numerator is (e_max − e), NOT (e − e_min) — so a LARGE void ratio gives a SMALL relative density.**

> **That direction is easy to invert, and option (b) here happens to be symmetric so the error would not show. With e = 0.60 the correct answer would be 75 per cent and the inverted formula would give 25 per cent — so the check is to reason the DIRECTION: a loose soil has a HIGH void ratio and a LOW relative density.**

> **The two limits e_max and e_min are determined by standard laboratory tests: the loosest state by pouring the sand gently into a mould, and the densest by vibration and tamping under a surcharge.**

**Why relative density is used for SAND rather than void ratio itself:**

> **A void ratio of 0.70 means nothing on its own — it could be loose or dense depending on the sand:**

| Sand | e_max | e_min | e = 0.70 means |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A well-graded sand** | **0.75** | **0.35** | **D_r = 12.5 % — very LOOSE** ← |
| **A uniform fine sand** | **0.90** | **0.50** | **D_r = 50 % — MEDIUM** |
| **A uniform coarse sand** | **1.00** | **0.65** | **D_r = 86 % — DENSE** ← |

> **So the SAME void ratio describes a very loose sand in one case and a dense one in another, depending on the grading — and only the relative density is comparable between sands.**

> **That is precisely why the index exists: it NORMALISES the void ratio against the particular soil's own achievable range, so that a figure from one sand can be compared with a figure from another.**

> **A WELL-GRADED sand achieves lower void ratios at both ends, because its fine particles fill the voids between the coarse ones — which is the same packing argument met in the grading discussion.**

**The classification and what it governs:**

| Relative density | Classification | Typical N₆₀ | Typical φ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0-15 %** | **VERY LOOSE** | **0-4** | **Below 28°** |
| **15-35 %** | **LOOSE** | **4-10** | **28-30°** |
| **35-65 %** | **MEDIUM DENSE** | **10-30** | **30-36°** ← 50 % |
| **65-85 %** | **DENSE** | **30-50** | **36-41°** |
| **85-100 %** | **VERY DENSE** | **Above 50** | **Above 41°** |

> **So this sand at 50 per cent is MEDIUM DENSE, with an expected friction angle around 32 to 34 degrees and an SPT N value around 15 to 25.**

> **The correlations in that table are how the relative density is actually estimated in the field — since e_max, e_min and the in-situ e cannot be measured directly in a sand without a sample that is impossible to obtain undisturbed.**

> **A sand cannot be sampled undisturbed by ordinary means: the act of pushing a tube into it changes its density.**

> **So the practical route is REVERSED from the laboratory one: the SPT or CPT is performed in situ, and the relative density is INFERRED from the penetration resistance using correlations of exactly that kind.**

> **That is a good instance of a laboratory-defined index being used through a field correlation, and it is why the SPT retains its place despite its crudeness.**

**Why relative density matters so much for sand — the two consequences:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHEAR STRENGTH — φ rises with density** | **From 28° very loose to over 41° very dense — a large range** ← |
| **SETTLEMENT — a loose sand compresses substantially under load** | **And it does so QUICKLY, unlike clay** |
| **LIQUEFACTION susceptibility** | **A LOOSE saturated sand can liquefy in an earthquake; a dense one dilates and does not** ← |
| **Permeability** | Falls with density |
| **Bearing capacity** | Rises steeply with φ |

> **The LIQUEFACTION consequence is the one of greatest importance in Nepal, and the mechanism turns on density in a way worth understanding:**

> **A LOOSE saturated sand, when sheared rapidly, tends to CONTRACT. Water cannot escape in the time available, so the pore pressure RISES, the effective stress falls toward zero, and the sand loses its strength entirely — it liquefies.**

> **A DENSE saturated sand, when sheared, tends to DILATE — to expand. That generates NEGATIVE pore pressure, which INCREASES the effective stress and makes the sand STRONGER.**

> **So the same material, at different densities, responds to earthquake shaking in OPPOSITE ways: loose sand liquefies and dense sand stiffens.**

> **The dividing line is the CRITICAL VOID RATIO, and a relative density above roughly 70 to 75 per cent is generally taken as non-liquefiable.**

> **That is why GROUND IMPROVEMENT by densification — vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction, stone columns — is the standard remedy for a liquefiable site: raising the relative density past that threshold converts a contractive soil into a dilative one.**

> **And it is why the Kathmandu valley's and the Terai's loose saturated sand deposits are assessed for liquefaction as a matter of course: much of that material sits below the threshold, and the consequence in an earthquake is the loss of all bearing capacity at once.**

examTip.trick: **D_r = (e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min) = 0.20/0.40 = 50 %.** The in-situ value sits midway between the limits, which confirms it.
examTip.trap: **The numerator is (e_max − e), not (e − e_min)** — a LOOSE soil has a HIGH void ratio and a LOW relative density. Reason the direction rather than recalling the formula.
examTip.mnemonic: **The same void ratio can mean loose in one sand and dense in another** — which is why the index normalises against each soil's own range. And above about 70-75 % D_r a saturated sand DILATES on shearing rather than contracting, so it does not liquefy.

questions.stem: The water content at which a soil reaches its MINIMUM VOLUME on drying, and below which no further shrinkage occurs, is the:
questions.solution:
**The SHRINKAGE LIMIT.**

**The consistency limits in order of decreasing water content:**

| State | Boundary | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **LIQUID** | — | Flows like a viscous fluid |
| — | **LIQUID LIMIT (w_L)** | **The boundary between the LIQUID and PLASTIC states** |
| **PLASTIC** | — | **Can be moulded and retains its shape** |
| — | **PLASTIC LIMIT (w_P)** | **The boundary between the PLASTIC and SEMI-SOLID states** |
| **SEMI-SOLID** | — | **Crumbles when moulded; still shrinks on drying** |
| — | **SHRINKAGE LIMIT (w_S)** | **The boundary between the SEMI-SOLID and SOLID states** ← |
| **SOLID** | — | **NO FURTHER VOLUME CHANGE on drying** ← |

> **So the shrinkage limit is the LOWEST of the three limits, and the ordering is  w_S < w_P < w_L.**

> **Option (c) PLASTICITY INDEX is not a limit at all but the DIFFERENCE between two of them (w_L − w_P), which makes it a well-made distractor — a real quantity of the wrong kind.**

**What happens physically at the shrinkage limit — the mechanism:**

> **As a saturated soil dries, water leaves the voids and the soil SHRINKS, the particles drawing together under the surface tension of the receding menisci.**

> **That continues while the soil remains SATURATED — the volume reduction equals the volume of water lost.**

> **At the SHRINKAGE LIMIT the particles come into their closest packing and can move no further.**

> **Beyond that point further drying removes water and AIR ENTERS THE VOIDS instead — so the water content falls while the VOLUME STAYS CONSTANT.**

| Drying stage | Water content | Volume | Saturation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Above the shrinkage limit** | **Falling** | **FALLING — shrinkage occurs** | **100 % — still saturated** ← |
| **AT the shrinkage limit** | **w_S** | **MINIMUM reached** | **100 %, just** ← |
| **Below the shrinkage limit** | **Falling further** | **CONSTANT — no more shrinkage** | **Falling — air enters** ← |

> **So the shrinkage limit is the water content at which the soil is JUST SATURATED at its minimum volume — and that is the definition from which the computation follows.**

**The computation, since the test is a volumetric one:**

> **w_S = [(V_d γ_w / M_d) − (1/G)] × 100**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **V_d** | **Volume of the OVEN-DRIED soil pat** |
| **M_d** | **Mass of the oven-dried soil** |
| **G** | Specific gravity of the solids |

> **The volume of the dried pat is measured by MERCURY DISPLACEMENT, which is the test's characteristic feature — mercury is used because it does not wet the soil and so does not enter its pores.**

> **And the specific gravity can be worked out FROM the shrinkage test if it is not known, which is a useful by-product of the same measurement.**

**Why the shrinkage limit matters — the applications:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Assessing SHRINK-SWELL potential** | **A LOW shrinkage limit means the soil goes on shrinking to a low water content — so it undergoes LARGE volume changes** ← |
| **Predicting cracking of a clay subgrade or a canal lining** | **Shrinkage cracks admit water and destroy the layer** ← |
| **Foundation depth in expansive soil** | **The founding level must be below the zone of seasonal moisture change** ← |
| **Suitability of a soil as a fill or a liner** | A high-shrinkage clay makes a poor fill |
| **Computing the SHRINKAGE INDEX (w_P − w_S)** | The range over which the soil is semi-solid |
| **Shrinkage RATIO and volumetric shrinkage** | Quantifying the movement |

> **The EXPANSIVE SOIL application is the one of greatest consequence and the relation is worth stating clearly:**

> **A soil with a LOW shrinkage limit and a HIGH liquid limit has a wide range over which it changes volume, and it is therefore the most troublesome.**

> **Black cotton soil — montmorillonitic clay — is the classic case: liquid limits of 50 to 100 per cent and shrinkage limits of 10 per cent or less, giving enormous seasonal movement.**

> **Such soil swells on wetting with pressures of 100 to 300 kPa, which is far more than a light structure can resist, and shrinks on drying leaving open cracks tens of millimetres wide and metres deep.**

> **The engineering consequences are severe and specific:**

| Consequence | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **Light structures, floors and boundary walls are LIFTED and CRACKED** | **Found BELOW the active zone (1.5-3.5 m), or on under-reamed piles** ← |
| **Pavements heave and crack** | **Replace or stabilise the subgrade; provide a moisture barrier** |
| **Canal linings crack and leak** | Lime or cement stabilisation of the subgrade |
| **Cracks admit water directly to depth, accelerating the cycle** | **Surface sealing and drainage away from the structure** ← |
