> **The UNDER-REAMED PILE is the classical Indian and Nepali answer to expansive soil and it deserves a note: a pile with one or more bulbs (under-reams) formed at its base anchors the structure BELOW the active zone.**

> **The bulb resists UPLIFT — which is the actual problem, since the soil swells and tries to lift the foundation — and an ordinary friction pile could not.**

> **So the under-ream is not there to increase bearing capacity but to provide ANCHORAGE AGAINST HEAVE, which is the reverse of a pile's usual purpose and is why the detail exists.**

**The three limits and the tests that determine them, as a set:**

| Limit | Test |
|---|---|
| **LIQUID LIMIT** | **CASAGRANDE apparatus — the groove closes over 10 mm in 25 blows; or the CONE PENETROMETER, 20 mm penetration** ← |
| **PLASTIC LIMIT** | **Rolling a thread by hand until it CRUMBLES at 3 mm diameter** ← |
| **SHRINKAGE LIMIT** | **Volume of the oven-dried pat by MERCURY DISPLACEMENT** ← |

> **All three are performed on REMOULDED soil passing the 425 μm sieve, which is the essential limitation of the whole family: the limits describe what the soil IS — its mineralogy and its fines — and say nothing about its in-situ structure, density or strength.**

> **So the index tests classify a soil and cannot design a foundation on it — which is why they are cheap, quick and universally performed, and why a triaxial or consolidation test is required as well.**

examTip.trick: **Order: w_S < w_P < w_L.** The SHRINKAGE LIMIT is the lowest — the water content at which the soil is JUST saturated at its minimum volume. Below it, air enters and the volume stops changing.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) plasticity index is not a limit but a DIFFERENCE (w_L − w_P)** — a real quantity of the wrong kind.
examTip.mnemonic: **A LOW shrinkage limit with a HIGH liquid limit is the worst combination** — a wide range of volume change, which is black cotton soil. The remedy is to found BELOW the active zone, and the UNDER-REAMED pile's bulb resists UPLIFT, not bearing.

questions.stem: Water seeps upward through a soil with a hydraulic gradient of 0.5. The seepage pressure at a depth of 4 m is:
questions.solution:
**19.6 kPa.**

**The seepage pressure:**

> **p_s = i γ_w z**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **i** | **Hydraulic gradient** | **0.5** |
| **γ_w** | **Unit weight of water** | **9.81 kN/m³** |
| **z** | **Depth over which the gradient acts** | **4 m** |

**The computation:**

> **p_s = 0.5 × 9.81 × 4 = 19.62 kPa ≈ 19.6 kPa** ✓

> **Option (b) 39.2 kPa is the value with the gradient omitted (γ_w z = 39.24), which is the designed trap — it is the HYDROSTATIC pressure at 4 m, a real and different quantity.**

> **Option (c) 9.8 kPa is γ_w alone, and option (d) 4.9 kPa is half of it.**

**What seepage pressure IS and why it matters:**

> **When water flows through a soil, it exerts a DRAG on the particles in the direction of flow — the SEEPAGE FORCE.**

> **The head lost to friction as the water passes through the pores is transferred to the soil skeleton as a body force, and the seepage pressure is that transferred head expressed as a pressure.**

| Direction of flow | Effect on the soil |
|---|---|
| **DOWNWARD seepage** | **ADDS to the effective stress — the soil is pressed together and becomes STRONGER** ← |
| **UPWARD seepage** | **SUBTRACTS from the effective stress — the soil is lifted and becomes WEAKER** ← |
| **Horizontal seepage** | Acts laterally; relevant to slope stability |

> **So the DIRECTION is everything, and the case in this question — UPWARD flow — is the dangerous one:**

> **σ' = γ' z − i γ_w z**

> **For a soil with γ' = 9.19 kN/m³ at 4 m depth:**

> **σ' without seepage = 9.19 × 4 = 36.8 kPa**

> **σ' with this upward seepage = 36.8 − 19.6 = 17.2 kPa** — LESS THAN HALF.

> **So an upward gradient of only 0.5 has removed 53 per cent of the soil's effective stress, and hence more than half its shear strength.**

**The CRITICAL HYDRAULIC GRADIENT — the limiting case:**

> **Setting σ' = 0 gives the gradient at which the soil loses ALL its strength:**

> **γ' z = i_c γ_w z, so  i_c = γ'/γ_w**

> **For this soil:  i_c = 9.19/9.81 = 0.94**

| Gradient | Condition |
|---|---|
| **0** | Full effective stress; the soil is at its strongest |
| **0.5** | **Effective stress halved — as in this question** ← |
| **i_c ≈ 0.94-1.0** | **σ' = ZERO. The soil has NO strength: QUICK CONDITION, BOILING, PIPING** ← |
| **Above i_c** | The soil is lifted bodily; particles are carried away |

> **The critical gradient works out close to 1.0 for almost every soil, and that is a genuinely useful fact:**

> **γ' is typically 8 to 11 kN/m³ and γ_w is 9.81, so the ratio is between about 0.8 and 1.1 for the whole range of soils.**

> **So the practical rule is that AN UPWARD GRADIENT APPROACHING UNITY DESTROYS ANY SOIL — roughly a metre of head lost over a metre of soil.**

> **And note that the critical gradient is INDEPENDENT of the soil's grain size, permeability or strength: it depends only on the submerged unit weight, which varies little.**

> **A dense gravel and a loose silt have nearly the same critical gradient — though the silt reaches it far more easily, since its low permeability means a large head loss over a short distance.**

**Where upward seepage occurs in practice — the situations to recognise:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The BASE of an excavation below the water table** | **The classic case — water flows up into the excavation and can boil the base** ← |
| **Downstream of a weir or a dam, at the exit** | **The EXIT GRADIENT — hence Khosla's criterion** ← |
| **Behind a sheet pile wall, at the dredge line** | Sheet pile design must check it |
| **Downstream toe of an earth dam** | **PIPING — the leading cause of earth dam failure** ← |
| **A sump being pumped inside an excavation** | **Draws the flow UP through the base — which is why external dewatering is safer** ← |

> **The EXCAVATION case is the one an engineer meets most often, and the two ways of dealing with it are worth contrasting:**

| Method | Effect on the base |
|---|---|
| **Pumping from a SUMP INSIDE the excavation** | **Draws water UPWARD through the base — creates the very gradient that boils it** ← |
| **DEWATERING from OUTSIDE with wellpoints or deep wells** | **LOWERS the water table below the base, so no upward flow crosses it at all** ← |

> **So sump pumping treats the symptom and creates the hazard, while external dewatering removes the cause — and that is why deep excavations in water-bearing ground are dewatered from outside as a matter of course.**

> **An excavation whose base is boiling cannot be worked in, cannot be founded on, and progressively loses material — so the ground level falls and the problem worsens.**

> **The other remedies are to LENGTHEN the seepage path (a deeper cut-off or sheet pile), to LOAD the base (a filter blanket of graded gravel, which adds weight without impeding the flow), or to reduce the head by staged excavation.**

> **The FILTER BLANKET is the elegant one: a layer of graded gravel over the excavation base adds effective weight to resist the uplift AND allows the water through without carrying particles with it — increasing the resisting force without increasing the driving head.**

> **Which is the same principle as the launching apron and the graded filter in a dam: work with the seepage rather than against it, and prevent the SOIL from moving rather than the WATER.**

examTip.trap: **Option (b) 39.2 kPa omits the gradient** — that is the HYDROSTATIC pressure at 4 m, a real and different quantity. The seepage pressure needs the i.
examTip.mnemonic: **DOWNWARD seepage strengthens soil; UPWARD seepage weakens it** — and i_c = γ'/γ_w ≈ 1 for every soil, so an upward gradient near unity destroys any of them. Which is why excavations are dewatered from OUTSIDE, never by a sump inside that draws water up through the base.

questions.stem: Darcy's law for flow through soil is valid so long as the flow remains laminar, that is for a Reynolds number less than about:
questions.solution:
**About 1.**

**The relation:**

> **Darcy's law  v = k i  is LINEAR — the velocity is directly proportional to the hydraulic gradient.**

> **That linearity holds only while the flow is LAMINAR, and for flow through a porous medium the transition occurs at a Reynolds number of about 1:**

> **Re = v d ρ / μ**, with d taken as the effective grain size (D₁₀).

| Reynolds number | Flow regime | Darcy's law |
|---|---|---|
| **Below 1** | **LAMINAR** | **VALID** ← |
| **1 to 10** | **Transitional** | **Departs progressively** |
| **Above 10** | **Turbulent** | **INVALID — v is no longer proportional to i** |

> **Option (a) 2000 is the pipe-flow transition value, which makes it the designed distractor — and the difference between 1 and 2000 is startling enough to require explanation.**

**Why the transition occurs at Re ≈ 1 rather than 2000 — the reason:**

> **The Reynolds number's transition value depends on the GEOMETRY of the flow passage, and a soil's pores are nothing like a pipe:**

| | **PIPE flow** | **Flow through SOIL pores** |
|---|---|---|
| **Passage** | **A smooth, straight, uniform circular tube** | **A tortuous, irregular, constantly changing network of pores** ← |
| **Length scale used** | **The pipe DIAMETER** | **The effective GRAIN size** |
| **Direction changes** | **None** | **CONSTANT — every pore turns the flow** ← |
| **Transition Re** | **2000** | **About 1** |

> **The essential point is that flow through soil is CONTINUALLY ACCELERATING, DECELERATING AND CHANGING DIRECTION as it threads between the grains.**

> **Each of those changes generates local eddies and inertial losses, so turbulence develops at a vastly lower Reynolds number than in a smooth straight pipe.**

> **So the two transition values are not inconsistent — they describe entirely different geometries, and the Reynolds number is a comparison of inertial to viscous forces whose critical value is specific to the flow's shape.**

> **That is worth understanding generally: a Reynolds number's critical value is not a universal constant but a property of the geometry, which is why open channel flow, pipe flow, flow round a sphere and flow through soil all have different transition values.**

**When Darcy's law FAILS in practice — the situations that matter:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Flow through COARSE GRAVEL or ROCKFILL** | **Grain sizes of tens of millimetres give Re well above 1 — Darcy's law does not apply** ← |
| **Flow through the ROCKFILL shell of a dam, or a rockfill drain** | Non-Darcy flow; a power-law relation is used |
| **Flow very close to a pumping well, where velocities are highest** | **The turbulent zone around the well screen causes extra head loss** ← |
| **Flow through fissured or karstic rock** | Conduit flow, not porous-medium flow |
| **Flow through CLAY at VERY LOW gradients** | **The OTHER end — see below** ← |

> **The WELL LOSS case is worth knowing because it explains a real observation: the drawdown at a pumping well is always greater than the theory predicts, and the excess is attributed to TURBULENT well loss at and near the screen.**

> **So a well's drawdown is written as  s = B Q + C Q²  — the first term the Darcian aquifer loss, the second the turbulent well loss — and a STEP DRAWDOWN TEST separates them.**

> **The distinction is practical: aquifer loss is a property of the ground and cannot be reduced, while well loss is a property of the well's construction and CAN be reduced by better screen design and development.**

> **So a well with a large C is a badly made well, and the test identifies it.**

**The CLAY exception at the other extreme, since it completes the picture:**

> **At VERY LOW hydraulic gradients in clay, Darcy's law also departs from linearity — but for the opposite reason.**

> **The water closest to the clay particles is strongly held by electrochemical forces (adsorbed water) and does not flow freely.**

> **So there appears to be a THRESHOLD GRADIENT below which flow is negligible, and the relation is not linear through the origin.**

> **The existence and magnitude of that threshold is debated, and the practical consequence is modest — but it means Darcy's law is bounded at BOTH ends: invalidated by turbulence at high velocities and by adsorbed water effects at very low gradients.**

> **Between those bounds, which covers virtually all seepage through sands, silts and clays under ordinary gradients, it is an excellent law — and its LINEARITY is what makes the whole mathematical apparatus of seepage tractable.**

**Why Darcy's linearity is such a gift, worth stating:**

> **Because v = ki is LINEAR, the equation governing steady seepage is LAPLACE'S EQUATION:**

> **∂²h/∂x² + ∂²h/∂z² = 0**

> **Laplace's equation is one of the most-studied equations in mathematics, and its solutions have properties that make seepage analysis possible:**

| Property | Consequence for seepage |
|---|---|
| **Solutions can be SUPERPOSED** | **The effect of several wells can be added** ← |
| **FLOW NETS can be drawn — orthogonal families of curves** | **A graphical solution with a pencil** ← |
| **CONFORMAL MAPPING gives exact solutions for simple boundaries** | **Which is exactly what Khosla's theory uses** ← |
| **Numerical solution is straightforward** | Finite difference and finite element methods |
| **The same equation governs heat conduction and electrostatics** | **So electrical analogue models were used before computers** |

> **The last row is historically interesting and conceptually illuminating: because the same equation governs the flow of electricity through a conductor, seepage problems were once solved by building a CONDUCTING PAPER OR ELECTROLYTIC TANK MODEL of the structure and measuring the voltage distribution.**
> **The equipotential lines of the electrical model ARE the equipotential lines of the seepage problem, and they can be traced directly.**

> **So a difficult seepage problem was solved by turning it into an easy electrical one — and that only works because Darcy's law is linear, which is why the transition at Re ≈ 1 defines the boundary of the whole method.**

examTip.trick: **Darcy's law needs Re < about 1** — not 2000. Option (a) is the PIPE-flow transition, and the difference is real: soil pores turn the flow constantly, so turbulence begins at a far lower Reynolds number.
examTip.trap: **A critical Reynolds number is a property of the GEOMETRY, not a universal constant** — pipe flow, channel flow, flow round a sphere and flow through soil all transition at different values.
examTip.mnemonic: **Darcy fails in COARSE GRAVEL and near a PUMPING WELL (turbulent well loss, the CQ² term).** And its LINEARITY is what makes seepage governed by LAPLACE'S equation — hence flow nets, superposition, and Khosla's conformal mapping.

questions.stem: The standard size of the shear box used in the direct shear test is:
questions.solution:
**60 mm × 60 mm.**

**The standard apparatus:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Shear box plan size** | **60 mm × 60 mm (a 36 cm² area)** ← |
| **Specimen thickness** | **About 20-25 mm** |
| **Larger box, for gravelly soils** | **100 mm × 100 mm, or 300 mm × 300 mm for coarse material** |
| **Rate of shearing** | **Slow enough for the drainage condition intended** |

> **Option (a) 38 mm × 76 mm is the standard TRIAXIAL specimen size (38 mm diameter × 76 mm long — a 2:1 ratio), which makes it the designed distractor: a real standard dimension for a different test.**

> **Options (c) and (d) are the larger shear boxes used for coarse material, so they are real sizes for special cases.**

**Why the box has to be enlarged for coarse soil — the reason behind the sizes:**

> **A test specimen must be large enough that it behaves as a CONTINUUM rather than as a few individual particles.**

> **The conventional requirement is that the specimen's least dimension be at least 6 to 10 TIMES the maximum particle size.**

| Box size | Maximum particle size testable |
|---|---|
| **60 × 60 mm** | **About 6-10 mm — fine soils, sands** ← |
| **100 × 100 mm** | **About 10-16 mm** |
| **300 × 300 mm** | **About 30-50 mm — gravels and rockfill** |

> **A gravel tested in a 60 mm box would have a few large stones spanning the shear plane, and the result would describe those particular stones rather than the material.**

> **So the box size is dictated by the grading, and using too small a box for a coarse soil gives a result that is not reproducible and not meaningful.**

**What the test measures and how:**

> **The specimen is held in a box SPLIT HORIZONTALLY at mid-height.**

> **A NORMAL LOAD is applied through a loading pad, and the two halves are then forced to slide relative to one another while the SHEAR FORCE is measured.**

> **The test is repeated on identical specimens at THREE OR MORE different normal loads, and the peak shear stress from each is plotted against its normal stress.**

> **The FAILURE ENVELOPE through those points gives:**

| From the plot | Parameter |
|---|---|
| **The INTERCEPT on the shear stress axis** | **COHESION c** |
| **The SLOPE of the line** | **ANGLE OF INTERNAL FRICTION φ** ← |

> **So a minimum of three specimens is required, and a single test gives only one point and no parameters at all — which is worth knowing, since a "direct shear test" means a set of three or more.**

**The advantages and the honest limitations:**

| Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE, quick and cheap** | **Drainage CANNOT be controlled** ← |
| **Suitable for SANDS, where drainage is not an issue** | **Pore pressure CANNOT be measured** ← |
| **Ideal for testing along a PREDETERMINED plane — a joint, an interface, a pre-existing slip surface** ← | **The failure plane is FORCED, and may not be the weakest** ← |
| **Large boxes possible, for coarse material** | **Stress distribution on the plane is NON-UNIFORM** |
| **Suits RESIDUAL strength testing (with reversals)** | **Only a limited displacement is possible before the box halves separate** ← |
| **The interface between soil and a structural material can be tested directly** | Rotation of the principal planes is not controlled |

> **The FORCED FAILURE PLANE is the fundamental objection: the soil must fail on the horizontal plane where the box splits, whether or not that is its weakest plane — so the measured strength can exceed the true minimum.**

> **And the STRESS NON-UNIFORMITY is real: the stress concentrates near the edges of the box, so the specimen does not fail simultaneously across the plane and the "failure" is progressive.**

> **Those two objections are why the TRIAXIAL test is the reference method for anything but free-draining sand — the specimen there fails on its own weakest plane under a reasonably uniform stress state, with the drainage controlled and the pore pressure measured.**

**Where the direct shear test is nevertheless the RIGHT test — the cases it suits:**

| Situation | Why the shear box is appropriate |
|---|---|
| **Routine testing of SANDS and gravels** | **Drainage is free anyway, so the inability to control it does not matter** ← |
| **Testing along a PRE-EXISTING slip surface** | **The plane is known and IS the weakest — the forced plane is a virtue** ← |
| **Testing a soil-to-structure INTERFACE — soil against concrete, steel or a geomembrane** | **The interface is placed at the split, and the interface friction angle is measured directly** ← |
| **RESIDUAL strength, by repeated reversals** | Large displacement accumulated |
| **Coarse material needing a large specimen** | Large boxes are practicable |

> **The INTERFACE application is genuinely important and is easy to overlook: the friction angle between soil and CONCRETE, or between soil and a GEOMEMBRANE, is what governs a retaining wall's base friction, a pile's shaft resistance, and the stability of a lined slope.**

> **That angle cannot be measured in a triaxial test at all, and the shear box measures it directly by placing the structural material in the lower half of the box.**

> **Typical results: soil-to-concrete friction of about (2/3)φ to φ for a rough cast surface, and considerably less for a smooth one or for a geomembrane — where values as low as 10 to 20 degrees are found and have caused lined-slope failures.**

> **The RING SHEAR apparatus deserves a closing mention as the shear box's specialised successor for one purpose: because the specimen is annular and rotates continuously, UNLIMITED displacement is possible.**

> **That is the only way to reach a soil's true RESIDUAL strength — the strength after very large displacement, which governs the stability of a slope containing an old landslide surface.**

> **A shear box's few millimetres of travel cannot reach it, and the residual strength can be substantially below the peak — which is why an old slip surface can reactivate under a load the intact soil would carry easily.**

examTip.trick: **60 mm × 60 mm is the standard shear box.** Option (a) 38 × 76 mm is the standard TRIAXIAL specimen (2:1 ratio) — a real dimension for a different test.
examTip.trap: **The box must be at least 6-10 times the maximum particle size**, which is why 100 mm and 300 mm boxes exist for gravels. A gravel in a 60 mm box measures individual stones, not the material.
examTip.mnemonic: **The FORCED failure plane is usually a defect and sometimes a virtue** — it is exactly what you want when testing a KNOWN plane: a pre-existing slip surface, or a soil-to-concrete or soil-to-geomembrane INTERFACE, which no triaxial test can measure.

questions.stem: A clay has an unconfined compressive strength of 80 kPa in its undisturbed state and 20 kPa after remoulding at the same water content. Its sensitivity is:
questions.solution:
**4.0.**

**The definition:**

> **SENSITIVITY  S_t = (unconfined compressive strength UNDISTURBED) / (unconfined compressive strength REMOULDED, at the same water content)**

**The computation:**

> **S_t = 80 / 20 = 4.0** ✓

> **Option (a) 0.25 is the ratio INVERTED — and it can be rejected without arithmetic, because remoulding always WEAKENS a clay, so the sensitivity is ALWAYS GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO 1.**

> **A value below 1 would mean remoulding made the clay stronger, which does not occur.**

> **The essential requirement of the definition is "AT THE SAME WATER CONTENT": the strength loss must be due to the destruction of STRUCTURE, not to added water.**

> **Remoulding a clay with water added would weaken it for a quite different reason, and the test would measure nothing about its structure.**

**The classification and what each band means:**

| Sensitivity | Classification | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **About 1** | **INSENSITIVE** | Remoulding costs nothing |
| **1 to 2** | **Slightly sensitive** | — |
| **2 to 4** | **MEDIUM sensitive** | ← 4.0 sits at the boundary |
| **4 to 8** | **SENSITIVE** | Significant strength loss on disturbance |
| **8 to 16** | **EXTRA sensitive** | — |
| **Above 16** | **QUICK CLAY** | **Turns to a LIQUID when disturbed** ← |

> **So this clay at 4.0 is at the boundary between medium sensitive and sensitive — it loses three quarters of its strength when remoulded, which is substantial.**

**Where the strength comes from, and why remoulding destroys it:**

> **An undisturbed clay's strength has two sources:**

| Source | Destroyed by remoulding? |
|---|---|
| **FRICTION and interlocking between particles at their present density** | **NO — the density is unchanged** |
| **STRUCTURE — the flocculated, edge-to-face arrangement of the platy particles, and any cementation at their contacts** | **YES, completely** ← |

> **A clay deposited in water settles as a FLOCCULATED, open, card-house structure held together by electrochemical attraction at the particle edges, and often strengthened over time by cementation and by thixotropic effects.**

> **REMOULDING breaks that structure down and reorients the particles into a DISPERSED, parallel arrangement — and the strength associated with the structure is lost.**

> **The particles are still there and the water content is unchanged, so the loss is entirely structural.**

> **That also explains THIXOTROPY: a remoulded clay left undisturbed at constant water content REGAINS part of its strength over days or weeks, as the particles slowly reorganise and the bonds re-form.**

> **So sensitivity and thixotropy are two aspects of the same structural strength — one its destruction, the other its partial recovery.**

**Why sensitivity matters — the practical consequences:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **SAMPLING disturbance falsifies the laboratory strength** | **A sensitive clay sampled roughly tests far weaker than it is in the ground** ← |
| **PILE DRIVING remoulds the clay around the shaft** | **The shaft resistance immediately after driving is much less than the long-term value** ← |
| **Excavation and trafficking destroy a sensitive subgrade** | **A firm clay becomes a slurry once worked** ← |
| **A landslide in a sensitive clay can RUN like a liquid** | **Quick clay flowslides travel kilometres over nearly flat ground** ← |
| **Vibration from construction can trigger strength loss** | Piling, blasting, compaction |

> **The SAMPLING consequence is why the field VANE SHEAR test matters so much in soft sensitive clay: the test is performed IN PLACE, so the clay is never sampled, transported or trimmed.**

> **A laboratory unconfined compression test on a sensitive clay recovered by a thick-walled sampler can give half the true strength or less — an error that is conservative and wasteful, and of unknown magnitude.**

> **The PILE DRIVING consequence is the practical one for foundation design and it has a name: the strength lost by remoulding during driving is regained over weeks as the clay reconsolidates and thixotropically recovers.**

> **That recovery is called SET-UP or FREEZE, and a driven pile's capacity can double in the weeks after driving.**

> **So a pile load-tested immediately after driving will underestimate its long-term capacity substantially — which is why a waiting period before testing is specified, and why re-driving a pile after a delay requires far more effort than it did originally.**

**QUICK CLAY, since it is the extreme case and a genuinely remarkable material:**

> **A quick clay has a sensitivity above 16 and can exceed 100. Undisturbed it will support a building; remoulded it flows like a liquid at the same water content.**

> **Its origin is specific: a marine clay deposited in salt water develops a flocculated structure stabilised by the salt in its pore fluid.**

> **If the land is later uplifted and FRESH WATER leaches the salt out over millennia, the structure remains — metastably — but its stabilising mechanism has gone.**

> **The clay is then a house of cards standing at a water content far above its remoulded liquid limit, and a modest disturbance collapses it entirely.**

> **The result is a RETROGRESSIVE FLOWSLIDE: a small initial failure liquefies, flows away, removes support from the ground behind it, which liquefies in turn — and the failure eats backward for hundreds of metres.**

> **Such slides are known chiefly in Norway, Sweden and eastern Canada, where the geological sequence of marine deposition, uplift and leaching occurred — and they are not a feature of Nepali geology.**

> **But the general principle is: A SOIL'S STRENGTH CAN DEPEND ON A STRUCTURE THAT IS METASTABLE, and a soil that has stood for millennia is not thereby proved stable under disturbance.**

> **That applies to the collapsible loess and the sensitive residual soils that DO occur in the region, and it is why disturbance-sensitivity is assessed rather than assumed away.**

examTip.trick: **S_t = undisturbed strength ÷ remoulded strength, AT THE SAME WATER CONTENT = 80/20 = 4.0.**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 0.25 inverts it — and can be rejected without arithmetic, since remoulding always weakens a clay, so S_t ≥ 1.** The "same water content" clause is essential: the loss must be structural, not from added water.
examTip.mnemonic: **Remoulding destroys STRUCTURE, not density** — which is why a remoulded clay slowly regains strength (THIXOTROPY), and why a driven pile's capacity doubles in the weeks after driving (SET-UP). And a sensitive clay sampled roughly tests far weaker than it is, which is the argument for the field VANE test.

questions.stem: For a normally consolidated sand with an angle of internal friction of 30°, the coefficient of earth pressure AT REST is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 0.50.**

**Jaky's relation:**

> **K₀ ≈ 1 − sin φ**

> **For φ = 30°:  K₀ = 1 − 0.5 = 0.50** ✓

**The three earth pressure coefficients for φ = 30°, which must be kept apart:**

| State | Coefficient | Value at φ = 30° | Wall movement |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **K_a = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ)** | **0.333** | **The wall moves AWAY from the soil** |
| **AT REST** | **K₀ ≈ 1 − sin φ** | **0.500** ← | **NO movement** |
| **PASSIVE** | **K_p = (1+sinφ)/(1−sinφ)** | **3.000** | **The wall moves INTO the soil** |

> **Options (b) 0.33 and (d) 3.0 are the ACTIVE and PASSIVE coefficients for the same soil, which makes them the designed distractors — and note that K₀ lies BETWEEN them, as it must.**

> **That ordering is the reliable check: K_a < K₀ < K_p always, and a value outside that range is wrong.**

> **Option (c) 0.67 is 1 − sin 30° computed as 1 − 0.33, or a similar slip.**

**Why the at-rest state exists and when it applies:**

> **The AT-REST condition is the state of the soil BEFORE any wall movement — the natural state of a soil deposit under its own overburden, with NO lateral strain.**

> **It applies wherever the retaining structure is RIGID enough that essentially no movement occurs:**

| Structure | Earth pressure state |
|---|---|
| **A BASEMENT WALL, braced by the floors** | **AT REST — it cannot move** ← |
| **A rigid box culvert or an underground tank** | **AT REST** |
| **A bridge ABUTMENT integral with the deck** | **AT REST, or close to it** ← |
| **A heavily braced excavation support** | **At rest to active, depending on the bracing's stiffness** |
| **A free-standing gravity retaining wall** | **ACTIVE — it moves enough** |
| **A wall being pushed into the soil (an anchor block, a wall toe)** | **PASSIVE** |

> **The BASEMENT WALL case is the practically important one and it is frequently got wrong:**

> **A basement wall is restrained at the top by the ground floor slab and at the bottom by the base slab, so it CANNOT rotate or translate.**

> **Designing it for ACTIVE pressure (K_a = 0.33) rather than AT-REST pressure (K₀ = 0.50) UNDERSTATES the load by 50 per cent.**

> **That is a substantial and unsafe error, and it arises because the active case is the one met first and most often.**

> **The general rule follows: A RIGID, UNYIELDING STRUCTURE MUST BE DESIGNED FOR AT-REST PRESSURE, and only a structure free to move a little may be designed for active pressure.**

**How much movement is needed — the quantitative basis of that rule:**

| State | Wall rotation required, as a fraction of the height |
|---|---|
| **ACTIVE, dense sand** | **0.001 (0.1 %)** |
| **Active, loose sand** | **0.004 (0.4 %)** |
| **Active, stiff clay** | **0.01** |
| **Active, soft clay** | **0.02** |
| **PASSIVE, dense sand** | **0.02 (2 %)** ← |
| **Passive, loose sand** | **0.06 (6 %)** |

> **So the ACTIVE state needs a very SMALL movement — a millimetre or two on a 3 m wall — while the PASSIVE state needs 20 to 60 times as much.**

> **That asymmetry has two consequences worth stating:**

> **FIRST — the active state develops almost immediately, so any wall that has moved perceptibly is experiencing active pressure. A wall need not be designed for at-rest pressure merely because it is stiff; it must be UNABLE TO MOVE.**

> **SECOND — the PASSIVE state requires movement that a structure usually cannot tolerate, which is why passive resistance is taken with a large factor of safety or ignored entirely.**

> **A designer counting on full passive resistance at a wall's toe has assumed a displacement of 2 to 6 per cent of the embedment depth, which would in most cases have failed the structure for other reasons first.**

**The OVERCONSOLIDATED case, since Jaky's relation applies to normally consolidated soil:**

> **For an OVERCONSOLIDATED soil, K₀ is HIGHER:**

> **K₀(OC) ≈ K₀(NC) × √(OCR)**

| OCR | K₀ for φ = 30° |
|---|---|
| **1 (normally consolidated)** | **0.50** ← |
| **4** | **0.50 × 2 = 1.00** |
| **9** | **0.50 × 3 = 1.50** ← |

> **So a heavily overconsolidated clay can have K₀ EXCEEDING 1 — the horizontal stress GREATER than the vertical.**

> **The reason is a matter of history: the soil was once under a much greater vertical load and developed a correspondingly large horizontal stress. When the overburden was removed by erosion, the vertical stress fell substantially and the horizontal stress was LOCKED IN, relieved only partially.**

> **So the soil retains a memory of its former loading in its horizontal stress — which is a genuinely striking fact and one with practical consequences:**

| Consequence of a high K₀ | Note |
|---|---|
| **Basement walls and shafts in overconsolidated clay carry much higher lateral pressure than K₀ = 0.5 would suggest** | **London Clay, with K₀ up to 2, is the classic case** ← |
| **An excavation in such clay HEAVES and squeezes inward strongly** | The locked-in stress is released |
| **Slopes cut in it fail long afterward, as the stress relieves and the clay softens** | **Delayed failures decades after cutting** ← |

> **The DELAYED SLOPE FAILURE phenomenon is worth knowing: cuttings in overconsolidated clay have failed 30, 50 and 70 years after construction, as the locked-in horizontal stress slowly relieved, the clay softened toward its residual strength, and the factor of safety fell below 1.**

> **So a cutting that has stood for decades in such material is not thereby proved stable — which is the same lesson as the metastable clay structure, arriving from a different direction.**

examTip.trick: **K₀ ≈ 1 − sin φ = 0.50 for φ = 30°.** Check the ordering: K_a (0.33) < K₀ (0.50) < K_p (3.0), always. Options (b) and (d) are the other two coefficients.
examTip.trap: **A BASEMENT WALL cannot move, so it must be designed for AT-REST pressure** — using K_a understates the load by 50 %. Active pressure requires the wall to be free to move, not merely to be stiff.
examTip.mnemonic: **Active needs 0.1-0.4 % rotation; PASSIVE needs 2-6 % — twenty to sixty times as much**, which is why passive resistance is discounted. And an OVERCONSOLIDATED clay can have K₀ above 1: it remembers its former overburden in a locked-in horizontal stress.

questions.stem: The minimum factor of safety normally required for a retaining wall against SLIDING is:
questions.solution:
**1.5.**

**The stability checks for a retaining wall and their required factors:**

| Check | Minimum factor of safety | Against |
|---|---|---|
| **SLIDING (translation along the base)** | **1.5** ← | **Horizontal thrust exceeding the base friction** |
| **OVERTURNING (rotation about the toe)** | **1.5 to 2.0** | **The thrust's moment exceeding the restoring moment** |
| **BEARING capacity of the founding soil** | **2.5 to 3.0** | **Crushing of the soil beneath the base** ← |
| **Overall (deep-seated) SLOPE failure** | **1.5** | A failure surface passing beneath the whole wall |
| **No tension at the heel** | **The resultant within the middle third** | Loss of contact |

> **Option (d) 3.0 is the BEARING CAPACITY factor from the same set of checks, which makes it a well-made distractor — and the fact that the bearing factor is twice the sliding factor is worth understanding rather than merely noting.**

**Why the bearing factor is so much larger than the sliding factor:**

| Consideration | Sliding | Bearing |
|---|---|---|
| **Certainty of the resisting parameter** | **Base friction — reasonably predictable, and measurable by a shear box interface test** | **Soil bearing capacity — depends on c, φ, geometry and the bearing capacity theory used; much less certain** ← |
| **Consequence of failure** | **Movement, and often self-arresting as the passive resistance mobilises** | **A bearing failure is SUDDEN and the wall rotates and collapses** ← |
| **Warning** | **Movement is visible** | **Little** |
| **Convention for soil bearing generally** | — | **2.5-3.0 is the standard for any foundation** |

> **So the larger factor reflects the greater uncertainty in the soil's bearing capacity and the more abrupt failure mode — which is the same reasoning behind every partial factor: the factor is a measure of the UNCERTAINTY, not of the importance.**

**The SLIDING check in detail, since it is the subject:**

> **FoS_sliding = (total resisting force) / (total driving force)**

| Force | Note |
|---|---|
| **DRIVING: the horizontal component of the active thrust P_a** | Plus any water pressure and surcharge |
| **RESISTING: base FRICTION = μ × ΣV = tan δ × ΣV** | **δ is the base friction angle, commonly taken as (2/3)φ to φ for a rough cast base** ← |
| **RESISTING: base ADHESION, where the founding soil is cohesive** | c_a × base area |
| **RESISTING: PASSIVE resistance on the front face and the key** | **Often IGNORED or heavily discounted — see below** ← |

> **The PASSIVE RESISTANCE term is the one requiring judgement, and there are good reasons to discount it:**

| Reason to discount the passive term | Note |
|---|---|
| **It requires substantial MOVEMENT (2-6 % of the depth) to develop** | **Movement that would itself constitute a failure** ← |
| **The soil in front may be EXCAVATED later — for a drain, a cable, a service trench** | **A trench dug along the toe removes the passive resistance entirely** ← |
| **The front soil may be loose backfill rather than undisturbed ground** | Its strength is unknown |
| **It may be eroded or scoured away** | Particularly near a watercourse |

> **The FUTURE EXCAVATION objection is the decisive practical one: a wall whose stability depends on the soil in front of it will fail when someone digs a trench along its toe — and that is not a hypothetical event but a routine one in an urban street.**

> **So the prudent practice is to check sliding WITHOUT the passive term, and to treat any passive resistance as a reserve rather than as a resistance relied upon.**

> **A SHEAR KEY beneath the base is the usual remedy where friction alone is insufficient: a downstand into the founding soil that must be sheared through, mobilising the soil's own strength rather than surface friction.**

**Where the checks come from, and the order to perform them:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute the earth pressure and the water pressure, and any surcharge** |
| **2** | **Compute the wall's self-weight and the weight of soil on the base (for a cantilever wall)** |
| **3** | **Check OVERTURNING about the toe** |
| **4** | **Check SLIDING along the base** ← |
| **5** | **Compute the base pressure distribution and check BEARING capacity, and that no tension occurs at the heel** |
| **6** | **Check overall stability against a deep-seated failure surface** |
| **7** | **Design the wall's sections for bending and shear** |

> **Note that step 5's two requirements are distinct: the maximum pressure must be within the safe bearing capacity, AND the resultant must lie within the middle third so that the whole base remains in compression.**

> **The middle-third rule is why the base is proportioned as it is: for a resultant within the middle third, the eccentricity e ≤ B/6, and the pressure distribution stays trapezoidal rather than becoming triangular with a zero at the heel.**

> **And step 6 is the one most often omitted and occasionally decisive: a wall can be perfectly stable in itself and slide away on a deep failure surface through the soft soil beneath it, carrying the wall, its backfill and the ground behind it together.**

> **That is a slope stability problem rather than a wall problem, and it must be analysed as one.**

**And the design measure that removes most of the difficulty, worth restating:**

> **The single largest cause of retaining wall failure is WATER PRESSURE behind the wall, and it is entirely avoidable:**

| Provision | Effect |
|---|---|
| **GRANULAR, free-draining backfill** | **No pore pressure builds up; no cohesion to be lost; no swelling** ← |
| **A DRAINAGE LAYER or a geocomposite drain against the wall** | Conducts water down to the outlet |
| **WEEP HOLES through the wall, or a longitudinal drain to an outlet** | **Releases the water — and they must be kept clear** ← |
| **A filter to prevent the drain clogging with fines** | Or the drainage fails silently |
| **Surface sealing and drainage away from the wall crest** | Keeps the water out in the first place |

> **The arithmetic makes the case: a saturated backfill with the water table at the top more than DOUBLES the thrust on a wall, because water acts with K = 1 while soil acts with K = 1/3.**

> **So a wall designed correctly for a drained backfill and then allowed to saturate is loaded to twice its design thrust — and a factor of safety of 1.5 does not survive a doubling of the load.**

> **Which is why a blocked weep hole is not a maintenance detail but a route to collapse, and why the drainage provisions are the part of a retaining wall design least worth economising on.**

examTip.trick: **Sliding 1.5, overturning 1.5-2.0, BEARING 2.5-3.0.** Option (d) 3.0 is the bearing factor from the same set of checks.
examTip.trap: **Discount the PASSIVE resistance in front of the wall** — it needs 2-6 % movement to develop, and someone will eventually dig a trench along the toe. Check sliding without it, and use a SHEAR KEY if friction is insufficient.
examTip.mnemonic: **A saturated backfill more than DOUBLES the thrust** (water acts with K = 1, soil with K = 1/3) — and a factor of 1.5 does not survive a doubled load. So a blocked weep hole is a route to collapse, not a maintenance detail.

questions.stem: The downward drag exerted on a pile shaft by the surrounding soil when that soil settles more than the pile is called:
questions.solution:
**NEGATIVE SKIN FRICTION**, also called downdrag.

**The mechanism — and why the sign reverses:**

> **A pile normally derives part of its capacity from SKIN FRICTION: as the pile settles relative to the soil, the soil resists that movement and exerts an UPWARD friction on the shaft.**

> **That is POSITIVE skin friction, and it HELPS.**

> **NEGATIVE skin friction occurs when the RELATIVE MOVEMENT IS REVERSED — when the SOIL settles MORE than the pile:**

| Case | Relative movement | Friction on the shaft | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **POSITIVE skin friction** | **The PILE moves down relative to the soil** | **UPWARD** | **Supports the pile — part of its capacity** |
| **NEGATIVE skin friction** | **The SOIL moves down relative to the pile** ← | **DOWNWARD** ← | **ADDS to the pile's load** ← |

> **So the same interface friction acts in opposite directions depending on which moves more, and the pile that was being helped is now being loaded.**

> **Option (d) POSITIVE skin friction is therefore the same physical mechanism with the movement reversed, which makes it the natural distractor.**

**When negative skin friction occurs — the situations to recognise:**

| Situation | Why the soil settles |
|---|---|
| **A pile driven through a recently placed FILL** | **The fill consolidates under its own weight** ← |
| **A pile through a soft clay layer that is CONSOLIDATING under a new surcharge or fill** | **The classic case — a piled structure on filled ground** ← |
| **GROUNDWATER LOWERING in the area** | **Falling pore pressure raises the effective stress and the soil consolidates** ← |
| **A pile through a layer being loaded by an adjacent embankment or building** | Load transferred laterally |
| **Collapsible or leaching soils** | Structural collapse of the soil |
| **Vibration-induced settlement of loose sand** | — |

> **The GROUNDWATER LOWERING case is worth emphasising because the cause can be remote and the effect unexpected: pumping in the neighbourhood lowers the water table, the soil consolidates over a wide area, and piles that were designed years earlier acquire a downdrag load nobody anticipated.**

> **That is the same mechanism as regional subsidence, seen from the pile's point of view.**

**The magnitude, and why it is a serious matter:**

> **The downdrag force is the shaft friction acting downward over the settling layer's thickness:**

> **Q_neg = (perimeter) × (thickness of the settling layer) × (unit skin friction)**

> **For a 400 mm square pile through 8 m of consolidating fill with a unit friction of 25 kPa:**

> **Q_neg = (4 × 0.4) × 8 × 25 = 1.6 × 8 × 25 = 320 kN**

> **That is a very substantial additional load — comparable with the pile's design working load in many cases — and it acts permanently.**

> **The consequences are twofold and both must be checked:**

| Consequence | Check required |
|---|---|
| **The pile carries MORE LOAD than the structure applies** | **The pile's STRUCTURAL capacity (the section's compressive strength) must carry the sum** ← |
| **The load must be carried by the SOIL BELOW the settling layer** | **End bearing plus the positive friction in the competent stratum must carry structure load PLUS downdrag** ← |
| **The pile SETTLES more than expected** | Serviceability |

> **The first consequence is the one most often overlooked: a pile designed for 800 kN of structural load and subjected to 320 kN of downdrag is carrying 1120 kN in its shaft, and the concrete section must be adequate for that total.**

> **A pile can therefore be crushed by downdrag even where the founding stratum is entirely adequate.**

**The remedies, in order of how commonly they are used:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **BITUMEN COATING (slip layer) on the shaft over the settling layer** | **A soft bitumen coating lets the soil slide past the pile with very little shear transfer — reducing downdrag by 70-90 %** ← |
| **Provide for the downdrag in the design — larger section, deeper founding** | **The straightforward and often the cheapest answer** |
| **A SLEEVE or casing around the shaft through the settling layer** | Isolates the shaft entirely |
| **PRELOAD the fill before piling, so the settlement happens first** | **Removes the cause** ← |
| **Use fewer, larger piles** | **Reduces the total perimeter, and hence the downdrag, for the same capacity** ← |
| **Ground improvement to reduce the settlement** | Vertical drains, stone columns |

> **The BITUMEN SLIP COATING is the classic engineered solution and it is genuinely effective: a 1 to 2 mm layer of soft bitumen on the shaft shears at a very low stress, so the settling soil slides past rather than dragging the pile down.**

> **Its limitations are practical: the coating must survive driving (which it often does not, for a driven pile through granular fill), and it must not extend into the bearing stratum where positive friction is wanted.**

> **The FEWER, LARGER PILES remedy is worth noting because it is counter-intuitive and correct: downdrag is proportional to the PERIMETER, while capacity is roughly proportional to the AREA — so for a given total capacity, larger piles have less perimeter and therefore less downdrag.**

> **Four 600 mm piles have less total perimeter than nine 400 mm piles of the same total area, so the downdrag is less.**

> **That is a design decision available at no cost, and it also reduces the number of pile caps and the piling time.**

**And the related pile phenomena, for context, since the sign of the movement governs several:**

| Phenomenon | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **NEGATIVE skin friction (downdrag)** | **The soil settles more than the pile** ← |
| **POSITIVE skin friction** | The pile settles more than the soil |
| **UPLIFT (tension) on a pile in expansive soil** | **The soil SWELLS and lifts the pile — the reverse again** ← |
| **Set-up (freeze)** | **Capacity gained after driving, as the remoulded clay reconsolidates** |
| **Relaxation** | Capacity LOST after driving, in some dense sands and shales |
| **Group efficiency** | The group's capacity differs from the sum of its piles' |
| **NEUTRAL PLANE** | **The depth at which the pile and the soil settle equally — above it the friction is negative, below it positive** ← |

> **The NEUTRAL PLANE is the concept that makes downdrag analysis rigorous and it is worth knowing: there is a depth at which the pile and the soil move together, and the friction changes sign there.**

> **Above the neutral plane the soil settles more and drags the pile down; below it the pile settles more and the soil supports it.**

> **So the downdrag is computed only over the depth ABOVE the neutral plane, and its location is found by requiring the pile's force and settlement to be compatible with the soil's.**

> **That refinement usually reduces the computed downdrag relative to the simple assumption that the whole settling layer contributes — which is why the simple calculation above is conservative, and why a rigorous analysis is worth doing where the downdrag governs.**

examTip.trick: **The sign depends on WHICH MOVES MORE: pile down relative to soil gives POSITIVE (helpful) friction; SOIL down relative to pile gives NEGATIVE (loading) friction.** Same interface, opposite direction.
examTip.trap: **Downdrag loads the pile's own SECTION, not just the founding stratum** — a pile can be crushed by downdrag even where the bearing stratum is fine. Check the structural capacity for structure load PLUS downdrag.
examTip.mnemonic: **Downdrag ∝ PERIMETER while capacity ∝ AREA — so FEWER, LARGER piles suffer less downdrag** for the same capacity. And a soft BITUMEN slip coating cuts it by 70-90 %, letting the soil slide past.

questions.stem: A plate load test on a CLAY using a 300 mm square plate gives a settlement of 4 mm at the design pressure. The settlement of a 1.2 m square footing at the same pressure would be about:
questions.solution:
**About 16 mm.**

**The scaling relation for CLAY:**

> **S_footing / S_plate = B_footing / B_plate**

> **The settlement is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to the width, for a cohesive soil at the same pressure.**

**The computation:**

> **S_f = 4 × (1200/300) = 4 × 4 = 16 mm** ✓

> **Option (a) 4 mm assumes no scaling at all, and options (b) and (c) correspond to scaling factors of 2 and 3.**

**Why the settlement scales with the width — the physical reason:**

> **A wider footing at the same PRESSURE stresses a much GREATER DEPTH of soil:**

| Footing width | Depth significantly stressed (about 1.5-2 B) |
|---|---|
| **300 mm plate** | **About 0.5 m** |
| **1.2 m footing** | **About 2 m** ← |

> **So the large footing compresses four times the thickness of soil at comparable stress levels, and it settles four times as much.**

> **That is the essential insight and it explains why a plate load test cannot be read directly: THE PLATE SAMPLES A MUCH SHALLOWER ZONE THAN THE FOOTING WILL STRESS.**

**The critical difference between CLAY and SAND — the trap in this topic:**

| Soil | Scaling relation | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **CLAY (cohesive)** | **S_f/S_p = B_f/B_p — DIRECTLY proportional** ← | **The modulus is roughly constant with depth, so the settlement scales with the stressed depth** |
| **SAND (cohesionless)** | **S_f/S_p = [B_f(B_p + 0.3) / B_p(B_f + 0.3)]²** ← | **The modulus INCREASES with depth (confinement), which partly offsets the greater stressed depth** ← |

> **Computing the SAND case for the same numbers, to show the difference:**

> **S_f = 4 × [1.2(0.3 + 0.3) / 0.3(1.2 + 0.3)]² = 4 × [0.72/0.45]² = 4 × 1.6² = 4 × 2.56 = 10.2 mm**

> **So the same plate result gives 16 mm on clay and 10 mm on sand — a difference of 60 per cent, from the soil type alone.**

> **The reason is that a sand's stiffness RISES with depth, because confinement increases the modulus. The deeper soil that the large footing stresses is therefore stiffer than the shallow soil the plate stressed, and the settlement grows less than proportionally.**

> **A clay's modulus is much less dependent on confining stress, so no such offset occurs.**

> **Applying the clay relation to a sand OVERSTATES the settlement (conservative but wasteful), and applying the sand relation to a clay UNDERSTATES it (unsafe) — so the soil type must be established before the scaling is applied.**

**The BEARING CAPACITY scaling, which runs the other way and is a separate matter:**

| Soil | Bearing capacity scaling |
|---|---|
| **CLAY** | **q_footing = q_plate — INDEPENDENT of width** ← |
| **SAND** | **q_footing / q_plate = B_footing / B_plate — proportional to width** ← |

> **Note that the two soils behave OPPOSITELY for the two quantities:**

| | **SETTLEMENT** | **BEARING CAPACITY** |
|---|---|---|
| **CLAY** | **Scales WITH width** | **INDEPENDENT of width** |
| **SAND** | **Scales less than width** | **Scales WITH width** |

> **The reason for the bearing capacity behaviour: a clay's undrained strength c_u is independent of the confining stress, so q_u = c_u N_c does not depend on the footing's size.**

> **A sand's strength comes from friction and rises with the confining stress, which rises with the footing's width — so a wider footing on sand has a proportionally higher bearing capacity.**

> **That double reversal is genuinely confusing and it is the substance of the topic. The way to keep it straight is to reason from the mechanism each time rather than to memorise four rules:**

> **ASK: does this soil's stiffness or strength depend on confining stress? For sand, yes; for undrained clay, no. Every one of the four relations follows from that single question.**

**The plate load test's own limitations, which are why the scaling is needed at all:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The plate stresses a SHALLOW zone only — about 2 plate widths** | **A soft layer below that depth is COMPLETELY MISSED** ← |
| **Size effect requires the scaling relations above** | The subject of this question |
| **For CLAY, the test gives only the IMMEDIATE settlement** | **CONSOLIDATION settlement, which may be far larger and takes years, is not measured at all** ← |
| **The test is short — hours** | Time-dependent behaviour is invisible |
| **It is affected by the water content at the time of testing** | Seasonal variation |
| **It requires a substantial reaction load** | Practical difficulty |

> **The MISSED SOFT LAYER is the most serious limitation and it has caused real failures: a plate test on a firm crust 1 m thick over soft clay gives an excellent result and tells you nothing about the soft clay that the building will actually stress.**

> **So a plate load test must ALWAYS be accompanied by a borehole to establish that no weaker stratum lies within the zone the real foundation will stress — which is to say, to a depth of 1.5 to 2 times the FOOTING width, not the plate width.**

> **And the CONSOLIDATION limitation is decisive for clay: the test measures the immediate elastic settlement, which for a clay is often the smaller part of the total.**

> **The consolidation settlement must be computed separately from oedometer tests, and adding the two gives the total — so a plate load test on clay answers only part of the question even after the size scaling is applied.**

> **That is why the test is used chiefly on SANDS and GRAVELS, where consolidation is immediate and the test's short duration is not a limitation — and why for a clay a consolidation test is the more informative measurement.**

examTip.trick: **For CLAY, settlement scales DIRECTLY with width: S_f = 4 × (1200/300) = 16 mm.** A wider footing stresses a proportionally deeper zone of soil.
examTip.trap: **SAND uses the squared bracket relation and gives only 10 mm for the same data** — because a sand's modulus RISES with depth, partly offsetting the deeper stressed zone. Applying the clay rule to sand is wasteful; the reverse is unsafe.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ask one question: does this soil's stiffness or strength depend on CONFINING STRESS?** Sand yes, undrained clay no — and all four size-effect rules follow. And a plate test MISSES any soft layer below about two plate widths, so a borehole is mandatory.

questions.stem: Cavitation in a hydraulic machine or conduit begins when the local pressure falls to:
options: The vapour pressure of the liquid at the prevailing temperature
questions.solution:
**The VAPOUR PRESSURE of the liquid at the prevailing temperature.**

**What happens at that pressure:**

> **A liquid BOILS when its pressure falls to its vapour pressure — and that is a statement about PRESSURE, not about temperature.**

> **Water boils at 100 °C because that is the temperature at which its vapour pressure equals one atmosphere.**

> **Reduce the pressure and it boils at a lower temperature:**

| Temperature | Vapour pressure of water |
|---|---|
| **5 °C** | **0.87 kPa** |
| **20 °C** | **2.34 kPa** ← |
| **40 °C** | **7.38 kPa** |
| **60 °C** | **19.9 kPa** |
| **100 °C** | **101.3 kPa — one atmosphere** ← |

> **So water at 20 °C boils if its absolute pressure falls to 2.34 kPa — which in gauge terms is about −99 kPa, very nearly a perfect vacuum.**

> **Option (c) ZERO ABSOLUTE pressure is the designed distractor and the distinction matters: cavitation begins BEFORE a perfect vacuum is reached, at the vapour pressure — and the gap, though small at ordinary temperatures, is what makes the phenomenon possible at all.**

> **Option (b) atmospheric pressure is far too high: pressures below atmospheric are entirely normal in a pipeline and cause no cavitation.**

**The DAMAGE mechanism — why cavitation destroys metal:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1** | **The pressure falls to the vapour pressure; VAPOUR CAVITIES (bubbles) form** |
| **2** | **The bubbles are carried by the flow into a region of HIGHER pressure** |
| **3** | **They COLLAPSE — implode — extremely rapidly** ← |
| **4** | **The collapse is asymmetric, driving a MICROJET of liquid at the nearby surface** |
| **5** | **Local pressures of hundreds of megapascals over microscopic areas** ← |
| **6** | **Repeated millions of times, the surface is PITTED and eroded** |

> **The key point is that the damage is done by the COLLAPSE, not by the formation — so the pitting appears DOWNSTREAM of the low-pressure region, where the pressure has recovered.**

> **That is diagnostically useful: pitting on a turbine runner's outlet side, or on a pipe wall a short distance downstream of a valve, indicates cavitation upstream of the damage rather than at it.**

> **And the pressures generated are extraordinary — comparable with the yield strength of steel — which is why a material as hard as stainless steel is progressively destroyed by a process involving nothing but water.**

**The symptoms, which are recognisable:**

| Symptom | Note |
|---|---|
| **A noise like GRAVEL passing through the machine** | **The classic and unmistakable sign** ← |
| **Vibration** | Irregular, and it can be severe |
| **A DROP in efficiency, head and discharge** | The vapour occupies volume that water should |
| **PITTED, spongy-looking metal on inspection** | **A characteristic honeycombed appearance, not a smooth wear** ← |
| **Erratic operation, surging** | — |

> **The GRAVEL NOISE is the first indication in practice, and it is worth knowing because it identifies the problem immediately: nothing else in a pump or turbine sounds like it.**

**Where cavitation occurs — the low-pressure points:**

| Location | Why the pressure is low there |
|---|---|
| **PUMP SUCTION side, just at the impeller inlet** | **The lowest pressure in the whole system; governed by the NPSH** ← |
| **Reaction TURBINE runner exit and draft tube** | **The draft tube deliberately creates sub-atmospheric pressure — see below** ← |
| **Downstream of a partly closed VALVE** | Severe local constriction |
| **The throat of a venturi, if the constriction is severe** | Limits how far a meter can be constricted |
| **SPILLWAY surfaces at irregularities or offsets** | **Has destroyed concrete spillway linings** ← |
| **Propeller and pump impeller blade tips** | High local velocity |
| **A pipe summit where the HGL falls below the pipe** | The siphon case |

> **The DRAFT TUBE case is the instructive one because the low pressure is INTENTIONAL: the draft tube's whole purpose is to create sub-atmospheric pressure at the runner exit, recovering the kinetic energy.**

> **So a reaction turbine deliberately operates close to the cavitation limit, and the machine's SETTING LEVEL above the tailwater is what keeps it on the safe side.**

> **The criterion is the CAVITATION COEFFICIENT:**

> **σ = (H_a − H_v − H_s) / H**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **H_a** | **Atmospheric pressure head — and it FALLS WITH ALTITUDE** ← |
| **H_v** | **VAPOUR pressure head — and it RISES WITH TEMPERATURE** ← |
| **H_s** | **The SETTING — height of the runner above the tailwater** |
| **H** | Net head |

> **σ must exceed a critical value σ_c that depends on the turbine's specific speed — and higher specific speed machines (Kaplans) are more cavitation-prone, so they need a smaller or negative setting.**

> **The two environmental terms deserve emphasis because both work against a Nepali installation:**

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **ALTITUDE reduces H_a** | **10.3 m at sea level, 8.1 m at 2000 m — 2.2 m less margin** ← |
| **Higher water TEMPERATURE raises H_v** | **0.24 m at 20 °C, 0.75 m at 40 °C — a further 0.5 m lost** |

> **So a turbine selected from a manufacturer's sea-level data and installed at 2000 m has about 2.2 m less cavitation margin than the data assume — and it will cavitate.**

> **The altitude correction is therefore a required design step for any Nepali hill installation, and neglecting it is a documented error rather than a theoretical caution.**

**The remedies, all of which raise the local pressure or tolerate the damage:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **LOWER the machine — reduce H_s, or set the runner below tailwater** | **The direct remedy, at the cost of excavation** ← |
| **Reduce the suction lift on a pump** | Same principle |
| **Increase the suction pipe diameter, and shorten it** | Reduces the friction loss ahead of the pump |
| **Reduce the flow rate, or run the machine nearer its design point** | Part-load operation often cavitates worse |
| **AERATE the low-pressure region** | **Admitting a little air cushions the collapse — used on spillways** ← |
| **Use cavitation-resistant materials — stainless steel, or weld overlays** | **Tolerates rather than prevents** |
| **Smooth the surfaces; eliminate offsets and irregularities** | Particularly on spillways |

> **The AERATION remedy is worth understanding because it is counter-intuitive: deliberately introducing AIR into the flow reduces cavitation damage.**

> **The air cushions the bubble collapse, so the microjets and the pressure spikes are much reduced — and a few per cent of entrained air is enough.**

> **That is why high spillways are fitted with AERATOR RAMPS or steps that entrain air into the boundary layer: the flow's velocity cannot be reduced, so the collapse is cushioned instead.**

> **It is a good example of mitigating a mechanism rather than removing its cause, adopted because the cause — a very high velocity on a concrete surface — cannot be removed at all.**

examTip.trick: **Cavitation begins at the liquid's VAPOUR PRESSURE — 2.34 kPa absolute for water at 20 °C** — not at zero absolute pressure. Boiling is a statement about PRESSURE, not temperature.
examTip.trap: **The damage is done by the COLLAPSE, not the formation** — so the pitting appears DOWNSTREAM of the low-pressure region, where the pressure has recovered. That is diagnostically useful.
examTip.mnemonic: **σ = (H_a − H_v − H_s)/H, and BOTH environmental terms work against a Nepali hill site** — altitude cuts H_a by 2.2 m at 2000 m, and warm water raises H_v. A turbine set from sea-level data will cavitate. And AERATION cushions the collapse where the velocity cannot be reduced.

questions.stem: A fluid that requires a certain minimum shear stress to be exceeded before it begins to flow at all is called:
questions.solution:
**A BINGHAM PLASTIC**, also called an ideal plastic.

**The classification of fluids by their shear behaviour:**

| Type | Relation between τ and du/dy | Character | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IDEAL (inviscid) fluid** | **τ = 0 always** | **No viscosity — a mathematical idealisation** | None real |
| **NEWTONIAN** | **τ = μ (du/dy), μ CONSTANT** | **A straight line THROUGH THE ORIGIN** ← | **Water, air, oils, most liquids** |
| **DILATANT (shear-thickening)** | **τ ∝ (du/dy)ⁿ, n > 1** | **Apparent viscosity RISES with shear rate** | **Dense cornflour suspension, some slurries** |
| **PSEUDOPLASTIC (shear-thinning)** | **τ ∝ (du/dy)ⁿ, n < 1** | **Apparent viscosity FALLS with shear rate** | **Paint, blood, polymer solutions, drilling mud** |
| **BINGHAM PLASTIC (ideal plastic)** | **τ = τ₀ + μ (du/dy)** | **A straight line with a POSITIVE INTERCEPT — a YIELD STRESS τ₀** ← | **FRESH CONCRETE, toothpaste, drilling mud, sewage sludge** ← |
| **Thixotropic** | Viscosity falls with TIME under constant shear | Time-dependent | Some gels, sensitive clays |
| **Rheopectic** | Viscosity rises with time under shear | Time-dependent | Rare |

> **The defining feature of a Bingham plastic is the YIELD STRESS τ₀ — the INTERCEPT on the shear stress axis.**

> **Below τ₀ the material does not flow at all; it behaves as a SOLID. Above τ₀ it flows, and thereafter like a Newtonian fluid with a constant plastic viscosity.**

> **So the graph is a straight line NOT passing through the origin, and that single feature distinguishes it from every other type.**

> **Option (a) NEWTONIAN is the designed distractor because a Bingham plastic's line is also STRAIGHT — the difference is entirely whether it passes through the origin.**

**FRESH CONCRETE as a Bingham plastic — the case that matters most:**

> **This is not an analogy but an accurate description, and it explains two things at once:**

| Observation | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **A slump cone HOLDS ITS SHAPE when the mould is lifted** | **The shear stress from its own weight is BELOW the yield stress, so it does not flow** ← |
| **VIBRATION makes concrete flow into the formwork** | **The vibrator supplies momentary shear stress EXCEEDING τ₀, so the material flows until the vibration stops** ← |
| **It stops flowing the instant the vibrator is withdrawn** | The stress falls below τ₀ again |
| **A wetter mix slumps more** | More water reduces τ₀ |
| **A superplasticised mix flows without vibration** | **The admixture reduces τ₀ dramatically — which is what self-compacting concrete is** ← |

> **So the slump test and the poker vibrator are both explained by one material property, and understanding concrete as a Bingham plastic makes both intelligible rather than being separate facts.**

> **SELF-COMPACTING CONCRETE is the practical culmination: by using a polycarboxylate superplasticiser to reduce the yield stress almost to zero while keeping the plastic viscosity high enough to prevent segregation, a concrete is made that FLOWS UNDER ITS OWN WEIGHT and needs no vibration at all.**

> **That is a deliberate manipulation of the two Bingham parameters independently — τ₀ down for flow, μ up for stability — and it is why it took so long to achieve: reducing the yield stress by adding water raises the flow AND causes segregation, and only a chemical admixture separates the two effects.**

**The two-parameter description, and why one number is insufficient:**

> **A Newtonian fluid is described by ONE number, its viscosity.**

> **A Bingham plastic needs TWO — the yield stress τ₀ and the plastic viscosity μ_p — and they govern different aspects of the behaviour:**

| Parameter | Governs |
|---|---|
| **YIELD STRESS τ₀** | **Whether the material flows AT ALL; the slump; the ability to be pumped from rest; the formwork pressure** ← |
| **PLASTIC VISCOSITY μ_p** | **How FAST it flows once moving; the resistance to segregation; the pumping pressure at a given rate** ← |

> **That is why the slump test alone is an incomplete description of workability: it measures essentially the YIELD STRESS and says nothing about the plastic viscosity.**

> **Two concretes of identical slump can behave quite differently — one flowing readily and segregating, the other stiff but cohesive — because their plastic viscosities differ.**

> **Which is precisely why the slump test's limitations were noted earlier, and why rheometers measuring both parameters are used for self-compacting and high-performance concrete where the distinction matters.**

**The OTHER civil engineering Bingham materials, since concrete is not the only one:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **FRESH CONCRETE and cement paste** | ← |
| **DRILLING MUD (bentonite slurry)** | **Its yield stress is essential: it SUSPENDS the cuttings when circulation stops, instead of letting them settle and jam the drill** ← |
| **Bentonite slurry in a DIAPHRAGM WALL trench** | **Supports the trench walls AND holds the excavated material in suspension** ← |
| **Sewage sludge** | Pumping design must allow for the yield stress |
| **Grout** | Penetration into a soil depends on the yield stress |
| **MUDFLOWS and DEBRIS FLOWS** | **Modelled as Bingham fluids — which is why they stop abruptly on a slope rather than thinning out** ← |

> **The DRILLING MUD case shows the yield stress being exploited rather than tolerated: a Newtonian fluid would let the cuttings settle the moment the pump stopped, jamming the hole.**

> **A mud with a yield stress holds them in suspension indefinitely, so drilling can be interrupted safely — and the mud is designed for that property.**

> **The DEBRIS FLOW application is worth noting for Nepal: a debris flow's characteristic behaviour — travelling far on a modest slope and then stopping abruptly, leaving a steep-fronted deposit — is exactly what a Bingham fluid does.**

> **A Newtonian fluid would spread out thinly and indefinitely. The yield stress is what makes a debris flow stop where it does and pile up rather than spreading, and it is why the deposits have the lobate, steep-margined form seen after every monsoon in the hills.**

> **So modelling a debris flow requires a yield stress, and predicting its RUNOUT distance — which is what a hazard map needs — depends on estimating that parameter.**

examTip.trick: **A BINGHAM PLASTIC's graph is a STRAIGHT LINE with a POSITIVE INTERCEPT — the yield stress τ₀.** Below τ₀ it behaves as a solid. A Newtonian line is also straight but passes through the ORIGIN.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the near miss — both lines are straight.** The distinction is entirely the intercept, which is why the slump cone holds its shape until vibration supplies stress above τ₀.
examTip.mnemonic: **Concrete needs TWO parameters: τ₀ (does it flow at all — the slump) and μ_p (how fast, and does it segregate).** Slump measures only the first, which is why two concretes of equal slump can behave differently — and why self-compacting concrete lowers τ₀ chemically while keeping μ_p up.

questions.stem: A vertical rectangular gate 3 m wide and 4 m high has its top edge at the water surface. The total hydrostatic force on the gate is:
questions.solution:
**235.4 kN.**

**The relation for the total force on a plane surface:**

> **F = γ A h̄**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **γ** | **Unit weight of water** | **9.81 kN/m³** |
| **A** | **AREA of the surface** | **3 × 4 = 12 m²** |
| **h̄** | **Depth of the CENTROID of the area** | **4/2 = 2 m** |

**The computation:**

> **F = 9.81 × 12 × 2 = 235.44 kN ≈ 235.4 kN** ✓

> **Option (b) 117.7 kN is exactly half — the result of using h̄ = 1 m, or of halving the area.**

> **Option (c) 470.9 kN is double — the result of using h̄ = 4 m, that is the FULL DEPTH rather than the centroid depth.**

> **Option (d) 78.5 kN is a third of the answer.**

> **So the errors available are all in the depth term, and the safeguard is to write down explicitly that h̄ is the depth of the CENTROID, not of the bottom edge.**

**Why the centroid depth is the right one — the derivation:**

> **The pressure varies linearly with depth: p = γh.**

> **The force on an element dA at depth h is γ h dA, and integrating:**

> **F = ∫ γ h dA = γ ∫ h dA = γ (A h̄)**

> **because ∫h dA is by definition the FIRST MOMENT of the area about the surface line, which equals A h̄.**

> **So the total force equals the pressure AT THE CENTROID multiplied by the area — which is a general result for any plane surface at any inclination.**

> **Equivalently: the AVERAGE pressure over the surface is the pressure at its centroid, and force = average pressure × area.**

**The alternative route, which is often quicker for a vertical rectangle:**

> **The pressure distribution is a TRIANGLE from zero at the surface to γh at the bottom:**

> **Pressure at the base = 9.81 × 4 = 39.24 kPa**

> **Force per metre of width = area of the pressure triangle = ½ × 4 × 39.24 = 78.48 kN/m**

> **Total force = 78.48 × 3 = 235.4 kN** ✓

> **Note that 78.48 kN/m — the force per metre width — happens to be option (d), which is therefore the answer to a different question: the force on a ONE-METRE-WIDE strip.**

> **That is a well-made distractor, since "force per metre run" is a common way of expressing such a result and a candidate might stop there.**

**The LOCATION of the force, since a gate design needs both:**

> **For a vertical rectangle with its top edge AT the surface:**

> **h̄_cp = 2d/3 = 2 × 4/3 = 2.67 m below the surface**

> **which is d/3 = 1.33 m above the base.**

> **The general relation:  h̄_cp = h̄ + I_G/(A h̄) = 2 + (3 × 4³/12)/(12 × 2) = 2 + 16/24 = 2.67 m** ✓

> **So the resultant of 235.4 kN acts 1.33 m above the base, and the moment about a bottom hinge is 235.4 × 1.33 = 313 kNm.**

> **That moment is what the gate's hoisting mechanism must overcome and what its structure must carry — which is why the location matters as much as the magnitude.**

> **And the two quantities depend on DIFFERENT geometric properties, which is worth restating:**

| Quantity | Depends on |
|---|---|
| **The MAGNITUDE of the force** | **The depth of the CENTROID (the first moment of area)** ← |
| **The LOCATION of the force** | **The SECOND MOMENT of area as well** ← |

**Where this calculation is used, and one warning:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sluice and lock GATE design** | **Both the force and its location** ← |
| **Dam and retaining wall stability** | The water thrust and its overturning moment |
| **Tank and reservoir wall design** | Bending moments in the wall |
| **Caisson and cofferdam bulkheads** | Panel design |
| **Culvert and pipe flap valves** | — |

> **The warning concerns the WATER ON BOTH SIDES case, which is the commonest real situation and is easily mishandled:**

> **A sluice gate usually has water on BOTH sides at different levels, and the NET force is the difference between the two.**

| Case | Net force |
|---|---|
| **Water only on the upstream side, to depth 4 m** | **235.4 kN** ← this question |
| **Water 4 m upstream, 2 m downstream** | **235.4 − (9.81 × 3 × 2 × 1) = 235.4 − 58.9 = 176.5 kN** |
| **Equal levels both sides** | **ZERO net force** ← |

> **And the NET force acts at a different location from either component, so its position must be found by taking moments of the two triangular distributions rather than by using the 2d/3 rule.**

> **That is where the arithmetic gets careless: the 2d/3 shortcut applies to a SINGLE triangular distribution with its apex at the surface, and it does not apply to the net of two.**

> **So for a gate with water on both sides, the two forces and their two locations are computed separately and combined — which is more work and is the only correct route.**

examTip.trick: **F = γ A h̄ = 9.81 × 12 × 2 = 235.4 kN**, where h̄ is the depth of the CENTROID — 2 m, not 4 m.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 470.9 kN uses the FULL depth as h̄, and option (d) 78.5 kN is the force per METRE OF WIDTH** — a real intermediate result, and a natural place to stop.
examTip.mnemonic: **MAGNITUDE needs the centroid depth; LOCATION needs the second moment too** (here 2d/3 = 2.67 m down, so 1.33 m above the base). And for a gate with water BOTH sides, compute the two forces and locations separately — the 2d/3 shortcut does not apply to their net.

questions.stem: The principle that the pressure at a point in a fluid at rest is the same in ALL DIRECTIONS is known as:
questions.solution:
**PASCAL'S LAW.**

**The statement and its proof:**

> **PASCAL'S LAW: the pressure at a point in a fluid AT REST is the same in all directions.**

> **The proof is a neat one and takes a few lines. Consider a small triangular wedge of fluid at rest, with faces of area dA_x, dA_y and dA_s:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Write the force balance in the x and y directions for the wedge** |
| **2** | **The pressure forces act NORMAL to each face (a fluid at rest can carry no shear)** ← |
| **3** | **The WEIGHT of the wedge is proportional to its VOLUME, hence to the CUBE of its size** |
| **4** | **The pressure forces are proportional to the AREAS, hence to the SQUARE of its size** |
| **5** | **As the wedge shrinks to a point, the weight (size³) vanishes FASTER than the pressure forces (size²)** ← |
| **6** | **So in the limit the weight is negligible, and the balance requires p_x = p_y = p_s** ✓ |

> **Step 5 is the elegant part: the result holds AT A POINT precisely because the weight term disappears faster than the pressure terms as the element shrinks.**

> **And step 2 is the condition on which everything rests: a fluid AT REST cannot sustain shear stress, so all forces on its faces are normal. That is why the law applies only to a static fluid.**

**Why the law requires the fluid to be AT REST — the important qualification:**

> **In a MOVING fluid, VISCOUS SHEAR STRESSES exist, and the normal stresses on planes of different orientation are NOT all equal.**

> **The "pressure" in a moving viscous fluid is then defined as the AVERAGE of the three normal stresses, and it is not identical to any one of them.**

> **So Pascal's law is exactly true for a static fluid and approximately true for a moving one — the departure being of the order of the viscous stresses, which for water at ordinary velocities is very small.**

> **That is why the law is used freely in hydraulics without qualification, and it is worth knowing that the qualification exists.**

**The applications, which are what make the law important:**

| Application | How it uses the law |
|---|---|
| **HYDRAULIC PRESS / hydraulic jack** | **Pressure applied at a small piston is transmitted UNDIMINISHED to a large piston, multiplying the force by the area ratio** ← |
| **Hydraulic brakes, hydraulic jacks, hydraulic lifts** | The same principle |
| **HYDRAULIC ACCUMULATOR and intensifier** | Energy storage and pressure multiplication |
| **The gate and dam pressure calculations** | Pressure acts normal to the surface, whatever its orientation |
| **MANOMETERS** | **Pressure is transmitted through the connecting fluid unchanged at the same level** ← |
| **Hydraulic governors and servomotors** | Turbine control |

> **The HYDRAULIC PRESS is the classic demonstration and the arithmetic is worth seeing:**
