> **A force of 100 N on a piston of 10 cm² area generates a pressure of 100/0.001 = 100 kPa.**

> **That pressure acts on a large piston of 1000 cm² (0.1 m²), giving a force of 100 × 0.1 = 10,000 N.**

> **So the force is multiplied ONE HUNDRED TIMES — the ratio of the areas.**

> **And note what is NOT multiplied: the WORK. The small piston must move 100 times as far as the large one, so the work done is the same at both ends (less friction).**

> **That is the hydraulic equivalent of a lever, and it obeys the same conservation: force is multiplied and distance is divided.**

> **A jack that lifts 10 tonnes with a hand force of 100 N requires a great many strokes, and the number of strokes is exactly what the energy balance demands.**

**The other options, since each is a fundamental principle in its own right:**

| Principle | Statement | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| **PASCAL'S LAW** | **Pressure at a point is equal in all directions** | **A fluid AT REST** ← |
| **ARCHIMEDES' PRINCIPLE** | **The buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced** | **A body immersed or floating in a fluid at rest** |
| **BERNOULLI'S THEOREM** | **p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant along a streamline** | **STEADY, incompressible, frictionless FLOW** ← |
| **NEWTON'S LAW OF VISCOSITY** | **τ = μ (du/dy)** | **A fluid IN MOTION with a velocity gradient** ← |

> **Note that the four divide neatly by whether the fluid is at rest or moving:**

> **PASCAL and ARCHIMEDES belong to HYDROSTATICS — fluid at rest.**

> **BERNOULLI and NEWTON'S VISCOSITY LAW belong to fluid in MOTION.**

> **So the stem's phrase "at rest" already excludes two of the four options, which is a useful way through the question.**

**And the hydrostatic pressure variation, since it is Pascal's law's companion:**

> **Pascal's law says the pressure at a POINT is the same in all directions. It does NOT say the pressure is the same everywhere.**

> **The pressure VARIES WITH DEPTH:**

> **dp/dz = −γ,  so  p = γ h**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pressure is the same at all points at the same LEVEL in a connected fluid at rest** | **The basis of every manometer, and of a level in a tank** ← |
| **Pressure increases linearly with depth** | 9.81 kPa per metre of water |
| **The shape of the vessel is IRRELEVANT** | **The HYDROSTATIC PARADOX — see below** ← |

> **The HYDROSTATIC PARADOX is worth a note because it surprises people: the pressure on the base of a vessel depends only on the DEPTH of liquid, not on the vessel's shape or the weight of liquid it contains.**

> **So a narrow tall vessel and a wide flaring one of the same depth exert the SAME pressure on their bases — even though one contains far more water.**

> **The apparent paradox is resolved by noticing that in the flaring vessel part of the water's weight is carried by the SLOPING WALLS, and in a narrowing one the walls carry an upward reaction.**

> **The total force on the base is pressure × base area in both cases, and the difference from the liquid's weight is accounted for by the walls — so the vertical equilibrium is satisfied and there is no paradox, only a misleading intuition.**

examTip.trick: **PASCAL'S LAW: pressure at a point in a fluid AT REST is equal in all directions.** The stem's "at rest" excludes Bernoulli and Newton's viscosity law immediately — both apply to fluid in motion.
examTip.trap: **Pascal's law is about a POINT, not about everywhere** — the pressure still VARIES with depth (p = γh). What is equal at all points of the same LEVEL in a connected fluid is the basis of every manometer.
examTip.mnemonic: **The proof works because the WEIGHT scales as size³ while the pressure forces scale as size²** — so the weight vanishes faster as the element shrinks to a point. And a hydraulic press multiplies FORCE by the area ratio and divides DISTANCE by it: the work is unchanged.

questions.stem: Flow in which the velocity at a given point does not change with TIME is described as:
questions.solution:
**STEADY flow.**

**The two distinctions that are constantly confused:**

| Term | Condition | With respect to |
|---|---|---|
| **STEADY flow** | **∂V/∂t = 0 — the velocity at a POINT does not change with TIME** ← | **TIME** |
| **UNSTEADY flow** | **∂V/∂t ≠ 0** | Time |
| **UNIFORM flow** | **∂V/∂s = 0 — the velocity does not change with POSITION along the flow** ← | **SPACE** |
| **NON-UNIFORM flow** | **∂V/∂s ≠ 0** | Space |

> **So STEADY concerns TIME and UNIFORM concerns SPACE, and the two are entirely independent — which gives four possible combinations, all of which occur:**

| Combination | Example |
|---|---|
| **STEADY UNIFORM** | **Flow at a constant rate through a long pipe of constant diameter; uniform flow in a long prismatic channel** ← |
| **STEADY NON-UNIFORM** | **Flow at a constant rate through a TAPERING pipe; gradually varied flow in a channel** ← |
| **UNSTEADY UNIFORM** | **A changing flow rate in a long constant-diameter pipe — rare and possible** |
| **UNSTEADY NON-UNIFORM** | **A flood wave passing down a natural river — the general and commonest real case** ← |

> **Option (a) UNIFORM is therefore the designed distractor: it is the spatial counterpart of the temporal condition the stem describes.**

> **The reliable way to keep them apart: STEADY relates to a CLOCK, UNIFORM relates to a RULER.**

**Why the distinction matters — what each assumption permits:**

| Assumption | What it allows |
|---|---|
| **STEADY flow** | **The time derivatives vanish, so the continuity and momentum equations become far simpler — ORDINARY rather than partial differential equations in many cases** ← |
| **UNIFORM flow** | **The spatial derivatives vanish; in open channel flow the depth is constant and the bed slope equals the friction slope** ← |
| **Both** | The simplest case, and the basis of Manning's and Chezy's equations |

> **The UNIFORM FLOW assumption is what makes Manning's equation possible, and that is worth stating explicitly:**

> **In uniform open channel flow, the depth does not change along the channel, which means the gravity component driving the flow exactly balances the friction resisting it.**

> **So the BED SLOPE equals the ENERGY (friction) SLOPE, and Manning's equation can use the bed slope — a measurable geometric quantity — in place of the friction slope, which is not directly measurable.**

> **That substitution is the whole basis of normal-depth computation, and it is valid ONLY for uniform flow.**

> **In GRADUALLY VARIED flow the two slopes differ, the depth changes along the channel, and a step-by-step computation of the water surface profile is required instead.**

**The other classifications of flow, since options (c) and (d) name two:**

| Classification | Categories | Criterion |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | **STEADY / unsteady** | ∂/∂t |
| **Space** | **UNIFORM / non-uniform** | ∂/∂s |
| **Viscous behaviour** | **LAMINAR / turbulent** | **Reynolds number — whether the flow is orderly or chaotic** ← |
| **Rotation of fluid elements** | **ROTATIONAL / irrotational** | **Whether fluid elements SPIN about their own axes (vorticity)** ← |
| **Compressibility** | Compressible / incompressible | Mach number |
| **Dimensionality** | One-, two-, three-dimensional | How many coordinates the velocity depends on |

> **The LAMINAR/TURBULENT and ROTATIONAL/IRROTATIONAL distinctions are worth a sentence each, since both are offered:**

> **LAMINAR flow moves in orderly parallel layers, with no mixing between them; TURBULENT flow is chaotic, with intense cross-mixing. The Reynolds number decides which occurs.**

> **IRROTATIONAL flow has zero VORTICITY — fluid elements translate and deform without spinning about their own axes.**

> **That sounds abstract and has a very practical consequence: an irrotational flow has a VELOCITY POTENTIAL, and the whole apparatus of potential flow theory — flow nets, complex variables, conformal mapping — applies to it.**

> **Which is exactly why seepage through soil and flow around a body outside its boundary layer can be analysed by flow nets: both are treated as irrotational.**

> **And it is why the boundary layer must be excluded: the shear within it makes the flow there strongly ROTATIONAL, so potential theory fails precisely at the surface where the drag is generated — which is D'Alembert's paradox again.**

**A caution about STEADY flow that is worth stating, since the assumption is made so freely:**

> **Turbulent flow is NEVER strictly steady: the velocity at a point fluctuates continuously and randomly, even when the discharge is constant.**

> **What is meant by "steady turbulent flow" is that the TIME-AVERAGED velocity does not change with time — the mean is steady while the instantaneous value is not.**

> **So the term is used in a MEAN sense throughout hydraulics, and the fluctuations are handled separately (as turbulent stresses, or as a source of the friction factor).**

> **That is not a quibble: the fluctuations are what cause the mixing, the sediment suspension and much of the erosion, so the unsteadiness that the "steady" assumption averages away is physically important.**

> **It is simply not important for computing the discharge — which is what the assumption is made for.**

examTip.trick: **STEADY relates to a CLOCK (∂V/∂t = 0); UNIFORM relates to a RULER (∂V/∂s = 0).** They are independent, so all four combinations occur.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) UNIFORM is the spatial counterpart** of the temporal condition described. A tapering pipe at constant discharge is STEADY and NON-UNIFORM.
examTip.mnemonic: **UNIFORM flow is what makes Manning's equation valid** — only then does the BED slope equal the FRICTION slope, letting a measurable geometry replace an unmeasurable energy gradient. Gradually varied flow needs a step-by-step profile computation instead.

questions.stem: The MOMENTUM equation is preferred to the energy equation for analysing a flow situation when:
options: The energy loss is unknown or difficult to evaluate
questions.solution:
**When the ENERGY LOSS is unknown or difficult to evaluate.**

**The essential difference between the two equations:**

| | **ENERGY equation (Bernoulli with losses)** | **MOMENTUM equation** |
|---|---|---|
| **Conserved quantity** | **ENERGY — a SCALAR** | **MOMENTUM — a VECTOR** ← |
| **Requires knowledge of** | **The ENERGY LOSS h_L between the two sections** ← | **Only the external FORCES on the control volume** ← |
| **Gives** | Pressures and velocities | **FORCES, and the relation between depths or velocities** |
| **Loss term** | **Must be known or estimated** | **NOT required — losses are internal to the control volume** ← |
| **Direction** | Not applicable (scalar) | **Must be applied in a chosen DIRECTION** |

> **The decisive point is in the fourth row: the momentum equation does not require the losses to be known, because whatever energy is dissipated inside the control volume does NOT affect the momentum balance.**

> **Momentum is conserved regardless of how much energy is turned into heat and turbulence — so the momentum equation can be applied across a violently dissipative region where the energy equation cannot.**

> **That is precisely why it is the tool for a hydraulic jump.**

**The classic applications, which all share that characteristic:**

| Application | Why momentum rather than energy |
|---|---|
| **HYDRAULIC JUMP** | **The energy loss is LARGE and UNKNOWN in advance — indeed the loss is what we want to FIND** ← |
| **FORCE ON A PIPE BEND** | **A force is wanted, and the energy equation gives no forces** ← |
| **Force on a sluice gate or a plate** | Same |
| **SUDDEN ENLARGEMENT in a pipe** | **The loss is unknown; the momentum equation DERIVES it (Borda-Carnot)** ← |
| **Force of a JET on a vane or a turbine bucket** | **The whole basis of impulse turbine analysis** ← |
| **Surge and bore propagation** | Dissipative, unsteady |
| **Force on a body in a flow (drag)** | A force is wanted |

> **The SUDDEN ENLARGEMENT case is the most illuminating because it shows the two equations being used TOGETHER:**

> **The MOMENTUM equation is applied to relate the pressures and velocities without knowing the loss.**

> **The ENERGY equation is then applied with an unknown loss term h_L.**

> **Eliminating the pressure difference between the two yields h_L = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g.**

> **So the loss is DERIVED rather than assumed — and that is only possible because the momentum equation supplied an independent relation that did not contain it.**

> **The same procedure gives the hydraulic jump's energy loss: momentum relates the two depths, and energy then computes the loss between them.**

> **That pairing — momentum to relate the states, energy to find the loss — is the standard method for any dissipative transition, and it is worth recognising as a pattern rather than as two separate derivations.**

**Why the other options are wrong, and instructively so:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **(a) Frictionless flow** | **If the flow were frictionless, the loss would be ZERO and KNOWN — so the ENERGY equation would work perfectly. This is the case where momentum is LEAST needed** ← |
| **(b) Uniform velocity distribution** | **A convenience for BOTH equations (it makes α and β equal 1). It does not favour either** |
| **(c) Steady flow** | **A simplification for both. The momentum equation has an unsteady form too** |

> **Option (a) inverts the reasoning exactly, which makes it the best distractor: frictionless flow is the ideal case for the ENERGY equation, not the reason to abandon it.**

**The requirements of the momentum equation, since it is not free of conditions:**

> **ΣF = ρ Q (V₂ − V₁), applied in a chosen direction, requires:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **A clearly defined CONTROL VOLUME** | **All the forces crossing its boundary must be identified** ← |
| **ALL external forces accounted for** | **Pressure forces on the ends, the weight component, the reaction from the boundary, and friction on the walls** ← |
| **A chosen DIRECTION for the equation** | It is a vector equation, applied one component at a time |
| **The MOMENTUM CORRECTION factor β where the velocity is non-uniform** | Usually taken as 1 for turbulent flow |
| **Steady flow, or the unsteady term retained** | — |

> **The commonest error is omitting a force — usually the PRESSURE FORCE on the control volume's end faces, or the WEIGHT component where the control volume is inclined.**

> **In the hydraulic jump analysis, for instance, the pressure forces on the two end sections are the hydrostatic thrusts γ y²/2 per unit width, and the friction on the short bed length is neglected — and that neglect is the analysis's only approximation.**

> **So the momentum equation trades the need to know the ENERGY LOSS for the need to know all the FORCES, and its accuracy rests on the completeness of that force accounting.**

**The SPECIFIC FORCE function, which is the momentum equation in open channel form:**

> **For a rectangular channel per unit width:**

> **F = y²/2 + q²/(g y)**

| Term | Represents |
|---|---|
| **y²/2** | **The hydrostatic PRESSURE force per unit width, divided by γ** |
| **q²/(g y)** | **The MOMENTUM flux per unit width, divided by γ** |

> **The momentum equation across a jump states that the SPECIFIC FORCE is EQUAL on both sides — and the two depths satisfying that equality are the SEQUENT depths.**

> **Plotting F against y gives a curve with a MINIMUM, and that minimum occurs at the CRITICAL DEPTH — the same depth at which the specific ENERGY is minimum.**

> **That coincidence is worth noting: the critical depth minimises BOTH the specific energy and the specific force, which is why it is such a special condition and why Fr = 1 characterises it from either point of view.**

> **And the two curves together explain the jump completely: the specific force is conserved (a vertical line on the F-y plot connects the two depths), while the specific energy is NOT (the two depths lie on different energy values, the difference being the loss).**

> **So a hydraulic jump is a transition at constant specific FORCE and reduced specific ENERGY — which is the whole phenomenon stated in one sentence.**

examTip.trick: **The momentum equation does not need the ENERGY LOSS — whatever is dissipated inside the control volume does not affect the momentum balance.** That is why it handles a hydraulic jump, where the loss is the unknown.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) inverts the reasoning: frictionless flow has ZERO KNOWN loss, so the ENERGY equation works perfectly there** — it is the case where momentum is least needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use them TOGETHER for a dissipative transition: MOMENTUM relates the two states, then ENERGY computes the loss.** That derivation gives both the sudden-enlargement loss and the hydraulic jump loss. And a jump conserves specific FORCE while reducing specific ENERGY.

questions.stem: For laminar flow in a circular pipe at a Reynolds number of 1600, the Darcy friction factor is:
questions.solution:
**0.040.**

**The relation for laminar pipe flow:**

> **f = 64 / Re**

**The computation:**

> **f = 64/1600 = 0.040** ✓

> **Option (d) 0.064 is 64/1000 — the correct formula with a mis-read Reynolds number.**

> **Option (b) 0.016 is 16/1000, or 64/4000 — the value at the turbulent transition.**

> **Option (c) 0.025 is a typical TURBULENT friction factor for a commercial pipe, offered here where the flow is laminar — which is the conceptual distractor.**

**Confirming that the flow IS laminar — the check that must be made first:**

> **Re = 1600 is below 2000, so the flow is LAMINAR and the relation f = 64/Re applies.** ✓

| Reynolds number | Regime | Friction factor |
|---|---|---|
| **Below 2000** | **LAMINAR** | **f = 64/Re — EXACT, and independent of roughness** ← |
| **2000-4000** | **TRANSITIONAL** | **Unpredictable; avoided in design** |
| **Above 4000** | **TURBULENT** | **From Colebrook-White or the Moody diagram; depends on Re AND roughness** |

> **Had the Reynolds number been above 4000, the formula would not apply at all — so establishing the regime is the first step, not an afterthought.**

**Why the laminar relation is EXACT while the turbulent ones are empirical:**

> **f = 64/Re is not a correlation but an exact theoretical result, derived from the HAGEN-POISEUILLE solution:**

> **The laminar velocity profile in a circular pipe can be solved exactly from the Navier-Stokes equations, because the flow is orderly and the equations become tractable.**

> **That solution gives:  h_f = 32 μ L V/(ρ g D²)**

> **Equating it to the Darcy-Weisbach form h_f = f L V²/(2gD) and solving for f:**

> **f L V²/(2gD) = 32 μ L V/(ρ g D²)**

> **f = 64 μ/(ρ V D) = 64/Re** ✓

> **So the 64 is a consequence of the parabolic velocity profile and nothing else — which is why it is exact, why it contains no roughness term, and why it can be trusted absolutely within the laminar range.**

> **Turbulent flow admits no such solution, which is why its friction factor rests on the Colebrook-White correlation and the Moody diagram.**

**The ROUGHNESS INDEPENDENCE, which is the striking feature:**

> **f = 64/Re contains NO roughness term at all: a laminar flow's friction is the same in a smooth glass tube and a rough cast iron one of the same diameter.**

> **The reason is physical: in laminar flow the fluid moves in orderly layers, and the layer at the wall is stationary.**

> **The roughness projections lie WITHIN that slow-moving layer and never disturb the flow — so the fluid never "feels" them.**

> **In TURBULENT flow the roughness projections penetrate the thin viscous sublayer and shed eddies into the turbulent core, which is exactly what generates the additional friction.**

> **That contrast explains the whole structure of the Moody diagram:**

| Region of the Moody diagram | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **LAMINAR (Re < 2000)** | **A single straight line f = 64/Re; roughness curves CONVERGE onto it** ← |
| **Turbulent, SMOOTH-pipe region** | **The roughness is submerged in the sublayer; f depends on Re alone** |
| **Turbulent TRANSITION region** | **f depends on BOTH Re and ε/D — the curved part of the diagram** |
| **FULLY ROUGH turbulent region** | **f depends on ε/D ALONE — the horizontal lines to the right** ← |

> **The FULLY ROUGH region's horizontal lines mean that beyond a certain Reynolds number the friction factor stops changing with the flow rate — so h_f becomes exactly proportional to V², which is what the empirical formulae (Hazen-Williams, Manning) assume.**

> **That is why those formulae work well for water mains at ordinary velocities and poorly for laminar or transitional flow: they are valid in the region where f is constant.**

**Why LAMINAR pipe flow is almost never encountered with water — the practical context:**

> **For water at 20 °C (ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s) in a 100 mm pipe, laminar flow requires:**

> **V < 2000 × 10⁻⁶/0.1 = 0.02 m/s**

> **Two centimetres per second — a barely perceptible trickle, and a discharge of only 0.16 litres per second in a 100 mm pipe.**

> **So laminar flow in a water pipe of any engineering size is essentially unattainable, and every water supply, drainage and irrigation calculation deals with turbulent flow.**

> **Where laminar flow DOES occur:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **SEEPAGE through soil** | **The basis of Darcy's law — and the reason it is LINEAR in velocity** ← |
| **Flow of VISCOUS liquids — oils, grouts, bitumen, sludge** | High viscosity gives a low Reynolds number |
| **Flow in very fine tubes and capillaries** | Small D |
| **Lubrication films** | Very small dimensions |
| **Flow in a drip irrigation emitter** | Small passages, low velocity |

> **The SEEPAGE case is the one that matters most in civil engineering, and the connection is worth making explicitly:**

> **Because seepage is laminar, its head loss is proportional to the FIRST power of the velocity — which is Darcy's law v = ki.**

> **Because pipe flow is turbulent, its head loss is proportional to V².**

> **So the linear relation that makes the whole mathematics of groundwater flow tractable — Laplace's equation, flow nets, superposition — exists ONLY because the Reynolds number in soil pores is very small.**

> **And in coarse rockfill, where it is not small, Darcy's law fails and the analysis becomes far harder — which is the same point arrived at from the other direction.**

examTip.trick: **f = 64/Re = 64/1600 = 0.040** — but CHECK the regime first: Re = 1600 is below 2000, so the flow is laminar and the relation applies.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 0.025 is a typical TURBULENT friction factor** offered where the flow is laminar. Above Re = 4000 the formula does not apply at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **f = 64/Re is EXACT (from the Hagen-Poiseuille parabolic profile) and contains NO roughness** — the projections lie inside the stationary wall layer and are never felt. In water, laminar flow needs V < 0.02 m/s in a 100 mm pipe, so it is essentially unattainable — except in SEEPAGE, which is why Darcy's law is linear.

questions.stem: In the Hardy Cross method of pipe network analysis, the flow correction ΔQ computed for a loop is applied:
options: Only to the pipe carrying the largest head loss
Only to the pipes in which the assumed flow is positive
To every pipe in the loop, in the same rotational sense
Only to the pipe common to two adjacent loops
questions.solution:
**To EVERY pipe in the loop, in the SAME ROTATIONAL SENSE.**

**Why it must be applied to every pipe — the reason is continuity:**

> **The Hardy Cross method begins with an assumed flow distribution that SATISFIES CONTINUITY at every junction: inflow equals outflow at each node.**

> **The iteration must PRESERVE that continuity, or the solution would drift away from a physically possible flow.**

> **Applying the same ΔQ to every pipe in the loop, in a consistent rotational sense, does exactly that:**

| At any junction on the loop | Effect of the correction |
|---|---|
| **One loop pipe brings ΔQ IN** | **+ΔQ** |
| **The next loop pipe carries ΔQ OUT** | **−ΔQ** |
| **NET change at the junction** | **ZERO — continuity is preserved** ← |

> **So the correction circulates around the loop and cancels at every node, which is why it can be applied without recomputing the junction balances.**

> **That is the method's central device: the iteration adjusts only the LOOP condition (zero head loss round the loop) while the JUNCTION condition (continuity) remains satisfied automatically.**

> **Applying the correction to only some pipes — options (a), (b) and (d) — would violate continuity at the junctions where the corrected and uncorrected pipes meet, and the iteration would not converge to a valid solution.**

**The two conditions the method enforces — Kirchhoff's laws for water:**

| Condition | Statement | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTINUITY at each junction** | **Σ Q at a node = 0** | **The INITIAL assumption, and preserved by the loop-wide correction** ← |
| **ZERO head loss round each closed loop** | **Σ h_f = 0** | **The ITERATION — this is what ΔQ corrects** ← |

> **The second condition is the physical statement that the head at any point is UNIQUE: travelling round a closed loop and returning to the start, the net change in head must be zero.**

> **That is precisely Kirchhoff's voltage law, and the first condition is Kirchhoff's current law — so a pipe network is an electrical circuit with h_f in place of voltage and Q in place of current.**

> **The only difference is that the resistance is NON-LINEAR: h_f = r Qⁿ with n ≈ 2, whereas an electrical resistance is linear.**

> **That non-linearity is why the solution must be ITERATIVE rather than obtained by solving simultaneous equations directly, and it is the whole reason the Hardy Cross method exists.**

**The correction formula and where it comes from:**

> **ΔQ = − Σ h_f / (n Σ |h_f / Q|)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Σ h_f** | **The ALGEBRAIC sum of the head losses round the loop — clockwise positive, anticlockwise negative** ← |
| **n** | **The exponent in h_f = r Qⁿ — 2 for Darcy-Weisbach, 1.85 for Hazen-Williams** ← |
| **Σ|h_f/Q|** | **The sum of the ABSOLUTE values of h_f/Q for every pipe in the loop** ← |

> **The formula is a NEWTON-RAPHSON step: it is the loop imbalance divided by the derivative of that imbalance with respect to Q.**

> **Since d(h_f)/dQ = n r Q^{n−1} = n h_f/Q, the denominator is the sum of those derivatives — and the correction is the classic "function divided by its derivative".**

> **Recognising it as Newton-Raphson explains two things: why it converges quadratically once close to the solution, and why the ABSOLUTE values are used in the denominator (the derivatives all have the same sign, since they represent resistance) while the numerator is ALGEBRAIC (the imbalance can be either way).**

> **Mixing those up — taking the numerator absolute, or the denominator algebraic — is the commonest error in the method and it prevents convergence.**

**The procedure in full:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Assume a flow distribution SATISFYING CONTINUITY at every junction** ← |
| **2** | **Choose a sign convention — clockwise positive — and identify the loops** |
| **3** | **Compute h_f for each pipe, with its sign** |
| **4** | **Compute Σh_f and Σ|h_f/Q| for each loop, and hence ΔQ** |
| **5** | **Apply ΔQ to EVERY pipe in the loop, in the same rotational sense** ← |
| **6** | **For a pipe COMMON to two loops, apply BOTH corrections** ← |
| **7** | **Repeat until every loop's Σh_f is acceptably small** |

> **Step 6 is where option (d) has its grain of truth: a pipe shared between two loops receives the correction from EACH loop, so it gets two corrections rather than one.**

> **That is not the same as the correction being applied ONLY to the common pipe, which is what the option states — but it is why the option is plausible.**

> **And the signs must be handled carefully there: a pipe that is clockwise in one loop is anticlockwise in the adjacent one, so the two corrections may partly cancel.**

**And the method's place today, stated honestly:**

> **The Hardy Cross method was devised in 1936 for hand computation, and it is no longer how networks are analysed in practice: EPANET and similar programs solve the whole system simultaneously by a global gradient method, which converges faster and handles pumps, valves, tanks and water quality as well.**

> **The method remains worth knowing for two reasons:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **It makes plain WHAT the software is solving** | **The two conditions, and the non-linearity that requires iteration** ← |
| **A hand check of ONE loop is the best way to detect a badly built model** | **A model with a wrong pipe length or a missing connection will show as a loop that does not balance** ← |

> **The second reason is the practical one: a network model's output is plausible-looking whatever is wrong with its input, and an independent hand check of a single loop's head balance catches gross errors that inspection of the input would not.**

> **That is a general habit worth having with any numerical model — verify one part by hand, because the software will converge just as confidently on a wrong problem as on a right one.**

examTip.trick: **Applying the SAME ΔQ to every pipe in the loop preserves CONTINUITY** — it brings ΔQ into each junction and takes it out again, so the node balance is untouched. The iteration then corrects only the loop condition.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) has a grain of truth: a pipe COMMON to two loops receives BOTH corrections** — with careful attention to sign, since it is clockwise in one loop and anticlockwise in the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **The numerator Σh_f is ALGEBRAIC (the imbalance can go either way); the denominator Σ|h_f/Q| is ABSOLUTE (all resistances).** Mixing them up prevents convergence. It is a Newton-Raphson step — function over derivative.

questions.stem: For the most economical (best hydraulic) trapezoidal channel section:
options: The hydraulic radius equals the depth of flow
The hydraulic radius equals half the depth of flow
The bed width equals the depth of flow
The side slope must be 1 vertical to 1 horizontal
questions.solution:
**The HYDRAULIC RADIUS equals HALF the depth of flow: R = y/2.**

**What "most economical" means:**

> **A channel is MOST ECONOMICAL (or of BEST HYDRAULIC SECTION) when it carries the MAXIMUM DISCHARGE for a given cross-sectional AREA — or equivalently, requires the MINIMUM AREA for a given discharge.**

> **From Manning's equation  Q = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}, with A, n and S fixed, Q is maximised when R is maximised.**

> **And R = A/P, so with A fixed, R is maximised when the WETTED PERIMETER P is MINIMISED.**

> **So the condition is: MINIMUM WETTED PERIMETER for the given area — which also minimises the excavation, the lining and the friction, all at once.**

**The conditions for the best trapezoidal section:**

| Condition | Statement |
|---|---|
| **R = y/2** | **The hydraulic radius is HALF the depth** ← |
| **A semicircle centred at the water surface, of radius y, is TANGENT to the bed and both sides** | **The geometric statement of the same thing** ← |
| **The sloping side length equals HALF the top width** | **For the best trapezoid** |
| **For the OPTIMUM side slope, the section is HALF A REGULAR HEXAGON** | **Side slope 1 vertical to 1/√3 horizontal, that is 60° to the horizontal** ← |

> **Option (a) R = y is the value for a WIDE RECTANGULAR channel (where R approaches y as the width grows), which makes it a plausible near-miss.**

> **Option (c) B = y is a condition sometimes met but not the general one, and option (d) prescribes a side slope that the soil rather than hydraulics determines.**

**The corresponding result for a RECTANGULAR channel, since it is the simpler case:**

> **For the best rectangular section:  B = 2y — the width is TWICE the depth.**

> **And then R = A/P = (2y × y)/(2y + 2y) = 2y²/4y = y/2** ✓

> **So the SAME condition R = y/2 holds for the best rectangular section as for the best trapezoidal one — which is a satisfying generality and worth knowing.**

> **In fact R = y/2 characterises the best section for a rectangle, a trapezoid and a triangle alike, and the reason is the semicircle condition: in every case the most efficient section is the one that best approximates a semicircle.**

**Why a SEMICIRCLE is the ideal, and why it is rarely used:**

> **Of all shapes, the SEMICIRCLE has the minimum wetted perimeter for a given area — so it is the theoretically most efficient channel section of all.**

| Section | Wetted perimeter for A = 10 m² |
|---|---|
| **SEMICIRCLE** | **7.93 m — the minimum possible** ← |
| **Best trapezoid (half hexagon)** | **8.06 m** |
| **Best rectangle** | **8.94 m** |
| **A wide shallow rectangle, B = 10y** | **12.6 m** |

> **So the best trapezoid is within 2 per cent of the theoretical ideal, and the best rectangle within 13 per cent — while a badly proportioned section is far worse.**

> **The semicircle is nevertheless rarely built, for entirely practical reasons:**

| Objection to a semicircular channel | Note |
|---|---|
| **Difficult and expensive to EXCAVATE and to FORM** | **A curved invert in earth or rock is far harder than plane surfaces** ← |
| **The sides are VERTICAL at the water surface, so an earth channel would collapse** | **Only a lined or pipe channel can hold that shape** ← |
| **Precast forms are needed for the lining** | Cost |
| **A trapezoid is easily cut by machine** | Practicality |

> **So the TRAPEZOID is the practical answer: it captures 98 per cent of the semicircle's efficiency using plane surfaces that a machine can cut and a lining can follow.**

> **And semicircular sections ARE used where the practical objections do not apply: in precast concrete channels, in sewers (where the pipe is circular anyway), and in flumes.**

**Why the theoretical optimum is often NOT adopted, which is the honest qualification:**

| Constraint that overrides the hydraulic optimum | Note |
|---|---|
| **SIDE SLOPE stability — the soil dictates it** | **The optimum 60° side slope is far too steep for most soils; a stable slope may be 1:1.5 or 1:2** ← |
| **The best section is DEEP and NARROW** | **Deep excavation is expensive, and a high water table or rock may forbid it** ← |
| **Freeboard and bank width requirements** | Add to the excavation |
| **A LINED channel's velocity limits** | May require a different area |
| **Silting and scouring (regime) requirements in an unlined channel** | **Kennedy and Lacey may fix the section instead** ← |
| **Land acquisition — a wide shallow channel takes more land** | Pulls the other way |

> **The SIDE SLOPE constraint is decisive in practice: the hydraulically optimal side slope of 1 vertical to 0.577 horizontal (60°) is stable only in rock or in a lined channel.**

> **An earth channel in ordinary soil needs 1:1.5 or flatter, so the "best" section is computed SUBJECT TO that imposed side slope rather than freely.**

> **That constrained optimum still gives R = y/2 and still minimises the perimeter for the given slope — so the condition remains useful, applied within the constraint.**

> **And the REGIME requirement is the more fundamental override for an unlined alluvial channel: Kennedy's or Lacey's theory fixes the section from the silt-carrying requirement, and the hydraulically most efficient section is simply irrelevant there.**

> **So the "most economical section" is the right criterion for a LINED channel of given capacity, and it is not the criterion for an unlined alluvial canal — which is a distinction worth being clear about, since the two topics sit side by side in the syllabus and answer different questions.**

examTip.trick: **R = y/2 for the best section** — and the same condition holds for the best RECTANGLE (B = 2y), trapezoid and triangle, because each is the closest approach to a SEMICIRCLE.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) R = y is the value for a WIDE rectangular channel**, where R approaches the depth. And the optimum side slope (60°, half a hexagon) is far too steep for most soils.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Most economical" means MINIMUM WETTED PERIMETER for the area** — which minimises excavation, lining and friction together. But for an UNLINED alluvial canal the REGIME theories fix the section instead, and hydraulic efficiency is irrelevant there.

questions.stem: The combined return of water to the atmosphere by evaporation from the soil and transpiration from plants is called:
questions.solution:
**EVAPOTRANSPIRATION.**

**The components of the hydrologic cycle, and what each term means:**

| Process | Definition |
|---|---|
| **PRECIPITATION** | Water reaching the ground as rain, snow, hail or dew |
| **INTERCEPTION** | **Precipitation caught by VEGETATION and building surfaces and evaporated before ever reaching the ground** ← |
| **INFILTRATION** | **Water entering the soil SURFACE from above** ← |
| **PERCOLATION** | **Movement of water DOWNWARD THROUGH the soil, below the root zone, toward the water table** ← |
| **EVAPORATION** | **Water changing to vapour from an open water or soil surface** |
| **TRANSPIRATION** | **Water taken up by plant roots and released as vapour through the leaves** |
| **EVAPOTRANSPIRATION (ET)** | **EVAPORATION plus TRANSPIRATION, combined** ← |
| **RUNOFF** | Water flowing over the surface to a channel |
| **Depression storage** | Water held in surface hollows |
| **Detention storage** | Water in transit over the surface |

> **Each option offered is a genuine and distinct process, so the option set is a test of the terminology of the hydrologic cycle.**

> **The INFILTRATION against PERCOLATION distinction in the middle rows is worth fixing, since the two are often used loosely as synonyms:**

> **INFILTRATION is water CROSSING THE SURFACE — entering the soil.**

> **PERCOLATION is water MOVING DOWNWARD WITHIN the soil, past the root zone.**

> **So infiltration is a surface process governing how much rainfall enters the ground rather than running off, and percolation is a subsurface process governing how much of that reaches the water table as recharge.**

> **Water can infiltrate and NOT percolate — being held in the root zone and later transpired — which is exactly what an irrigation engineer wants.**

**Why EVAPORATION and TRANSPIRATION are combined into one term:**

> **They are combined for a practical reason: THEY CANNOT BE SEPARATED IN THE FIELD.**

> **A cropped field loses water both from its soil surface and through its plants, simultaneously and from the same water supply — and no measurement distinguishes them.**

> **What can be measured is the TOTAL loss, by a lysimeter or by a water balance, and that total is the evapotranspiration.**

> **And it is the total that matters for design: the irrigation requirement depends on the water leaving the field, not on the route it takes.**

> **So the combined term is not a convenience but a recognition that the separable quantity is not the measurable one.**

**POTENTIAL and ACTUAL evapotranspiration — the distinction that matters:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **POTENTIAL evapotranspiration (PET)** | **The ET that WOULD occur from a well-watered reference crop, limited only by the ENERGY and the atmospheric demand** ← |
| **ACTUAL evapotranspiration (AET)** | **The ET that DOES occur, which is less where the soil moisture is insufficient** ← |
| **Reference crop ET (ET₀)** | PET for a standard short grass reference |
| **CROP evapotranspiration (ET_c)** | **ET₀ × the CROP COEFFICIENT K_c for the crop and its growth stage** ← |

> **The distinction is the whole basis of irrigation scheduling:**

> **PET is set by the WEATHER — radiation, temperature, humidity, wind. It is what the atmosphere DEMANDS.**

> **AET is limited by the SOIL MOISTURE available. When the soil dries, the plant cannot meet the demand and AET falls below PET.**

| Condition | AET relative to PET |
|---|---|
| **Soil at or near FIELD CAPACITY** | **AET = PET — the plant transpires freely** ← |
| **Soil moisture depleted** | **AET < PET — the plant closes its stomata and suffers stress** ← |
| **Soil at the WILTING POINT** | **AET → 0; the crop dies** |

> **So the purpose of irrigation is to keep the soil moisture high enough that AET can equal PET — because whenever AET falls below PET the crop is under stress and the yield is reduced.**

> **And the irrigation SCHEDULE follows directly: water is applied when the soil moisture has fallen to a stated fraction of the available water, before the stress begins.**

> **Typically irrigation is applied when 50 per cent of the AVAILABLE water (the water between field capacity and wilting point) has been depleted — the exact figure depending on the crop's sensitivity and the growth stage.**

**The CROP COEFFICIENT, since it converts a weather quantity into a crop requirement:**

> **ET_c = K_c × ET₀**

| Growth stage | Typical K_c |
|---|---|
| **Initial (after sowing, little canopy)** | **0.3 to 0.5 — mostly soil evaporation** ← |
| **Crop development** | Rising |
| **MID-SEASON (full canopy)** | **1.0 to 1.2 — the peak demand** ← |
| **Late season (ripening)** | **Falling to 0.3 to 0.6** |

> **So the same weather produces quite different crop water requirements at different stages, and the peak demand occurs at full canopy — which is why the irrigation schedule is not uniform through the season.**

> **And the low initial K_c explains why the KOR watering, though critical for the crop's survival, is not the season's largest water requirement: the canopy is small and most of the loss is from the soil.**

> **The kor watering is critical because of TIMING and the crop's vulnerability, not because of quantity — which is a distinction worth having, since the canal is sized on the kor and the seasonal total is governed by the mid-season demand.**

**The methods of estimating ET, and the honest position on them:**

| Method | Data required | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **LYSIMETER — direct measurement** | An instrumented tank of soil and crop | **The reference against which all others are calibrated; laborious** ← |
| **PENMAN-MONTEITH (FAO 56)** | **Radiation, temperature, humidity, wind** | **The international standard — and it needs data most Nepali stations do not have** ← |
| **BLANEY-CRIDDLE** | **Temperature and daylight hours only** | **Simple; widely used in India and Nepal for exactly that reason** ← |
| **Pan evaporation × a pan coefficient** | A Class A pan record | Practical where a pan exists |
| **Hargreaves, Thornthwaite** | Temperature | Approximations |

> **The choice among them is dictated by DATA AVAILABILITY rather than by preference, and that is worth stating plainly: Penman-Monteith is the best method and requires measurements that are not made at most stations in Nepal.**

> **So Blaney-Criddle or a pan-based estimate is used, with the understanding that it is an approximation — and the resulting uncertainty is one reason irrigation systems carry the generous efficiencies and factors discussed earlier.**

> **Improving the estimate requires improving the METEOROLOGICAL NETWORK rather than the formula, which is a matter of national infrastructure rather than of engineering technique.**

examTip.trick: **EVAPOTRANSPIRATION = evaporation (from soil and water) + transpiration (through plants).** They are combined because they cannot be separated in the field — only the total is measurable.
examTip.trap: **INFILTRATION is water CROSSING the surface; PERCOLATION is water moving DOWN within the soil past the root zone.** Water can infiltrate and not percolate — held in the root zone, which is what irrigation wants.
examTip.mnemonic: **PET is what the WEATHER demands; AET is what the SOIL MOISTURE allows.** Irrigation exists to keep AET equal to PET, since any shortfall is crop stress. And ET_c = K_c × ET₀ — K_c is only 0.3-0.5 early and 1.0-1.2 at full canopy.

questions.stem: At a POINT OF CONTRAFLEXURE in a beam:
options: The bending moment is zero and changes sign
The slope of the beam is zero
questions.solution:
**The BENDING MOMENT is ZERO and CHANGES SIGN.**

**The definition, precisely:**

> **A POINT OF CONTRAFLEXURE (point of inflexion) is a section at which the bending moment passes through ZERO while REVERSING its sign — from sagging to hogging, or the reverse.**

> **Both parts of the definition are necessary:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **M = 0** | **Necessary — but not sufficient on its own** ← |
| **M CHANGES SIGN there** | **The distinguishing feature** ← |

> **A moment can be zero WITHOUT a contraflexure point: at the free end of a cantilever and at the simple supports of a simply supported beam, M = 0 and does NOT change sign.**

> **So the ends of a simply supported beam are not points of contraflexure, though the moment is zero there — which is worth being clear about.**

**Why the other options are wrong, and each is instructive:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| **(a) Shear force zero** | **The point of MAXIMUM BENDING MOMENT, since dM/dx = V** ← |
| **(b) Bending moment zero, changing sign** | ✓ |
| **(c) Maximum deflection** | **Where the SLOPE is zero, since deflection is a maximum when dy/dx = 0** |
| **(d) Slope zero** | **The point of maximum DEFLECTION, and at a fixed support** |

> **Option (a) is the designed distractor because it is the OPPOSITE extreme: where the shear is zero the moment is at its MAXIMUM, and where the moment is zero the shear is generally at its largest.**

> **So the two conditions identify opposite features of the same diagrams, and confusing them inverts the answer.**

**Why contraflexure matters — the DETAILING consequence:**

> **The bending moment's SIGN determines WHICH FACE of a member is in TENSION, and reinforcement must be placed on the tension face:**

| Moment | Tension face | Reinforcement |
|---|---|---|
| **SAGGING (positive)** | **BOTTOM** | **Main steel at the BOTTOM** |
| **HOGGING (negative)** | **TOP** | **Main steel at the TOP** ← |

> **So at a point of contraflexure the reinforcement must CHANGE FROM ONE FACE TO THE OTHER — and locating those points is what determines where top steel can be curtailed and where bottom steel must begin.**

> **That is the practical purpose of finding them, and it is why a continuous beam's reinforcement drawing shows bars stopping and starting at particular distances from the supports.**

> **And it is why the curtailment rule matters: a bar may not simply stop at the theoretical contraflexure point but must extend a further DEVELOPMENT LENGTH (or 12φ) beyond it, since at that point it is still carrying force.**

**Where contraflexure points occur — the cases to recognise:**

| Beam | Points of contraflexure |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLY SUPPORTED, downward load only** | **NONE — the moment is sagging throughout** ← |
| **CANTILEVER, downward load only** | **NONE — hogging throughout** ← |
| **OVERHANGING beam** | **One or two, between each support and the overhang** ← |
| **FIXED at both ends, central point load** | **TWO, at L/4 from each end** ← |
| **Fixed both ends, UDL** | **Two, at 0.211 L from each end** |
| **PROPPED CANTILEVER, UDL** | **ONE, at L/4 from the fixed end** |
| **CONTINUOUS beam** | **One or two in each span, near the supports** ← |
| **A COLUMN in a sway frame** | **One, near mid-height — which is why L_e = 0.5L for a fixed-fixed column** ← |

> **The FIRST TWO rows are worth stating because they answer a common misconception: a simply supported beam under downward load has NO point of contraflexure, so its reinforcement stays at the bottom throughout.**

> **Contraflexure requires the moment to reverse, which requires either a HOGGING region — from continuity, fixity or an overhang — or an upward load.**

> **So the presence of contraflexure points is a signature of RESTRAINT or CONTINUITY, and a determinate simply supported span has none.**

**The COLUMN case in the last row, which connects two topics:**

> **The EFFECTIVE LENGTH of a column is defined as the distance between its POINTS OF CONTRAFLEXURE in the buckled shape — that is, between the points of zero moment.**

| End condition | Buckled shape | Effective length |
|---|---|---|
| **Hinged-hinged** | **A half sine wave; zero moment AT the ends** | **L** |
| **Fixed-fixed** | **Contraflexure points at the QUARTER POINTS** | **0.5 L** ← |
| **Fixed-hinged** | **One contraflexure point at 0.707 L from the fixed end** | **0.707 L** |
| **Fixed-free** | **The contraflexure point is a mirror-image L beyond the free end** | **2 L** |

> **So the effective length table met in the column topic is entirely a statement about contraflexure points — and sketching the buckled shape and marking the zero-moment points recovers every value.**

> **That is why the geometric definition is worth holding rather than the four numbers: it generates them, and it applies to intermediate cases the table does not list.**

**How to LOCATE a contraflexure point, since the calculation is often required:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Write the bending moment expression M(x) for the relevant portion of the beam** |
| **2** | **SET M(x) = 0** |
| **3** | **Solve for x** |
| **4** | **CHECK that the sign actually reverses there, and that x lies within the portion for which the expression is valid** ← |

> **Step 4 is where errors occur: solving M(x) = 0 may give a root OUTSIDE the range for which that expression applies, which is not a contraflexure point at all.**

> **A worked example — an overhanging beam of span 6 m with a 2 m overhang carrying 10 kN/m throughout:**

> **Total load on the overhang = 20 kN at 1 m from the support, so its moment about the support is 20 kNm hogging.**

> **Reactions: taking moments, R_A = (10 × 8 × 4 − ... ) — the arithmetic depends on the arrangement, and the method is what matters: write M(x) between the supports, set it to zero, and solve the resulting quadratic.**

> **For a UDL the expression is quadratic, so there are TWO roots — and typically one lies within the span (a genuine contraflexure point) and one outside it (to be discarded).**

> **Which is exactly why step 4 exists, and why an answer must be checked against the geometry rather than taken from the algebra.**

examTip.trick: **M = 0 AND the sign REVERSES — both parts are needed.** The ends of a simply supported beam have M = 0 and no sign change, so they are not contraflexure points.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) describes the OPPOSITE extreme** — where the SHEAR is zero the MOMENT is maximum (dM/dx = V). The two conditions identify opposite features of the same diagrams.
examTip.mnemonic: **Contraflexure is where the reinforcement must move from one FACE to the other** — which is what fixes curtailment. And a column's EFFECTIVE LENGTH is just the distance between its contraflexure points, which generates the whole 0.5L / L / 2L table from a sketch.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span L carries a uniformly distributed load w over its entire span. The shear force at MIDSPAN is:
questions.solution:
**ZERO.**

**The reasoning, which follows from symmetry alone:**

> **The reaction at each support is wL/2.**

> **The shear force at a distance x from the left support is:**

> **V(x) = wL/2 − w x**

> **At midspan, x = L/2:**

> **V = wL/2 − w(L/2) = 0** ✓

> **So the load carried by the left half of the beam exactly equals the left reaction, and no shear is transmitted across the midspan section.**

> **By symmetry it could not be otherwise: a symmetric beam under symmetric load has zero shear at its centre, since a non-zero shear would have to act in opposite senses on the two identical halves.**

**Why the distractors are placed as they are:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **(a) wL/2** | **The MAXIMUM shear force, at the SUPPORTS** ← |
| **(b) wL/4** | **The shear at the QUARTER POINT (x = L/4)** |
| **(c) wL/8** | **wL²/8 is the maximum MOMENT — the coefficient with the wrong dimensions offered as a shear** ← |
| **(d) Zero** | ✓ |

> **Option (c) is the instructive one: wL²/8 is the famous maximum bending moment for this beam, and "wL/8" is that coefficient with an L dropped — so the option is dimensionally a shear and numerically a corrupted moment.**

> **A dimensional check does not catch it (wL/8 is a force), but noticing that 8 belongs to the MOMENT and 2 to the SHEAR does.**

**The complete shear and moment picture for this beam:**

| Position x | Shear force V | Bending moment M |
|---|---|---|
| **0 (left support)** | **+wL/2 — MAXIMUM** ← | **0** |
| **L/4** | **+wL/4** | **3wL²/32** |
| **L/2 (midspan)** | **ZERO** ← | **wL²/8 — MAXIMUM** ← |
| **3L/4** | **−wL/4** | **3wL²/32** |
| **L (right support)** | **−wL/2** | **0** |

> **The pattern is the essential one: WHERE THE SHEAR IS ZERO THE MOMENT IS MAXIMUM, and where the moment is zero the shear is maximum.**

> **That is not a coincidence but a direct consequence of  dM/dx = V:**

> **The moment is stationary — at a maximum or minimum — exactly where its derivative, the shear, vanishes.**

> **So the two diagrams are related as a function and its derivative, and every feature of one corresponds to a feature of the other:**

| Feature of the SHEAR diagram | Corresponding feature of the MOMENT diagram |
|---|---|
| **Crosses ZERO** | **MAXIMUM or minimum** ← |
| **Is CONSTANT** | Moment varies LINEARLY |
| **Varies LINEARLY (under a UDL)** | Moment is PARABOLIC |
| **Has a STEP (at a point load)** | Moment has a KINK (change of slope) |
| **The AREA under it between two points** | **The CHANGE in moment between those points** ← |
| **Is maximum** | The moment's slope is steepest |

> **The AREA relation in the fifth row is the most useful of these for construction, and it works here:**

> **Area of the shear diagram from 0 to L/2 = ½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8**

> **which IS the midspan moment** ✓

> **So the maximum moment can be obtained by computing the AREA of a triangle, with no moment equation at all — and the check that the moment returns to zero at the far support is that the total area under the shear diagram is zero (the positive and negative triangles cancel).**

**Where the shear diagram's zero is NOT at midspan — the general case:**

> **The zero-shear point coincides with midspan only for a SYMMETRIC load. For any unsymmetrical loading it lies elsewhere, and finding it is the first step in locating the maximum moment:**

| Loading on a simply supported span | Zero shear, and hence maximum moment, at |
|---|---|
| **UDL over the whole span** | **MIDSPAN** ← |
| **UDL over the LEFT HALF only** | **x = 3L/8 from the left — not midspan** ← |
| **A single point load at distance a** | **AT the load** |
| **Two unequal point loads** | At one of them — whichever the shear crosses zero under |
| **A triangular load, maximum at the right** | At x = 0.577 L from the left |

> **The SECOND row is worth noting because it was computed earlier for a specific beam: a UDL over the left half gives reactions in the ratio 3:1, and the shear crosses zero at 3L/8 rather than at L/2.**

> **So the habit to form is: FIND WHERE THE SHEAR CROSSES ZERO, and do not assume midspan.**

> **For a symmetric case the two coincide and the assumption costs nothing; for an unsymmetrical one it gives the wrong section and an understated moment.**

**And a note on why the shear at midspan being zero does NOT mean the section is unimportant:**

> **The midspan section carries the MAXIMUM MOMENT and NO SHEAR — so it is designed entirely for flexure.**

> **The support sections carry the MAXIMUM SHEAR and NO MOMENT — so they are designed entirely for shear.**

> **That separation is convenient and is why a beam's flexural reinforcement is greatest at midspan while its shear reinforcement (stirrups) is closest-spaced at the supports.**

> **A reinforcement drawing showing the reverse — heavy stirrups at midspan and light ones at the supports — is a signature of a fundamental misunderstanding, and it does occur.**

examTip.trick: **V(x) = wL/2 − wx, which is ZERO at x = L/2.** By symmetry it must be: a non-zero shear would act in opposite senses on two identical halves.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) wL/8 is the moment coefficient with an L dropped** — the 8 belongs to the MOMENT (wL²/8) and the 2 to the SHEAR (wL/2). A dimensional check will not catch it; knowing which coefficient goes with which will.
examTip.mnemonic: **Where the SHEAR is zero the MOMENT is maximum, because dM/dx = V.** And the AREA under the shear diagram is the CHANGE in moment — here ½ × L/2 × wL/2 = wL²/8 directly. But do not assume midspan: a half-span UDL puts it at 3L/8.

questions.stem: The strain energy stored per unit volume of a material when it is stressed up to the ELASTIC LIMIT is called the:
questions.solution:
**The MODULUS OF RESILIENCE.**

**The related terms, distinguished precisely:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **STRAIN ENERGY (U)** | **The total energy stored in a body by virtue of its deformation** |
| **RESILIENCE** | **The TOTAL strain energy stored in a body** |
| **PROOF RESILIENCE** | **The strain energy stored at the ELASTIC LIMIT — the maximum energy the body can store WITHOUT permanent deformation** ← |
| **MODULUS OF RESILIENCE** | **PROOF RESILIENCE PER UNIT VOLUME** ← |
| **TOUGHNESS (modulus of toughness)** | **The energy per unit volume absorbed up to FRACTURE — the WHOLE area under the stress-strain curve** ← |

> **So the sequence is: resilience is an energy, proof resilience is that energy at a particular state, and the MODULUS of resilience is that quantity PER UNIT VOLUME.**

> **The word MODULUS in this context means "per unit volume", exactly as it does in "modulus of toughness" — which is a useful thing to know, since the term otherwise looks like a stiffness.**

> **Option (a) RESILIENCE is the same quantity WITHOUT the per-unit-volume normalisation, which makes it the designed distractor.**

**The computation, since it is a simple area:**

> **On a stress-strain diagram, the strain energy per unit volume is the AREA UNDER THE CURVE.**

> **Up to the elastic limit the curve is a straight line, so the area is a TRIANGLE:**

> **Modulus of resilience = ½ × σ_e × ε_e = ½ σ_e (σ_e/E) = σ_e²/(2E)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **σ_e** | **Stress at the elastic limit** |
| **ε_e** | **Strain at the elastic limit** |
| **E** | Young's modulus |

> **For mild steel with σ_e = 250 MPa and E = 200 GPa:**

> **Modulus of resilience = 250²/(2 × 200,000) = 62,500/400,000 = 0.156 MPa = 156 kJ/m³**

> **And note the form σ_e²/(2E): the resilience goes as the SQUARE of the elastic limit stress and INVERSELY as the stiffness.**

> **So a material that is STRONG and FLEXIBLE stores the most energy elastically — which is exactly why SPRING STEEL is both high-strength and used in a form that permits large deflection.**

**RESILIENCE against TOUGHNESS — the distinction that matters most:**

| | **RESILIENCE** | **TOUGHNESS** |
|---|---|---|
| **Energy absorbed** | **UP TO THE ELASTIC LIMIT** | **UP TO FRACTURE** ← |
| **Recoverable?** | **YES — fully, on unloading** ← | **NO — mostly dissipated in plastic work** |
| **Area under the stress-strain curve** | **The initial TRIANGLE** | **The ENTIRE area** ← |
| **Favoured by** | **HIGH strength, LOW stiffness** | **HIGH strength AND HIGH ductility** ← |
| **Application** | **SPRINGS, and anything that must store and return energy** | **Structures that must survive impact, blast or earthquake** ← |
| **Material example** | **Spring steel, rubber** | **Mild steel** |

> **The distinction is between energy STORED and energy ABSORBED, and it selects quite different materials:**

> **A spring must store energy and give it back, so it must remain ELASTIC — high resilience is wanted and ductility is irrelevant.**

> **A structure under impact or earthquake must ABSORB energy and need not return it, so PLASTIC deformation is welcome — high toughness is wanted, and it comes chiefly from DUCTILITY.**

> **That is why a high-carbon spring steel, which is strong and brittle, would be a very poor structural material despite its high resilience: it stores energy well and absorbs almost none.**

> **And it is the quantitative form of the argument for ductility met repeatedly in this syllabus: a ductile material's toughness comes overwhelmingly from the area under the PLASTIC portion of its curve, which is many times the elastic triangle.**

| Material | Modulus of resilience | Modulus of toughness |
|---|---|---|
| **Mild steel** | **Modest** | **VERY LARGE — the plastic plateau dominates** ← |
| **High-carbon spring steel** | **LARGE** | **Modest — little plastic strain** |
| **Cast iron** | Small | **Very small — it fractures with almost no plastic strain** ← |
| **Rubber** | **Very large** | Large |

> **The CAST IRON row makes the earlier point quantitatively: its toughness is very small, which is precisely why it fails without warning and why it was abandoned for structural framing.**

**Where strain energy is USED — the energy methods:**

| Method | Statement | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **CASTIGLIANO'S FIRST theorem** | **δ = ∂U/∂P — the deflection at a load's point equals the partial derivative of the strain energy with respect to that load** ← | **Deflections of trusses, curved members, frames** |
| **Castigliano's second theorem** | ∂U/∂δ = P | — |
| **VIRTUAL WORK (unit load method)** | **Apply a unit load and equate external and internal virtual work** | **Deflections of any structure; the most general method** ← |
| **Strain energy method for indeterminacy** | **Minimise U with respect to the redundant** | Indeterminate structures |
| **Impact loading** | **Equate the falling weight's potential energy to the strain energy stored** ← | Impact stress in a bar or beam |

> **The IMPACT application is the most direct use of resilience and it explains a design principle worth knowing:**

> **A falling weight's energy must be absorbed as strain energy, so:**

> **W(h + δ) = ½ P δ, from which the impact load P and the stress follow.**

> **The consequence is that a STIFFER member suffers a HIGHER impact stress, because it deforms less and therefore must reach a greater force to absorb the same energy.**

> **So under impact, FLEXIBILITY IS PROTECTIVE — the opposite of the intuition that a stronger, stiffer member is always safer.**

> **That is why a rope is used to arrest a fall rather than a chain, why a crash barrier is designed to deform, and why a rigid connection can fail under an impact that a flexible one survives.**

> **And it is the same principle as base isolation in earthquake engineering: reducing the structure's stiffness reduces the force it attracts, at the cost of greater displacement.**

examTip.trick: **MODULUS OF RESILIENCE = proof resilience PER UNIT VOLUME = σ_e²/(2E)** — the area of the elastic triangle under the stress-strain curve. "Modulus" here means per unit volume, not a stiffness.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) RESILIENCE is the same energy WITHOUT the per-unit-volume normalisation.** And TOUGHNESS is the whole area up to FRACTURE, which for mild steel is many times the elastic triangle.
examTip.mnemonic: **RESILIENCE is energy STORED (recoverable — springs); TOUGHNESS is energy ABSORBED (dissipated — impact and earthquake).** Hence a strong brittle spring steel is a poor structural material. And under IMPACT, a stiffer member suffers a HIGHER stress — flexibility is protective.

questions.stem: A steel bar is subjected to a uniaxial tensile stress of 200 MPa. Taking E = 200 GPa and Poisson's ratio 0.3, the volumetric strain is:
questions.solution:
**4.0 × 10⁻⁴.**

**The relation for uniaxial stress:**

> **Volumetric strain  ε_v = (σ/E)(1 − 2μ)**

**The computation:**

> **Axial strain  ε = σ/E = 200/200,000 = 1.0 × 10⁻³**

> **ε_v = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × (1 − 2 × 0.3) = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × 0.4 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴** ✓

> **Option (a) 1.0 × 10⁻³ is the AXIAL strain, with the (1 − 2μ) factor omitted — the designed trap, since it is the intermediate result.**

> **Option (b) 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ is the LATERAL strain (μ × axial = 0.3 × 10⁻³), and option (c) 7.0 × 10⁻⁴ is (1 − μ) × axial.**

> **So every distractor is a real strain from the same problem, which makes the option set a test of which quantity is asked for.**

**Where the (1 − 2μ) comes from — the derivation in three lines:**

> **Under a tensile stress in the x direction only:**

| Direction | Strain |
|---|---|
| **x (axial)** | **ε_x = +σ/E** |
| **y (lateral)** | **ε_y = −μ σ/E** |
| **z (lateral)** | **ε_z = −μ σ/E** |

> **The volumetric strain is the SUM of the three linear strains (for small strains):**

> **ε_v = ε_x + ε_y + ε_z = (σ/E)(1 − μ − μ) = (σ/E)(1 − 2μ)** ✓

> **So the bar gets LONGER in one direction and THINNER in two, and the net volume change is the sum of the three effects.**

> **The fact that ε_v is the SUM of the linear strains is worth knowing in itself: for a small deformation, the volumetric strain of any element equals the sum of the three orthogonal linear strains, whatever the stress state.**

> **That is why the general form is  ε_v = (σ_x + σ_y + σ_z)(1 − 2μ)/E — the volume change depends only on the SUM of the normal stresses, and not on how they are distributed among the three directions.**

**What the answer means — the volume INCREASES:**

> **ε_v = +4.0 × 10⁻⁴, that is a volume INCREASE of 0.04 per cent.**

> **So a bar in TENSION gets BIGGER in volume, even though it gets thinner: the lengthening more than compensates for the two contractions.**

> **The reason is in the arithmetic: the axial strain is +1 unit and each lateral strain is −0.3, so the net is 1 − 0.6 = +0.4.**

> **Since μ < 0.5 for every real material, (1 − 2μ) is always POSITIVE — so a bar in tension ALWAYS increases in volume and a bar in compression always decreases.**

> **That is the general result, and it holds for every material except the limiting incompressible case.**

**The LIMITING case at μ = 0.5, which is where the relation becomes interesting:**

| Poisson's ratio | (1 − 2μ) | Volumetric strain |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | **1.0** | **Equal to the axial strain — no lateral contraction at all (cork)** |
| **0.25** | **0.5** | Half the axial strain |
| **0.3 (steel)** | **0.4** | **4.0 × 10⁻⁴ here** ← |
| **0.5** | **ZERO** | **NO VOLUME CHANGE — the material is INCOMPRESSIBLE** ← |
| **Above 0.5** | **NEGATIVE** | **Volume would DECREASE under tension — physically impossible** ← |

> **The row at μ = 0.5 is the reason Poisson's ratio cannot exceed a half, and it is a cleaner argument than the bulk-modulus one:**

> **At μ = 0.5 the lateral contractions exactly cancel the axial extension, so the volume is unchanged — the material deforms at CONSTANT VOLUME.**

> **Above 0.5 the volume would DECREASE under tension, which would mean the material could store energy by being pulled apart — and a stable material cannot do that.**

> **So 0.5 is a hard upper bound, and it corresponds to INCOMPRESSIBILITY.**

**Where the constant-volume condition is used, since it is not merely a limit:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **UNDRAINED behaviour of SATURATED CLAY** | **No water can leave, so the volume cannot change — μ = 0.5 is the CORRECT value, not an approximation** ← |
| **RUBBER and elastomeric bearings** | **μ ≈ 0.4999 — which is why a rubber bearing is stiff in compression and flexible in shear** ← |
| **PLASTIC deformation of metals** | **Plastic flow occurs at constant volume, so μ_effective = 0.5 in the plastic range** ← |
| **Immediate settlement of a footing on clay** | The elastic formula uses μ = 0.5 |

> **The RUBBER BEARING case is worth explaining because it is the basis of a whole class of structural bearings:**

> **Because rubber is nearly incompressible, a rubber pad CONFINED between steel plates cannot change volume — so it cannot compress vertically either, except by bulging at its edges.**

> **Restraining that bulge (by bonding thin steel shims into the pad) makes it VERY STIFF vertically while leaving it FLEXIBLE in shear, since shear involves no volume change.**

> **That combination — stiff vertically, flexible horizontally — is exactly what a bridge bearing needs: it must carry the deck's weight and permit thermal movement and rotation.**

> **So a laminated elastomeric bearing exploits the incompressibility directly, and the number of steel shims is the design variable that sets the vertical stiffness.**

> **And it is the same property that makes a rubber base isolator work in seismic design: very stiff under gravity, very flexible laterally, so the structure's lateral period is lengthened and the earthquake force it attracts is reduced.**

examTip.trick: **ε_v = (σ/E)(1 − 2μ) = 1.0×10⁻³ × 0.4 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴.** The volumetric strain is the SUM of the three linear strains: +1 axial and −0.3 twice.
examTip.trap: **Every distractor is a real strain from the same problem** — 1.0×10⁻³ is the AXIAL strain (the intermediate result), 3.0×10⁻⁴ the LATERAL strain. Read which is asked.
examTip.mnemonic: **(1 − 2μ) is why μ cannot exceed 0.5: at 0.5 the volume is unchanged (INCOMPRESSIBLE), above it the volume would fall under tension.** Which is exactly why μ = 0.5 is CORRECT for undrained clay and why confined rubber is stiff vertically and flexible in shear.

questions.stem: In the theory of simple bending, the assumption that plane sections remain plane after bending leads directly to the conclusion that:
options: Strain varies linearly across the depth of the section
Stress is uniform across the depth of the section
Strain is uniform across the depth of the section
Stress varies as the square of the distance from the neutral axis
questions.solution:
**STRAIN varies LINEARLY across the depth.**

**The chain of reasoning — and the order matters:**

> **The assumption is geometric: a plane section perpendicular to the axis before bending remains PLANE and perpendicular after bending.**

> **So the section simply ROTATES about the neutral axis.**

| Step | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1. The section rotates as a plane** | **The extension of any fibre is PROPORTIONAL to its distance from the neutral axis** ← |
| **2. Strain = extension / original length** | **STRAIN varies LINEARLY with y: ε = y/R** ← |
| **3. IF the material obeys HOOKE'S LAW (σ = Eε)** | **STRESS also varies linearly: σ = E y/R** ← |
| **4. Combined with moment equilibrium** | **σ = M y/I — the flexure formula** |

> **The order is the essential point: the assumption gives LINEAR STRAIN directly and unconditionally, and linear STRESS only if Hooke's law additionally holds.**

> **So strain linearity is a GEOMETRIC consequence and stress linearity is a MATERIAL consequence — and that distinction is not a pedantic one, as the next section shows.**

**Why the distinction matters — where stress is NOT linear:**

| Situation | Strain distribution | Stress distribution |
|---|---|---|
| **Elastic bending of steel** | **LINEAR** | **LINEAR** |
| **A steel beam bent BEYOND YIELD** | **STILL LINEAR** ← | **NOT linear — it plateaus at f_y** ← |
| **REINFORCED CONCRETE at the ultimate limit state** | **STILL LINEAR** ← | **NOT linear — the code's parabolic-plus-rectangular stress block** ← |
| **A composite section of two materials** | **LINEAR (strain is continuous)** | **DISCONTINUOUS at the interface, since E differs** ← |

> **The REINFORCED CONCRETE row is the one that matters most in this syllabus, and it explains the whole basis of limit state design:**

> **IS 456's ultimate limit state analysis retains the plane-sections assumption — so the STRAIN is still linear, running from 0.0035 at the compression face to the steel's strain at its level.**

> **But the STRESS is emphatically not linear: concrete's stress-strain curve is parabolic to 0.002 strain and then constant, and the steel's is bilinear.**

> **So the stress block is parabolic-plus-rectangular, and the coefficients 0.36 f_ck and 0.42 x_u come from integrating THAT shape rather than a triangle.**

> **That is why the whole apparatus works: the geometry (linear strain) survives into the plastic range, and only the material relation changes.**

> **A designer who assumed linear STRESS at the ultimate limit state would be using the working-stress method's triangular block, and would get quite different — and unconservative — coefficients.**

**The COMPOSITE SECTION case, since it is the other important departure:**

> **In a composite beam — steel and concrete, or two timbers, or a flitched beam — the strain is continuous across the interface (the materials are bonded and must deform together).**

> **But σ = Eε, and E differs — so the STRESS JUMPS at the interface.**

> **That is handled by the MODULAR RATIO method: the section is transformed into an equivalent section of ONE material by multiplying the widths by m = E₁/E₂.**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Choose one material as the reference** |
| **2** | **Multiply the other material's width by the MODULAR RATIO m = E_other/E_reference** ← |
| **3** | **Analyse the transformed section by the ordinary flexure formula** |
| **4** | **Convert the stresses back: the stress in the transformed material is m times the computed value** ← |

> **Step 4 is the one most often forgotten: the transformation gives the correct STRAINS and the correct MOMENT, and the stress in the transformed material must be multiplied back by m.**

> **The same modular-ratio idea is what underlies the working-stress design of reinforced concrete, where m is taken as 280/(3σ_cbc) — and it is why that method treats the steel as an equivalent area of concrete m times larger.**

**The other assumptions of simple bending theory, since they come as a set:**

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **The material is HOMOGENEOUS and ISOTROPIC** | **Fails for timber, and for reinforced concrete** |
| **The material obeys HOOKE'S LAW, with the same E in tension and compression** | **Fails beyond yield, and for concrete and cast iron** ← |
| **PLANE SECTIONS remain plane** | ← this question; survives into the plastic range |
| **The beam is initially STRAIGHT, of uniform cross-section** | Curved beams need a modified theory |
| **The radius of curvature is LARGE compared with the depth** | **Fails for a DEEP beam** ← |
| **The load acts in a PLANE OF SYMMETRY** | **Fails for unsymmetrical bending — an angle section** ← |
| **Transverse sections remain PERPENDICULAR to the axis (no shear deformation)** | **Fails for a deep beam, where shear deflection matters** ← |

> **The DEEP BEAM failures in rows five and seven are the same one seen twice, and they define the theory's limit: for a span-to-depth ratio below about 2, plane sections do NOT remain plane, the strain is not linear, and flexure theory does not apply at all.**

> **Such members are designed by STRUT-AND-TIE modelling instead, as noted in the shear discussion — and the reason is precisely that this question's assumption has failed.**

> **So the assumption examined here is not a formality: it is the foundation of beam theory, it is remarkably robust (surviving into the plastic range and across composite sections), and knowing WHERE it fails identifies exactly which members need a different method.**

examTip.trick: **Plane sections remaining plane gives LINEAR STRAIN directly — a GEOMETRIC consequence.** Linear STRESS follows only if HOOKE'S LAW additionally holds, which is a MATERIAL consequence.
examTip.trap: **At the ultimate limit state the STRAIN is still linear and the STRESS is NOT** — hence IS 456's parabolic-plus-rectangular block, from which 0.36 f_ck and 0.42 x_u come. Assuming linear stress there gives the working-stress triangle and wrong coefficients.
examTip.mnemonic: **The assumption is remarkably robust — it survives into the plastic range and across composite sections** (where strain is continuous and STRESS jumps, handled by the modular ratio). It fails only for DEEP beams (L/d below about 2), which need strut-and-tie modelling.

questions.stem: The ratio of the Euler crippling load for a column with BOTH ENDS FIXED to that for the same column with BOTH ENDS HINGED is:
questions.solution:
**4.**

**The reasoning:**

> **P_cr = π² E I / L_e²**

> **The only difference between the two cases is the EFFECTIVE LENGTH:**

| End condition | L_e | P_cr |
|---|---|---|
| **Both HINGED** | **L** | **π²EI/L²** |
| **Both FIXED** | **0.5 L** | **π²EI/(0.5L)² = 4 π²EI/L²** ← |

> **Ratio = 4** ✓

> **Since P_cr goes as 1/L_e², halving the effective length QUADRUPLES the load — and that squared relation is the whole content of the answer.**

**The full set of ratios, for the four standard cases:**

| End condition | L_e | P_cr relative to hinged-hinged |
|---|---|---|
| **Both FIXED** | **0.5 L** | **4** ← |
| **Fixed-hinged** | **0.707 L** | **2** |
| **Both HINGED** | **L** | **1 (the reference)** |
| **Fixed-FREE** | **2 L** | **0.25** |

> **So the four cases span a range of SIXTEEN TO ONE, from fixed-fixed to fixed-free — and options (b) 2 and (d) 8 are near the fixed-hinged ratio and a doubling of the answer respectively.**

> **The ratio 2 for the fixed-hinged case is worth noting: 1/0.707² = 1/0.5 = 2 exactly, since 0.707 = 1/√2.**

**Why END RESTRAINT is such good value — the practical consequence:**

> **Quadrupling a column's capacity by fixing its ends costs NOTHING in material: no larger section, no better steel, only a connection detailed to resist moment.**

> **Compare the alternatives for the same fourfold increase:**

| To quadruple the buckling capacity | Cost |
|---|---|
| **FIX both ends instead of pinning them** | **A moment connection — a base plate with bolts at a lever arm, a welded or bolted end plate** ← |
| **QUADRUPLE the moment of inertia** | **Roughly double the section depth, or a much heavier section** |
| **Use a stronger steel** | **NOTHING — Euler's formula contains no yield strength** ← |
| **HALVE the unbraced length by adding an intermediate BRACE** | **One extra member — also very good value** ← |

> **The third row is the one worth restating because it is counter-intuitive and important: EULER'S FORMULA CONTAINS E AND I BUT NOT f_y.**

> **So a slender column's buckling load is entirely independent of its steel's strength, and specifying a high-strength steel for a slender strut is wasted money.**

> **To strengthen a slender column, change its GEOMETRY (a better-shaped section) or its RESTRAINT (fixity, or a brace) — not its material.**

> **And the fourth row is the cheapest intervention of all in practice: bracing a pin-ended column at midheight halves its unbraced length and quadruples its capacity for the cost of one light member.**

**The essential caution — that the theoretical ratio is NOT the design ratio:**

> **The values 0.5, 0.707, 1 and 2 assume PERFECT restraint, which nothing provides.**

> **IS 800 gives more conservative design values:**

| Condition | Theoretical L_e | IS 800 design L_e | Design ratio to hinged |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Effectively held in position AND restrained in direction at both ends** | **0.5 L** | **0.65 L** | **2.4, not 4** ← |
| **Held in position both ends, restrained in direction at one** | 0.707 L | **0.80 L** | 1.56 |
| **Held in position both ends, direction restrained at neither** | **L** | **1.0 L** | **1** |
| **One end fixed, other free** | 2 L | **2.0 L** | 0.25 |

> **So the DESIGN benefit of fixing both ends is a factor of (1/0.65)² = 2.4, not 4 — and claiming the theoretical 4 would overstate the capacity by 66 per cent.**
