> **The reason for the code's conservatism is that a real "fixed" end provides restraint that depends on the STIFFNESS of the members framing into it, and a column framing into a slender beam is far from fixed.**

> **So the question's answer — 4 — is the correct answer to the question asked about EULER'S formula, and it is not the number a designer would use.**

> **That distinction between the theoretical mechanism and the design provision is worth being explicit about, because both appear in examinations and they differ.**

**And the more refined treatment, since it explains where the code's values come from:**

> **The effective length of a column in a real FRAME depends on the relative stiffness of the columns and the beams at each joint, expressed through a stiffness ratio:**

> **β₁, β₂ = (Σ column stiffness at the joint) / (Σ column stiffness + Σ beam stiffness)**

| Situation | Effective length |
|---|---|
| **Beams very STIFF relative to the columns** | **The joint approaches FIXED; L_e → 0.5 L (non-sway)** ← |
| **Beams very FLEXIBLE relative to the columns** | **The joint approaches PINNED; L_e → L or more** ← |
| **A SWAY frame** | **L_e can EXCEED L, sometimes greatly** ← |

> **The SWAY case is the one that catches designers: in an unbraced frame free to sway, the effective length can be 1.2 L, 2 L or more — so a column in a sway frame is far weaker than the same column in a braced one.**

> **That is why BRACING a frame, or providing shear walls, does more than resist lateral load: it converts every column in the frame from a sway column to a non-sway one, and substantially increases their capacities.**

> **So a bracing system pays for itself twice — once in lateral stability and once in column capacity — which is worth knowing when its cost is being questioned.**

examTip.trick: **P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², and fixing both ends halves L_e from L to 0.5L — so the load QUADRUPLES.** The four cases span 16 : 1 overall.
examTip.trap: **The theoretical ratio 4 is NOT the design ratio.** IS 800 uses 0.65L rather than 0.5L for fixed-fixed, giving (1/0.65)² = 2.4 — because no real connection is perfectly fixed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Euler's formula contains E and I but NOT f_y — so high-strength steel is wasted on a slender column.** Change the GEOMETRY or the RESTRAINT instead. And bracing a frame pays twice: lateral stability AND converting every column from sway to non-sway.

questions.stem: In a loaded beam, the rate of change of the bending moment with respect to distance along the beam is equal to:
questions.solution:
**The SHEAR FORCE.**

**The differential relations for a beam, in full:**

> **Starting from the load and integrating upward:**

| Relation | Statement |
|---|---|
| **dV/dx = −w** | **The rate of change of SHEAR equals MINUS the load intensity** ← |
| **dM/dx = V** | **The rate of change of MOMENT equals the SHEAR FORCE** ← this question |
| **d²M/dx² = −w** | Combining the two |
| **M = EI (d²y/dx²)** | **The moment-curvature relation** |
| **dy/dx = θ** | **The SLOPE** |
| **y** | **The DEFLECTION** |

> **So the complete chain, from load to deflection, is a sequence of INTEGRATIONS:**

> **LOAD  →  SHEAR  →  MOMENT  →  (÷EI)  →  CURVATURE  →  SLOPE  →  DEFLECTION**

> **and each arrow is one integration (with a constant of integration fixed by a boundary condition).**

> **That is the DOUBLE INTEGRATION METHOD, and options (c) and (d) name two further links in the same chain — which is what makes them plausible distractors.**

**The consequences of dM/dx = V — three that are used constantly:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The moment is MAXIMUM where the shear is ZERO** | **Since a maximum requires the derivative to vanish** ← |
| **The AREA under the shear diagram between two points equals the CHANGE in moment** | **The integral form — the fastest way to construct a moment diagram** ← |
| **The moment diagram's SLOPE at any point equals the shear there** | **So a steep moment diagram means a large shear** ← |

> **The SECOND consequence is the practically useful one and it is worth demonstrating:**

> **For a simply supported beam of span L under a UDL w, the shear diagram is a triangle from +wL/2 to −wL/2.**

> **The area of the positive triangle, from the support to midspan, is ½ × (L/2) × (wL/2) = wL²/8.**

> **That IS the midspan moment** ✓ — obtained by computing a triangle's area, with no moment equation written at all.

> **And the total area under the whole shear diagram is zero (the two triangles cancel), which confirms that the moment returns to zero at the far support — a self-check on the whole construction.**

> **So a moment diagram can be built from a shear diagram by accumulating areas, and the arithmetic is elementary geometry.**

**The DEGREE relations, which follow from the integrations and catch drawing errors:**

| Loading | Shear diagram | Moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **NO load** | **CONSTANT (0th degree)** | **LINEAR (1st)** |
| **POINT load** | **A STEP** | **A KINK — a change of slope** |
| **UNIFORM load (UDL)** | **LINEAR (1st)** | **PARABOLIC (2nd)** ← |
| **LINEARLY VARYING load** | **PARABOLIC (2nd)** | **CUBIC (3rd)** |
| **An applied COUPLE** | **No change** | **A STEP** ← |

> **Each integration raises the degree by one, so the moment diagram is always one degree "smoother" than the shear diagram, which is one degree smoother than the load.**

> **Checking a sketched diagram against that rule catches most errors immediately: a UDL producing a triangular moment diagram, or a point load producing a curved moment diagram, is wrong on sight.**

> **And the COUPLE row is worth noting because it is the exception to the pattern: an applied moment produces a STEP in the moment diagram and NO change in the shear diagram at all — which is the reverse of a point load's behaviour.**

**MACAULAY'S METHOD, since it is how the double integration is done in practice:**

> **The difficulty with double integration is that a beam with several loads has a DIFFERENT moment expression in each segment, requiring separate integration and matching of constants at every boundary.**

> **MACAULAY'S METHOD avoids all of that with a notational device: terms are written in ANGLE BRACKETS ⟨x − a⟩, with the rule that**

> **⟨x − a⟩ = 0 whenever x < a, and equals (x − a) whenever x ≥ a.**

> **So a single expression covers the whole beam, and it is integrated once — with the bracket terms simply switching on as each load is passed:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **ONE expression for the whole beam** | **Not one per segment** ← |
| **TWO constants of integration only** | **Fixed by the two boundary conditions** ← |
| **Continuity at the load points is automatic** | The device guarantees it |
| **Extends to UDLs, couples and partial loads** | With the appropriate bracket powers |

> **That is a substantial saving: a beam with four loads would otherwise need five expressions, ten constants and eight matching conditions.**

> **The essential discipline in using it is that a bracket term must be integrated AS A BRACKET — ∫⟨x−a⟩dx = ⟨x−a⟩²/2 — and never expanded, since expanding destroys the switching property.**

> **Expanding the brackets is the commonest error, and it produces an expression that is correct in the last segment and wrong in all the others.**

**And the alternative methods, since double integration is not always the best route:**

| Method | Best for |
|---|---|
| **Double integration (with Macaulay)** | **A general beam with several loads; gives the whole deflection curve** ← |
| **MOMENT-AREA method** | **The slope and deflection at ONE point; uses the M/EI diagram's AREA and CENTROID** ← |
| **CONJUGATE BEAM method** | **The same, recast as a fictitious beam loaded with M/EI — deflections become moments** ← |
| **Strain energy / Castigliano** | **Trusses, frames and curved members** |
| **Unit load (virtual work)** | **The most general — any structure, any redundancy** |

> **The CONJUGATE BEAM method is worth a note because it is the same set of differential relations exploited in reverse:**

> **Since d²y/dx² = M/EI has exactly the form of d²M/dx² = −w, the DEFLECTION of the real beam behaves mathematically like the MOMENT of a fictitious beam loaded with M/EI.**

> **So a deflection problem becomes a moment problem, which requires no integration at all — only statics.**

> **That is a genuinely elegant device and it exists entirely because of the relation this question asks about: the whole chain from load to deflection is one repeated integration, so any two links in it are analogous.**

examTip.trick: **dM/dx = V and dV/dx = −w.** The full chain LOAD → SHEAR → MOMENT → CURVATURE → SLOPE → DEFLECTION is a sequence of integrations, and options (c) and (d) are further links in it.
examTip.trap: **Each integration raises the DEGREE by one** — so a UDL gives a LINEAR shear and PARABOLIC moment. A UDL with a triangular moment diagram is wrong on sight. And an applied COUPLE steps the MOMENT and leaves the shear unchanged.
examTip.mnemonic: **The AREA under the shear diagram is the CHANGE in moment** — so ½ × L/2 × wL/2 = wL²/8 gives the midspan moment by geometry alone. And in MACAULAY'S method, never expand the brackets: integrate them as brackets or the switching property is destroyed.

questions.stem: A flexible cable carrying a load uniformly distributed over its HORIZONTAL SPAN hangs in the shape of:
questions.solution:
**A PARABOLA.**

**The two cable shapes, which depend on how the load is distributed:**

| Load distribution | Shape | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Uniform per unit HORIZONTAL length** | **PARABOLA** ← | **A suspension bridge, where the deck's weight is uniform along the span** ← |
| **Uniform per unit length ALONG THE CABLE** | **CATENARY** ← | **A cable hanging under its OWN WEIGHT — a transmission line, a chain** ← |

> **Option (b) CATENARY is therefore the designed distractor, and it is the correct answer to the other load case — which is the whole substance of this question.**

**Why the two differ, and why the difference is usually small:**

> **A cable's own weight is distributed along its LENGTH, and the cable is longer than its horizontal span — more so near the supports where it is steepest.**

> **So a self-weight load is MORE CONCENTRATED near the supports than a load uniform per horizontal metre, and the resulting curve is slightly different.**

| Sag-to-span ratio | Difference between the parabola and the catenary |
|---|---|
| **1/10 or flatter** | **Under 1 per cent — negligible** ← |
| **1/5** | **A few per cent** |
| **1/2 or steeper** | **Substantial** |

> **Since practical cables and suspension bridges have sag-to-span ratios of about 1/8 to 1/12, THE PARABOLA IS AN EXCELLENT APPROXIMATION EVEN FOR SELF-WEIGHT — and it is far easier to work with, since the catenary involves hyperbolic functions.**

> **So the parabola is used in practice for both cases, and the catenary is reserved for steeply sagging cables where the error would matter.**

> **That is worth knowing as a practical matter and not merely as a distinction: the exact answer is the catenary and the used answer is the parabola.**

**The parabolic cable's properties — the working results:**

> **For a cable of span L with sag h at midspan, carrying w per unit horizontal length:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **HORIZONTAL tension H (constant throughout)** | **H = w L²/(8 h)** ← |
| **Maximum tension, at the SUPPORTS** | **T_max = √(H² + (wL/2)²)** ← |
| **Minimum tension, at the LOWEST point** | **H — the horizontal component alone** ← |
| **Length of the cable (approximately)** | **L(1 + 8h²/3L² − 32h⁴/5L⁴ …)** |

> **The HORIZONTAL TENSION being CONSTANT along the cable is the key property and it deserves explanation: a cable can carry no shear and no moment, so at every section the only internal force is TENSION along the cable's own direction.**

> **The horizontal component of that tension must be the same everywhere, since no horizontal force is applied between the supports.**

> **So H is constant, the VERTICAL component varies from zero at the lowest point to wL/2 at each support, and the total tension is therefore LEAST at the bottom and GREATEST at the supports.**

> **Which is why a cable fails at its anchorage or its saddle rather than at midspan, and why those are the details that receive the attention.**

**The relation H = wL²/(8h) and the ARCH analogy:**

> **That expression is IDENTICAL to the horizontal thrust of a three-hinged parabolic arch under a UDL — which is not a coincidence.**

| | **CABLE** | **ARCH** |
|---|---|---|
| **Shape under a UDL** | **PARABOLA (sagging)** | **PARABOLA (rising)** |
| **Internal force** | **TENSION throughout** ← | **COMPRESSION throughout** ← |
| **Horizontal force at the supports** | **wL²/(8h) — pulling INWARD** | **wL²/(8h) — pushing OUTWARD** |
| **Bending moment** | **ZERO — a cable cannot carry moment** | **ZERO — for this load and shape** |

> **So an arch is an INVERTED CABLE, and the funicular shape met in the arch discussion is exactly this parabola turned upside down.**

> **That is the physical basis of the funicular principle: a cable finds by itself the shape in which it carries a given load in pure tension, and inverting that shape gives a structure carrying the same load in pure compression.**

> **It is also a practical design method: hanging a chain with weights representing the loads gives, by inversion, the ideal arch shape for those loads — which is how Gaudí designed the Sagrada Família's structure, using hanging string models.**

> **And it explains why the sag-to-rise ratio matters so much in both: H goes as 1/h, so a FLAT cable or a FLAT arch generates an enormous horizontal force.**

| Sag or rise h | H for w = 20 kN/m, L = 100 m |
|---|---|
| **25 m (h/L = 1/4)** | **1000 kN** |
| **12.5 m (1/8)** | **2000 kN** |
| **5 m (1/20)** | **5000 kN** ← |
| **2 m (1/50)** | **12,500 kN** |

> **So a very flat cable requires an enormous anchorage — which is why suspension bridge cables sag substantially and why a nearly straight cable (a tie rod) is a quite different structural proposition.**

**Where cables are used, since the shape governs the design:**

| Structure | Note |
|---|---|
| **SUSPENSION BRIDGE main cables** | **Load uniform per horizontal metre (the deck) — a PARABOLA** ← |
| **TRANSMISSION LINES** | **Self-weight only — a CATENARY, though the parabola is used for flat spans** ← |
| **Cable-stayed bridges** | Straight stays, not a hanging cable |
| **Cable roofs and tension membranes** | **The shape follows the load; a saddle shape resists uplift** ← |
| **Guy ropes, ropeways, cableways** | **Common in Nepal's hills for goods transport** ← |
| **Prestressing tendons in a draped profile** | Parabolic, to match the moment diagram |

> **The PRESTRESSING application in the last row is a neat closure: a prestressing tendon is draped in a PARABOLA precisely so that its upward force on the beam is uniform, opposing a uniform downward load.**

> **So the parabola appears there for exactly the reason it appears in a cable — it is the shape whose curvature produces a uniform transverse force — and the load balancing method of prestressed design is that observation used deliberately.**

> **A parabolic tendon with the right force can BALANCE the dead load entirely, leaving the beam with no deflection and no flexural stress under that load — which is as close as structural engineering comes to elegance.**

examTip.trick: **Uniform per HORIZONTAL length gives a PARABOLA (a suspension bridge deck); uniform ALONG THE CABLE gives a CATENARY (self-weight).** Option (b) is the other load case.
examTip.trap: **For sag ratios flatter than about 1/10 the two differ by under 1 %** — so the parabola is used in practice even for self-weight, because the catenary needs hyperbolic functions.
examTip.mnemonic: **H = wL²/(8h) is IDENTICAL to a three-hinged parabolic arch's thrust — an arch is an INVERTED CABLE.** And H goes as 1/h, so a FLAT cable needs an enormous anchorage. A parabolic prestressing tendon exerts a UNIFORM upward force, which is load balancing.

questions.stem: Castigliano's first theorem states that the deflection at the point of application of a load is given by:
options: The partial derivative of the total strain energy with respect to that load
The second derivative of the bending moment at that point
The integral of the shear force over the span
The product of the load and the span divided by EI
questions.solution:
**The PARTIAL DERIVATIVE of the total strain energy with respect to that load.**

**The statement:**

> **δ = ∂U / ∂P**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **δ** | **The deflection at the point of application of P, IN THE DIRECTION of P** ← |
| **U** | **The TOTAL strain energy stored in the whole structure** |
| **P** | **The load in question** |

> **And the companion result for rotation:**

> **θ = ∂U / ∂M** — the rotation at the point of application of a couple M equals the partial derivative of the strain energy with respect to that couple.

> **So a FORCE derivative gives a DEFLECTION and a MOMENT derivative gives a ROTATION — which follows from the requirement that force × displacement and moment × rotation both have the dimensions of work.**

**Why the theorem is so useful — what it replaces:**

| Alternative method | Effort |
|---|---|
| **Double integration** | **Requires the moment expression along the whole member and two integrations, with boundary conditions** |
| **Moment-area** | Requires the M/EI diagram's area and centroid |
| **CASTIGLIANO** | **Requires only the strain energy expression, and a differentiation** ← |

> **The saving is greatest for structures where the moment expression is awkward or the geometry is not a simple beam:**

| Structure | Why Castigliano suits it |
|---|---|
| **TRUSSES** | **U = Σ (F² L)/(2AE) over the members — a SUM, not an integral** ← |
| **CURVED members — hooks, links, rings** | **The moment varies with angle; integration along the arc is natural** ← |
| **Rigid FRAMES** | Each member contributes its own energy term |
| **Structures with several load types together** | Axial, bending, shear and torsion energies simply add |
| **INDETERMINATE structures** | **Via the second theorem — see below** |

> **The TRUSS case is where the method is most obviously superior: the strain energy is a SUM over the members, so the deflection becomes:**

> **δ = ∂/∂P [Σ F²L/(2AE)] = Σ (F L/AE)(∂F/∂P)**

> **which is exactly the UNIT LOAD (virtual work) formula for a truss deflection — and that is not a coincidence: Castigliano's theorem and the unit load method give the same expression, arrived at from energy and from virtual work respectively.**

> **So a candidate who knows either has the other.**

**The strain energy expressions, since the theorem needs them:**

| Action | Strain energy |
|---|---|
| **AXIAL force** | **U = ∫ F² dx/(2AE), or Σ F²L/(2AE) for members of constant force** ← |
| **BENDING** | **U = ∫ M² dx/(2EI)** ← |
| **SHEAR** | **U = ∫ (β V² dx)/(2AG) — usually NEGLIGIBLE for a slender beam** ← |
| **TORSION** | **U = ∫ T² dx/(2GJ)** |

> **Note that every one has the same form: (action)² × length / (2 × the relevant stiffness) — which makes them easy to reconstruct rather than remember individually.**

> **And the SHEAR term is customarily neglected for a slender beam, where it contributes perhaps 1 to 3 per cent of the deflection — but it is NOT negligible for a DEEP beam, where it can dominate.**

> **That is another manifestation of the deep-beam problem: for L/d below about 4, shear deflection becomes significant, and below about 2 it is the larger part.**

**The DUMMY LOAD device, which extends the theorem's reach:**

> **Castigliano's theorem gives the deflection AT A LOAD, IN THE DIRECTION OF THAT LOAD. What if the deflection is wanted where there is no load, or in another direction?**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Apply a FICTITIOUS (dummy) load Q at the point and in the direction required** ← |
| **2** | **Write the strain energy INCLUDING Q** |
| **3** | **Differentiate: δ = ∂U/∂Q** |
| **4** | **SET Q = 0 in the result** ← |

> **Step 4 is the device: the dummy load is introduced only to be differentiated with respect to, and then removed.**

> **That is a legitimate operation because the derivative is evaluated at Q = 0, so the answer describes the structure as it actually is.**

> **It is the same trick as the unit load method's fictitious unit load, and it makes the theorem entirely general.**

**CASTIGLIANO'S SECOND THEOREM, and the theorem of least work:**

> **The second theorem states  ∂U/∂δ = P — the load required to produce a given deflection is the derivative of the strain energy with respect to that deflection.**

> **Its practical importance is in INDETERMINATE analysis, through the THEOREM OF LEAST WORK:**

> **For a redundant force R in an indeterminate structure, the compatibility condition is  ∂U/∂R = 0**

> **because the redundant's corresponding displacement is ZERO (a redundant support does not move, a redundant member's ends do not separate).**

| So the procedure is | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Choose the redundant R and release it** | Making the structure determinate |
| **2. Express all forces in terms of the loads AND R** | — |
| **3. Write U in terms of R** | — |
| **4. Set ∂U/∂R = 0 and solve for R** ← | **The redundant takes the value that MINIMISES the strain energy** ← |

> **The last line is the theorem of least work, and it is a genuinely striking statement: AN INDETERMINATE STRUCTURE DISTRIBUTES ITS FORCES SO AS TO MINIMISE ITS TOTAL STRAIN ENERGY.**

> **That is a variational principle of the same family as Fermat's principle in optics and the principle of least action in mechanics — nature choosing the configuration that minimises a quantity.**

> **And it has a practical corollary worth carrying: since strain energy is minimised, the forces distribute themselves toward the STIFFER load paths — which is the energy-based statement of "load flows to stiffness" met in the propped cantilever discussion.**

> **So that rule of thumb is not an observation but a consequence of a minimum principle, and it can be relied upon rather than merely remembered.**

examTip.trick: **δ = ∂U/∂P for a deflection; θ = ∂U/∂M for a rotation.** A FORCE derivative gives a DISPLACEMENT, a MOMENT derivative a ROTATION — because both products must have the dimensions of work.
examTip.trap: **For a deflection where there is no load, apply a DUMMY load Q, differentiate, then SET Q = 0.** That is legitimate because the derivative is evaluated at Q = 0, describing the real structure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Every strain energy term has the same form: (action)² × length ÷ (2 × stiffness)** — so they need not be memorised separately. And ∂U/∂R = 0 for a redundant is the THEOREM OF LEAST WORK: a structure distributes forces to MINIMISE strain energy, which is why load flows to stiffness.

questions.stem: In the moment distribution method, the DISTRIBUTION FACTOR for a member meeting at a joint is:
options: Its length divided by the total length of all members at the joint
Its moment divided by the total moment at the joint
Its stiffness divided by the sum of the stiffnesses of all members at the joint
questions.solution:
**Its STIFFNESS divided by the SUM of the stiffnesses of all the members meeting at that joint.**

**The definition:**

> **DF = k / Σk**, where k is the member's rotational stiffness at that joint.

> **And since all the distribution factors at a joint are fractions of the same total:**

> **Σ DF at any joint = 1.0** — which is the essential check on every joint's factors.

**The member stiffnesses, since the factors depend on them:**

| Far end of the member | Stiffness k | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **4EI/L** | **The standard case** ← |
| **HINGED (pinned)** | **3EI/L** | **Three quarters of the fixed value** ← |
| **A member with a FIXED far end, in relative terms** | **I/L** | **Only RELATIVE stiffnesses matter, so 4E cancels** ← |

> **The third row is the practical simplification: since the distribution factor is a RATIO of stiffnesses, any common factor cancels — so I/L can be used in place of 4EI/L throughout, provided E is the same for all members.**

> **But the 3EI/L for a hinged far end does NOT cancel to I/L: it becomes (3/4)(I/L), and forgetting that reduction is a real error.**

> **So the working rule is: use I/L for a member fixed at the far end, and 0.75 I/L for one hinged there.**

**A worked example, since the factors are easily got wrong:**

> **A joint B where three members meet: BA (span 6 m, I = 2I₀, far end A FIXED), BC (span 4 m, I = I₀, far end C HINGED), and BD (a column 3 m long, I = I₀, far end D FIXED):**

| Member | Far end | Relative stiffness | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BA** | **FIXED** | **I/L = 2I₀/6** | **0.333 I₀** |
| **BC** | **HINGED** | **0.75 × I/L = 0.75 × I₀/4** | **0.188 I₀** |
| **BD** | **FIXED** | **I/L = I₀/3** | **0.333 I₀** |
| **TOTAL Σk** | — | — | **0.854 I₀** |

> **The distribution factors are each member's stiffness divided by that total:**

| Member | DF |
|---|---|
| **BA** | **0.333/0.854 = 0.390** |
| **BC** | **0.188/0.854 = 0.220** |
| **BD** | **0.333/0.854 = 0.390** |
| **Σ DF** | **1.000** ✓ |

> **The factors summing to UNITY is the check to make at every joint, and it catches most arithmetic errors at once.**

> **Note that BA and BD have EQUAL factors despite BA having twice the second moment of area: BA's greater length exactly offsets it, since stiffness goes as I/L and 2I₀/6 = I₀/3.**

**Why the factors take that form — the physical reasoning:**

> **When a moment is applied at a joint, the joint ROTATES, and every member meeting there rotates by the SAME amount (the joint is rigid).**

> **Each member then resists that rotation in proportion to its own STIFFNESS — so each carries a share of the applied moment proportional to its stiffness.**

> **That is why the distribution is by stiffness and not by length, area or anything else — and it is another instance of LOAD FLOWING TO STIFFNESS, which is now appearing for the third time in this chapter.**

> **Option (a) is the designed distractor because LENGTH does appear in the stiffness — but INVERSELY, and combined with I. A long member is LESS stiff and takes LESS moment, which is the opposite of what option (a) implies.**

**The moment distribution procedure, since the factor is one step of it:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute the FIXED END MOMENTS for every member, treating each as fixed at both ends** ← |
| **2** | **Compute the DISTRIBUTION FACTORS at every joint, checking they sum to 1** ← |
| **3** | **At each joint, sum the fixed end moments — the UNBALANCED moment** |
| **4** | **BALANCE the joint: distribute the NEGATIVE of the unbalanced moment among the members in proportion to their DFs** ← |
| **5** | **CARRY OVER half of each distributed moment to the member's far end** ← |
| **6** | **Repeat from step 3 — the carry-overs create new imbalances** |
| **7** | **Continue until the carry-overs are negligibly small; sum all the columns** |

> **The CARRY-OVER FACTOR of ONE HALF in step 5 is the method's other key number, and it applies when the far end is FIXED.**

> **For a member with a HINGED far end the carry-over is ZERO — nothing can be carried to a hinge, since a hinge cannot sustain a moment.**

> **So the two numbers to have are: DF = k/Σk, and carry-over = ½ to a fixed end, 0 to a hinge.**

> **And the reason the method converges is that each cycle carries over only half of a diminishing quantity, so the corrections shrink geometrically — usually to negligibility within three or four cycles.**

**Why the method matters, and its place today:**

> **Moment distribution (Hardy Cross, 1930 — the same engineer as the pipe network method) was the practical means of analysing indeterminate frames for four decades, and it has two enduring virtues:**

| Virtue | Note |
|---|---|
| **It requires NO simultaneous equations** | **A frame with twenty redundants is solved by arithmetic alone** ← |
| **It gives PHYSICAL INSIGHT into how moments distribute** | **You can see the load flowing to the stiff members** ← |
| **A single joint can be checked by hand** | **Verifying a computer model** ← |
| **It converges reliably** | Each cycle halves the error |

> **Modern practice uses matrix stiffness analysis in software, which solves the whole system at once and handles any structure.**

> **But the second and third virtues remain valuable: moment distribution shows WHY a stiffer beam attracts more moment, and it allows a hand check of one joint of a computer model — which, as with the Hardy Cross pipe method, is the best defence against a plausible-looking wrong answer.**

> **That both of Hardy Cross's iterative methods survive for the same reason — insight and hand-checkability rather than efficiency — is a fair comment on what a numerical method is for.**

examTip.trick: **DF = k/Σk, and the factors at any joint must SUM TO 1.0** — the check to make every time. Use relative stiffness I/L for a member FIXED at the far end and 0.75 I/L for one HINGED there.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) has length appearing — but INVERSELY, inside the stiffness.** A LONGER member is LESS stiff and takes LESS moment, the opposite of what that option implies.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two numbers run the method: DF = k/Σk, and CARRY-OVER = ½ to a fixed end, ZERO to a hinge** (a hinge cannot hold a moment). And the distribution by stiffness is "load flows to stiffness" again — the same principle as the propped cantilever.

questions.stem: For dead load calculation, the unit weight of REINFORCED concrete is taken as:
questions.solution:
**25 kN/m³.**

**The unit weights required for dead load calculation (IS 875 Part 1):**

| Material | Unit weight (kN/m³) |
|---|---|
| **REINFORCED cement concrete** | **25** ← |
| **PLAIN cement concrete** | **24** |
| **Cement mortar / plaster** | **20.4** |
| **BRICK masonry** | **19 to 20** |
| **Stone masonry (coursed rubble)** | **20.4 to 26.5** |
| **STEEL** | **78.5** |
| **Timber** | **6 to 8** |
| **Water** | **9.81** |
| **Soil, moist** | **18 to 20** |
| **Lime concrete** | **19** |
| **Glass** | **25** |

> **The distinction between REINFORCED (25) and PLAIN (24) concrete is small and real: the steel occupies perhaps 1 to 2 per cent of the volume at a unit weight three times the concrete's, which accounts for the difference.**

> **Option (c) 20 kN/m³ is close to the brick masonry and moist soil figures, and option (d) 18 kN/m³ is a typical soil value — so the option set draws from the same table.**

**Why the DEAD LOAD deserves care, despite being the "easy" load:**

> **Dead load is the one load that is present ALWAYS, acts on EVERY member, and is under the designer's own control — so an error in it propagates everywhere and is never relieved.**

> **And it is frequently the LARGER part of the total load:**

| Structure | Dead load as a proportion of the total |
|---|---|
| **A concrete building floor** | **60 to 75 per cent** ← |
| **A long-span bridge** | **Approaching 90 per cent** ← |
| **A light steel roof** | **20 to 30 per cent** |
| **A warehouse floor with heavy storage** | **30 to 40 per cent** |

> **The BRIDGE row makes the strongest point: for a long span, the structure spends most of its capacity carrying ITSELF, and the live load it can carry is what remains.**

> **That is why long-span design is dominated by reducing self-weight — lighter decks, higher-strength materials, and eventually cable-supported forms in which the deck's weight is carried by cables rather than by the deck's own bending.**

> **And it is why a heavier concrete would not simply be a stronger one: increasing a long-span member's size increases the load it must carry, and beyond a point the addition is self-defeating.**

**What is easily OMITTED from a dead load calculation — the practical hazard:**

| Item | Note |
|---|---|
| **FLOOR FINISHES — screed, tiles, marble** | **50 mm of screed and tiles is about 1.2 kN/m² — comparable with a residential live load of 2.0** ← |
| **CEILING, plaster and services below the slab** | 0.3 to 0.5 kN/m² |
| **PARTITION walls** | **Often taken as an equivalent uniform load of 1.0 to 1.5 kN/m² where their position is not fixed** ← |
| **Waterproofing and roof screed to falls** | **A screed laid to falls can be 150 mm at its thickest** ← |
| **Suspended services, ducts, sprinklers** | — |
| **FUTURE finishes or overlays** | **A pavement or a floor may be resurfaced without the slab being strengthened** ← |

> **The FLOOR FINISH item is the one most often underestimated: a 50 mm screed with 20 mm of marble weighs about 1.2 to 1.5 kN/m², which on a residential floor is comparable with the entire live load.**

> **So omitting or understating the finishes can be a 20 per cent error in the total load — and it is an error in the direction of unsafety, since the finishes will certainly be there.**

> **The PARTITION allowance deserves its note because of how it is handled: where partitions may be moved or added, their weight is not applied at their drawn positions but as an EQUIVALENT UNIFORM LOAD over the floor, so that the slab is adequate wherever they are put.**

> **That is a sensible device, and it fails when a heavy masonry partition is later built on a slab designed for a 1.0 kN/m² allowance — which is a common cause of excessive deflection in altered buildings.**

**The DEAD LOAD's other property — that it can be BENEFICIAL, and must then be reduced:**

> **Dead load usually acts against the structure, and sometimes it acts FOR it:**

| Situation | Dead load's role | Load factor |
|---|---|---|
| **A beam carrying its own weight** | **ADVERSE** | **1.5** |
| **A retaining wall resisting OVERTURNING** | **BENEFICIAL — the weight resists** | **0.9** ← |
| **A footing resisting UPLIFT from wind** | **BENEFICIAL** | **0.9** ← |
| **A basement resisting FLOTATION** | **BENEFICIAL** | **0.9, and the calculation is often critical** ← |
| **A dam resisting sliding** | **BENEFICIAL** | Reduced |

> **The principle is the general one met earlier: a load factor EXCEEDS 1 when the load's effect is ADVERSE and falls BELOW 1 when it is BENEFICIAL — because overstating a helpful load is unsafe.**

> **The FLOTATION case in the fourth row is worth a closing note because it produces a counter-intuitive design requirement:**

> **An empty basement below the water table is a buoyant box, and it will FLOAT if the uplift exceeds its weight.**

> **The critical moment is during CONSTRUCTION, when the structure above has not been built and the dewatering is switched off — so the basement is at its lightest and the water table at its highest.**

> **The remedies are to keep dewatering until sufficient dead load is in place, to provide tension piles or ground anchors, to thicken the base slab, or to flood the basement deliberately if the water rises unexpectedly.**

> **And basements HAVE floated — cracking their slabs and lifting out of the ground — so it is a real check and not a theoretical one.**

examTip.trick: **RCC 25 kN/m³, plain concrete 24, brick masonry 19-20, steel 78.5, water 9.81.** The RCC/PCC difference is the steel occupying 1-2 % of the volume at three times the density.
examTip.trap: **Floor FINISHES are the most-omitted dead load** — 50 mm of screed and tiles is 1.2-1.5 kN/m², comparable with a residential live load of 2.0. Omitting them is a 20 % error in the unsafe direction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead load is 60-75 % of a concrete floor's total and approaching 90 % on a long-span bridge** — which is why long spans are dominated by reducing self-weight. And where it is BENEFICIAL (overturning, uplift, flotation) it is factored DOWN to 0.9.

questions.stem: As per IS 1893, the seismic ZONE FACTOR Z for Zone V is:
questions.solution:
**0.36.**

**The zone factors:**

| Seismic zone | Zone factor Z | Intensity |
|---|---|---|
| **II** | **0.10** | **Low** |
| **III** | **0.16** | **Moderate** |
| **IV** | **0.24** | **Severe** |
| **V** | **0.36** ← | **VERY SEVERE — the highest** |

> **Note that Zone I was abolished and merged into Zone II in the 2002 revision, so the scale now runs from II to V.**

> **Options (a) 0.10 and (b) 0.24 are the Zone II and Zone IV factors — real values from the same table — while option (d) 0.48 is above the maximum.**

**What Z represents — and the definition is worth being precise about:**

> **Z is TWICE the expected peak ground acceleration, expressed as a fraction of g, for the MAXIMUM CONSIDERED EARTHQUAKE (MCE).**

> **The factor of 2 in the definition appears because A_h = (Z/2)(I/R)(S_a/g), and the Z/2 converts the MCE level to the DESIGN BASIS EARTHQUAKE (DBE) — taken as half the MCE.**

| Level | Definition | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| **MAXIMUM CONSIDERED EARTHQUAKE (MCE)** | **The most severe shaking reasonably expected at the site** | **Z = 0.36 g in Zone V** ← |
| **DESIGN BASIS EARTHQUAKE (DBE)** | **HALF the MCE — the level the structure is designed to resist with repairable damage** | **Z/2 = 0.18 g** ← |

> **So a Zone V structure is designed for a peak ground acceleration of 0.18 g, and is expected to SURVIVE 0.36 g with damage but without collapse.**

> **That two-level philosophy is the heart of seismic design and it is worth stating explicitly:**

| Earthquake level | Expected performance |
|---|---|
| **A MODERATE (DBE-level) earthquake** | **The structure resists it WITHOUT SIGNIFICANT STRUCTURAL DAMAGE, though non-structural damage may occur** ← |
| **A SEVERE (MCE-level) earthquake** | **The structure may suffer SERIOUS STRUCTURAL DAMAGE but must NOT COLLAPSE — life is protected** ← |

> **So the code does NOT promise an undamaged building after a major earthquake. It promises that the building will not fall down and kill its occupants.**

> **Designing for no damage under the MCE would be economically impossible for ordinary buildings, and the two-level approach is the deliberate compromise — with the R factor providing the ductility that makes survival-with-damage possible.**

**NEPAL's seismic zoning, since the country is not in the Indian zone map:**

> **Nepal has its own code, NBC 105, which zones the country separately — and the essential fact is that NEPAL LIES ENTIRELY IN A REGION OF HIGH SEISMIC HAZARD.**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Tectonic setting** | **The INDIAN plate underthrusting the EURASIAN plate along the Main Himalayan Thrust** ← |
| **Convergence rate** | **About 20 mm per year, of which roughly half is accommodated on the Himalayan front** |
| **Consequence** | **Strain accumulates and is released in great earthquakes** ← |
| **Historical great earthquakes** | **1255, 1344, 1408, 1505, 1833, 1934 (Bihar-Nepal, M 8.0), 2015 (Gorkha, M 7.8)** |
| **Equivalent Indian zoning** | **Nepal's territory corresponds to Indian Zones IV and V** ← |

> **The 2015 GORKHA earthquake is the recent reference and its lessons are directly relevant to this syllabus:**

| Observation from 2015 | Engineering lesson |
|---|---|
| **Unreinforced masonry and adobe suffered catastrophically** | **The R = 1.5 assigned to unreinforced masonry is not a formality** ← |
| **Engineered reinforced concrete frames largely performed well** | **Ductile detailing works** |
| **Non-engineered RC frames with masonry infill failed** | **SOFT STOREY and SHORT COLUMN failures were widespread** ← |
| **Traditional timber-framed buildings often outperformed masonry** | **Low mass and ductile connections** |
| **Kathmandu valley showed SITE AMPLIFICATION** | **Soft lake-bed sediments amplified the long-period motion** ← |

> **The SOFT STOREY failure is the one worth naming because it is entirely avoidable and remains common: a ground floor left open for shops or parking, with masonry infill above, has a ground storey far more flexible than the storeys above.**

> **The whole building's seismic displacement then concentrates in that one storey, its columns are overwhelmed, and the building drops onto its ground floor.**

> **The remedies are to provide shear walls or braced bays in the open storey, or to design its columns for the amplified forces — and the failure occurs because the infill above is treated as non-structural in the analysis while acting structurally in the event.**

**The other factors in A_h, since Z is one of four:**

> **A_h = (Z/2)(I/R)(S_a/g)**

| Factor | Represents | Range |
|---|---|---|
| **Z** | **The site's seismic HAZARD** | **0.10 to 0.36** ← |
| **I** | **The building's IMPORTANCE** | **1.0 ordinary; 1.5 hospitals, schools, emergency buildings** |
| **R** | **DUCTILITY, redundancy and overstrength of the structural system** | **1.5 unreinforced masonry to 5.0 a ductile SMRF** |
| **S_a/g** | **DYNAMIC amplification at the structure's period, and the soil type** | **Plateau 2.5** |

> **Working a Zone V example to show the magnitudes: an ordinary ductile RC frame (I = 1.0, R = 5.0) with a period in the plateau range (S_a/g = 2.5) on medium soil:**

> **A_h = (0.36/2)(1.0/5.0)(2.5) = 0.18 × 0.2 × 2.5 = 0.09**

> **So the design base shear is 9 per cent of the seismic weight — which is a substantial lateral load and far less than the 0.36 g the ground may actually experience.**

> **The difference is made up by DUCTILITY, which is what the R = 5 represents — and that is the whole logic of the method restated in numbers.**

examTip.trick: **Zone II 0.10, III 0.16, IV 0.24, V 0.36.** Zone I was abolished in 2002. Options (a) and (b) are the Zone II and IV factors.
examTip.trap: **Z is TWICE the design ground acceleration** — the Z/2 in A_h converts the MCE level to the DBE, taken as half. So a Zone V structure is designed for 0.18 g and must survive 0.36 g without collapse.
examTip.mnemonic: **The code promises SURVIVAL, not absence of damage: no significant structural damage in a moderate quake, and NO COLLAPSE in a severe one.** Nepal corresponds to Indian Zones IV-V throughout — and the 2015 lesson was SOFT STOREY and SHORT COLUMN failures in non-engineered frames.

questions.stem: The rule that, for given materials and full compaction, the strength of concrete depends inversely on the water-cement ratio is known as:
questions.solution:
**ABRAMS' LAW** (Duff Abrams, 1918).

**The statement:**

> **For a given cement and aggregate, and for FULLY COMPACTED concrete, the compressive strength depends ONLY on the WATER-CEMENT RATIO:**

> **f_c = A / B^(w/c)**

> **where A and B are empirical constants for the materials used.**

> **The relation is a decreasing exponential: strength FALLS as the water-cement ratio RISES, steeply at first and less so at high ratios.**

| Water-cement ratio | Approximate 28-day strength (OPC) |
|---|---|
| **0.35** | **50 MPa and above** |
| **0.45** | **About 40 MPa** |
| **0.50** | **About 33 MPa** ← |
| **0.60** | **About 25 MPa** |
| **0.70** | **About 18 MPa** |
| **0.80** | **About 13 MPa** |

> **The other options are genuine relations by other workers — Feret's rule expresses strength in terms of the volumes of cement, water and air, and Bolomey's formula is a linear form of the same idea — but Abrams' is the name attached to the law as stated.**

**The two conditions on which the law depends — and they matter:**

| Condition | Why it is essential |
|---|---|
| **The concrete must be FULLY COMPACTED** | **See below — this is the whole qualification** ← |
| **The materials (cement, aggregate) are given** | The constants A and B depend on them |

> **THE FULL COMPACTION CONDITION IS WHERE THE LAW'S PRACTICAL LIMIT LIES, and it produces the characteristic strength-against-water-content curve:**

| Water-cement ratio | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **VERY LOW (below about 0.3 without admixtures)** | **The mix is too STIFF to compact fully; entrapped air remains, and the strength is LOW despite the low ratio** ← |
| **OPTIMUM** | **Just enough water to permit full compaction — MAXIMUM strength** ← |
| **ABOVE the optimum** | **Full compaction is easy, and Abrams' law governs: strength falls as w/c rises** ← |

> **So the actual strength-against-w/c curve RISES to a peak and then FALLS, and Abrams' law describes only the falling branch.**

> **The rising branch exists because a mix too dry to compact retains air voids, and EACH 1 PER CENT OF ENTRAPPED AIR COSTS ABOUT 5 PER CENT OF STRENGTH — the same figure met in the air entrainment discussion.**

> **A concrete compacted to only 90 per cent of full density loses roughly half its potential strength, which swamps any benefit from a low water content.**

> **That is why the theoretical minimum water-cement ratio is not the practical one, and why superplasticisers are so valuable: they permit full compaction at a water-cement ratio the mix could not otherwise be worked at.**

**Why the water-cement ratio governs strength — the mechanism:**

> **Cement hydration produces a solid gel that fills space. The water that is NOT consumed by hydration remains as CAPILLARY PORES in the hardened paste.**

| More water means | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **More capillary pores when the excess water leaves** | **Higher POROSITY** ← |
| **Higher porosity** | **LOWER strength — strength falls steeply with porosity** ← |
| **Higher porosity** | **Higher PERMEABILITY, hence poorer DURABILITY** ← |
| **A more dilute paste** | Weaker bonding |

> **The DURABILITY consequence in the third row is at least as important as the strength one, and it is why the codes set a MAXIMUM water-cement ratio for each exposure class INDEPENDENTLY of the strength requirement:**

| Exposure | Maximum w/c | Minimum grade |
|---|---|---|
| **Mild** | **0.55** | **M20** |
| **Moderate** | **0.50** | **M25** |
| **Severe** | **0.45** | **M30** |
| **Very severe** | **0.45** | **M35** |
| **Extreme** | **0.40** | **M40** |

> **So a mix might reach M30 strength at a water-cement ratio of 0.55 with a rich cement content — and it would still be REJECTED for severe exposure, because its PERMEABILITY would be too high.**

> **That is the durability requirement acting independently of strength, and it is why the two are specified separately.**

**The theoretical minimum water for hydration, since it bounds the whole subject:**

| Requirement | Water-cement ratio |
|---|---|
| **CHEMICALLY combined water for complete hydration** | **About 0.23 to 0.25** ← |
| **Water held in the GEL PORES (physically adsorbed)** | **A further 0.15 or so** |
| **TOTAL for complete hydration with no capillary pores** | **About 0.38 to 0.40** ← |
| **Practical minimum for workability without admixtures** | **About 0.40 to 0.45** |
| **With superplasticisers** | **0.25 to 0.35 achievable** ← |

> **The 0.38 figure is the theoretically interesting one: BELOW it, there is not enough water to hydrate all the cement, so some cement remains unhydrated permanently.**

> **That sounds wasteful and is not: the unhydrated cement grains act as very hard, very well-bonded fine aggregate, and such concretes are extremely strong and extremely impermeable.**

> **High-performance concretes deliberately operate at w/c of 0.25 to 0.30 with a substantial unhydrated cement fraction, achieving 80 to 120 MPa — and the unhydrated cement also provides an AUTOGENOUS HEALING capacity, hydrating later if a crack admits water.**

> **So the "complete hydration" condition is not the optimum for strength, and the law's exponential form continues to hold well below it — which is a striking confirmation of a rule formulated a century ago on far weaker concretes.**

examTip.trick: **ABRAMS' LAW: for given materials and FULL COMPACTION, strength depends only on the water-cement ratio** — f_c = A/B^(w/c), a decreasing exponential.
examTip.trap: **The FULL COMPACTION condition is the whole qualification.** Below the optimum the mix is too stiff to compact, air remains, and the strength FALLS — each 1 % of entrapped air costs about 5 %. So the real curve rises to a peak and then falls; Abrams describes only the falling branch.
examTip.mnemonic: **The codes cap w/c by EXPOSURE independently of strength (0.55 mild down to 0.40 extreme)** — because w/c governs PERMEABILITY and hence durability, not only strength. And about 0.38 is the theoretical water for complete hydration; high-performance concrete runs below it deliberately.

questions.stem: The water-cement ratio theoretically required for COMPLETE hydration of cement, including the water held in the gel pores, is about:
questions.solution:
**About 0.38.**

**The breakdown of that figure:**

| Component | Water-cement ratio | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **CHEMICALLY COMBINED water** | **About 0.23** | **Water that enters the hydration products chemically — it cannot be driven off without decomposing them** ← |
| **GEL PORE water** | **About 0.15** | **Physically adsorbed within the gel's own fine pores — it is part of the gel structure** ← |
| **TOTAL for complete hydration** | **About 0.38** ← | **Below this, some cement CANNOT hydrate** |

> **Option (a) 0.20 is close to the chemically combined water alone, which makes it a well-made distractor: it is a real component of the total, offered as the total.**

> **And option (d) 0.50 is a typical practical water-cement ratio for ordinary concrete — above the theoretical requirement, as practical mixes generally are.**

**What happens ABOVE and BELOW that ratio:**

| Water-cement ratio | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **BELOW 0.38** | **Insufficient water for complete hydration — some cement remains UNHYDRATED permanently** ← |
| **EXACTLY 0.38** | **Just enough; in principle no capillary pores and no unhydrated cement** |
| **ABOVE 0.38** | **The excess water occupies space that becomes CAPILLARY PORES when it leaves** ← |

> **So the excess water above 0.38 is what creates the capillary porosity — and capillary porosity is what governs both strength and permeability.**

> **That is the mechanism behind Abrams' law expressed in terms of the pore structure: more water means more capillary pores means lower strength and higher permeability.**

> **And it explains why the relation is so strong: strength falls very steeply with porosity, roughly exponentially, so a modest increase in water produces a substantial loss.**

**Why UNHYDRATED CEMENT is not the waste it appears — the important qualification:**

> **Operating below 0.38 leaves cement unhydrated, which sounds like paying for material that does nothing.**

> **In fact those unhydrated grains are among the best components of the mix:**

| Property of unhydrated cement grains | Note |
|---|---|
| **Extremely HARD and STRONG** | Harder than most aggregates |
| **PERFECTLY BONDED to the surrounding gel** | **They were the source of it — there is no interface to fail** ← |
| **Very FINE, filling the smallest spaces** | Reduces porosity further |
| **Capable of LATER hydration** | **AUTOGENOUS HEALING — a crack admitting water lets them hydrate and seal it** ← |

> **So a low-water-cement-ratio concrete is not one with wasted cement but one with a superior microstructure, and the unhydrated fraction is a feature rather than a defect.**

> **HIGH-PERFORMANCE CONCRETE exploits it deliberately: at w/c of 0.25 to 0.30, perhaps a third of the cement never hydrates, and strengths of 80 to 120 MPa result.**

> **The AUTOGENOUS HEALING property is genuinely useful: fine cracks in such concrete seal themselves when water reaches them, because the unhydrated cement at the crack face hydrates and the products fill the crack.**

> **That has been observed in practice in water-retaining structures, where fine cracks leak initially and stop leaking within weeks.**

**Why practical mixes use MORE than 0.38 — the workability constraint:**

> **A paste at w/c 0.38 without admixtures is far too stiff to place and compact, so extra water is added purely for WORKABILITY:**

| Purpose of the water | Note |
|---|---|
| **Chemical — hydration** | **0.23** |
| **Physical — gel pores** | **0.15** |
| **WORKABILITY — to make the mix placeable** | **The remainder, and usually the largest part** ← |

> **So in an ordinary concrete at w/c 0.50, roughly a quarter of the water is there only to allow the mix to be handled — and it becomes capillary porosity afterward.**

> **That is the central tension in concrete technology: WATER IS NEEDED FOR PLACING AND HARMFUL AFTERWARD.**

> **Every development in concrete technology of the past fifty years has been an attempt to resolve it:**

| Development | How it resolves the tension |
|---|---|
| **PLASTICISERS** | **Same workability with 5-10 % less water** |
| **SUPERPLASTICISERS** | **15-30 % less water — the decisive advance** ← |
| **Self-compacting concrete** | **Flows without vibration at a low w/c** ← |
| **Better GRADING and rounded aggregate** | Less water needed for the same workability |
| **MINERAL admixtures — fly ash, slag, silica fume** | **Improve workability AND refine the pore structure** ← |
| **Vacuum dewatering** | Removes excess water AFTER placing |
| **Vibration and better compaction plant** | Permits a drier mix to be placed |

> **The SUPERPLASTICISER is the technology that made high-performance concrete possible, and its mechanism is worth a sentence: the polymer adsorbs onto the cement grains and disperses them, either by electrostatic repulsion or (for polycarboxylates) by steric hindrance.**

> **Cement grains naturally flocculate into clumps that trap water; dispersing them releases that trapped water and makes it available for lubrication.**

> **So a superplasticiser does not add water — it liberates the water already present, which is why the same workability is achieved with 30 per cent less.**

> **The VACUUM DEWATERING entry is a different and ingenious approach: the concrete is placed at a workable ratio and the excess water is then SUCKED OUT through a filter mat before setting.**

> **The mix is workable when it needs to be and low-water when it hardens — which resolves the tension directly rather than by chemistry, and is used for industrial floors where a hard, low-porosity surface is wanted.**

examTip.trick: **About 0.38 total: 0.23 CHEMICALLY combined plus 0.15 in the GEL PORES.** Option (a) 0.20 is the chemical component alone — a real part offered as the whole.
examTip.trap: **Water ABOVE 0.38 becomes CAPILLARY POROSITY when it leaves** — which is the mechanism behind Abrams' law. Strength falls steeply with porosity, so a modest extra of water costs a great deal.
examTip.mnemonic: **Below 0.38 some cement never hydrates — and that is a FEATURE: the grains are hard, perfectly bonded, and give AUTOGENOUS HEALING.** The central tension is that water is needed for PLACING and harmful AFTERWARD, which is what superplasticisers resolve by dispersing flocculated grains.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the maximum strain in concrete at the outermost compression fibre in FLEXURE is taken as:
questions.solution:
**0.0035.**

**The two concrete strain limits, which must be kept apart:**

| Loading | Maximum concrete strain |
|---|---|
| **FLEXURE (bending)** | **0.0035** ← |
| **AXIAL COMPRESSION (pure)** | **0.002** ← |
| **Combined axial load and bending** | **Between the two, interpolated: 0.0035 − 0.75 × (strain at the least compressed fibre)** |

> **Option (a) 0.002 is the AXIAL compression limit, which makes it the designed distractor — both are IS 456 values and they are constantly interchanged.**

**Why the flexural strain limit EXCEEDS the axial one — the reason:**

> **In PURE AXIAL compression, the whole section is at the same strain. When the most-stressed material reaches its capacity, the entire section fails at once — there is nowhere for the load to go.**

> **In FLEXURE, the strain VARIES across the depth. As the extreme fibre approaches its limit, it sheds stress to the less-strained material below it.**

> **That REDISTRIBUTION lets the extreme fibre strain beyond the value it could sustain in uniform compression, because it is RESTRAINED and SUPPORTED by the less-strained concrete adjacent to it.**

> **So the 0.0035 is not a different material property but the same material behaving differently under a strain GRADIENT — and the 75 per cent extra reflects that support.**

> **The interpolation rule for combined loading follows naturally: as the section moves from pure bending toward pure axial compression, the strain gradient flattens and the limit falls from 0.0035 toward 0.002.**

**Where the 0.0035 is used — it defines the whole ultimate limit state:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **It fixes one end of the STRAIN DIAGRAM** | **The other end is the steel's strain, and the neutral axis position follows** ← |
| **It defines the LIMITING neutral axis depth x_u,max** | **Through the strain compatibility with the steel's yield strain** ← |
| **It defines the STRESS BLOCK's shape** | Parabolic to 0.002, then rectangular to 0.0035 |
| **It gives the coefficients 0.36 and 0.42** | From integrating that block |

> **The STRESS BLOCK's two-part shape follows directly from the concrete's stress-strain curve and the two strain values:**

| Strain range | Stress | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| **0 to 0.002** | **RISING parabolically to 0.446 f_ck** | **PARABOLA** ← |
| **0.002 to 0.0035** | **CONSTANT at 0.446 f_ck** | **RECTANGLE** ← |

> **So the 0.002 appears in the FLEXURAL analysis too — not as the limit, but as the strain at which the concrete reaches its peak stress and the curve turns from parabolic to flat.**

> **That is why both numbers are needed and why they are confused: 0.002 is where the stress PEAKS, and 0.0035 is where the concrete CRUSHES.**

> **Between them the concrete is at full stress and increasing strain — which is what gives it a modest ductility and makes the rectangular part of the block possible.**

**Deriving x_u,max from the strain diagram, since it is the limit's main consequence:**

> **At the balanced condition, the concrete reaches 0.0035 at the same instant the steel reaches its design yield strain:**

> **Steel's limiting strain = 0.87 f_y/E_s + 0.002**

> **By similar triangles on the strain diagram:**

> **x_u,max/d = 0.0035 / (0.0035 + steel's limiting strain)**

| Grade | Steel's limiting strain | x_u,max/d |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.87 × 250/2×10⁵ + 0.002 = 0.00309** | **0.0035/0.00659 = 0.531** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.00180 + 0.002 = 0.00380** | **0.0035/0.00730 = 0.479** ← |
| **Fe 500** | **0.00217 + 0.002 = 0.00417** | **0.0035/0.00767 = 0.456** |

> **So the whole x_u,max table is generated by the 0.0035 together with each steel's yield strain — and it need not be memorised separately.**

**Why the limit matters — WARNING before failure:**

> **The 0.0035 is a CRUSHING strain, and crushing of concrete is a BRITTLE, sudden failure.**

> **The entire structure of IS 456's flexural design is arranged so that the STEEL YIELDS FIRST:**

| Section type | What happens first | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| **UNDER-reinforced (x_u < x_u,max)** | **STEEL yields; the section deflects and cracks widely; the neutral axis rises; the concrete crushes LATER** | **DUCTILE, with ample warning** ← |
| **BALANCED (x_u = x_u,max)** | **Both at once** | The boundary |
| **OVER-reinforced (x_u > x_u,max)** | **CONCRETE crushes while the steel is still elastic** | **BRITTLE, sudden, NO warning** ← |

> **IS 456 PROHIBITS over-reinforced sections, and x_u,max — derived from this 0.0035 — is how the prohibition is expressed numerically.**

> **So the strain limit is not merely a material datum but the origin of the code's central safety provision, and the chain runs:**

> **0.0035 → x_u,max → the under-reinforced requirement → ductile failure with warning.**

> **That chain is worth being able to state, because it explains why a number describing concrete's crushing determines how much STEEL a beam may contain — which is otherwise a puzzling connection.**

**And a note on where the 0.0035 comes from:**

> **It is an experimental value: tests on concrete in flexure show the extreme fibre reaching strains of about 0.003 to 0.004 before crushing, with some dependence on the strength.**

> **HIGHER-strength concrete is LESS ductile and crushes at a LOWER strain — so 0.0035 is conservative for M20 and less so for M60.**

> **Codes dealing with high-strength concrete accordingly reduce the limit (to 0.003 or below above about M60), and IS 456's 0.0035 is appropriate for the normal-strength range it covers.**

> **CONFINEMENT reverses the trend dramatically: concrete confined by close spiral or hoop reinforcement can sustain strains of 0.01 to 0.02 — five times the unconfined value — which is exactly the ductility that seismic detailing is provided to obtain.**

examTip.trick: **0.0035 in FLEXURE, 0.002 in pure AXIAL compression.** Option (a) is the axial value — both are IS 456 numbers and are constantly swapped.
examTip.trap: **0.002 also appears in flexure — as the strain where the stress PEAKS and the block turns from parabolic to rectangular.** So both numbers are in the same diagram: 0.002 peak stress, 0.0035 crushing.
examTip.mnemonic: **The flexural limit is HIGHER because a strain GRADIENT lets the extreme fibre be supported by less-strained concrete beside it.** And the chain 0.0035 → x_u,max → under-reinforced requirement is why a concrete crushing strain limits how much STEEL a beam may hold.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the maximum spacing of MAIN reinforcement in a solid slab is:
options: d or 100 mm, whichever is less
questions.solution:
**3d or 300 mm, whichever is LESS** (d being the effective depth).

**The slab reinforcement spacing rules:**

| Reinforcement | Maximum spacing |
|---|---|
| **MAIN (principal) steel** | **3d or 300 mm, whichever is LESS** ← |
| **DISTRIBUTION (secondary) steel** | **5d or 450 mm, whichever is less** ← |

> **Option (c) 5d or 450 mm is the DISTRIBUTION steel rule, which makes it the designed distractor — both are IS 456 values from the same clause.**

> **The distribution steel is permitted a WIDER spacing because it carries no calculated load: its purposes are shrinkage and temperature control, load distribution and holding the main bars, none of which requires close spacing.**

**Why a maximum spacing is specified at all — the purposes:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **CRACK CONTROL** | **Widely spaced bars leave wide cracks between them; closer bars distribute the same total steel into more, finer cracks** ← |
| **Ensuring the steel is DISTRIBUTED across the slab** | **A concentrated bunch of bars would leave regions unreinforced** ← |
| **Effective load DISTRIBUTION to the reinforcement** | Local loads must reach a bar |
| **Resisting a concentrated load anywhere on the slab** | — |

> **The CRACK CONTROL purpose is the principal one and it is worth understanding, because it explains why the SPACING is limited independently of the AREA of steel:**

> **A given area of steel can be provided as a few large bars widely spaced, or many small bars closely spaced.**

> **Both give the same STRENGTH, and they give quite different CRACK WIDTHS:**

| Arrangement | Strength | Crack pattern |
|---|---|---|
| **FEW LARGE bars, widely spaced** | **The same** | **FEWER, WIDER cracks** ← |
| **MANY SMALL bars, closely spaced** | **The same** | **MORE, FINER cracks** ← |

> **Since crack WIDTH governs durability — a wide crack admits water and chlorides to the steel — the closely spaced arrangement is superior for the same steel area.**

> **So the spacing rule enforces a serviceability requirement that the strength calculation does not address at all, and it is why a slab is reinforced with 10 mm bars at 150 mm rather than 16 mm bars at 380 mm.**

> **The general principle: FOR CRACK CONTROL, MANY SMALL BARS ARE BETTER THAN FEW LARGE ONES OF THE SAME TOTAL AREA.**

> **And that principle extends beyond slabs: it is why side-face reinforcement is required in deep beams, and why a large-diameter bar is a poor choice in a member where cracking matters.**

**The MINIMUM spacing rules, which bound the other end:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal clear distance between bars** | **The GREATEST of: the largest bar diameter; the maximum aggregate size plus 5 mm** ← |
| **Vertical clear distance between layers** | **The greatest of: 15 mm; two thirds of the maximum aggregate size; the largest bar diameter** |

> **The MAXIMUM AGGREGATE SIZE appearing in both is the practical constraint: the concrete must be able to pass BETWEEN the bars, and an aggregate larger than the gap will arch across it and leave a void.**

> **So the minimum spacing is a CONCRETING requirement and the maximum spacing a CRACKING requirement — the two rules serve entirely different purposes and bound the arrangement from opposite sides.**

**The other slab reinforcement provisions, as a working set:**

| Provision | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Maximum spacing, MAIN steel** | **3d or 300 mm, whichever is less** ← |
| **Maximum spacing, DISTRIBUTION steel** | **5d or 450 mm, whichever is less** |
| **MINIMUM steel (mild steel)** | **0.15 % of the gross area** |
| **Minimum steel (HYSD)** | **0.12 % of the gross area** ← |
| **MAXIMUM bar diameter** | **One EIGHTH of the total slab thickness** ← |
| **Nominal cover** | By exposure — 20 mm mild, 30 mm moderate |
| **Span/depth ratio (simply supported one-way slab)** | **20, modified for the tension steel percentage** |

> **The MAXIMUM BAR DIAMETER rule (D/8) is easy to overlook and is a real constraint on thin slabs:**

> **A 100 mm slab may not use bars larger than 12.5 mm, and a 125 mm slab is limited to about 16 mm.**

> **The reason is that a large bar in a thin slab has too little concrete around it to develop bond and to control cracking, and it forces the effective depth down disproportionately.**

> **So a thin slab needing more steel must use MORE bars rather than LARGER ones — which is consistent with the crack-control principle above.**

**And the DISTRIBUTION steel's direction, since it is where slabs are most often detailed wrongly:**

| Slab type | Main steel | Distribution steel |
|---|---|---|
| **ONE-WAY slab** | **Along the SHORT span, at the BOTTOM** | **Along the LONG span, ABOVE the main steel** ← |
| **TWO-WAY slab** | **BOTH directions are main steel** | **None as such** |
| **Cantilever slab** | **Along the span, at the TOP** ← | **Perpendicular, below the main steel** |

> **In a ONE-WAY slab the distribution steel is placed ON TOP of the main steel, which means the main steel gets the GREATER effective depth — as it should, since it carries the moment.**
> **Reversing them reduces the effective depth by one bar diameter, which on a 100 mm slab is a 10 per cent loss of capacity for nothing.**

> **And in a CANTILEVER the main steel is at the TOP, so the distribution steel goes BENEATH it — the mirror image, and the detail most often got wrong on site because the habit is to place the distribution bars second.**

> **A cantilever slab with its main bars beneath the distribution bars has lost effective depth exactly where it can least afford to, which is a small error with a real consequence.**

examTip.trick: **MAIN steel: 3d or 300 mm, whichever is LESS. DISTRIBUTION steel: 5d or 450 mm.** Option (c) is the distribution rule.
examTip.trap: **The spacing rule enforces CRACK CONTROL, which the strength calculation does not address** — the same steel area as many small bars gives more, FINER cracks than as few large ones.
examTip.mnemonic: **MINIMUM spacing is a CONCRETING rule (the aggregate must pass between the bars); MAXIMUM spacing is a CRACKING rule.** And in a one-way slab the distribution steel sits ON TOP of the main steel — reversed in a CANTILEVER, where the main steel is at the top.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the EFFECTIVE SPAN of a simply supported slab or beam is taken as:
options: The clear span plus the effective depth, or the centre-to-centre distance between supports, whichever is LESS
Always the centre-to-centre distance between supports
Always the clear span between the supports
The clear span plus the full width of both supports
questions.solution:
**The CLEAR SPAN PLUS THE EFFECTIVE DEPTH, or the CENTRE-TO-CENTRE distance between supports, whichever is LESS.**

**The IS 456 effective span rules:**

| Member | Effective span |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported beam or slab** | **The LESSER of: clear span + effective depth; or centre to centre of supports** ← |
| **CONTINUOUS beam or slab, support width ≤ 1/12 of the clear span** | **Centre to centre of supports** |
| **Continuous, support width > 1/12 of the clear span, END span** | **The lesser of: clear span + half the effective depth; or clear span + half the support width** |
| **Continuous, intermediate span with wide supports** | **The CLEAR SPAN** |
| **CANTILEVER** | **The length to the face of the support PLUS half the effective depth** ← |
| **Cantilever at the end of a continuous beam** | **The length to the centre of the support** |
| **FRAMES** | **Centre to centre of the members** |

> **So the rule is not a single formula but a small table, and the simply supported case is the "lesser of two" form.**

**Why the effective span is not simply the clear span — the reasoning:**

> **The load on a beam is not transferred to the support at a single point: the reaction is DISTRIBUTED across the bearing width.**

> **Its RESULTANT acts somewhere within the support — neither at the face nor necessarily at the centre.**

| Support condition | Where the reaction's resultant acts |
|---|---|
| **A NARROW support** | **Close to the centre — so centre-to-centre is the sensible span** ← |
| **A WIDE support** | **Nearer the INNER face, since the beam lifts off the outer part** ← |

> **So for a wide support, taking the span as centre-to-centre would OVERSTATE it — the load is not really being carried over that full distance.**

> **The "clear span plus effective depth" expression approximates the true position of the resultant: it places it about d/2 inside each face, which corresponds roughly to where the reaction concentrates on a wide bearing.**

> **And the "whichever is LESS" clause selects automatically between the two: for a narrow support the centre-to-centre distance is the smaller and governs; for a wide one, clear span plus d governs.**

> **That is why the rule takes its form — it is not an arbitrary convention but an approximation to the reaction's real position, written so that the correct approximation is selected by the geometry.**

**A worked comparison, since the difference can be significant:**

> **A slab of 4.0 m clear span with an effective depth of 150 mm:**

| Support width | Clear span + d | Centre to centre | EFFECTIVE SPAN (the lesser) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **230 mm** | **4.00 + 0.15 = 4.15 m** | **4.00 + 0.23 = 4.23 m** | **4.15 m** ← |
| **150 mm** | **4.15 m** | **4.00 + 0.15 = 4.15 m** | **4.15 m — equal** |
| **100 mm** | **4.15 m** | **4.00 + 0.10 = 4.10 m** | **4.10 m** ← |
| **450 mm (a wide beam)** | **4.15 m** | **4.00 + 0.45 = 4.45 m** | **4.15 m** ← |

> **So for the wide support the rule saves 0.30 m of span — about 7 per cent — and since the moment goes as the SQUARE of the span, that is a 14 per cent reduction in the design moment.**

> **Using the centre-to-centre span throughout, as option (b) proposes, would be conservative but wasteful — and by a margin worth having on a repetitive floor.**

**The CANTILEVER rule, since it differs in form and is often got wrong:**

> **A cantilever's effective span is the length to the FACE of the support PLUS HALF the effective depth — an ADDITION, not a "lesser of".**

> **The reason is that a cantilever's critical section is at the support face, and the effective root of the cantilever lies slightly inside it where the reaction concentrates.**

> **So the effective length is slightly GREATER than the projection, which is conservative — as it should be, given a cantilever's lack of redundancy.**

> **And the exception in the sixth row of the table matters: a cantilever at the END of a CONTINUOUS beam takes its length to the CENTRE of the support, because the continuity means the beam does not simply bear on the support but passes through it.**

**Why the effective span matters so much — where it propagates:**

| Quantity | Dependence on the span |
|---|---|
| **Bending MOMENT** | **∝ L²** ← |
| **SHEAR force** | **∝ L** |
| **DEFLECTION** | **∝ L⁴** ← |
| **Span/depth ratio check** | **Directly** |

> **The DEFLECTION dependence on L⁴ is the striking one: a 7 per cent error in the span is a 31 per cent error in the computed deflection.**

> **So the effective span must be got right before the span/depth check is applied, and a designer using the centre-to-centre span for a wide-supported slab will find it failing a deflection check it would actually pass.**

> **And the L² dependence of the moment means that the small distinction between 4.10 m and 4.45 m — under 9 per cent — changes the design moment by 18 per cent, which on a large floor is a real quantity of steel and concrete.**

> **That is why the rule exists in the code at all: for a single beam the difference is trivial, and over a whole building it is not.**
tags: span dependence of moment and deflection

examTip.trick: **Simply supported: the LESSER of (clear span + effective depth) and (centre to centre).** The "lesser of" clause selects automatically — centre-to-centre for a narrow support, clear span + d for a wide one.
examTip.trap: **A CANTILEVER's rule is an ADDITION, not a "lesser of": length to the support face PLUS half the effective depth.** And a cantilever at the end of a CONTINUOUS beam takes its length to the support CENTRE.
examTip.mnemonic: **Moment ∝ L² and DEFLECTION ∝ L⁴** — so a 7 % span error is a 14 % moment error and a 31 % deflection error. The rule exists because over a whole building that difference is a real quantity of material.

questions.stem: In a two-way restrained slab, TORSION reinforcement is required:
options: At all four corners equally, in two layers
Only at a corner where both edges are continuous
At a corner where BOTH edges are discontinuous, in four layers, of area equal to three quarters of the maximum midspan steel
It is never required in a slab
questions.solution:
**At a corner where BOTH edges are DISCONTINUOUS, in FOUR layers, of area equal to THREE QUARTERS of the maximum midspan steel.**

**The IS 456 requirement, set out fully:**

| Corner condition | Torsion steel required |
|---|---|
| **BOTH edges DISCONTINUOUS (simply supported)** | **FULL torsion steel: 0.75 × A_st(midspan), in FOUR layers** ← |
| **ONE edge continuous, one discontinuous** | **HALF the above: 0.375 × A_st(midspan)** ← |
| **BOTH edges CONTINUOUS** | **NONE required** ← |

> **The FOUR LAYERS are: two at the TOP (one in each direction) and two at the BOTTOM (one in each direction) — a mesh at each face.**

> **And the steel extends from the corner a distance of ONE FIFTH OF THE SHORTER SPAN in each direction.**

> **Option (b) reverses the condition, which makes it the designed distractor: torsion steel is needed where the edges are DISCONTINUOUS, not continuous.**

**Why the requirement runs that way — the mechanism:**

> **A two-way slab restrained at its edges tends to LIFT AT ITS CORNERS when loaded, because the slab deflects into a dish shape and the corners are the last parts to follow.**

> **If the corner is HELD DOWN — by the weight of a wall above, by continuity with an adjacent panel, or by a monolithic connection — that restraint prevents the lift and generates TWISTING MOMENTS in the slab.**

> **Those twisting moments produce PRINCIPAL TENSILE STRESSES on the diagonal, and concrete cracks perpendicular to them:**

| Face | Direction of the principal tension | Crack direction |
|---|---|---|
| **TOP of the slab at the corner** | **Along the diagonal TOWARD the corner** | **Cracks PERPENDICULAR to that diagonal** ← |
| **BOTTOM of the slab at the corner** | **Along the diagonal AWAY from the corner** | **Cracks perpendicular, at right angles to the top crack** ← |

> **So the cracking runs in DIFFERENT DIRECTIONS on the two faces — which is exactly why FOUR layers are needed rather than two.**

> **A mesh at the top and a mesh at the bottom together provide reinforcement crossing both crack directions, and either alone would leave one face unreinforced against its own crack.**

> **That is the reason for the four layers, and it is worth knowing because two layers is the natural but insufficient assumption.**

**Why a CONTINUOUS edge needs none:**

> **Where a corner's edges are continuous with adjacent panels, the adjacent panels themselves restrain the corner and carry the twisting moment.**

> **The continuity reinforcement over the support — which is present anyway to carry the hogging moment — also serves the torsional function.**

> **So no additional steel is required, and the requirement scales with the amount of discontinuity: full steel for two discontinuous edges, half for one, none for none.**

> **That graduated requirement is a sensible piece of code writing — the provision matches the severity of the condition rather than being applied uniformly.**

**Where the corner effect shows in the moment coefficients:**

> **IS 456's Annex D gives moment coefficients for two-way RESTRAINED slabs (corners held down, torsion steel provided) and separately for SIMPLY SUPPORTED slabs with corners NOT held down:**

| Slab condition | Moment coefficients | Corner steel |
|---|---|---|
| **RESTRAINED — corners held down, torsion steel provided** | **LOWER moments** ← | **Required as above** |
| **SIMPLY SUPPORTED — corners free to lift** | **HIGHER moments** ← | **None, but the slab is weaker** |

> **So holding the corners down and providing torsion steel REDUCES the midspan moments — the corner restraint helps the slab carry its load.**

> **That is the practical payoff: the torsion steel is not merely a defensive measure against cracking but the price of using the lower, restrained-slab moment coefficients.**

> **A designer who uses the restrained coefficients and omits the corner steel has taken the benefit without providing the condition it depends on — which is a real and not uncommon error, and it produces exactly the corner cracking the steel was to prevent.**

**The corner lift phenomenon in practice, since it is observable:**

| Observation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A simply supported slab's corners visibly LIFT under load** | **Demonstrable on a model, and measurable on a real slab** ← |
| **Diagonal cracks at the corners of an inadequately reinforced slab** | **Running at 45° across the corner on the top face** ← |
| **A wall or a parapet at the corner is enough to hold it down** | **And thereby generates the twisting moment** |
| **Slabs cast monolithically with edge beams are restrained** | The usual condition in practice |

> **The third row is worth noting because it produces the requirement unexpectedly: a designer may treat a slab as simply supported and detail it accordingly, while the actual construction — a monolithic edge beam, or a wall above — restrains the corners in fact.**

> **The slab then develops twisting moments it was not reinforced for, and cracks.**

> **So the safer practice is to provide corner reinforcement wherever the corner might be restrained, which in monolithic construction is almost everywhere — and the quantity is modest.**

**And the related TORSION provisions for BEAMS, since the topic connects:**

| Aspect | Beam torsion |
|---|---|
| **When torsion must be designed for** | **EQUILIBRIUM torsion (the member must carry it for equilibrium) — always** ← |
