| **When it may be neglected** | **COMPATIBILITY torsion (it arises only from restraint and can be relieved by cracking)** ← |
| **Reinforcement required** | **CLOSED stirrups plus longitudinal bars distributed round the perimeter** ← |
| **Design method** | Equivalent bending moment and equivalent shear |

> **The EQUILIBRIUM against COMPATIBILITY distinction is the important one and it parallels the slab case:**

> **A CANOPY beam carrying a projecting slab must resist the torsion or the canopy falls — equilibrium torsion, which must be designed for in full.**

> **A SPANDREL beam twisted because the slab framing into it wants to rotate can simply CRACK and relieve the torsion, redistributing the moment to the slab — compatibility torsion, which may be neglected provided minimum reinforcement is present.**

> **So the question to ask of any torsion is: IS THE STRUCTURE IN EQUILIBRIUM WITHOUT IT? If not, it must be designed for; if so, it may be relieved.**

> **The slab corner case is a compatibility effect — the slab would stand without the corner restraint, at higher midspan moments — which is why the code offers the choice between restraining the corners (with steel) and not restraining them (with higher moments).**

examTip.trick: **Both edges DISCONTINUOUS: full torsion steel, 0.75 × midspan steel, in FOUR layers, over one fifth of the shorter span.** One edge continuous: half. Both continuous: none.
examTip.trap: **FOUR layers, not two — because the corner cracks run in DIFFERENT directions on the top and bottom faces**, so a mesh is needed at each face.
examTip.mnemonic: **Holding the corners down REDUCES the midspan moments** — the torsion steel is the price of using the restrained-slab coefficients. Taking the lower moments while omitting the steel is a real error that produces exactly the corner cracking it was to prevent.

questions.stem: As per IS 800, the maximum permissible slenderness ratio for a steel member carrying COMPRESSION resulting from dead and imposed loads is:
questions.solution:
**180.**

**The IS 800 slenderness limits:**

| Member and loading | Maximum λ = L_e/r |
|---|---|
| **A member carrying COMPRESSION from dead and imposed loads** | **180** ← |
| **A TENSION member subject to REVERSAL of stress from wind or earthquake** | **180** |
| **A member subjected to compression resulting ONLY from wind or earthquake, provided the deformation does not adversely affect the stress in any part** | **250** ← |
| **A member normally carrying TENSION but subject to reversal from wind or earthquake** | **350** ← |
| **A TENSION member (other than a pretensioned tie)** | **400** |
| **Compression flange of a beam against lateral torsional buckling** | 300 |

> **Every option offered is a real IS 800 limit for a different case, so the option set requires the member's role and loading to be matched.**

> **The pattern that organises the table: COMPRESSION members are limited most strictly, and TENSION members most loosely — because slenderness is a BUCKLING concern and tension members do not buckle.**

**Why a slenderness limit exists at all, quite apart from the strength calculation:**

> **The design capacity calculation already accounts for slenderness through the buckling curves — a very slender member simply has a very low capacity.**

> **So why prohibit slenderness beyond a limit, rather than letting the low capacity govern?**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **HANDLING and ERECTION damage** | **A very slender member bends under its own weight and is easily bent during transport and lifting** ← |
| **VIBRATION and "flutter" under wind or machinery** | **A slender member has a low natural frequency and can vibrate visibly and audibly** ← |
| **SAG under self-weight** | **Unsightly, and it introduces an initial eccentricity that reduces the capacity further** ← |
| **Sensitivity to accidental loads and impact** | A slender strut is easily damaged |
| **The design formulae's reliability falls at extreme slenderness** | Initial imperfections dominate |
| **Very low capacity makes the member near-useless anyway** | At λ = 250 the capacity is a small fraction of the yield load |

> **The HANDLING reason is the practically decisive one: a member with λ above about 200 cannot be lifted, transported or erected without bending, and it arrives on site already imperfect.**

> **So the limit is largely a CONSTRUCTABILITY provision rather than a strength one — which is why it is expressed as an absolute prohibition rather than as a reduction factor.**

> **That is the same class of rule as the maximum steel percentage in a column: a limit imposed by what can actually be built rather than by what can be calculated.**

**Why TENSION members are permitted such high slenderness:**

> **A tension member cannot buckle — tension straightens it rather than bending it — so slenderness does not reduce its strength at all.**

> **Its limit of 400 is imposed purely for the handling, sag and vibration reasons above.**

> **And that is why the limits drop when REVERSAL is possible:**

| Member | Limit | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure tension, no reversal** | **400** | Handling only |
| **Tension with reversal from wind or earthquake** | **350** | It becomes a compression member briefly |
| **Compression from wind or earthquake only** | **250** | Compression, but transient |
| **Compression from dead and imposed loads** | **180** ← | **Compression, and PERMANENT** |

> **So the ladder from 400 down to 180 tracks how severely and how permanently the member is in compression — which makes the four values intelligible rather than arbitrary.**

> **A member that is in compression ALWAYS gets the strictest limit; one that is in compression only during a rare event gets a looser one; one never in compression gets the loosest.**

**Computing the slenderness ratio, since the limit is applied to it:**

> **λ = L_e / r_min**

| Term | Note |
|---|---|
| **L_e** | **The EFFECTIVE length, from the end conditions — 0.65L to 2.0L per IS 800** |
| **r_min** | **The MINIMUM radius of gyration — about the WEAKEST axis** ← |

> **The r_min requirement is the one most often mishandled: a member buckles about its WEAKEST axis, so the smallest radius of gyration governs — not the one about the axis of bending.**

> **For an I-section that is the MINOR (y-y) axis, whose r is typically a quarter of the major-axis value — so an I-section used as a column is far more slender than its depth suggests.**

> **And for an ANGLE the weakest axis is neither of the geometric axes but the MINOR PRINCIPAL axis (the v-v axis), whose r is smaller still — which is why a single angle strut is such an inefficient member.**

| Section | r_min relative to the overall size |
|---|---|
| **Circular hollow section** | **0.35 D — the same about every axis** ← |
| **Square hollow section** | **0.4 D, the same about both axes** |
| **I-section** | **About 0.2 to 0.25 of the FLANGE WIDTH, not the depth** ← |
| **Single ANGLE** | **About 0.19 of the leg length, about the v-v axis** ← |

> **The table shows why a HOLLOW SECTION is the efficient compression member: its radius of gyration is the same about every axis, so there is no weak direction to govern.**

> **An I-section wastes capacity because its major-axis strength cannot be used — the minor axis fails first — unless it is braced about the minor axis, which is exactly what a strut in a braced frame has.**

> **So the choice of section for a compression member is governed by r_min, and the practical rule follows: use a section whose radii of gyration are similar about both axes, or brace the weak axis.**

> **A single angle used as a long strut, with its very small v-v radius and its inevitable eccentric connection, is the worst common case — and it is used constantly in light trusses because it is cheap and easy to connect.**

examTip.trick: **180 for compression from dead and imposed loads.** The ladder: 180 (permanent compression), 250 (compression from wind/earthquake only), 350 (tension with reversal), 400 (pure tension).
examTip.trap: **Every option is a real IS 800 limit for another case.** The ladder tracks how SEVERELY and how PERMANENTLY the member is in compression — which makes the four values intelligible rather than arbitrary.
examTip.mnemonic: **The limit is largely a CONSTRUCTABILITY rule, not a strength one** — a member above λ ≈ 200 bends under its own weight during handling. And λ uses r_MIN, about the WEAKEST axis: for an I-section the minor axis, for an angle the v-v principal axis.

questions.stem: For load-bearing brick masonry in a seismically active region, the cement-sand mortar mix generally specified is:
questions.solution:
**1 : 4 or richer.**

**The mortar mixes and their applications:**

| Cement : sand | Compressive strength (approximate) | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **1 : 3** | **Very high** | **Structural repairs, machine foundations, rich pointing** |
| **1 : 4** | **High** | **LOAD-BEARING masonry in seismic regions; heavily loaded walls; foundations below plinth** ← |
| **1 : 5** | **Moderate** | Load-bearing walls in general |
| **1 : 6** | **Modest** | **Ordinary brickwork in non-seismic areas; partition walls** ← |
| **1 : 8 and leaner** | **Low** | **Non-load-bearing partitions only** |
| **Lime mortars and cement-lime** | **Low but WORKABLE and forgiving** | **Traditional and conservation work** |

> **Options (a) and (b) are real mixes for lighter duty, which makes them the designed distractors — the question turns on the SEISMIC requirement.**

**Why a seismic region requires a richer mortar — the reasoning:**

> **Masonry's weakness is TENSION and SHEAR, and both are carried by the MORTAR JOINTS rather than by the units:**

| Property | Governed by |
|---|---|
| **COMPRESSIVE strength of the masonry** | **Mainly the UNITS, with the mortar contributing** |
| **TENSILE and FLEXURAL strength** | **Almost entirely the MORTAR and its BOND to the units** ← |
| **SHEAR strength** | **The mortar's bond and friction** ← |
| **Behaviour under cyclic (earthquake) loading** | **The joints — which is where the cracking and sliding occur** ← |

> **An earthquake loads a wall IN SHEAR (in its own plane) and IN BENDING (out of plane), and both are joint-governed.**

> **So the mortar's strength and, more importantly, its BOND to the bricks determine how the wall performs — and a lean mortar has poor bond.**

> **That is why the seismic codes specify a richer mix: not for compressive strength, which a lean mortar could supply, but for BOND and SHEAR.**

**Why a mortar should NOT be stronger than necessary — the qualification that matters:**

> **It is tempting to conclude that richer is always better, and it is not:**

| Consequence of an excessively rich mortar | Note |
|---|---|
| **The mortar becomes STRONGER than the BRICKS** | **Cracks then pass THROUGH the bricks rather than along the joints** ← |
| **Cracking is CONCENTRATED into few wide cracks rather than distributed** | **Fewer, wider cracks are worse than many fine ones** ← |
| **Greater SHRINKAGE, hence shrinkage cracking** | A rich cement mortar shrinks more |
| **Reduced ability to accommodate MOVEMENT** | **A weaker mortar deforms and redistributes; a rigid one cracks** ← |
| **Repointing becomes destructive** | The mortar cannot be removed without damaging the units |
| **Cost** | Cement is the expensive component |

> **The FIRST TWO rows express the classical masonry principle: THE MORTAR SHOULD BE THE WEAKER COMPONENT, so that cracking occurs in the joints where it can be repaired, rather than through the units where it cannot.**

> **That principle is why conservation work on historic masonry uses LIME mortars: a cement mortar in an old soft-brick wall is far stronger than the bricks, and the resulting cracks destroy the bricks themselves.**

> **So the seismic requirement for 1:4 and the conservation requirement for a weak lime mortar are not contradictory — they apply to different masonry with different units, and both follow from the same principle of matching the mortar to the unit.**

> **For modern fired bricks of 7.5 to 10 MPa, a 1:4 mortar is appropriately matched. For a soft historic brick of 3 MPa it would not be.**

**The functions of mortar, since the mix is chosen to serve them:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **BIND the units into a monolithic mass** | The primary structural function |
| **DISTRIBUTE the load evenly over the units' bearing faces** | **Bricks are not perfectly flat; mortar accommodates the irregularity** ← |
| **Accommodate DIMENSIONAL variation in the units** | Bricks vary by several millimetres |
| **SEAL the joints against water and air penetration** | Durability and weathertightness |
| **Provide the TENSILE and SHEAR capacity** | ← the seismic requirement |
| **Provide appearance** | Pointing |

> **The LOAD DISTRIBUTION function in the second row explains why a mortar joint must be neither too thin nor too thick:**

| Joint thickness | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Too THIN (below about 6 mm)** | **Cannot accommodate the units' irregularity; point contacts develop and bricks crack** ← |
| **10 mm — the standard** | **The design value; the modular brick dimensions assume it** ← |
| **Too THICK (above about 15 mm)** | **The mortar's lower strength and higher deformability reduce the masonry's strength; more shrinkage** ← |

> **The 10 mm standard joint is what makes modular bricks work: the 190 mm brick plus a 10 mm joint gives the 200 mm module, so dimensions work out in round hundreds.**

> **And it is why brickwork gauge is checked on site — a wall built with 15 mm joints will be the wrong height after twenty courses, and its strength will be lower than designed.**

**The seismic masonry provisions of which the mortar is one part:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **A rich mortar — 1:4 or richer** | ← this question |
| **HORIZONTAL BANDS at plinth, sill, lintel and roof levels** | **The most important measure — the LINTEL band above all** ← |
| **VERTICAL reinforcement at corners, wall junctions and opening jambs** | Resists out-of-plane bending |
| **Limits on the SIZE and POSITION of openings** | **Openings weaken the piers between them, and one near a corner is worst** ← |
| **Limits on wall LENGTH between cross walls, and on height** | Slenderness |
| **A rigid ROOF DIAPHRAGM tied to the walls** | So the walls act as a box |
| **Good QUALITY units, well soaked, properly bonded** | The basics |

> **The BANDS remain the single most effective measure, for the reason given earlier: masonry has essentially no tensile strength, and the bands supply the tensile continuity that ties the walls into a box rather than leaving them as separate panels free to fall outward.**

> **A rich mortar improves each wall's own shear strength; the bands make the walls act together.**

> **Both are needed, and of the two the bands matter more — which is why a limited budget should provide bands in a 1:6 mortar rather than 1:4 mortar without bands.**

> **That is a genuine and useful priority judgement for the low-cost construction that dominates Nepali housing, and it is the kind of decision an engineer is asked to make in practice.**

examTip.trick: **1:4 or richer for load-bearing masonry in a seismic region** — not for compressive strength, which a leaner mix could give, but for BOND and SHEAR, which the joints carry.
examTip.trap: **Richer is not always better: the MORTAR SHOULD BE WEAKER THAN THE UNITS**, so cracks run in the repairable joints rather than through the bricks. That is why conservation work uses LIME mortar in soft historic brickwork.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 10 mm joint is the standard — 190 mm brick plus 10 mm gives the 200 mm module.** Too thin cannot accommodate the units' irregularity; too thick weakens the wall. And of the seismic measures, the BANDS matter more than the mortar: bands in 1:6 beat 1:4 without bands.

questions.stem: The PEAK FACTOR used to convert average daily water demand to peak hourly demand for a town of moderate population is generally taken as:
questions.solution:
**2.7.**

**The standard peak factors, which multiply the AVERAGE daily demand:**

| Demand | Peak factor | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **AVERAGE daily demand** | **1.0** | The base |
| **MAXIMUM DAILY demand** | **1.8** | **The average of the maximum day in the year** ← |
| **MAXIMUM HOURLY demand** | **1.5 × the maximum daily** | **= 1.5 × 1.8 = 2.7 of the average** ← |
| **PEAK (maximum hourly of the maximum day)** | **2.7** ← | **The design figure for distribution** |
| **Fire demand added separately** | — | Coincident with maximum daily |

> **So the 2.7 is not an independent figure but the PRODUCT of the two: 1.8 for the peak DAY and a further 1.5 for the peak HOUR within it.**

> **Options (a) 1.5 and (b) 1.8 are the two component factors offered separately, and (c) 2.0 is the peak factor for a very large city — every distractor is a real number from the same derivation.**

**Which factor governs which component of the system — the essential application:**

| Component | Designed for |
|---|---|
| **SOURCE (river intake, well field, reservoir yield)** | **MAXIMUM DAILY demand — a source cannot be sized for a peak hour, and storage absorbs the hourly variation** ← |
| **Water TREATMENT plant** | **MAXIMUM DAILY demand** ← |
| **PUMPS and rising main to the service reservoir** | **Maximum daily, over the pumping hours** |
| **SERVICE RESERVOIR** | **Sized to absorb the difference between the steady supply and the varying demand** ← |
| **DISTRIBUTION mains** | **MAXIMUM HOURLY demand — or maximum daily plus fire demand, whichever is greater** ← |

> **The division is the important idea: the SOURCE and the TREATMENT PLANT are sized on the maximum DAY, while the DISTRIBUTION network is sized on the maximum HOUR.**

> **What makes that possible is the SERVICE RESERVOIR, which sits between them and absorbs the hourly variation: the plant produces steadily through the day, the reservoir fills when demand is low and empties when it is high, and the network draws at the varying rate.**

> **Without the reservoir, the treatment plant would have to be sized for the peak hour — 50 per cent larger for no benefit, since it would run at part load nearly all the time.**

> **So the service reservoir is an economic device as much as an operational one, and that is the clearest way to state its purpose.**

**Why the peak factor FALLS as the population RISES:**

| Population | Typical peak factor |
|---|---|
| **Under 50,000** | **3.0 and above** ← |
| **50,000 to 200,000** | **2.5 to 3.0** |
| **Above 200,000** | **2.0 to 2.5** ← |
| **A single house** | **Extremely high — perhaps 10 or more** ← |

> **The reason is STATISTICAL AVERAGING: in a small community, everybody bathes and cooks at nearly the same hour, so the demands coincide and the peak is sharp.**

> **In a large city the habits are more varied and the peaks of different districts do not align, so the aggregate curve is flatter.**

> **The single-house row makes the principle vivid: a house's demand is zero for most of the day and very high for a few minutes, so its instantaneous peak factor is enormous — which is why individual service pipes are sized by fixture-unit methods rather than by any average.**

> **The same averaging principle appears throughout engineering — in the live load reduction permitted on columns carrying many floors, and in the diversity factor applied to electrical loads.**

**The design PER CAPITA demand, since the peak factor multiplies it:**

| Component | Litres per capita per day |
|---|---|
| **DOMESTIC** | **135 (Indian standard for a piped supply with sewerage)** ← |
| **Industrial and commercial** | 20 to 25 |
| **Public purposes — parks, street washing** | 10 |
| **Fire fighting** | 1 |
| **LOSSES and wastage (unaccounted for water)** | **55 — the LARGEST non-domestic item** ← |
| **TOTAL design figure** | **About 200 to 270 lpcd for a well-served town** ← |

> **Nepal's own norms are lower and vary by settlement type — around 45 lpcd for a rural water supply, 65 to 100 for a small town, and higher in urban Kathmandu — reflecting service levels rather than any difference in need.**

> **The LOSSES row deserves the emphasis: unaccounted-for water at 55 lpcd out of 200 is roughly 25 to 30 per cent of the supply, and in many South Asian systems the real figure is 40 per cent or more.**

> **That is the single largest opportunity in most water supply systems: reducing losses from 40 per cent to 20 per cent frees a quarter of the supply at a fraction of the cost of a new source.**

> **And it is why LEAK DETECTION and DISTRICT METERING have become the priority in system improvement — new sources are expensive and contentious, while the water already being produced and lost is not.**

**The other design decisions the peak factor participates in:**

> **DESIGN PERIOD — the number of years ahead for which a component is sized:**

| Component | Design period |
|---|---|
| **Storage DAMS and large sources** | **50 years — hard to extend** ← |
| **Infiltration works, wells** | 30 years |
| **Water TREATMENT plant** | **15 years, extended in modules** ← |
| **Pipe mains and distribution** | **30 years — the pipe is cheap, the trench is not** ← |
| **Pumps** | **10 years — short-lived and easily replaced** ← |

> **The logic is consistent: the design period is LONG where extension is DIFFICULT or where the marginal cost of extra capacity is small, and SHORT where the component is easily added to or replaced.**

> **The PIPE row makes the point best — laying a larger pipe costs little more than a smaller one because the excavation, bedding and reinstatement dominate, and relaying it later means digging up the street again.**

> **So pipes are sized generously and pumps are not, and the design periods reflect that rather than any difference in the pipes' or pumps' physical life.**

examTip.trick: **2.7 = 1.8 (peak DAY) × 1.5 (peak HOUR within it).** Options (a) and (b) are the two components offered separately.
examTip.trap: **SOURCE and TREATMENT PLANT are sized on the maximum DAY; DISTRIBUTION MAINS on the maximum HOUR.** The SERVICE RESERVOIR between them absorbs the hourly variation — which is what saves the plant from being 50 % larger.
examTip.mnemonic: **The peak factor FALLS as population rises** — statistical averaging: in a small town everyone bathes at the same hour. And note LOSSES at 55 lpcd out of ~200: reducing unaccounted-for water is the cheapest new source most systems have.

questions.stem: The principal purpose of a BREAK PRESSURE TANK in a gravity water supply pipeline in hilly terrain is to:
options: Store water to meet the peak hourly demand
Remove silt and suspended matter from the flow
Limit the STATIC HEAD in the pipe below the tank by exposing the flow to atmospheric pressure
Provide a chlorination point along the main
questions.solution:
**To LIMIT THE STATIC HEAD in the pipeline below it, by breaking the continuous water column and exposing the flow to atmospheric pressure.**

**Why the problem arises — the arithmetic of a hill pipeline:**

> **In a gravity system, the STATIC HEAD at any point is simply the vertical distance below the water surface at the source, and it does not depend on the pipe's length or its route:**

> **Pressure (m of water) = vertical drop; and 10 m of head ≈ 1 bar ≈ 0.1 MPa**

| Vertical drop from the source | Static pressure at the low point |
|---|---|
| **50 m** | **5 bar** |
| **100 m** | **10 bar** ← |
| **200 m** | **20 bar** ← |
| **500 m** | **50 bar** ← |

> **A Nepali hill supply may take water from a spring several hundred metres above the village it serves, and the pressure at the bottom would then far exceed what ordinary pipe can hold.**

| Pipe | Typical pressure rating |
|---|---|
| **HDPE PE80, PN 6** | **6 bar — about 60 m of head** ← |
| **HDPE PN 10** | **10 bar — 100 m** ← |
| **HDPE PN 16** | 16 bar |
| **GI medium class** | **About 20-25 bar** |
| **Ductile iron** | Higher still |

> **So a 250 m drop would burst PN 10 pipe two and a half times over — and the response of specifying a heavier pipe for the whole length is expensive and often impossible to obtain.**

**What the break pressure tank does:**

| Feature | Effect |
|---|---|
| **A small covered tank, OPEN TO THE ATMOSPHERE, on the pipeline** | **The water column is interrupted** ← |
| **Pressure at the tank returns to ZERO gauge** | **The static head below it is measured from the TANK's water level, not the source's** ← |
| **Placed at intervals down the fall** | **Each tank resets the head, so no reach exceeds the pipe's rating** ← |
| **Inlet controlled by a float valve, with an overflow** | Prevents the tank overtopping when demand falls |

> **A 250 m fall with two break pressure tanks becomes three reaches of about 83 m each, every one of which PN 10 pipe will carry comfortably.**

> **That is the whole idea: THE TANK CONVERTS ONE UNMANAGEABLE HEAD INTO SEVERAL MANAGEABLE ONES, at the cost of a small masonry or ferrocement structure.**

> **Options (a), (b) and (d) all name real functions of other structures on the same pipeline — a SERVICE RESERVOIR stores for peak demand, a SEDIMENTATION or silt tank removes suspended matter, and chlorination is done at the reservoir — so the option set is drawn entirely from the same system.**

**The other appurtenances on a transmission main, since each answers a specific hazard:**

| Appurtenance | Position | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **AIR VALVE (air release / vacuum breaker)** | **At the HIGH points (summits)** ← | **Releases accumulated air, which would otherwise form a lock and throttle the flow; and ADMITS air on draining, to prevent the pipe COLLAPSING under vacuum** ← |
| **WASHOUT / scour valve** | **At the LOW points** ← | **Drains the main for maintenance and flushes out accumulated silt** ← |
| **SLUICE / gate valve** | At intervals and at branches | **Isolates a section for repair without shutting the whole main** ← |
| **REFLUX (non-return / check) valve** | On pumping mains | Prevents reverse flow when the pump stops |
| **PRESSURE RELIEF valve** | Where surge is expected | Limits transient pressure |
| **BREAK PRESSURE TANK** | **At intervals down a steep fall** ← | **This question** |
| **THRUST BLOCKS** | **At bends, tees, reducers and dead ends** ← | **Resist the unbalanced force from the change of momentum and pressure** ← |

> **The AIR VALVE entry deserves its emphasis because its two functions are opposite and both matter:**

> **Air comes out of solution and collects at summits, where it forms a pocket that reduces the effective bore and can stop the flow entirely — an "air lock", and a very common cause of a gravity scheme delivering far less than its design flow.**

> **And in the other direction, draining a pipeline without admitting air creates a partial vacuum. A thin-walled pipe has very little resistance to EXTERNAL pressure and will collapse — which is why the same fitting must also let air IN.**

> **The rule to carry: AIR VALVES AT THE PEAKS, WASHOUTS IN THE VALLEYS.**

**WATER HAMMER, since the break pressure tank helps with it too:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cause** | **A sudden change of velocity — a valve closed quickly, a pump stopping** ← |
| **Magnitude** | **The pressure rise can be MANY TIMES the static head** ← |
| **The Joukowsky equation** | **Δp = ρcΔv, with c the wave celerity — about 1,200 m/s in steel, 300-500 m/s in HDPE** ← |
| **Controls** | **Close valves SLOWLY; surge tanks; air vessels; relief valves; flywheels on pumps** ← |
| **The break pressure tank's role** | **It provides a free surface, so the surge wave is reflected and dissipated rather than travelling the whole line** ← |

> **The CELERITY figures in the third row carry a useful practical point: HDPE's much lower wave speed means it develops a far smaller surge pressure than steel for the same velocity change — roughly a third to a quarter.**

> **A flexible pipe absorbs the shock by expanding slightly, and a rigid one cannot. So plastic pipe is more forgiving of hydraulic transients as well as cheaper to lay, which is one more reason it dominates rural water supply.**

**And the practical design points for the tank itself:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Keep it SMALL** | **It is not a reservoir — a few minutes' storage is enough** ← |
| **COVER it and screen every opening** | **An open tank on a hillside is a contamination point and a mosquito breeding site** ← |
| **Provide an OVERFLOW sized for the full inflow** | **The tank must not surcharge and pressurise the reach above** ← |
| **Provide a washout and access for cleaning** | Silt accumulates |
| **Site it where it can be REACHED for maintenance** | **A tank that cannot be visited will not be maintained** ← |
| **Protect against freezing at high altitude** | Bury or insulate |

> **The COVER requirement is the one most often neglected in practice and the most consequential: a break pressure tank sits on the line AFTER the source protection and BEFORE the village, so contamination entering there reaches every consumer.**

> **Numerous rural schemes deliver contaminated water from a protected spring for exactly this reason — the fault is not at the source but at an unscreened tank halfway down the hill.**

examTip.trick: **A break pressure tank exposes the flow to ATMOSPHERE, so the static head below it is measured from the TANK's level, not the source's.** 10 m of head ≈ 1 bar; a 250 m fall with two tanks becomes three reaches of ~83 m.
examTip.trap: **Static head depends only on the VERTICAL DROP — not on the pipe's length or route.** All four options name real functions on the same pipeline: storage is the service reservoir's, silt removal the sedimentation tank's.
examTip.mnemonic: **AIR VALVES AT THE PEAKS, WASHOUTS IN THE VALLEYS.** The air valve works both ways — it releases air locks and ADMITS air on draining, or the pipe collapses under vacuum. And always COVER and SCREEN the tank: it sits downstream of the source protection.

questions.stem: The process of COAGULATION in water treatment primarily removes:
options: COLLOIDAL and fine suspended matter that will not settle
questions.solution:
**COLLOIDAL and fine suspended matter that will not settle** under gravity alone.

**Why colloids will not settle — the problem coagulation solves:**

| Particle | Size | Settling time through 1 m of water |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravel** | **10 mm** | **About 1 second** |
| **Coarse sand** | **1 mm** | **About 10 seconds** |
| **Fine sand** | **0.1 mm** | **About 2 minutes** |
| **Silt** | **0.01 mm** | **About 2 hours** |
| **Bacteria** | **0.001 mm (1 µm)** | **About 8 days** ← |
| **COLLOIDS** | **0.001 to 1 µm** | **Months to YEARS — effectively NEVER** ← |

> **So plain sedimentation removes sand and silt and is useless against colloids, and the colloids are what make water turbid and coloured.**

> **Two things keep them suspended:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **Their tiny mass — Brownian motion exceeds gravity** | Thermal agitation keeps them dispersed |
| **Their SURFACE CHARGE — almost all natural colloids carry a NEGATIVE charge, so they REPEL one another** ← | **The dominant cause, and the one coagulation attacks** |

**How coagulation works — the two distinct stages:**

| Stage | Mechanism | Mixing |
|---|---|---|
| **COAGULATION** | **DESTABILISATION — the coagulant's positive ions neutralise the colloids' negative charge, so they no longer repel** ← | **RAPID / FLASH mixing, 30-60 seconds, high velocity gradient** ← |
| **FLOCCULATION** | **AGGREGATION — the destabilised particles collide and grow into visible FLOC** ← | **SLOW, GENTLE mixing, 20-40 minutes** ← |

> **The MIXING requirements are opposite, and that is the practically important point:**

> **Coagulation needs VIOLENT mixing so the coagulant disperses through the whole volume before it hydrolyses — it has only seconds to act.**

> **Flocculation needs GENTLE mixing so that particles are brought into contact often enough to collide, but not so violently that the fragile floc already formed is torn apart.**

> **Mixing too vigorously in the flocculation basin destroys the floc; mixing too little means the particles never meet. The velocity gradient G is the parameter used to specify it — around 700 s⁻¹ for flash mixing and 20 to 70 s⁻¹ for flocculation.**

**The coagulants:**

| Coagulant | Formula | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **ALUM (aluminium sulphate)** | **Al₂(SO₄)₃·18H₂O** | **The most common; effective pH 6.5 to 8.5** ← |
| **Ferric chloride** | FeCl₃ | **Wider pH range, 4 to 11; heavier floc** ← |
| **Ferrous sulphate (copperas)** | FeSO₄·7H₂O | With lime |
| **Sodium aluminate** | NaAlO₂ | For soft waters |
| **Polyaluminium chloride (PAC)** | — | **Prehydrolysed — less pH depression, less sludge** ← |
| **Polyelectrolytes** | Organic polymers | **Coagulant AIDS — bridge particles, strengthen floc** ← |

> **ALUM's reaction consumes ALKALINITY and produces acid, which is the operational fact that matters:**

> **Al₂(SO₄)₃·18H₂O + 3Ca(HCO₃)₂ → 2Al(OH)₃↓ + 3CaSO₄ + 6CO₂ + 18H₂O**

> **The Al(OH)₃ precipitate is the FLOC — a gelatinous solid that both sweeps particles down with it and adsorbs colour and organics.**

> **The alkalinity consumption means a soft, low-alkalinity water will have its pH DEPRESSED below the effective range, and the coagulation will fail — so LIME or soda ash must be added to supply the alkalinity.**

> **That is the most common cause of poor coagulation in practice, and it is diagnosed by measuring the pH after dosing rather than before.**

**Determining the DOSE — the jar test:**

> **There is no formula: the optimum dose depends on the water's turbidity, alkalinity, pH, temperature and the nature of its colloids, and it CHANGES with the season.**

> **The JAR TEST is the standard method: six beakers of the raw water, dosed with increasing coagulant, flash-mixed, slow-mixed and settled in parallel, and the residual turbidity measured.**

| Observation from a jar test | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Turbidity falls with dose, reaches a minimum, then RISES again** | **RESTABILISATION — an overdose reverses the charge from negative to POSITIVE and the colloids repel once more** ← |
| **Floc forms but does not settle** | Too light — a coagulant aid or a heavier coagulant is needed |
| **No floc at all** | **pH out of range — check the alkalinity** ← |

> **The RESTABILISATION effect in the first row is the counter-intuitive one and it is real: MORE COAGULANT CAN GIVE WORSE WATER.**

> **An operator who responds to poor settling by increasing the dose may be making it worse, which is precisely why the jar test is run rather than the dose being guessed.**

**Where coagulation sits in the treatment train:**

> **Screening → aeration → COAGULATION (flash mix) → FLOCCULATION → SEDIMENTATION → FILTRATION → DISINFECTION → storage**

| Unit | Removes |
|---|---|
| **Plain sedimentation** | Coarse settleable solids |
| **COAGULATION + flocculation + sedimentation** | **Colloids, most turbidity, colour, some bacteria (60-90 %)** ← |
| **Rapid sand FILTRATION** | **Remaining floc and turbidity, more bacteria (98-99 %)** ← |
| **DISINFECTION** | **Pathogens — the final barrier** ← |

> **Option (c)'s disinfection is the LAST step of the train and a different process entirely — coagulation removes bacteria only incidentally, by enmeshing them in floc.**

> **And the MULTIPLE BARRIER principle that the train embodies is the essential public health idea: no single process is relied upon.**

> **Each stage removes a large fraction of what reaches it, so that a failure of one stage still leaves the water far from raw — and that redundancy, rather than any one process's efficiency, is what makes a treated supply safe.**

examTip.trick: **Coagulation removes COLLOIDS — particles of 0.001 to 1 µm that would take months to settle** because their NEGATIVE surface charge makes them repel one another.
examTip.trap: **COAGULATION needs VIOLENT flash mixing (30-60 s); FLOCCULATION needs GENTLE slow mixing (20-40 min).** Mixing vigorously in the flocculator destroys the floc it just made.
examTip.mnemonic: **Alum CONSUMES ALKALINITY and depresses pH** — the commonest cause of coagulation failure in soft water, cured by lime. And an OVERDOSE can RESTABILISE the colloids by reversing their charge: more coagulant, worse water. Hence the jar test.

questions.stem: The rate of filtration of a RAPID sand filter, compared with a SLOW sand filter, is approximately:
questions.solution:
**30 to 50 times greater.**

**The two filters compared:**

| Property | SLOW sand filter | RAPID (gravity) sand filter |
|---|---|---|
| **Filtration rate** | **100 to 200 litres/m²/hour (0.1-0.2 m/h)** | **3,000 to 6,000 litres/m²/hour (3-6 m/h)** ← |
| **Ratio** | **1** | **About 30 to 50 times** ← |
| **Effective size of sand** | **0.2 to 0.3 mm — FINE** | **0.4 to 0.7 mm — COARSER** |
| **Uniformity coefficient** | 2 to 3 | 1.3 to 1.7 |
| **Bed depth** | 0.9 to 1.1 m | 0.6 to 0.75 m |
| **AREA required** | **LARGE** ← | **Small** |
| **Pretreatment needed** | **NONE — plain sedimentation suffices** ← | **COAGULATION and flocculation ESSENTIAL** ← |
| **Cleaning** | **SCRAPING the top 20-25 mm, by hand, every 1-3 months** ← | **BACKWASHING, 24-48 hours, automatic** ← |
| **Bacterial removal** | **98 to 99.5 % — EXCELLENT** ← | **80 to 90 % — inferior** ← |
| **Turbidity of raw water tolerated** | **Below 30 NTU** | **Any, after coagulation** |
| **Loss of head** | 0.1 m initial to 0.7 m final | 0.3 m initial to 2.5-3.5 m final |
| **Skilled supervision** | **Not needed** ← | **Needed** |
| **Capital cost** | **High (land)** | **Lower** |
| **Operating cost** | **Low** ← | **Higher (power, chemicals)** |

**Why the slow filter is BETTER bacteriologically despite being slower — the mechanism:**

> **A slow sand filter does not work primarily by STRAINING. Its removal is largely BIOLOGICAL, and it depends on a layer that forms on its surface.**

> **The SCHMUTZDECKE (German, "dirt blanket") is a slimy biological mat of algae, bacteria, protozoa and their products that develops on the sand surface over the first days of operation:**

| What the schmutzdecke does | Note |
|---|---|
| **Strains very fine particles** | Its pores are far finer than the sand's |
| **BIOLOGICALLY consumes organic matter** | The bacteria in it feed on the water's organics |
| **PREDATION — protozoa eat the bacteria in the water** ← | **This is what gives the 99 %+ bacterial removal** |
| **Adsorbs colour and dissolved organics** | — |

> **So the removal is a LIVING process, and that has consequences:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A new or newly scraped filter must RIPEN before its water is used** | **Typically 1-2 days while the schmutzdecke re-forms** ← |
| **The filter must run CONTINUOUSLY** | **Interrupting the flow starves the biology** ← |
| **Chlorinated water must not be applied** | It would kill the layer |
| **Cold weather slows the biology** | Performance falls in winter |

> **The RIPENING requirement is the operational subtlety and the one most often violated: water filtered immediately after scraping is not properly treated, and must be run to waste.**

**Why a rapid filter MUST have coagulation before it:**

> **A rapid filter's sand is COARSER and its rate is 40 times higher, so straining alone would remove very little — the colloids would pass straight through.**

> **Its removal depends on the particles arriving already DESTABILISED and formed into floc, which then attaches to the sand grains by:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **Straining** | Only the largest floc |
| **SEDIMENTATION within the pores** | The pore spaces act as tiny settling basins |
| **ADSORPTION and adhesion to the grains** | **The principal mechanism, and it requires destabilised particles** ← |
| **Flocculation within the bed** | Particles collide as they pass |

> **So applying uncoagulated water to a rapid filter produces poor water AND a rapid loss of head — the fine material passes or blinds the surface.**

> **That is why coagulation is listed as ESSENTIAL rather than merely helpful: without it the rapid filter does not work at all.**

**BACKWASHING — the rapid filter's cleaning cycle:**

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Trigger** | **Head loss reaching 2.5-3 m, or breakthrough of turbidity, or a set time** ← |
| **Method** | **Reverse flow UPWARD at 0.6-0.9 m/min, expanding the bed by 30-50 %** ← |
| **Air scour** | Often applied first to break up the accumulated solids |
| **Duration** | 5 to 15 minutes |
| **Water used** | **1 to 5 per cent of the filter's output** ← |
| **Filter-to-waste after backwash** | **The first filtrate is turbid and is run to waste** ← |

> **The BED EXPANSION is the essential mechanism: the sand must be FLUIDISED so the grains separate and rub against one another, releasing the trapped floc.**

> **Too LITTLE expansion and the bed is not cleaned, so MUD BALLS form — agglomerations of sand and floc that grow, sink into the bed and destroy its uniformity.**

> **Too MUCH expansion and the sand is carried away over the wash-water troughs, losing media.**

> **And the FILTER-TO-WASTE step in the last row parallels the slow filter's ripening: immediately after backwashing, a rapid filter also produces its poorest water, because the grains are clean and their adsorptive surfaces have not yet been conditioned.**

> **So both filter types produce their worst water just after cleaning, for related reasons, and both require that first output to be discarded — which is a satisfying convergence between two very different processes.**

**Which to choose:**

| Prefer SLOW sand where | Prefer RAPID sand where |
|---|---|
| **Land is CHEAP and available** | **Land is scarce or expensive** |
| **Skilled operators are NOT available** ← | Skilled operation is assured |
| **Chemicals are hard to obtain** ← | Chemicals are readily supplied |
| **Raw water turbidity is LOW and steady** | **Turbidity is high or variable** ← |
| **Small towns and rural supplies** ← | **Large cities** |

> **For rural Nepal, the slow sand filter is often the better choice for exactly the reasons in the left column — it needs no chemicals, no power and no skilled operator, and its bacterial removal is superior.**

> **Its limitation is land and its intolerance of high turbidity, which for a Himalayan river carrying glacial silt in the monsoon is a serious one — so a roughing filter or a settling tank ahead of it is usually necessary.**

examTip.trick: **Slow 100-200 L/m²/h; rapid 3,000-6,000 L/m²/h — about 30 to 50 times.** Slow uses FINER sand (0.2-0.3 mm) and needs NO coagulation; rapid uses coarser sand and coagulation is ESSENTIAL.
examTip.trap: **The SLOW filter gives BETTER bacterial removal (98-99.5 % against 80-90 %)** — because its removal is BIOLOGICAL, by the SCHMUTZDECKE, with protozoa preying on bacteria. Slower is better here, not worse.
examTip.mnemonic: **Both filters give their WORST water just after cleaning** — the slow filter must RIPEN 1-2 days after scraping, the rapid filter runs FILTER-TO-WASTE after backwashing. Inadequate backwash expansion produces MUD BALLS.

questions.stem: The minimum SELF-CLEANSING velocity generally adopted in the design of a sanitary sewer is:
questions.solution:
**0.6 m/s.**

**The sewer velocity limits:**

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **MINIMUM — self-cleansing** | **0.6 m/s (some codes 0.8 m/s for storm sewers)** ← | **Below this, SOLIDS DEPOSIT and the sewer silts up** |
| **Desirable range** | **0.6 to 1.2 m/s** | Neither depositing nor eroding |
| **MAXIMUM — non-scouring** | **2.4 to 3.0 m/s** ← | **Above this, the sewer's lining ABRADES** |

> **Option (c) 1.2 m/s is the upper end of the desirable range and (d) 2.4 m/s the maximum — both real values, offered for the minimum.**

**Why a MINIMUM velocity is needed — the distinctive feature of sewer design:**

> **Sewage carries GRIT, sand, faecal solids and debris. If the velocity falls too low, these settle out on the invert.**

| Consequence of deposition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The cross-section is reduced, so the capacity falls** | And the velocity falls further — a self-worsening cycle ← |
| **The deposits decompose ANAEROBICALLY** | **Producing H₂S — odour, and CROWN CORROSION** ← |
| **Eventual BLOCKAGE and surcharge** | Sewage backs up into properties |
| **Expensive mechanical cleaning** | Rodding, jetting, or excavation |

> **The self-worsening character in the first row is what makes the minimum velocity a hard requirement rather than a preference: a sewer that begins to silt continues to silt, because the deposit reduces the section and slows the flow further.**

> **So a sewer that has silted does not recover on its own, and must be cleaned.**

**The CROWN CORROSION mechanism, since it is the most destructive consequence:**

| Step | Process |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Sewage goes SEPTIC (anaerobic) in slow-moving or deposited material** |
| **2** | **Sulphate-reducing bacteria produce HYDROGEN SULPHIDE (H₂S) in the liquid** ← |
| **3** | **H₂S is volatile and escapes into the sewer's air space above the flow** |
| **4** | **It dissolves in the moisture condensed on the CROWN (the top of the pipe)** ← |
| **5** | **AEROBIC Thiobacillus bacteria there oxidise it to SULPHURIC ACID (H₂SO₄)** ← |
| **6** | **The acid attacks the concrete's cement paste — the crown erodes and eventually collapses** ← |

> **The result is a sewer that is sound at its invert (permanently submerged, so no oxygen and no acid) and DESTROYED at its crown — which is diagnostic of the mechanism.**

> **The remedies follow directly from the steps: maintain velocity so the sewage does not go septic, VENTILATE so the H₂S is carried away, avoid long detention in rising mains, and use acid-resistant linings (PVC, HDPE, vitrified clay, or a sacrificial concrete thickness) where the risk is high.**

> **Crown corrosion has destroyed major sewers in warm climates within twenty years of construction, so it is not a marginal concern — and warm sewage, as in Nepal's Terai, accelerates it.**

**Why a MAXIMUM velocity is also needed:**

> **Sewage is ABRASIVE — it carries grit and sand — so a high velocity erodes the sewer's invert, particularly in concrete and brick sewers.**

| Material | Maximum permissible velocity |
|---|---|
| **Vitrified clay, cast iron** | **3.0 m/s and above — hard and resistant** |
| **Concrete, M25 and above** | **2.5 to 3.0 m/s** |
| **Stoneware** | 3.0 m/s |
| **Brick masonry** | **1.5 to 2.5 m/s — the softest** ← |

> **Where the topography forces a steep grade, DROP MANHOLES are used: the sewer runs at an acceptable grade between manholes and the level is dropped vertically within the manhole.**

> **That converts a continuous steep slope into a series of flat runs and vertical drops, keeping the flow velocity within limits while following steep ground — which is exactly the condition in Nepal's hill towns, so drop manholes are common there.**

**Achieving self-cleansing velocity at LOW flows — the real design difficulty:**

> **A sewer must carry the peak flow of the design year AND remain self-cleansing at the minimum flow of the first year of operation — and those may differ by a factor of ten or more.**

| Approach | Note |
|---|---|
| **Design so that the velocity at MINIMUM flow still reaches 0.6 m/s** | The direct requirement |
| **Use the smallest practicable diameter** | **Minimum 150 mm for a lateral, 200 mm for a street sewer** ← |
| **Steepen the gradient** | Limited by ground slope and excavation depth |
| **Use an EGG-SHAPED section for combined sewers** | **Narrow invert concentrates low flows and keeps velocity up** ← |
| **Provide FLUSHING arrangements** | Flushing tanks or manual flushing at the head of runs |
| **Build in STAGES rather than to the ultimate size at once** | — |

> **The EGG-SHAPED sewer is the classical solution and is worth understanding: a circular sewer running at a small depth has a wide, shallow flow with a large wetted perimeter relative to its area, so the hydraulic radius and hence the velocity are low.**

> **An egg-shaped section, narrow at the bottom, concentrates the same small flow into a deeper, narrower stream with a better hydraulic radius — so the low-flow velocity is maintained.**

> **They are expensive to build and are now rare, but the reasoning is sound and it explains a great many Victorian sewers still in service.**

**And the useful hydraulic property of a circular sewer running part full:**

| Depth of flow | Velocity relative to full | Discharge relative to full |
|---|---|---|
| **0.5 D (half full)** | **1.00 — the SAME as full** ← | **0.50** |
| **0.8 D** | **1.14 — the MAXIMUM** ← | **0.98** |
| **0.94 D** | 1.12 | **1.08 — the MAXIMUM discharge** ← |
| **1.0 D (just full)** | 1.00 | 1.00 |

> **The two counter-intuitive results in this table are worth remembering: a sewer running HALF FULL has the SAME velocity as one running full, and a sewer running at 0.94 D carries MORE than when it is just full.**

> **The reason is that near the crown the added area is small while the added wetted perimeter is large, so the hydraulic radius falls — and the velocity with it.**

> **The practical consequence is that sewers are designed to run at 0.5 to 0.8 of full depth at the peak flow, which gives good velocity, ventilation space above the flow, and a reserve of capacity.**

examTip.trick: **0.6 m/s minimum self-cleansing; 0.6-1.2 desirable; 2.4-3.0 maximum non-scouring.** Options (c) and (d) are the upper limits offered for the lower one.
examTip.trap: **Silting is SELF-WORSENING** — the deposit reduces the section, which lowers the velocity further. A silted sewer does not recover on its own.
examTip.mnemonic: **CROWN CORROSION: septic sewage → H₂S → escapes to the air space → oxidised by Thiobacillus on the moist crown → SULPHURIC ACID → the crown erodes while the invert stays sound.** And a sewer HALF FULL has the SAME velocity as full; at 0.94 D it carries MORE than full.

questions.stem: The BOD₅ test measures:
options: The oxygen required to oxidise all organic matter chemically
The dissolved oxygen present in the sample
The oxygen consumed by micro-organisms in 5 days at 20 °C in degrading BIODEGRADABLE organic matter
questions.solution:
**The oxygen consumed by MICRO-ORGANISMS in 5 days at 20 °C in degrading BIODEGRADABLE organic matter.**

**The standard conditions, all of which are part of the definition:**

| Condition | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Duration** | **5 days** ← | **A compromise — see below** |
| **Temperature** | **20 °C** ← | **A standard temperate value; the rate is temperature-dependent** |
| **Incubation** | **In the DARK** ← | **Light would allow algal photosynthesis to PRODUCE oxygen and falsify the result** |
| **Measurement** | **Initial DO minus final DO, on a diluted sample** | Sewage would exhaust the oxygen otherwise |
| **Seeding** | Micro-organisms added if the sample lacks them | Industrial wastes especially |

> **The DARK requirement in the third row is a real and necessary precaution rather than a formality: an unshaded bottle containing algae would show a LOWER oxygen consumption, or even an INCREASE, because photosynthesis adds oxygen.**

**Why FIVE days, which is the question most often asked about the test:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Complete oxidation of carbonaceous matter takes about 20 days** | **BOD₅ is only about 68 per cent of the ultimate BOD** ← |
| **Five days is a practical laboratory turnaround** | A result within a working week |
| **The origin is British** | **The longest time a river takes to reach the sea in Britain — so five days' oxygen demand was what mattered** ← |
| **After 5 days, NITRIFICATION begins to interfere** | **Nitrifying bacteria consume oxygen too, inflating the result** ← |

> **The historical origin in the third row is genuine and is a good illustration of how a standard becomes universal: a figure chosen for British rivers is now used worldwide, including in places where no river takes five days to reach anywhere.**

> **The NITRIFICATION point is the technically important one: beyond about five days, nitrifying bacteria begin oxidising ammonia to nitrate, consuming oxygen in a process quite separate from the degradation of organic carbon.**

> **So a longer test measures CARBONACEOUS plus NITROGENOUS demand together, and the five-day period conveniently ends just before nitrification becomes significant.**

> **Where a longer test is needed, a nitrification INHIBITOR is added and the result is reported as CBOD (carbonaceous BOD).**

**BOD compared with the other measures of organic strength:**

| Test | Measures | Time | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BOD₅** | **BIODEGRADABLE organic matter, biologically** | **5 days** ← | **The most meaningful, the slowest** |
| **COD** | **ALL oxidisable matter, chemically (dichromate)** | **3 hours** ← | **Always HIGHER than BOD; includes non-biodegradable matter** |
| **TOC** | **Total organic CARBON** | **Minutes** | Instrumental |
| **ThOD** | Theoretical oxygen demand, from the chemical formula | Calculated | — |

> **The COD/BOD RATIO is the useful diagnostic derived from the first two:**

| COD/BOD ratio | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **1.5 to 2.5** | **Readily BIODEGRADABLE — domestic sewage; biological treatment will work well** ← |
| **2.5 to 4** | Partially biodegradable |
| **Above 4** | **POORLY biodegradable — industrial waste, possibly TOXIC to the biology; biological treatment may fail** ← |

> **So the two tests together tell you what one alone cannot: whether biological treatment is the right process for the waste.**

> **A high COD with a low BOD means the waste contains a great deal of organic matter that the bacteria cannot eat — and putting it into an activated sludge plant will simply pass it through, or poison the plant.**

> **That is why an industrial effluent is characterised by both, and why a trade effluent discharge consent specifies both.**

**Typical values, for calibration:**

| Water | BOD₅ (mg/L) |
|---|---|
| **Pristine mountain stream** | **Below 1** |
| **Clean river** | **1 to 2** |
| **Acceptable for a river receiving discharge** | Below 3 |
| **Treated effluent, standard for discharge to a stream** | **20 to 30** ← |
| **WEAK domestic sewage** | **110** |
| **MEDIUM domestic sewage** | **220** ← |
| **STRONG domestic sewage** | **400** |
| **Dairy or brewery waste** | **1,000 to 3,000** ← |
| **Distillery spent wash** | **40,000 to 100,000** ← |

> **The last two rows show why industrial wastes are treated separately: a distillery's effluent is a hundred times the strength of sewage, and discharging it to a municipal plant would overwhelm the works.**

**The first-order kinetics, since BOD₅ is usually converted to ultimate BOD:**

> **BOD_t = L(1 − 10^(−kt)) where L is the ultimate BOD and k is the rate constant, about 0.1 per day at 20 °C for domestic sewage.**

> **At t = 5 days with k = 0.1: BOD₅ = L(1 − 10^(−0.5)) = L(1 − 0.316) = 0.684 L**

> **So BOD₅ ≈ 0.68 L, which is the 68 per cent quoted above, and L ≈ 1.46 × BOD₅.**

> **The temperature correction is k_T = k₂₀ × 1.047^(T−20), so at 30 °C the rate constant is 1.047¹⁰ = 1.58 times the 20 °C value — the reaction runs 58 per cent faster.**

> **That has a direct practical meaning for Nepal's Terai and for any warm climate: organic matter is degraded FASTER, so a river's oxygen is consumed more quickly and over a SHORTER distance downstream.**

> **Warm water also holds LESS dissolved oxygen at saturation — 7.5 mg/L at 30 °C against 9.1 at 20 °C — so the demand rises exactly as the supply falls.**

> **The two effects compound, which is why oxygen sag in a tropical river is deeper and closer to the outfall than the same discharge would cause in a temperate one.**

examTip.trick: **BOD₅: 5 days, 20 °C, in the DARK** — the dark matters, since algae would photosynthesise and ADD oxygen. Option (b) describes COD, option (c) the DO test.
examTip.trap: **BOD₅ is only about 68 % of the ULTIMATE BOD** (L ≈ 1.46 × BOD₅). Five days is chosen partly because NITRIFICATION begins interfering beyond it — a longer test measures carbonaceous plus nitrogenous demand together.
examTip.mnemonic: **COD/BOD tells you whether biological treatment will work: 1.5-2.5 readily biodegradable, above 4 poorly biodegradable or toxic.** And in a warm climate the demand rises (k × 1.58 at 30 °C) exactly as the saturation DO falls (7.5 against 9.1 mg/L).

questions.stem: In an ACTIVATED SLUDGE process, the sludge that is returned from the secondary clarifier to the aeration tank serves to:
options: Reduce the volume of sludge for disposal
Maintain the required concentration of MICRO-ORGANISMS in the aeration tank
Provide additional oxygen to the mixed liquor
Settle out the grit that escaped the grit chamber
questions.solution:
**Maintain the required concentration of MICRO-ORGANISMS in the aeration tank.**

**Why the return is essential — the core of the process:**

> **The activated sludge process treats sewage by growing a population of bacteria that consume its organic matter. The rate of treatment depends on HOW MANY bacteria are present.**

> **The incoming sewage supplies very few. If the process relied on them alone, the aeration tank would need a detention time of days rather than hours.**

> **By SETTLING the bacteria out in the clarifier and RETURNING them, the concentration in the aeration tank is built up to 20 or 30 times what the influent would supply — so the same treatment is achieved in 4 to 8 hours.**

| Quantity | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **MLSS — mixed liquor suspended solids in the aeration tank** | **1,500 to 4,000 mg/L** ← |
| **MLVSS — the volatile (biological) fraction** | **About 70-80 % of MLSS** |
| **Suspended solids in the raw sewage** | **200 to 400 mg/L** |
| **RETURN sludge ratio (Q_r/Q)** | **25 to 100 per cent of the influent flow** ← |
| **Return sludge concentration** | **8,000 to 12,000 mg/L** |
| **Aeration detention time** | **4 to 8 hours** ← |

> **So the recirculation is what makes the process compact — and "activated sludge" is named for exactly this: the settled sludge is "activated" (biologically alive and hungry) and is put back to work.**

**The distinction between RETURN and WASTE sludge, which the question's option (a) gestures at:**

| Stream | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **RETURN activated sludge (RAS)** | **Maintains the MLSS — the biology's population** ← |
| **WASTE activated sludge (WAS)** | **Removes the EXCESS growth, controlling the sludge age** ← |

> **Both are drawn from the clarifier underflow and they do opposite things: the return maintains the population and the waste limits it.**

> **The bacteria GROW as they consume the organic matter, so the population would increase without limit if none were removed. The wasting rate therefore controls the SLUDGE AGE:**

> **Sludge age (SRT) = mass of solids in the system / mass of solids wasted per day**

| Sludge age | Process | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **0.5 to 2 days** | **HIGH-RATE activated sludge** | Partial treatment, poor settling |
| **5 to 15 days** | **CONVENTIONAL activated sludge** ← | **The normal range** |
| **Above 10 days** | **NITRIFICATION becomes possible** ← | **Nitrifiers grow slowly and are washed out at short sludge ages** |
| **20 to 30 days** | **EXTENDED AERATION** ← | **Sludge largely self-digested; little waste sludge; simple operation** |

> **The NITRIFICATION threshold is the most useful entry: nitrifying bacteria reproduce far more slowly than the carbon-eating heterotrophs, so if the sludge is wasted faster than they can multiply, they are washed out and no nitrification occurs.**

> **So whether a plant nitrifies is determined largely by its sludge age — which is a design and operating decision, not an accident.**

> **And EXTENDED AERATION at 20-30 days is the choice for small works: the long sludge age means the bacteria consume their own cell material, so very little sludge needs disposal and the operation is simple and tolerant — at the cost of a much larger tank and more aeration energy.**

**The F/M ratio, the other control parameter:**

> **F/M = food to micro-organism ratio = (BOD applied per day) / (mass of MLVSS in the tank)**

| F/M (kg BOD / kg MLVSS / day) | Regime |
|---|---|
| **0.05 to 0.15** | **Extended aeration — starved bacteria, excellent settling, low sludge production** ← |
| **0.2 to 0.4** | **Conventional — the normal design range** ← |
| **0.4 to 1.5** | **High rate — well-fed bacteria, poor settling** ← |

> **The pattern: LOW F/M means STARVED bacteria, which settle WELL because they flocculate when hungry; HIGH F/M means well-fed dispersed growth which settles BADLY.**

> **That is a genuinely useful operating insight — a plant with poor settling is often overloaded, and reducing the load or increasing the MLSS improves the settling.**

**BULKING — the process's characteristic failure:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | **The sludge will not settle or compact in the clarifier; the blanket rises and solids are carried over into the effluent** ← |
| **Principal cause** | **FILAMENTOUS organisms — long thread-like bacteria that bridge between flocs and hold them apart** ← |
| **What favours filaments** | **Low DO, low F/M in some cases, nutrient deficiency (N or P), septic influent, low pH, high sulphide** ← |
| **How it is measured** | **SVI — sludge volume index; above 150 mL/g indicates bulking** ← |
| **Remedies** | Chlorinate the return sludge; correct DO and nutrients; a selector zone at the inlet |

> **BULKING is the single most common serious operating problem in activated sludge plants, and it is destructive because it defeats the whole process:**

> **If the sludge will not settle, it cannot be returned — so the MLSS falls, the treatment deteriorates, and the solids leave in the effluent, which is exactly what the plant exists to prevent.**

> **The SELECTOR is the modern preventive: a small, high-F/M contact zone at the head of the aeration tank where the returned sludge meets the raw sewage.**

> **Floc-forming bacteria take up substrate rapidly and store it; filaments cannot. So the selector gives the floc-formers a competitive advantage and the filaments are gradually eliminated — an elegant solution that manipulates the ecology rather than treating the symptom.**

**The NUTRIENT requirement, since its deficiency appears above:**

> **The rule of thumb is BOD : N : P = 100 : 5 : 1.**

> **Domestic sewage comfortably exceeds this, so nutrient deficiency is never a problem in a municipal plant.**

> **Many INDUSTRIAL wastes — sugar, distillery, paper, food processing — are rich in carbon and deficient in nitrogen and phosphorus, and their biological treatment fails or bulks until nutrients are DOSED.**

> **So a plant treating a carbohydrate-rich industrial waste may need urea and phosphoric acid added — which surprises operators used to removing nutrients rather than adding them.**

examTip.trick: **The RETURN sludge maintains the MLSS at 1,500-4,000 mg/L** — 20-30 times what the influent supplies, which is what compresses the treatment into 4-8 hours.
examTip.trap: **RETURN and WASTE sludge do OPPOSITE things** from the same clarifier underflow: the return maintains the population, the waste limits it and sets the SLUDGE AGE. Option (a) describes wasting, not returning.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sludge age above ~10 days is needed for NITRIFICATION** — nitrifiers grow slowly and wash out below it. **LOW F/M = starved bacteria = GOOD settling.** And BULKING (SVI > 150) from filamentous organisms is the classic failure — cured by a SELECTOR zone.

questions.stem: A SEPTIC TANK provides treatment principally by:
options: SEDIMENTATION of solids and ANAEROBIC digestion of the settled sludge
Aerobic oxidation in an aerated chamber
questions.solution:
**SEDIMENTATION of the solids and ANAEROBIC digestion of the settled sludge.**

**What a septic tank does and does not do:**

| Process | Occurs? | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **SEDIMENTATION of settleable solids** | **YES — the principal mechanism** ← | Forms the sludge layer at the bottom |
| **FLOTATION of grease and light solids** | **YES** | Forms the SCUM layer at the top |
| **ANAEROBIC digestion of the settled sludge** | **YES — slowly, over months** ← | Reduces the sludge volume |
| **AEROBIC treatment** | **NO — the tank is sealed and anaerobic** ← | Option (b) is wrong on this |
| **Substantial BOD removal** | **PARTIAL only — 30 to 50 per cent** ← | **The effluent is still strongly polluting** |
| **PATHOGEN removal** | **VERY LITTLE** ← | **The effluent is dangerous** |
| **Nutrient removal** | **Essentially none** | N and P pass through |

> **THE MOST IMPORTANT FACT ABOUT A SEPTIC TANK IS THAT ITS EFFLUENT IS NOT TREATED SEWAGE.**

> **It removes solids and reduces BOD by perhaps 40 per cent, and it leaves a liquid that is anaerobic, foul-smelling, still high in BOD and full of pathogens.**

> **A septic tank is therefore only the FIRST stage of an on-site system, and it MUST be followed by a means of disposing of the effluent into the ground:**

| Disposal method | Note |
|---|---|
| **SOAK PIT (soakaway)** | **Simplest; suits permeable soil and a low water table** ← |
| **DISPERSION TRENCHES / drain field** | **Perforated pipe in gravel; the preferred method where space allows** ← |
| **Evapotranspiration bed** | Where the soil is impermeable |
| **Sand filter or constructed wetland** | Where a higher standard is needed |
| **Discharge to a sewer or drain** | **NOT acceptable without further treatment** ← |

> **A septic tank discharging directly to a stream or an open drain — which is extremely common in South Asia including Nepal — is a public health hazard and provides very little benefit over raw discharge.**

**Design features and their reasons:**

| Feature | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Detention time** | **24 to 48 hours at the daily flow** ← | Long enough for solids to settle |
| **Number of compartments** | **Two (sometimes three); the first about 2/3 of the volume** ← | **The second catches carryover from the first** |
| **Length : width** | **2:1 to 4:1** | **Approaches plug flow; reduces short-circuiting** ← |
| **Liquid depth** | **1.0 to 2.0 m** | Space for sludge, clear zone and scum |
| **Free board** | **300 mm** | Scum accumulation |
| **INLET and OUTLET** | **T-pipes or baffles dipping BELOW the liquid surface** ← | **Prevents the SCUM from escaping and dissipates the inflow's energy** |
| **Outlet invert** | **50-75 mm BELOW the inlet invert** ← | Prevents backflow |
| **Desludging interval** | **1 to 3 years** ← | Sludge accumulates at 30-40 L per person per year |
| **VENT pipe** | **Above roof level** | **Releases methane and H₂S safely** ← |

> **The T-PIPE inlet and outlet deserve emphasis because their omission is the commonest construction fault:**

> **A plain outlet at the liquid surface allows the SCUM to flow out with the effluent, which blocks the soakaway and defeats the tank.**

> **The T-pipe draws the effluent from BELOW the scum and ABOVE the sludge — the clear middle zone — which is the only part of the tank's contents fit to discharge.**

**DESLUDGING, since neglecting it is how septic tanks fail:**

| What happens if desludging is neglected | Note |
|---|---|
| **The sludge layer rises until it reaches the outlet** | **Solids then discharge to the soakaway** ← |
| **The soakaway CLOGS irreversibly** | **Its replacement is far more expensive than desludging** ← |
| **The effective volume falls, so the detention time falls** | Poorer settling, worse effluent |
| **The tank eventually blocks entirely** | Sewage backs up |

> **So the tank is maintenance-dependent, and the maintenance is one operation every one to three years — cheap and simple, and very commonly neglected because the tank is out of sight and gives no warning until the soakaway has already failed.**

> **And a critical safety point: SEPTIC TANK GASES ARE LETHAL. The tank contains methane (explosive) and hydrogen sulphide (toxic, and it deadens the sense of smell so that the warning disappears as the danger rises), and it is OXYGEN-DEFICIENT.**

> **People die in septic tanks every year, usually a worker who enters and collapses, followed by a rescuer who enters after them.**

> **The tank must be ventilated and tested before entry, entry made with breathing apparatus and a harness, and a person stationed outside — and the desludging done by pump from outside wherever possible.**

**Why NOT to leave the sludge "to digest away":**

> **The anaerobic digestion in a septic tank does reduce the sludge, and it is SLOW and INCOMPLETE:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Temperature** | **Ambient — often 15-25 °C, well below the 35 °C of a heated digester** ← |
| **Mixing** | **None** ← |
| **Digestion time** | **Months** |
| **Result** | **Perhaps 50 % reduction in volatile solids over a long period — the remainder accumulates permanently** ← |

> **So the tank is not self-emptying, and a persistent inert residue accumulates regardless.**

> **The comparison with a proper anaerobic DIGESTER at a treatment works is instructive: heated to 35 °C, mixed, and retained 20-30 days, it achieves the same digestion in a month that a septic tank does not complete in years — and it collects the methane as a fuel rather than venting it.**

> **A septic tank is thus a very simple, very cheap, very robust device that does a small part of the job — and its value lies precisely in needing no power, no chemicals and no operator, which is why it remains the right answer for a dispersed rural population.**

examTip.trick: **Sedimentation plus ANAEROBIC digestion — the tank is sealed, so option (b)'s aerobic treatment is wrong.** Detention 24-48 h, two compartments, T-pipes at inlet and outlet.
examTip.trap: **Septic tank effluent is NOT treated sewage** — only 30-50 % BOD removal and essentially no pathogen removal. It MUST go to a soak pit or drain field, never to an open drain.
examTip.mnemonic: **The T-pipe draws from the clear middle zone, below the SCUM and above the SLUDGE** — a plain outlet lets scum out and blocks the soakaway. And septic tank gases kill: methane, H₂S (which deadens the sense of smell), and oxygen deficiency.

questions.stem: The residual chlorine to be maintained at the consumer's tap for a safe supply is generally:
questions.solution:
**0.2 mg/L** (commonly specified as 0.2 mg/L free residual chlorine after 30 minutes' contact, at the far end of the distribution system).

**The chlorine figures that must be kept apart:**

| Quantity | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Residual required at the CONSUMER'S TAP (far point)** | **0.2 mg/L** ← |
| **Residual leaving the treatment works** | **0.5 to 1.0 mg/L — higher, so that 0.2 survives the journey** ← |
| **Contact time required before the residual is measured** | **30 minutes minimum** ← |
| **Residual during an epidemic or after contamination** | **1.0 to 2.0 mg/L (superchlorination)** ← |
| **Taste threshold for most people** | **About 0.3 to 0.5 mg/L — so the residual is close to detectable** ← |
| **WHO guideline maximum** | 5 mg/L |

> **Option (c) 2.0 mg/L is the emergency figure and (d) 5.0 mg/L the guideline maximum, so both are real numbers from the same subject.**

**Why a residual is maintained at all — the essential idea:**

> **Disinfection at the works kills the pathogens present in the water AT THAT MOMENT. The RESIDUAL protects the water on its way to the consumer:**

| Threat during distribution | How the residual answers it |
|---|---|
| **Cross-connections and back-siphonage** | **The residual disinfects small ingresses** ← |
| **Ingress through leaking joints when the pressure drops** | **The great hazard in intermittent supplies** ← |
| **Regrowth of bacteria in the mains (biofilm)** | The residual suppresses it |
| **Contamination in service reservoirs** | — |
| **Contamination in domestic storage tanks** | — |

> **The residual is also a MONITORING tool, and this may be its greatest practical value: measuring free chlorine is a simple field test taking seconds, whereas a bacteriological test takes 24 to 48 hours in a laboratory.**

> **So an ABSENT residual is an immediate warning that something is wrong — either the dosing has failed or the water has been contaminated and has consumed the chlorine — and it is detected on the spot rather than two days later.**

> **That is why distribution monitoring is largely residual monitoring, with bacteriological sampling used to confirm.**

**INTERMITTENT SUPPLY, which is the condition in most of Nepal and much of South Asia:**

> **A supply that runs only a few hours a day is far more dangerous than a continuous one, and the reason is not obvious:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **When the mains EMPTY, they go to NEGATIVE or zero pressure** | **Contaminated groundwater and sewage are then SUCKED IN through leaking joints** ← |
| **A leaking main under pressure leaks OUT — which is safe** | **The same leak with no pressure lets contamination IN** ← |
| **The residual is consumed in the stagnant main** | No protection remains |
| **Households store water in tanks and vessels** | **Recontamination during storage and handling** ← |
| **The first flush after restoration is grossly contaminated** | Often not run to waste |

> **The SECOND ROW is the point that makes the whole issue clear: A LEAK IS ONLY SAFE WHILE THE PIPE IS PRESSURISED.**

> **The same crack that harmlessly loses water at 3 bar admits sewage at zero pressure — so the intermittent supply converts every leak in the network into a contamination point twice a day.**

> **This is why moving from intermittent to CONTINUOUS supply is regarded as the single most important improvement in South Asian urban water — more valuable than better treatment, because the treated water is being recontaminated after it leaves the works.**

> **And it is counter-intuitive to administrators, who see continuous supply as using more water. In fact it usually uses less, because the losses from the twice-daily filling surge and from household over-storage disappear.**

**The forms of chlorine residual, since "free" is specified:**

| Form | Composition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **FREE residual** | **HOCl (hypochlorous acid) and OCl⁻ (hypochlorite ion)** | **Fast, powerful disinfectant** ← |
| **COMBINED residual** | **CHLORAMINES — chlorine combined with ammonia** | **Much weaker (25-100 times) but LONGER-LASTING** ← |

> **HOCl is the effective species, and it predominates at LOW pH:**

| pH | Proportion as HOCl |
|---|---|
| **6.0** | **97 %** ← |
| **7.0** | **75 %** |
| **7.5** | **50 %** |
| **8.0** | **24 %** ← |
| **9.0** | **3 %** ← |

> **So disinfection is far more effective at pH 7 than at pH 8.5 — the same dose does perhaps three times the work — and the pH after treatment therefore matters a great deal.**

> **A water that has been softened by lime, or coagulated with sodium aluminate, may leave the works at pH 9 or above, and its chlorination will be correspondingly ineffective unless the pH is corrected first.**

**The BREAKPOINT curve, which explains the dosing:**

| Stage of increasing dose | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Chlorine is consumed by reducing agents — Fe²⁺, Mn²⁺, H₂S, organics. NO residual appears.** ← |
| **2** | **Chlorine reacts with AMMONIA to form CHLORAMINES. A COMBINED residual builds up.** ← |
| **3** | **Further chlorine DESTROYS the chloramines (oxidising them to nitrogen gas). The residual FALLS — to the BREAKPOINT.** ← |
| **4** | **Beyond the breakpoint, added chlorine appears as FREE residual.** ← |

> **The curve rises, falls, and rises again — and the falling middle section is the surprising part: ADDING MORE CHLORINE REDUCES THE RESIDUAL.**

> **An operator who measures a falling residual and responds by reducing the dose is moving in exactly the wrong direction, and the water will get worse.**

> **BREAKPOINT CHLORINATION means dosing past the breakpoint so that a FREE residual is obtained — and it also destroys the ammonia and the taste-and-odour-producing chloramines, so the water is better as well as better disinfected.**

**And the disinfection by-product concern, which limits how much chlorine may be used:**

> **Chlorine reacts with natural organic matter (humic and fulvic acids) to form TRIHALOMETHANES (THMs) — chloroform and its relatives — which are suspected carcinogens.**

| Control measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Remove the ORGANIC PRECURSORS before chlorinating** | **Enhanced coagulation, activated carbon — the best approach** ← |
| **Move the chlorination point LATER in the train** | **Post-chlorination rather than pre-chlorination** ← |
| **Use CHLORAMINES for the distribution residual** | Fewer THMs, longer-lasting |
| **Use an alternative primary disinfectant** | Ozone, UV, chlorine dioxide |

> **The risk balance deserves stating plainly, because it is often misrepresented: the THM risk is a small, long-term, statistical cancer risk, while the risk of INADEQUATE DISINFECTION is cholera, typhoid and death within days.**

> **Wherever the two are in tension, DISINFECTION WINS — and the historical case is decisive: the withdrawal of chlorination in Peru in 1991, partly over THM concerns, was followed by a cholera epidemic that killed thousands.**

examTip.trick: **0.2 mg/L free residual at the far tap after 30 minutes' contact** — with 0.5-1.0 leaving the works so that 0.2 survives. 2.0 is the emergency figure, 5.0 the WHO maximum.
examTip.trap: **On the BREAKPOINT curve, adding more chlorine can REDUCE the residual** (stage 3, where chloramines are destroyed). An operator who cuts the dose in response is going the wrong way.
examTip.mnemonic: **HOCl is the effective species and it predominates at LOW pH: 97 % at pH 6, 24 % at pH 8.** And an INTERMITTENT supply is dangerous because a leak is only safe while PRESSURISED — at zero pressure the same crack admits sewage.

questions.stem: An Initial Environmental Examination (IEE) differs from an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) in that the IEE is:
options: A LESS DETAILED study, required for projects of smaller scale or lower anticipated impact
Required only for projects that have already been built
A more detailed study than an EIA
Prepared by the contractor rather than the proponent
questions.solution:
**A LESS DETAILED study, required for projects of smaller scale or lower anticipated impact.**

**The tiered system of environmental assessment, as applied in Nepal:**

| Level | When required | Approving authority (Nepal) |
|---|---|---|
| **Brief Environmental Study (BES)** | **The smallest category of prescribed projects** ← | The concerned ministry |
| **INITIAL ENVIRONMENTAL EXAMINATION (IEE)** | **Medium-scale projects listed in the schedules — a smaller road, a modest water supply, a small hydropower scheme** ← | **The concerned ministry** |
| **ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT (EIA)** | **Large projects, and any project in a SENSITIVE AREA regardless of size** ← | **The Ministry of Forests and Environment** |

> **The tiering exists so that the depth of the study is proportionate to the risk: requiring a full EIA for a small rural water scheme would consume more resources than the scheme itself.**
