> **And the SENSITIVE AREA rule in the third row is the important qualification: a small project in a national park, a conservation area, a wetland or near a cultural heritage site requires a full EIA regardless of its size — because the receiving environment, not the project, determines the risk.**

**The stages of the assessment, common to both levels:**

| Stage | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **SCREENING** | **Decides WHICH level of study is required — BES, IEE or EIA** ← |
| **SCOPING** | **Decides WHAT the study will cover; identifies the significant issues and excludes the trivial** ← |
| **Terms of Reference (ToR), approved** | Fixes the scope formally |
| **BASELINE study** | **The existing environment — physical, biological, socio-economic and cultural** ← |
| **IMPACT prediction and evaluation** | **Magnitude, extent, duration; direct, indirect and cumulative** ← |
| **Analysis of ALTERNATIVES** | **Including the NO-PROJECT alternative** ← |
| **MITIGATION measures** | Avoid, minimise, mitigate, compensate |
| **Environmental Management Plan (EMP)** | **The mitigation measures with budgets, responsibilities and a schedule** ← |
| **MONITORING and auditing plan** | Baseline, compliance and impact monitoring |
| **PUBLIC CONSULTATION and disclosure** | **Public notice, hearings, recommendation of the local body** ← |
| **Review and approval** | By the authority |

> **SCOPING in the second row is where the quality of an assessment is largely decided, and it is the stage most often rushed: an assessment that studies everything equally studies nothing well, and one that omits a significant issue cannot be repaired later by any amount of detail elsewhere.**

> **The ANALYSIS OF ALTERNATIVES is the stage most often reduced to a formality, and it is the one with the greatest potential value — because the largest environmental gains come from choosing a better ALIGNMENT, SITE or TECHNOLOGY, not from mitigating a poor one.**

> **Including the NO-PROJECT alternative is not a bureaucratic requirement but the baseline against which every impact is measured, and it forces the question of whether the project's benefits justify its costs at all.**

**The MITIGATION hierarchy, which parallels the safety hierarchy:**

| Rank | Measure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **AVOID** | **Realign the road around the forest rather than through it** ← |
| **2** | **MINIMISE** | Reduce the footprint; work outside the breeding season |
| **3** | **MITIGATE / RESTORE** | Rehabilitate borrow pits; stabilise and revegetate slopes |
| **4 — last** | **COMPENSATE / OFFSET** | **Compensatory afforestation; resettlement compensation** ← |

> **As with the safety hierarchy, the ranking is real and the last resort is the weakest: compensatory afforestation nominally replaces a felled forest and does not replace a mature ecosystem, and resettlement compensation does not restore a community.**

> **So an assessment whose mitigation consists mainly of compensation has generally failed to influence the design, which is what the assessment exists to do.**

**The impacts a Nepali civil project typically raises:**

| Impact | Note |
|---|---|
| **SLOPE INSTABILITY and landslides from hill road cutting** | **The dominant impact of Nepali road building; spoil disposal is critical** ← |
| **Loss of forest and of habitat** | Compensatory afforestation required |
| **SPOIL and muck disposal into rivers** | **Side-casting from hill roads chokes streams and destabilises slopes below** ← |
| **Sedimentation of watercourses** | Affects fisheries and downstream water users |
| **Loss of land, houses and livelihoods; resettlement** | **Requires a Resettlement Action Plan** ← |
| **Impacts on downstream water users from a diversion** | **Environmental FLOW must be maintained** ← |
| **Quarrying and borrow area damage** | Rehabilitation required |
| **Dust, noise and vibration during construction** | Temporary but significant near settlements |
| **Impacts on cultural and religious sites** | Especially sensitive in Nepal |

> **THE SPOIL DISPOSAL ISSUE deserves the emphasis it is given, because it is the single most damaging and most avoidable practice in Nepali hill road construction:**

> **Excavated material side-cast down the slope buries vegetation, loads the slope below, blocks natural drainage and enters watercourses — causing landslides and sedimentation far beyond the road corridor.**

> **Proper practice is to identify designated spoil disposal sites in advance, to haul the material there, to compact and drain it, and to revegetate — all of which costs money that is routinely omitted from the estimate.**

> **The result is that the environmental cost of a cheaply built hill road is paid by the people living below it, which is precisely the sort of externality the assessment process exists to internalise.**

> **And the ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW requirement is the corresponding issue for hydropower: a diversion scheme must release a minimum flow (commonly 10 per cent of the minimum monthly average flow, or a figure from a specific study) into the dewatered reach, so that the river between the intake and the powerhouse is not left dry.**

**And the recurring weakness of the process, which is worth naming honestly:**

| Weakness | Note |
|---|---|
| **The assessment is prepared AFTER the design is fixed** | **So it cannot influence the alternatives it is supposed to evaluate** ← |
| **It is treated as a CLEARANCE to be obtained rather than a design tool** | ← |
| **The EMP's budget is not carried into the construction contract** | **So the mitigation is never funded or executed** ← |
| **MONITORING and auditing rarely happen** | The report is filed and forgotten |
| **Public consultation is nominal** | Notices posted where no one reads them |

> **The THIRD row is the most actionable for an engineer, and it is squarely within a civil engineer's control: if the EMP's measures are written into the BILL OF QUANTITIES as paid items, they get done; if they are left as general obligations, they do not.**

> **Making environmental mitigation a measured and paid item — spoil haulage to a designated site, bio-engineering of slopes, dust suppression, silt fencing — is the single most effective step available, and it turns the assessment from a document into work on the ground.**

examTip.trick: **IEE is the LESS detailed study for medium-scale projects; EIA is the full study for large ones — and for ANY project in a sensitive area regardless of size**, because the receiving environment determines the risk.
examTip.trap: **Mitigation hierarchy: AVOID → MINIMISE → MITIGATE → COMPENSATE.** An assessment whose mitigation is mostly compensation has failed to influence the design, which is what it exists to do.
examTip.mnemonic: **Write the EMP's measures into the BILL OF QUANTITIES as paid items** — spoil haulage, bio-engineering, silt fencing — or they will never be executed. And for Nepali hill roads, SPOIL DISPOSAL is the most damaging and most avoidable impact.

questions.stem: A crop has a base period of 120 days and a duty of 1,800 hectares per cumec. The DELTA for the crop is:
questions.solution:
**0.576 m (57.6 cm).**

**The relation and its derivation, which is worth reconstructing rather than memorising:**

> **Δ = 8.64 B / D**

> **where Δ is the delta in METRES, B the base period in DAYS, and D the duty in HECTARES PER CUMEC.**

> **Δ = 8.64 × 120 / 1,800 = 1,036.8 / 1,800 = 0.576 m** ←

**Where the 8.64 comes from:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **A duty D means 1 cumec running for the whole base period irrigates D hectares** | **The definition** ← |
| **Volume delivered** | **1 m³/s × B days × 86,400 s/day = 86,400 B cubic metres** ← |
| **Area irrigated** | **D hectares = D × 10,000 m²** ← |
| **Depth = volume / area** | **86,400 B / (10,000 D) = 8.64 B / D metres** ← |

> **So the 8.64 is simply 86,400 seconds in a day divided by 10,000 square metres in a hectare — and knowing that, the formula cannot be misremembered.**

> **The distractors are the characteristic slips: 0.432 is the answer with 8.64 halved (or B taken as 60), 1.152 is it doubled, and 0.288 is a quarter — all of them the result of mishandling the constant.**

**The three quantities and how they relate:**

| Term | Definition | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **DUTY (D)** | **The AREA a unit discharge will irrigate over the base period** ← | **hectares per cumec** |
| **DELTA (Δ)** | **The total DEPTH of water the crop requires over the base period** ← | **metres or cm** |
| **BASE PERIOD (B)** | **The period from the FIRST watering to the LAST, before harvesting** ← | **days** |

> **The relation is INVERSE: a HIGH duty means a SMALL delta, because one cumec spread over more land must give each hectare less depth.**

> **A high duty is therefore DESIRABLE — it means the water is being used efficiently, irrigating more land per unit of discharge.**

> **That is the point most often inverted, because "duty" sounds like a demand rather than a performance.**

**Typical deltas, for a sense of scale:**

| Crop | Delta (cm) | Base period (days) |
|---|---|---|
| **RICE (paddy)** | **100 to 150** ← | **120 to 150** |
| **Sugarcane** | **80 to 150** ← | **320 to 360 — nearly a full year** |
| **Wheat** | **30 to 40** | **100 to 120** |
| **Maize** | **25 to 45** | 100 |
| **Cotton** | **40 to 50** | 200 |
| **Gram, pulses** | **20 to 30** ← | 90 to 120 |
| **Vegetables** | 45 to 60 | Varies |

> **RICE's delta is three to four times that of wheat or gram, and that single fact drives most of the water-allocation difficulty in South Asian irrigation.**

> **Rice is grown under PONDED water rather than merely moist soil, so its requirement includes standing depth, percolation and evaporation from a free surface — none of which a dry-footed crop incurs.**

> **The consequence for a canal system is that the cropping PATTERN, not merely the area, determines the discharge required — and a shift toward rice can overwhelm a canal designed for a mixed pattern without a single extra hectare being irrigated.**

**The factors that affect duty, since improving it is the object of most irrigation engineering:**

| Factor | Effect on duty |
|---|---|
| **CANAL LINING** | **RAISES duty substantially — seepage losses may be 30-50 % of the flow in an unlined canal** ← |
| **Method of application — flood, furrow, sprinkler, DRIP** | **DRIP raises duty dramatically; flood irrigation wastes most** ← |
| **SOIL type** | **Sandy soil, high percolation, LOW duty; clayey soil, higher duty** ← |
| **CLIMATE — temperature, humidity, wind** | Hot and dry means higher evaporation and lower duty |
| **Crop and its variety** | As the table above |
| **Quality of the water** | Saline water needs extra for leaching, lowering duty |
| **Skill of the cultivator, and the water charge levied** | **Free or flat-rate water is used wastefully; volumetric charging raises duty** ← |
| **Rainfall during the base period** | Effective rainfall reduces the irrigation requirement |

> **The LAST-BUT-ONE row is worth stating plainly because it is an institutional rather than an engineering lever, and it is frequently the most powerful one available: where water is charged by the HECTARE rather than by the VOLUME, the farmer has no reason to economise, and lining a canal simply delivers more water to be wasted at the field.**

> **So improving duty is not only a matter of concrete in the channel — it requires the delivery to be measurable and the charge to follow the volume, which is a far harder reform than lining.**

**And the DUTY MEASURED AT DIFFERENT POINTS, since the same crop has several duties:**

| Point of measurement | Duty |
|---|---|
| **At the FIELD** | **HIGHEST — no conveyance losses yet incurred** ← |
| **At the outlet / watercourse head** | Lower |
| **At the distributary head** | Lower still |
| **At the CANAL HEAD (head of the main canal)** | **LOWEST — all conveyance losses included** ← |

> **So a duty figure is meaningless without saying WHERE it is measured, and the difference between field duty and canal-head duty is precisely the conveyance efficiency of the system.**

> **A system with a field duty of 2,000 ha/cumec and a canal-head duty of 1,200 ha/cumec is losing 40 per cent of its water between the head and the field — which is the diagnosis that justifies lining, and it can only be made if both figures are known.**

examTip.trick: **Δ = 8.64 B / D** with Δ in metres, B in days, D in ha/cumec. Here 8.64 × 120 / 1800 = **0.576 m**. The 8.64 is just 86,400 s/day ÷ 10,000 m²/ha — derive it and you cannot misremember it.
examTip.trap: **Duty and delta are INVERSELY related, and a HIGH duty is GOOD** — more land irrigated per cumec. The word sounds like a demand, which is why the relation is so often inverted.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rice's delta (100-150 cm) is three to four times wheat's (30-40)** — so the cropping PATTERN, not the area, sets the discharge. And duty is HIGHEST at the field and LOWEST at the canal head; the gap is the conveyance loss.

questions.stem: The GROSS COMMAND AREA (GCA) of an irrigation project differs from the CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA (CCA) in that the GCA includes:
options: Only the area actually sown in a given season
The total area enclosed by the project boundary, INCLUDING unculturable land such as villages, roads, ponds and rocky ground
The area irrigated in both crop seasons counted twice
Only the area that receives water by gravity
questions.solution:
**The TOTAL area enclosed by the irrigation boundary, INCLUDING land that cannot be cultivated** — villages, roads, canals, ponds, marsh, forest and barren ground.

**The hierarchy of command areas, from largest to smallest:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS COMMAND AREA (GCA)** | **The whole area that CAN be commanded — everything within the irrigation boundary, culturable or not** ← |
| **CULTURABLE COMMAND AREA (CCA)** | **GCA MINUS the unculturable area — the land that is fit for cultivation** ← |
| **Culturable CULTIVATED area** | The part of the CCA actually under crops |
| **Culturable UNCULTIVATED area** | Fit for cultivation but left fallow |
| **INTENSITY OF IRRIGATION** | **The percentage of the CCA actually irrigated in a crop SEASON** ← |

> **The relation to hold: GCA ⊃ CCA ⊃ cultivated area ⊃ irrigated area.**

> **Typically the CCA is 70 to 85 per cent of the GCA, the remainder being the unculturable fraction.**

**INTENSITY OF IRRIGATION, since it is the figure that turns area into discharge:**

> **Intensity = (area irrigated in a season / CCA) × 100 per cent**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is quoted SEPARATELY for each season** | **Kharif (monsoon) and Rabi (winter), and sometimes a hot-weather season** ← |
| **The ANNUAL intensity is their SUM** | **And it CAN EXCEED 100 per cent** ← |
| **An annual intensity above 100 %** | **Means the same land is cropped more than once a year — which is the object of irrigation** ← |

> **The point in the second and third rows is the one that surprises: an annual intensity of 150 per cent is not an arithmetic error but a genuine and desirable result, meaning that on average each hectare of the CCA carries one and a half crops a year.**

> **A well-run system with assured water may reach 180 to 200 per cent; a monsoon-dependent one may manage 100 per cent or less.**

> **So the intensity measures how hard the LAND is worked, not what proportion of it is served — and it is the single figure that best expresses what an irrigation project has actually achieved.**

**A worked example, since the terms combine in the design calculation:**

> **A project has a GCA of 12,000 hectares. Twenty per cent is unculturable. The rabi intensity is 60 per cent, and the crop's duty at the canal head is 1,500 ha/cumec.**

| Step | Working | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **CCA** | **12,000 × 0.80** | **9,600 ha** ← |
| **Area irrigated in rabi** | **9,600 × 0.60** | **5,760 ha** ← |
| **Discharge required at the head** | **5,760 / 1,500** | **3.84 cumecs** ← |

> **That chain — GCA to CCA to irrigated area to discharge — is the backbone of irrigation project design, and every term in it must be defined precisely or the discharge comes out wrong by a large factor.**

> **Using the GCA instead of the CCA in this example would give 4.8 cumecs, oversizing the canal by 25 per cent; ignoring the intensity would give 6.4 cumecs, oversizing it by two thirds.**

**The CROP SEASONS in the subcontinent, since intensity is quoted by season:**

| Season | Period | Crops |
|---|---|---|
| **KHARIF (monsoon)** | **June/July to October** ← | **Rice, maize, millet, cotton, sugarcane planting** |
| **RABI (winter)** | **October/November to March/April** ← | **Wheat, barley, gram, mustard, potato** |
| **ZAID / hot weather** | **March to June** | Vegetables, melons, fodder |

> **The irrigation demand is highest in RABI and lowest in KHARIF, which is the opposite of what the river offers:**

| Season | River flow | Irrigation demand |
|---|---|---|
| **KHARIF (monsoon)** | **HIGH — the rivers are in flood** ← | **LOW — the rain does most of the work** ← |
| **RABI (winter)** | **LOW — lean season flows** ← | **HIGH — no rain at all** ← |

> **THAT MISMATCH IS THE CENTRAL PROBLEM OF IRRIGATION PLANNING IN NEPAL AND NORTHERN INDIA, and it is worth stating explicitly because it determines what kind of project is appropriate.**

> **A RUN-OF-RIVER diversion can only take what the river is carrying at the time, so it serves the kharif well and the rabi poorly — which is why so many diversion schemes irrigate a large area in the monsoon and a fraction of it in winter.**

> **A STORAGE reservoir holds the monsoon surplus for release in the dry season, and that is precisely what converts a seasonal supply into a year-round one — at the cost of a dam, submergence and resettlement.**

> **So the intensity a project can achieve in rabi is largely determined by whether it has storage, and the GCA-CCA-intensity arithmetic above is where that difference shows up in numbers.**

examTip.trick: **GCA ⊃ CCA ⊃ cultivated ⊃ irrigated.** GCA is everything inside the boundary; CCA excludes villages, roads, ponds and rocky ground — typically 70-85 % of the GCA.
examTip.trap: **ANNUAL intensity can exceed 100 %** — it is the sum of the seasonal intensities, and above 100 % simply means the land carries more than one crop a year, which is the object of irrigation.
examTip.mnemonic: **GCA → CCA → × intensity → ÷ duty = discharge.** Using GCA instead of CCA here oversizes the canal by 25 %; ignoring intensity oversizes it by two thirds. And demand peaks in RABI exactly when the river is lowest — which is the case for STORAGE.

questions.stem: In KENNEDY'S theory of channel design, the CRITICAL VELOCITY RATIO (CVR, denoted m) is defined as the ratio of:
options: The channel's bed width to its depth
The silt carried to the silt capacity of the channel
The channel's actual velocity to the velocity of approach
The ACTUAL mean velocity in the channel to KENNEDY'S critical velocity for that depth
questions.solution:
**The ACTUAL mean velocity to KENNEDY'S CRITICAL VELOCITY for the same depth.**

> **m = V / V₀, where V₀ = 0.55 m y^0.64 in metric units, y being the depth of water in metres.**

> **(In Kennedy's original form the coefficient 0.55 already contains the CVR, so the working equation is usually written V₀ = 0.55 m y^0.64 with m the critical velocity ratio.)**

**What the CVR represents:**

| CVR value | Silt grade | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **m > 1** | **COARSER silt than the standard** | **The channel can carry more silt; it will SCOUR if the supply is insufficient** ← |
| **m = 1** | **The standard silt of Kennedy's Upper Bari Doab observations** | **Neither scouring nor silting** ← |
| **m < 1** | **FINER silt** | **The channel SILTS UP** ← |

| Silt | Typical m |
|---|---|
| **Coarse sand** | **1.1 to 1.2** |
| **Standard silt** | **1.0** |
| **Fine sand / light silt** | **0.8 to 0.9** ← |

> **So the CVR is Kennedy's device for adapting a single empirical relation to soils other than the one on which it was derived — which is both its usefulness and its principal weakness, since m must be estimated from experience rather than measured.**

**What Kennedy's theory sought to achieve — the idea of a NON-SILTING, NON-SCOURING channel:**

> **A canal carrying silty water has two failure modes, and they pull in opposite directions:**

| Velocity | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **TOO LOW** | **The silt DEPOSITS; the section fills; capacity falls** ← |
| **TOO HIGH** | **The bed and banks SCOUR; the section enlarges and the canal is damaged** ← |
| **CRITICAL** | **The silt is kept in suspension and carried through — the channel is in REGIME** ← |

> **Kennedy's observation, from twenty years of data on the Upper Bari Doab Canal, was that the silt-supporting power comes from the EDDIES GENERATED AT THE BED, rising to the surface — so it depends on the DEPTH of the channel and not on its width.**

> **That is why his critical velocity is a function of y alone, and it is the theory's defining assumption.**

**The limitations of Kennedy's theory, which is why Lacey superseded it:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **No equation for the BED WIDTH** | **The B/y ratio must be ASSUMED, so the solution is not unique — different assumptions give different "correct" channels** ← |
| **The CVR must be estimated by judgement** | Not measurable in advance |
| **Kutter's formula is needed for the slope, and its rugosity n must also be assumed** | Two assumptions compound |
| **Silt GRADE is not quantified** | **Only through the vague m** ← |
| **The silt CHARGE (concentration) is not considered at all** | ← |
| **Trial and error is required** | Cumbersome |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DECISIVE DEFECT: Kennedy's method tells you what velocity to aim at, and not what shape of channel to build.**

> **A designer must assume a B/y ratio, compute, and check — and any of a range of sections will satisfy the criterion, so the method does not determine the design.**

**LACEY'S REGIME THEORY, which addresses exactly that gap:**

| Aspect | Lacey's improvement |
|---|---|
| **The number of equations** | **THREE independent relations, so the section is FULLY DETERMINED** ← |
| **Silt quantified by** | **The SILT FACTOR f = 1.76√d, with d the mean particle size in mm** ← |
| **The slope is given by the theory** | **Not imported from Kutter** ← |
| **Concept of regime** | **INITIAL regime (shape adjusted only) and FINAL regime (shape, slope and section all adjusted)** ← |

> **The three working relations:**

| Quantity | Lacey relation |
|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = 4.75 √Q** ← |
| **Regime velocity** | **V = (Q f² / 140)^(1/6)** ← |
| **Regime slope** | **S = f^(5/3) / (3340 Q^(1/6))** ← |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = 0.47 (Q/f)^(1/3)** ← |
| **Regime SCOUR depth** | **R = 0.473 (Q/f)^(1/3)** — the same expression, used for foundation depths ← |

> **The SCOUR DEPTH relation in the last row is the one that reaches beyond canal design: it is used to fix the founding depth of bridge piers, guide bunds and weir aprons throughout the subcontinent.**

> **That a regime formula derived for stable canals should govern bridge foundation depths is a striking piece of engineering economy, and it is why Lacey's work matters far outside irrigation.**

**And the comparison that summarises both:**

| | KENNEDY | LACEY |
|---|---|---|
| **Basis** | **Critical velocity from bed eddies; depth only** | **Regime: eddies from the ENTIRE wetted perimeter** ← |
| **Silt described by** | **CVR, m — qualitative** | **Silt factor f — from the actual particle size** ← |
| **Equations available** | **One (plus imported Kutter)** | **Three — the section is determined** ← |
| **Slope** | Assumed, via Kutter | **Given by the theory** |
| **Result** | **A family of acceptable sections** | **A unique section** ← |

> **The conceptual advance in the first row is worth noting: Kennedy attributed the silt-carrying eddies to the BED alone, so only depth mattered; Lacey attributed them to the WHOLE wetted perimeter, which brings the width into the theory and is what makes a complete solution possible.**

> **Both are empirical and both are still used — Lacey for design, Kennedy for checking and for the intuition that a channel must be neither too slow nor too fast.**

examTip.trick: **CVR m = actual velocity ÷ Kennedy's critical velocity, with V₀ = 0.55 m y^0.64.** m > 1 coarser silt, m < 1 finer silt (the channel silts).
examTip.trap: **Kennedy gives NO equation for bed width** — B/y must be assumed, so a family of sections satisfies it. That is the defect Lacey's three relations remove.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacey: P = 4.75√Q, V = (Qf²/140)^(1/6), f = 1.76√d, and scour R = 0.473(Q/f)^(1/3)** — that last one fixes BRIDGE PIER founding depths across the subcontinent. Kennedy's eddies come from the BED (depth only); Lacey's from the whole WETTED PERIMETER.

questions.stem: The principal reason for LINING an irrigation canal is to:
options: Increase the roughness so that the flow is slowed
Allow a flatter bed slope to be used
Reduce SEEPAGE losses and prevent water logging of the adjoining land
Increase the quantity of silt the canal can carry
questions.solution:
**To reduce SEEPAGE losses, and with them the water logging of the adjoining land.**

**The magnitude of the loss, which is what justifies the cost:**

| Canal | Typical seepage loss |
|---|---|
| **Unlined canal in SANDY soil** | **Up to 50 per cent of the flow** ← |
| **Unlined canal in loam** | **25 to 35 per cent** ← |
| **Unlined canal in clay** | 10 to 20 per cent |
| **LINED canal** | **Reduced by 60 to 95 per cent of the unlined figure** ← |

> **Losing a third of the water between the headworks and the field is the ordinary condition of an unlined system, and it means that a third of the reservoir, the headworks and the main canal has been built to deliver nothing.**

**The full set of benefits, since seepage is only the first:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reduced SEEPAGE — more water delivered** | **The primary purpose** ← |
| **Prevention of WATER LOGGING and consequent SALINITY** | **Often the more valuable benefit — see below** ← |
| **A HIGHER velocity is permissible** | **Lining resists scour, so the canal can run faster** ← |
| **A SMALLER cross-section for the same discharge** | **Following from the higher velocity — less earthwork and less land acquired** ← |
| **A FLATTER slope becomes possible** | **Extending the command area to land the canal could not otherwise reach** ← (option b — a real benefit, but a consequence rather than the purpose) |
| **Lower MAINTENANCE — no silt clearance, no weed growth, no bank erosion** | **Weeds in an unlined canal can reduce capacity by a third** ← |
| **Stability of the banks; no breaches** | A breach in a large canal is a serious event |
| **No loss of land to a wide section** | — |

> **Option (b) is a genuine and important benefit, which makes it the best-made distractor — but a flatter slope is a CONSEQUENCE of lining, not the reason for it.**

> **And option (a) is the reverse of the truth: lining REDUCES the roughness, which is precisely what permits the higher velocity and the smaller section.**

| Surface | Manning's n |
|---|---|
| **Concrete lining, trowelled** | **0.013 to 0.015** ← |
| **Brick lining** | 0.015 to 0.017 |
| **Earth canal, clean and straight** | **0.022 to 0.025** ← |
| **Earth canal, weedy** | **0.030 to 0.040** ← |

> **From n = 0.025 to n = 0.014 is nearly a doubling of velocity for the same slope and section — which is where the smaller cross-section comes from.**

**WATER LOGGING, since it is the benefit most often underestimated:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **1 — Seepage from the canal raises the WATER TABLE in the surrounding land** ← | Continuously, year after year |
| **2 — The water table reaches the ROOT ZONE (within about 1.5 to 2 m of the surface)** | **The soil's air is displaced; roots cannot respire** ← |
| **3 — CAPILLARY rise brings water to the surface, where it EVAPORATES** ← | **The dissolved SALTS are left behind** |
| **4 — SALINITY and ALKALINITY build up in the topsoil** | **Year on year, irreversibly without treatment** ← |
| **5 — The land goes OUT OF CULTIVATION** | ← |

> **THE CRUEL IRONY OF THIS SEQUENCE DESERVES TO BE STATED: an irrigation project built to make land productive can, through its own seepage, destroy the land beside its canals.**

> **Large areas in Pakistan's Punjab and in parts of India were rendered saline in exactly this way during the twentieth century, and reclaiming them costs far more than lining the canal would have.**

> **So the water-logging benefit is not a secondary consideration attached to the water-saving one — in many systems it is the larger of the two, and it is the reason lining is specified even where water is not scarce.**

**The types of lining:**

| Lining | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cast in-situ CONCRETE** | **The most durable and most expensive; 50-100 mm thick** ← |
| **Shotcrete / guniting** | Suits repairs and irregular surfaces |
| **Precast concrete slabs** | Quick; joints are the weakness |
| **BRICK or stone masonry** | **Labour-intensive, which suits Nepali conditions; durable** ← |
| **Boulder / stone pitching in mortar** | Where stone is local |
| **COMPACTED EARTH or clay blanket** | **Cheapest; modest reduction only** ← |
| **Bentonite / soil-cement** | — |
| **PLASTIC membrane (LDPE/HDPE), buried under earth cover** | **Very effective and cheap; must be PROTECTED, since it is destroyed by sunlight, traffic and burrowing animals** ← |

> **The MEMBRANE entry carries a real caution: an exposed plastic membrane degrades in ultraviolet light within a season or two, and it must therefore be covered with a protective layer of earth or concrete.**

> **A membrane lining installed without adequate cover is a common false economy, and it fails completely rather than gradually.**

**And the DRAINAGE the lining does not remove the need for:**

> **Lining reduces the seepage that CAUSES water logging; it does not drain land that is already logged, nor deal with deep percolation from the fields themselves.**

| Remedy for water logging | Note |
|---|---|
| **LINING the canals and watercourses** | **Attacks the cause** ← |
| **SURFACE drains** | Remove ponded water and storm runoff |
| **SUB-SURFACE drains — tile or perforated pipe, or open ditches** | **Lower the water table directly** ← |
| **VERTICAL drainage — tube wells pumping the shallow aquifer** | **Lowers the table AND supplies usable irrigation water — CONJUNCTIVE USE** ← |
| **Controlled irrigation; volumetric charging** | Reduces over-application at the field |
| **Bio-drainage — deep-rooted trees along the canal** | Eucalyptus and similar; modest but cheap |
| **LEACHING with excess water plus gypsum, where salinity has set in** | **Reclamation, after the drainage is in place** ← |

> **The CONJUNCTIVE USE entry is the most elegant of these because it turns the problem into the solution: the water causing the logging is pumped out and applied to the crop, lowering the water table and augmenting the canal supply at the same time.**

> **It works only where the shallow groundwater is of usable quality — pumping saline water onto the fields would accelerate the salinity it is meant to relieve — so the water quality must be established before the tube wells are sunk.**

examTip.trick: **Seepage is up to 50 % in sandy soil, 25-35 % in loam — lining cuts it by 60-95 %.** Option (a) is backwards: lining REDUCES roughness (n from ~0.025 to ~0.014).
examTip.trap: **Option (b), a flatter slope, is a genuine benefit — but a CONSEQUENCE of lining, not the reason for it.** The higher permissible velocity is what allows both the flatter slope and the smaller section.
examTip.mnemonic: **Seepage → water table rises → capillary rise → evaporation leaves SALTS → the land goes out of cultivation.** An irrigation project can destroy the land beside its own canals, which is often the larger half of lining's benefit.

questions.stem: In BLIGH'S CREEP THEORY for the design of a weir floor, the creep length is taken as:
options: The horizontal distance between the upstream and downstream ends of the floor only
The sum of ALL horizontal and vertical distances along the contact surface, both weighted EQUALLY
The sum of the vertical distances only
The horizontal distances weighted fully and the vertical distances weighted one third
questions.solution:
**The sum of ALL the horizontal and vertical distances along the base of the structure, with both weighted EQUALLY.**

**Bligh's assumption and its consequence:**

> **Bligh assumed that water percolating under a weir travels along the contact surface between the floor and the subsoil, and that the loss of head is UNIFORM along that path — with no distinction between horizontal and vertical travel.**

> **L = C × H**

> **where L is the total creep length, H the seepage head, and C is BLIGH'S COEFFICIENT, depending on the soil:**

| Soil | Bligh's coefficient C |
|---|---|
| **Fine micaceous sand (Indo-Gangetic rivers)** | **15** ← |
| **Coarse-grained sand** | **12** |
| **Sand mixed with boulder and gravel** | **5 to 9** ← |
| **Light sand and mud** | 8 |

> **A HIGHER C means a LONGER creep path is required — so fine sand, through which water travels most readily and which is most easily piped away, demands the greatest length.**

> **The HYDRAULIC GRADIENT is simply the reciprocal: 1/C. So for fine sand the safe gradient is 1 in 15.**

**LANE'S WEIGHTED CREEP THEORY, which option (d) describes:**

> **Lane examined some 200 dams and found Bligh's equal treatment to be wrong: VERTICAL creep is far more effective at dissipating head than horizontal creep.**

> **L_w = (sum of vertical creep) + ⅓ × (sum of horizontal creep)**

| Theory | Horizontal weight | Vertical weight |
|---|---|---|
| **BLIGH** | **1** | **1** ← |
| **LANE** | **⅓** ← | **1** ← |

> **Option (d) is Lane's rule, which makes it the best-made distractor — a real and more accurate theory, offered for Bligh's.**

> **The practical implication of Lane's weighting is important: VERTICAL CUT-OFFS AND SHEET PILES ARE FAR MORE EFFECTIVE THAN A LONG HORIZONTAL FLOOR.**

> **Three metres of sheet pile does the work of nine metres of floor, at a fraction of the cost and the excavation — which is why modern weirs rely on deep cut-offs at each end rather than on extended aprons.**

**KHOSLA'S THEORY, which superseded both:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Basis** | **POTENTIAL FLOW theory — the actual flow net, solved mathematically, not an empirical creep path** ← |
| **Origin** | **Investigation of failures at structures designed correctly by Bligh's method** ← |
| **Method** | **The complex profile is split into simple standard FORMS, each solved exactly, then corrections applied** ← |
| **Corrections applied** | **For the FLOOR THICKNESS, for the MUTUAL INTERFERENCE of piles, and for the SLOPE of the floor** ← |
| **Key finding** | **The EXIT GRADIENT at the downstream end is the critical quantity, not the total creep length** ← |

> **KHOSLA'S CENTRAL INSIGHT — that the danger is concentrated at the DOWNSTREAM EXIT rather than distributed along the path — is the conceptual advance, and it explains why Bligh-designed works failed:**

> **Bligh's method could give an adequate total creep length while leaving the exit gradient dangerously steep, and it is at the exit that PIPING begins.**

> **The safe exit gradients:**

| Soil | Safe exit gradient |
|---|---|
| **Shingle** | **1 in 4 to 1 in 5** ← |
| **Coarse sand** | **1 in 5 to 1 in 6** |
| **Fine sand** | **1 in 6 to 1 in 7** ← |

> **And Khosla's other practical conclusion: A DEEP VERTICAL CUT-OFF AT THE DOWNSTREAM END IS ESSENTIAL, because it is what controls the exit gradient.**

> **An upstream cut-off reduces uplift; a DOWNSTREAM cut-off controls the exit gradient and prevents piping — and the downstream one must always be the deeper of the two.**

**PIPING, since it is the failure all three theories exist to prevent:**

| Stage | Process |
|---|---|
| **1** | **The exit gradient exceeds the critical value at the downstream toe** ← |
| **2** | **The seepage force lifts and carries away the finest soil particles** ← |
| **3** | **A small channel forms and works BACKWARD toward the upstream side** ← |
| **4** | **The channel enlarges as flow through it increases — a RUNAWAY process** ← |
| **5** | **The structure is undermined and collapses, often SUDDENLY** ← |

> **The RUNAWAY character in step 4 is what makes piping so dangerous: once begun, it accelerates, because a larger pipe carries more water which removes more soil.**

> **There is no equilibrium to arrest it, and failure can follow the first visible sign within hours.**

> **The critical hydraulic gradient at which it begins is i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e), which for typical values (G = 2.65, e = 0.65) is about 1.0 — and the safe exit gradients above are that value with a factor of safety of 4 to 7.**

**And the two protections against uplift and piping, which follow from all of this:**

| Measure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Adequate FLOOR THICKNESS downstream** | **The floor's WEIGHT resists the UPLIFT pressure beneath it — a thin floor is blown up from below** ← |
| **Deep DOWNSTREAM cut-off** | **Controls the exit gradient** ← |
| **Upstream cut-off and impervious apron** | **Lengthens the path and reduces uplift** ← |
| **INVERTED FILTER at the downstream end** | **Graded filter that lets WATER escape while retaining the SOIL — the direct defence against piping** ← |
| **Launching apron beyond it** | Protects against scour |

> **The INVERTED FILTER is the neatest of these because it addresses the mechanism rather than the head: piping requires soil particles to be carried away, and a properly graded filter permits the seepage to discharge harmlessly while holding every particle in place.**

> **Relieving the pressure without losing the soil is exactly what is wanted, and it is the same principle used behind retaining walls and in earth dam drains.**

examTip.trick: **BLIGH weights horizontal and vertical creep EQUALLY: L = C×H, with C = 15 fine sand, 12 coarse sand, 5-9 boulders.** Option (d) is LANE's rule (vertical 1, horizontal ⅓).
examTip.trap: **Lane's weighting means a VERTICAL cut-off is three times as effective as horizontal floor** — 3 m of sheet pile does the work of 9 m of apron, which is why modern weirs use deep cut-offs.
examTip.mnemonic: **Khosla's insight: the danger is the EXIT GRADIENT at the downstream toe, not the total creep length** — which is why Bligh-designed works still failed. Safe exit gradients 1 in 4 (shingle) to 1 in 7 (fine sand), and the DOWNSTREAM cut-off must be the deeper.

questions.stem: A SILT EJECTOR differs from a SILT EXCLUDER in that the ejector is located:
options: In the river upstream of the head regulator, and keeps silt out of the canal
On the crest of the weir, to pass silt over it
Across the undersluice pocket, to scour the river bed
In the CANAL, downstream of the head regulator, and removes silt that has ALREADY entered
questions.solution:
**In the CANAL, DOWNSTREAM of the head regulator — it removes silt that has already entered the canal.**

**The two devices compared, since the distinction is entirely one of position and timing:**

| | SILT EXCLUDER | SILT EJECTOR (silt extractor) |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | **In the RIVER, in the undersluice pocket, UPSTREAM of the head regulator** ← | **In the CANAL, some distance DOWNSTREAM of the head regulator** ← |
| **Function** | **PREVENTS silt from entering the canal** ← | **REMOVES silt that has already entered** ← |
| **How it works** | **Tunnels along the bed carry the silt-laden BOTTOM layer past the regulator and into the undersluices, so only the clearer upper water enters the canal** ← | **Silt settling on the canal bed is drawn off through a tunnel and returned to the river or an escape channel** ← |
| **Water used** | River water, escaping through the undersluices | **CANAL water — which is a real cost, since it is water already diverted** ← |
| **Timing** | **Preventive** ← | **Curative** ← |

> **The mnemonic that keeps them apart: the EXCLUDER EXCLUDES silt before it enters; the EJECTOR EJECTS silt that has entered.**

> **Option (a) describes the excluder exactly, which makes it the designed distractor — both are real structures and they are constantly interchanged.**

**Why either is needed — the physics of silt distribution:**

> **Silt is NOT uniformly distributed through the depth of a river. The coarser and heavier particles travel near the BED, and the water near the SURFACE is comparatively clear.**

| Layer | Silt content |
|---|---|
| **Near the SURFACE** | **Lowest, and finest particles** ← |
| **Mid depth** | Intermediate |
| **Near the BED** | **HIGHEST, and the coarsest particles** ← |

> **THAT STRATIFICATION IS THE WHOLE BASIS OF SILT CONTROL AT A HEADWORKS, and every device exploits it:**

| Device or feature | How it uses the stratification |
|---|---|
| **SILT EXCLUDER tunnels** | **Skim off the BOTTOM layer and pass it downstream** ← |
| **A HIGH crest (sill) on the head regulator** | **The canal draws from ABOVE the silt-laden bed layer** ← |
| **Locating the offtake on the OUTER bank of a bend** | **NO — the outer bank scours; the correct choice is discussed below** ← |
| **Divide wall and undersluice pocket** | Creates a still pocket where coarse material deposits and can be scoured away |
| **Settling basin (in a hydropower or canal intake)** | Slows the flow so the silt drops out |

> **THE BEND RULE deserves care because it is counter-intuitive and frequently misstated:**

> **At a river bend, the surface water flows toward the OUTER bank and the bottom water flows toward the INNER bank — a helical secondary current.**

> **The silt-laden bottom water therefore moves toward the INSIDE of the bend, which is why the inner bank builds up as a point bar and the outer bank scours into a deep pool.**

> **So an offtake on the OUTER (concave) bank draws the clearer SURFACE water and gets deep water at its mouth, while one on the inner bank draws the silt.**

> **The rule: TAKE OFF FROM THE OUTER BANK OF A BEND — the deep, scoured, relatively silt-free side.**

> **This is why so many traditional and modern intakes are sited on the concave bank, and it is the same principle exploited by the Tyrolean and side intakes of hill hydropower schemes.**

**The components of a diversion headworks, so the two devices can be located:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **WEIR or BARRAGE** | **Raises the water level to command the canal** ← |
| **UNDERSLUICES (scouring sluices)** | **A deeper bay next to the head regulator; keeps a clear pocket, scours deposited silt, and passes low flows** ← |
| **DIVIDE WALL** | **Separates the undersluice pocket from the weir proper, giving still water in front of the regulator** ← |
| **HEAD REGULATOR (canal head regulator)** | **Admits the design discharge into the canal and excludes floods** ← |
| **SILT EXCLUDER** | **Within the pocket, upstream of the regulator** ← |
| **FISH LADDER** | Permits migration past the weir |
| **Guide banks, marginal bunds, launching aprons** | River training |
| **Impervious and pervious floors, cut-offs** | Seepage and scour control |

> **The DIVIDE WALL and UNDERSLUICES work together and their purpose is worth stating: they create a POCKET of relatively still, deep water in front of the canal's mouth.**

> **Coarse material settles there rather than at the regulator's sill, and it is periodically flushed out through the undersluices by opening their gates — a scouring operation that is part of routine headworks management.**

> **The undersluice crest is therefore set LOWER than the weir crest, so that the pocket is the deepest part of the river at the site and the silt collects where it can be dealt with.**

**And the weir against the barrage, since both appear at a headworks:**

| | WEIR | BARRAGE |
|---|---|---|
| **How the level is raised** | **Mainly by the raised CREST itself** ← | **Mainly by GATES on a low crest** ← |
| **Control over the pond level** | **Little — the level depends on the flow** ← | **Full control at all discharges** ← |
| **Afflux upstream during floods** | **HIGHER — the crest obstructs** ← | **LOWER — the gates are opened and the flood passes freely** ← |
| **Silt disposal** | Poorer | **Better — gates can be operated to sluice silt through** ← |
| **Cost** | **Lower** ← | Higher |
| **Suits** | Small schemes, stable rivers | **Large schemes, alluvial rivers, where level control matters** ← |

> **The AFFLUX row is usually the deciding factor in flat alluvial country: a weir raises the flood level upstream over a long reach, requiring extensive marginal bunds and submerging land.**

> **A barrage, whose gates are lifted clear during a flood, causes far less afflux — so on a large river through populated flat land, the barrage's extra cost buys a great reduction in the flooding and land acquisition it causes.**

examTip.trick: **EXCLUDER EXCLUDES before entry (in the river, upstream of the regulator); EJECTOR EJECTS after entry (in the canal, downstream).** Option (a) describes the excluder.
examTip.trap: **Silt travels near the BED, clear water near the surface** — every silt-control device exploits that stratification, including the raised regulator sill and the excluder's bottom tunnels.
examTip.mnemonic: **Take an offtake from the OUTER (concave) bank of a bend** — the helical current sweeps bottom water and its silt toward the INNER bank, so the outer bank is deep and comparatively clear. And a BARRAGE beats a weir on afflux and level control.

questions.stem: The purpose of a LAUNCHING APRON provided at the toe of a guide bund is to:
options: Provide a layer of stone that SETTLES down the scour slope as scour develops, protecting the bund's toe
Act as an impervious blanket to reduce seepage under the bund
Serve as a roadway for maintenance vehicles
Increase the bund's height during floods
questions.solution:
**To provide a layer of stone that SETTLES ("launches") down the developing scour slope, armouring the toe as the scour deepens.**

**The mechanism, which is the reason for the name:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1 — Before the flood** | **The apron lies FLAT on the river bed, extending outward from the bund's toe** ← |
| **2 — Scour begins at the toe during the flood** | **The bed is eroded away from beneath the apron's outer edge** ← |
| **3 — The stone LAUNCHES** | **Deprived of support, the stones roll and slide down the face of the scour hole** ← |
| **4 — The launched stone forms a continuous armour on the scour slope** | **At the natural angle of repose, protecting the toe** ← |
| **5 — Equilibrium** | **Scour ceases once the slope is armoured** ← |

> **The apron is therefore a SELF-ADJUSTING protection: it responds to whatever depth of scour actually occurs, rather than having to be built to the full depth in advance.**

> **That is a genuinely elegant solution to a problem whose magnitude cannot be predicted precisely — and it is why the launching apron has survived unchanged since Bell devised it in the nineteenth century.**

**The design quantities, which follow from that mechanism:**

| Quantity | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Maximum SCOUR DEPTH** | **From Lacey: R = 0.473 (Q/f)^(1/3), then a multiplying factor by location** ← |
| **Scour factor at the NOSE of a guide bund** | **2.0 to 2.5 × R** ← |
| **At the transition / curved portion** | **1.5 × R** |
| **Along the straight shank** | **1.25 × R** |
| **Length of the apron** | **1.5 × D, where D is the scour depth BELOW the bed** ← |
| **Thickness laid flat** | **1.25 T, where T is the thickness required on the launched slope** ← |
| **Launched slope assumed** | **2 : 1 (horizontal : vertical)** ← |

> **The 1.5 D LENGTH and the 1.25 T THICKNESS both come from the same simple geometry: the stone must cover a slope of length D√(1+2²) = 2.24 D at the required thickness, and the flat apron must therefore contain that volume of stone.**

> **The extra thickness allows for the stone spreading and for some loss as it launches — so the rules are the volume calculation plus an allowance, not arbitrary factors.**

> **The NOSE FACTOR of 2 to 2.5 in the second row is the important one: scour is DEEPEST at the upstream nose of the guide bund, where the flow is turned most sharply, and the apron there must be correspondingly heavier.**

**GUIDE BUNDS themselves, since the apron protects them:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Purpose** | **To CONFINE and GUIDE the river through the waterway of a bridge or weir, preventing it from outflanking the structure** ← |
| **Form** | **A pair of embankments, one on each bank, usually curved (elliptical) upstream and with a short curved tail downstream** ← |
| **The upstream CURVED HEAD (nose)** | **Turns the flow gradually into the waterway; the most heavily attacked point** ← |
| **Length** | **Typically 1.0 to 1.5 times the waterway width upstream, 0.2 to 0.4 downstream** ← |
| **Slope pitching** | Stone pitching on the river face, with the launching apron at its toe |
| **Named after** | **Bell — hence "Bell's bunds"** |

> **The word OUTFLANKING in the first row names the failure the guide bund exists to prevent, and it is the characteristic disaster of a structure on an alluvial river:**

> **The river, unable to pass through the bridge or weir opening, cuts a new channel AROUND THE END of the structure through the soft bank material.**

> **The structure is then left standing in a dry or partly dry channel while the river flows past it — undamaged, and useless.**

> **Guide bunds and marginal bunds are the defence, and their extent must be enough to keep the river within the designed waterway even during an extreme flood with the channel at its most adverse position.**

**The other river training works, since the syllabus names them together:**

| Work | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **GUIDE BUNDS** | **Guide the flow through a structure** ← |
| **SPURS (groynes)** | **Project from the bank into the river to deflect the flow away from it, and to induce silting between them** ← |
| **MARGINAL BUNDS / LEVEES** | **Longitudinal embankments confining floods to the floodplain** ← |
| **Revetment / pitching** | Armours the bank in place |
| **Cut-offs** | Shorten an excessively meandering reach |
| **Bed bars, sills** | Control bed level |

> **SPURS deserve a note on their two types, since the distinction determines their behaviour:**

| Spur type | Orientation | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **ATTRACTING spur** | **Pointing DOWNSTREAM** | **Draws the flow TOWARD the bank — used to bring the deep channel to an intake** ← |
| **REPELLING spur** | **Pointing UPSTREAM (at about 60-70° to the bank)** | **Pushes the flow AWAY from the bank — the usual protective form** ← |
| **DEFLECTING spur** | Perpendicular | Local change of direction only |

> **The relation is worth remembering because it is the opposite of intuition: a spur pointing UPSTREAM, into the current, REPELS the flow from the bank, and one pointing downstream ATTRACTS it.**

> **A protective spur built pointing downstream because that seemed to offer less resistance will draw the river against the very bank it was meant to save — which is a real and expensive error.**

> **And the deepest scour at any spur occurs at its NOSE, so that is where the launching apron and the heaviest stone are needed, exactly as at the guide bund's head.**

examTip.trick: **The apron lies flat, the bed scours from beneath it, and the stone LAUNCHES down the scour slope to armour it** — a self-adjusting protection that need not be built to the full scour depth in advance.
examTip.trap: **Scour is deepest at the NOSE of a guide bund: 2.0-2.5 × Lacey's R**, against 1.5 at the transition and 1.25 along the shank. Apron length 1.5 D, thickness 1.25 T, launched slope 2:1.
examTip.mnemonic: **A spur pointing UPSTREAM REPELS the flow; one pointing DOWNSTREAM ATTRACTS it** — the opposite of intuition, and getting it backwards draws the river onto the bank you meant to protect. Guide bunds exist to prevent OUTFLANKING.

questions.stem: A cross-drainage work in which the natural DRAINAGE is carried OVER the canal, the canal flowing below with a free water surface, is called a:
questions.solution:
**A SUPER-PASSAGE.**

**The full family of cross-drainage works, which is the substance of this topic:**

| Work | What passes OVER | What passes UNDER | Flow condition below |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **The CANAL** | **The drainage** | **FREE surface (gravity)** ← |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** | **The CANAL** | **The drainage** | **UNDER PRESSURE (the drainage is syphoned)** ← |
| **SUPER-PASSAGE** | **The DRAINAGE** ← | **The CANAL** | **FREE surface** ← |
| **CANAL SYPHON (syphon)** | **The DRAINAGE** | **The CANAL** | **UNDER PRESSURE (the canal is syphoned)** ← |
| **LEVEL CROSSING** | **Both meet at the SAME level and mix; regulated by gates** ← | — | — |
| **INLET and OUTLET** | **A small drainage is admitted INTO the canal and taken out further along** ← | — | — |

> **The naming follows two questions, and answering them in order gives the right term every time:**

| Question | Answer determines |
|---|---|
| **1 — WHICH IS ON TOP, canal or drainage?** | **Canal on top → AQUEDUCT family. Drainage on top → SUPER-PASSAGE family** ← |
| **2 — Does the LOWER one flow freely or under pressure?** | **Free → aqueduct / super-passage. Pressure → SYPHON aqueduct / canal syphon** ← |

> **So an AQUEDUCT and a SUPER-PASSAGE are mirror images, and the word SYPHON in either name means only that the LOWER channel runs full and under pressure rather than with a free surface.**

> **The commonest confusion is between the super-passage and the canal syphon, since in both the drainage is on top — and the distinction is entirely whether the canal below has a free surface or is pressurised.**

**How the choice between them is made:**

| Governing condition | Choice |
|---|---|
| **Canal bed well ABOVE the drainage's high flood level** | **AQUEDUCT — the simplest and cheapest** ← |
| **Canal bed above the drainage bed, but the flood level would submerge the canal trough** | **SYPHON AQUEDUCT — the drainage bed is depressed and it runs under pressure** ← |
| **Drainage bed well ABOVE the canal's full supply level** | **SUPER-PASSAGE** ← |
| **Drainage above the canal, but the canal's water level would be in the way** | **CANAL SYPHON** ← |
| **Both at nearly the SAME level, and the drainage is small and clean** | **LEVEL CROSSING or INLET-OUTLET** ← |

> **THE RELATIVE LEVELS DECIDE THE STRUCTURE, and there is very little choice in the matter — which is why the first thing done at a proposed crossing is a levelling survey of the canal's full supply level against the drainage's bed and high flood levels.**

> **The design consequence is worth noting: the canal's alignment is usually fixed by the contour it must follow to command its area, so the canal level is the fixed quantity and the drainage must be accommodated around it.**

**Why a SYPHON is undesirable where it can be avoided:**

| Disadvantage of a syphon | Note |
|---|---|
| **SILT and debris DEPOSIT in the depressed barrel** | **The floor is below the natural bed, so anything carried settles there** ← |
| **It must be CLEANED regularly** | A maintenance burden that is often neglected |
| **A blocked barrel causes UPSTREAM FLOODING** | **The consequence of that neglect** ← |
| **Higher head loss** | — |
| **More expensive to build** | Deeper excavation, pressurised structure |

> **The SILTING problem in the first row is the practical reason engineers avoid syphons where the levels permit anything else: a syphon barrel is a sediment trap by construction, and it silts up in exactly the floods when it is most needed.**

> **Provision for cleaning — access, adequate barrel height, and sometimes a sloping floor — must be part of the design rather than an afterthought.**

**The other regulating structures named in this subchapter:**

| Structure | Function |
|---|---|
| **HEAD REGULATOR** | **At the offtake of a canal from the river or from a parent canal — controls the discharge admitted** ← |
| **CROSS REGULATOR** | **ACROSS a canal, downstream of an offtake — raises the upstream level so the offtake can draw its share at low flows** ← |
| **CANAL ESCAPE** | **Discharges SURPLUS water out of the canal, into a drain or river** ← |
| **CANAL OUTLET (module)** | **The small structure delivering water from a distributary to a watercourse** ← |
| **CANAL FALL (drop)** | **Lowers the canal bed where the ground slope exceeds the canal's design slope, dissipating the surplus energy** ← |

> **THE CROSS REGULATOR'S PURPOSE IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD, and it is worth stating clearly: it is not there to control the main canal's flow for its own sake, but to RAISE THE WATER LEVEL UPSTREAM of itself.**

> **When the canal runs at part supply, the water level falls, and an offtake whose sill is at the design level would draw nothing.**

> **Closing the cross regulator partly, immediately downstream of the offtake, backs the water up and restores the level at the offtake's mouth — so the distributary gets its share even at reduced supply.**

> **A head regulator and a cross regulator are therefore installed as a PAIR at every major offtake, and operated together.**

> **And the CANAL ESCAPE in the middle row is a safety device of the first importance: a canal whose supply cannot be reduced quickly — because the headworks are far upstream, or a distributary has been closed suddenly — will overtop and breach.**

> **A breach in a large canal empties it, floods the land below, and takes weeks to repair. The escape lets the surplus out harmlessly, and escapes are accordingly provided at intervals along every main canal and immediately upstream of every major structure.**

examTip.trick: **Two questions settle the name: (1) which is on TOP — canal on top = AQUEDUCT family, drainage on top = SUPER-PASSAGE family; (2) does the LOWER one flow FREE or under PRESSURE — pressure adds "syphon".**
examTip.trap: **Super-passage and canal SYPHON both carry the drainage over the canal** — the difference is only whether the canal below has a free surface (super-passage) or runs full under pressure (canal syphon).
examTip.mnemonic: **A syphon barrel is a SEDIMENT TRAP by construction** — its floor is below the natural bed, so it silts exactly when most needed. And a CROSS REGULATOR exists to RAISE the level upstream so an offtake can draw at part supply; it pairs with the head regulator.

questions.stem: A canal FALL is provided where:
options: The canal crosses a natural drainage channel
The canal needs to discharge its surplus water
Two canals of different levels have to be joined
The natural GROUND SLOPE is STEEPER than the canal's designed bed slope, so the surplus energy must be dissipated
questions.solution:
**Where the natural GROUND SLOPE is STEEPER than the canal's designed bed slope**, so that the accumulated surplus level is dropped at one point and the energy dissipated.

**Why the situation arises:**

> **A canal's bed slope is fixed by its hydraulic design — typically 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 10,000 for a large canal, chosen to give a non-silting, non-scouring velocity.**

> **The natural ground slope is whatever the country provides, and it is very often much steeper — perhaps 1 in 1,000.**

| Slope | Value |
|---|---|
| **Canal's design bed slope** | **1 in 5,000 (0.0002)** ← |
| **Natural ground slope** | **1 in 1,000 (0.001)** ← |
| **Divergence per kilometre** | **1.0 − 0.2 = 0.8 m per km** ← |

> **So after a kilometre the canal bed is 0.8 m above the ground; after five kilometres, 4 m — and the canal would be running along an ever-higher embankment.**

| Consequence of not providing a fall | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ever-increasing EMBANKMENT height** | **Costly earthwork, growing without limit** ← |
| **Risk of BREACH** | **A high embanked canal is dangerous; a breach floods the land below** ← |
| **Seepage through the embankment** | Water logging alongside |
| **The canal cannot COMMAND its area properly** | It becomes too high relative to the fields |

> **A FALL restores the canal to the ground surface by dropping its bed at one point — and the energy released must be destroyed, or it would scour the channel downstream.**

> **So a fall is two things at once: a LEVEL adjustment and an ENERGY DISSIPATOR, and the second is what governs its design.**

**Distinguishing it from the other structures the options name:**

| Option | The structure it actually describes |
|---|---|
| **(a) crossing a natural drainage** | **A CROSS-DRAINAGE work — aqueduct, super-passage, syphon** ← |
| **(b) discharging surplus water** | **A CANAL ESCAPE** ← |
| **(c) joining two canals of different levels** | Not a standard canal structure as described |
| **(d) ground steeper than the bed slope** | **A FALL — correct** ← |

> **Every distractor names a real canal structure's purpose, so the question turns on matching the function to the name.**

**Types of fall, in the order they were developed:**

| Fall | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ogee fall** | **The earliest; a smooth S-shaped profile that avoided a hydraulic jump — and therefore dissipated LITTLE energy, causing downstream scour** ← |
| **Rapid fall** | A long sloping glacis; used for small drops |
| **Stepped / cascade fall** | A series of steps; dissipates well |
| **Trapezoidal notch fall** | **Notches sized so that the upstream level is nearly independent of the discharge** ← |
| **Well type (cylinder / syphon well) fall** | Suits large drops with small discharge |
| **Simple vertical drop (Sarda type)** | **A raised crest with a vertical drop into a cistern** ← |
| **Glacis fall (straight and parabolic — Montague)** | **The modern standard: a sloping glacis on which a HYDRAULIC JUMP is formed and held** ← |
| **Baffle fall (Inglis)** | **A baffle wall in the cistern forces the jump to occur in a fixed position at all discharges** ← |

> **The progression through this list is a single idea being refined: HOW TO FORCE THE HYDRAULIC JUMP TO OCCUR WHERE IT IS WANTED.**

> **The OGEE fall's defect is instructive: by delivering the water smoothly it avoided the jump altogether, so the energy arrived downstream intact and scoured the canal — the smooth solution was the damaging one.**

> **The GLACIS fall works because a sloping apron converts the falling water into a supercritical stream, and the jump forms where it meets the downstream tailwater — dissipating 60 to 70 per cent of the energy in a short length.**

> **And the BAFFLE fall solves the remaining problem: the jump's position depends on the tailwater depth, which varies with discharge, so at part flow the jump can sweep out and the protection be bypassed. A baffle wall fixes its position for all discharges, which is why it is the preferred modern form.**

**FLUMED and NON-FLUMED falls, and the other functions a fall can serve:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **FLUMED fall** | **The waterway is NARROWED at the fall, so the structure is smaller and cheaper — but the velocity rises and more energy must be dissipated** ← |
| **A fall combined with a REGULATOR** | Common — the fall gives a convenient point for level control |
| **A fall combined with a BRIDGE** | The structure carries a road at little extra cost |
| **A fall used to generate POWER** | **A micro-hydropower installation on a canal fall — the head already exists** ← |
| **A fall as a METERING point** | **The crest acts as a weir, so the discharge can be measured** ← |

> **The POWER row is worth a closing note because it turns a liability into an asset: the energy that a fall exists to DESTROY can instead be USED.**

> **Canal-fall micro-hydro schemes need no dam, no reservoir and no new head — the drop is already there and the flow is already regulated — so their environmental and social costs are close to zero.**

> **Nepal's irrigation canals in the Terai contain a considerable number of such falls, and they represent a modest but genuinely low-impact power resource, of the kind that is easy to overlook precisely because the structure was built for another reason entirely.**

examTip.trick: **A FALL is needed when the GROUND slope exceeds the canal's DESIGN bed slope** — otherwise the canal ends up on an ever-higher embankment. It is both a level adjustment and an ENERGY DISSIPATOR.
examTip.trap: **Every distractor names a real structure: cross-drainage work (a), canal escape (b).** Match the function to the name.
examTip.mnemonic: **The whole history of fall design is forcing the HYDRAULIC JUMP to occur where wanted.** The smooth OGEE fall failed because it avoided the jump and sent the energy downstream; the GLACIS forms it; the BAFFLE fixes its position at all discharges.

questions.stem: The most damaging long-term consequence of WATER LOGGING in an irrigated area is:
options: An increase in the humidity of the local climate
The accumulation of SALTS in the root zone, rendering the soil saline or alkaline
An increase in the canal's silt load
A reduction in the canal's discharge capacity
questions.solution:
**The accumulation of SALTS in the root zone**, rendering the soil saline or alkaline and eventually taking it out of cultivation.

**The sequence, which explains why the damage is progressive and irreversible:**

| Step | Process |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Seepage from canals and over-irrigation raise the WATER TABLE** ← |
| **2** | **The water table reaches within about 1.5-2 m of the surface — the CRITICAL DEPTH** ← |
| **3** | **CAPILLARY action lifts water from the table to the surface** ← |
| **4** | **At the surface the water EVAPORATES, and the dissolved SALTS it carried are LEFT BEHIND** ← |
| **5** | **The process repeats daily; the salt concentration in the topsoil RISES without limit** ← |
| **6** | **The land becomes SALINE (white alkali) or ALKALINE (black alkali) and goes out of cultivation** ← |

> **STEPS 4 AND 5 CONTAIN THE WHOLE OF THE PROBLEM: the water leaves and the salt does not.**

> **Every litre evaporated deposits its dissolved solids permanently, so the soil acts as an accumulator — and even water of good quality, applied indefinitely with no drainage, will eventually salinise the land.**

> **This is why the condition is progressive rather than steady, and why it is so hard to reverse once established.**

**The immediate effects of water logging, before the salinity develops:**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Loss of soil AERATION** | **Roots need oxygen; saturated soil has none, and the roots suffocate** ← |
| **The root zone is restricted to the shallow layer above the table** | Poor anchorage and drought susceptibility |
| **SOIL TEMPERATURE falls** | **Wet soil warms slowly, delaying germination and growth** ← |
| **Beneficial soil BACTERIA are suppressed** | **Nitrification is an aerobic process and stops; nitrogen availability falls** ← |
| **Cultivation operations become impossible** | Machinery cannot enter the field |
| **Weeds and water-loving plants take over** | — |
| **Malaria and other vector-borne disease** | Standing water |

> **The BACTERIA row is worth its place: the nitrogen cycle in soil depends on aerobic bacteria, so a waterlogged soil not only suffocates the roots but stops supplying them with nitrogen — two injuries from the same cause.**

**The two kinds of salt-affected soil, since the remedies differ:**

| | SALINE (white alkali) | ALKALINE / SODIC (black alkali) |
|---|---|---|
| **Dominant salts** | **Chlorides and sulphates of Na, Ca, Mg** | **SODIUM carbonate and bicarbonate** ← |
| **pH** | **Below 8.5** | **ABOVE 8.5, often 9-10** ← |
| **Appearance** | **WHITE crust on the surface** ← | **BLACK, from dispersed organic matter** ← |
| **Soil STRUCTURE** | **Retained — the soil remains permeable** ← | **DESTROYED — the clay disperses and the soil becomes impermeable** ← |
| **Remedy** | **LEACHING with good water, plus drainage** ← | **Apply GYPSUM (calcium sulphate) to replace the sodium, THEN leach** ← |
| **Ease of reclamation** | **Easier** | **Much harder — the impermeability resists the very leaching required** ← |

> **THE STRUCTURE ROW EXPLAINS WHY SODIC SOIL IS THE WORSE OF THE TWO, and the mechanism is worth understanding:**

> **Sodium ions cause clay particles to DISPERSE (deflocculate) rather than clump together. The soil loses its crumb structure, becomes a dense impermeable mass, and water will neither enter it nor drain through it.**

> **So the treatment — leaching the salts out with water — cannot be applied, because the water cannot get in.**

> **GYPSUM breaks the deadlock: its calcium replaces the sodium on the clay's exchange sites, the clay flocculates, the structure and permeability return, and only then can the displaced sodium be leached away.**

> **Calcium restores what sodium destroyed, and the order of operations is essential — gypsum first, then leaching.**

**Prevention, which is far cheaper than reclamation:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **LINE the canals, distributaries and watercourses** | **Attacks the principal source of the seepage** ← |
| **Provide SUB-SURFACE DRAINAGE from the outset** | **Keeps the water table below the critical depth** ← |
| **CONJUNCTIVE USE — pump the shallow groundwater for irrigation** | **Lowers the table and augments the supply at once** ← |
| **Avoid OVER-IRRIGATION — volumetric charging, on-farm water management** | ← |
| **Provide adequate SURFACE drainage for storm runoff** | Often omitted entirely |
| **Include a LEACHING FRACTION in the irrigation schedule** | **Apply slightly more water than the crop needs, so salts are flushed DOWN rather than concentrated** ← |
| **Choose salt-tolerant crops where risk exists** | Barley, cotton, date palm |
| **Maintain the drains** | **A blocked drain is no drain at all** ← |

> **THE LEACHING FRACTION IN THE SIXTH ROW IS THE KEY IDEA IN PREVENTION, and it inverts the instinct to economise on water:**

> **Applying exactly the crop's requirement means every gram of salt delivered stays in the root zone. Applying a modest EXCESS — perhaps 10 to 20 per cent — carries the salts down below the roots.**

> **So a small deliberate over-application is protective, PROVIDED the excess can actually DRAIN AWAY.**

> **Without drainage, the same excess simply raises the water table and makes matters worse — which is why LEACHING AND DRAINAGE MUST BE PROVIDED TOGETHER, and why either alone can be harmful.**

> **That pairing is the single most important principle in the sustainable management of irrigated land, and the historical record supports it plainly: irrigation systems that provided drainage from the beginning have lasted for centuries, and those that did not have salinised, some of them in a few decades.**

examTip.trick: **Water table rises → capillary rise → evaporation → the water leaves and the SALT DOES NOT.** The soil accumulates salt indefinitely, so even good-quality water salinises land if there is no drainage.
examTip.trap: **SALINE (white, pH < 8.5, structure intact) is leached out; SODIC/alkaline (black, pH > 8.5) needs GYPSUM FIRST** — sodium disperses the clay and makes the soil impermeable, so leaching cannot work until calcium restores the structure.
examTip.mnemonic: **LEACHING AND DRAINAGE MUST GO TOGETHER.** A 10-20 % leaching fraction flushes salts below the root zone — but without drainage the same excess just raises the water table and makes it worse.

questions.stem: In the development of a hydropower project, the studies are normally carried out in the sequence:
options: RECONNAISSANCE study → pre-feasibility study → feasibility study → detailed design
Feasibility study → reconnaissance study → detailed design → pre-feasibility study
Detailed design → feasibility study → reconnaissance study
Pre-feasibility study → detailed design → reconnaissance study → feasibility study
questions.solution:
**RECONNAISSANCE → PRE-FEASIBILITY → FEASIBILITY → DETAILED DESIGN.**

**What each stage does, and what it costs:**

| Stage | Purpose | Basis of the data | Cost accuracy | Typical cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RECONNAISSANCE** | **Identify whether a site is worth investigating at all; compare alternative sites on a river** ← | **Maps, existing hydrology, a brief site visit** | **±40 % or worse** | **A fraction of 1 % of the project** |
| **PRE-FEASIBILITY** | **Select the best scheme layout and capacity; decide whether to proceed** ← | **Preliminary survey, some geology, regional hydrology** | **±25 %** | **0.5-1 %** |
| **FEASIBILITY** | **Establish technical, economic, environmental and financial viability; the basis for the LICENSE and for financing** ← | **Detailed topographic survey, drilling and geological investigation, gauged hydrology, EIA** | **±10-15 %** | **1-3 %** ← |
| **DETAILED DESIGN (tender design)** | **Produce drawings, specifications and tender documents for construction** ← | **All of the above plus supplementary investigation** | **±5-10 %** | **2-5 %** |

> **The sequence is one of PROGRESSIVELY NARROWING CHOICE AND INCREASING EXPENDITURE, and that is its logic: cheap studies eliminate poor options before expensive studies are spent on them.**

> **A reconnaissance may examine a dozen sites on a river and recommend two; a pre-feasibility takes those two and recommends one; the feasibility study establishes whether that one should be built.**

> **Spending feasibility-level money on a site that a reconnaissance would have rejected is the waste the sequence exists to prevent.**

**Why the FEASIBILITY study is the pivotal one:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is the basis on which the LICENSE is granted** | **In Nepal, the generation license follows an approved feasibility study and EIA** ← |
| **It is what LENDERS and investors examine** | **No financing is raised on a pre-feasibility** ← |
| **It fixes the INSTALLED CAPACITY** | **The single most consequential decision in the project** ← |
| **It includes the EIA and the resettlement plan** | Statutory requirements |
| **It is where the geology is actually investigated** | **And geology is where hydropower projects go wrong** ← |

> **THE GEOLOGY POINT IN THE LAST ROW DESERVES EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS THE CHARACTERISTIC RISK OF HYDROPOWER, and particularly of Himalayan hydropower:**

> **The Himalaya is young, tectonically active and structurally complex, with shattered rock, thrust zones, high in-situ stresses and unpredictable groundwater.**

> **A tunnel is bought by the metre and the rock is not visible until it is excavated, so the cost of a headrace tunnel can multiply if the ground proves worse than assumed.**

> **Cost and time overruns on Nepali and Indian Himalayan projects have very often been geological — squeezing ground, high water inflows, collapses — rather than hydrological or commercial.**

> **That is why the drilling and geological investigation carried out at feasibility stage is money exceptionally well spent, and why cutting it to save time is one of the most expensive economies available in this sector.**

**The other decisions taken during planning:**

| Decision | Note |
|---|---|
| **The TYPE of scheme** | **Storage, run-of-river, peaking run-of-river, or pumped storage** ← |
| **The INSTALLED CAPACITY** | **From the flow duration curve and the market — see below** ← |
| **The layout — dam site, headrace route, powerhouse position** | Governed by topography and geology |
| **Surface or UNDERGROUND powerhouse** | Underground where the valley is narrow or slopes unstable |
| **The number and type of units** | Reliability and part-load efficiency |
| **Transmission connection point** | **Often a binding constraint — a project without an evacuation line cannot sell power** ← |

> **The TRANSMISSION row is worth naming because it has repeatedly been the binding constraint in Nepal: projects have been completed and left unable to deliver their output because the transmission line was not ready.**

> **A generating license and a power purchase agreement are worth nothing without a physical connection, so the transmission plan belongs in the feasibility study rather than being treated as somebody else's responsibility.**

**And the STAGES OF PHYSICAL DEVELOPMENT that follow the studies:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Licensing — survey license, then generation license** | Survey license first, permitting the studies |
| **Financial closure** | **All financing agreements signed; see project finance** ← |
| **Construction — access roads first** | **In Nepal the ACCESS ROAD is often the first and most difficult work** ← |
| **Commissioning and testing** | Wet testing, trial run |
| **Commercial operation date (COD)** | **When the PPA's tariff begins to be earned** ← |
| **Operation, and eventual handover under a BOOT concession** | Typically after 25-35 years |

> **The ACCESS ROAD entry reflects a real feature of Himalayan projects: the site is often days from the nearest road, and every tonne of cement, steel and equipment must reach it.**

> **The access road is therefore built first, is a substantial project in itself, causes much of the scheme's environmental impact through spoil and slope disturbance, and frequently governs the construction programme.**

> **It is also the part of the project that benefits the local population most directly and permanently, which is why access roads feature so prominently in the local-benefit negotiations that accompany Nepali hydropower development.**

examTip.trick: **RECONNAISSANCE (±40 %) → PRE-FEASIBILITY (±25 %) → FEASIBILITY (±10-15 %) → DETAILED DESIGN.** Progressively narrowing choice, progressively increasing cost.
examTip.trap: **The FEASIBILITY study is the pivot** — it is the basis of the generation license, of financing, and of the installed-capacity decision, and it is where the GEOLOGY is finally investigated.
examTip.mnemonic: **Himalayan hydropower overruns are usually GEOLOGICAL, not hydrological** — a tunnel is bought by the metre and the rock is unseen until excavated. Cutting the drilling programme to save time is the most expensive economy in the sector.

questions.stem: A PEAKING RUN-OF-RIVER (PROR) hydropower plant differs from a simple run-of-river plant in that a PROR plant:
options: Has no intake structure at all
Operates only during the monsoon season
Has a PONDAGE that stores a few hours' flow, so generation can be concentrated in the peak demand hours
Requires a large storage reservoir with seasonal regulation
questions.solution:
**It has PONDAGE — a small storage holding a few hours' flow — so the day's water can be concentrated into the PEAK DEMAND hours.**

**The three types compared:**

| Type | Storage | Regulation period | Generation pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RUN-OF-RIVER (ROR)** | **NONE (or negligible)** | **None** | **Generates whatever the river offers, hour by hour** ← |
| **PEAKING ROR (PROR)** | **PONDAGE — typically 4 to 6 hours of flow** ← | **DAILY** ← | **Stores through the night and off-peak hours; releases at full capacity during the evening peak** ← |
| **STORAGE** | **A large RESERVOIR** | **SEASONAL or annual** ← | **Stores the monsoon surplus for release through the dry season** ← |

> **The distinction is one of the PERIOD over which the flow is regulated: none, a day, or a year.**
