> **Option (d) describes the STORAGE plant, which makes it the designed distractor — the difference between pondage and a reservoir is exactly the difference between daily and seasonal regulation.**

**Why peaking capability is so valuable — the economics:**

> **Electricity demand is not uniform. A typical Nepali daily load curve has a pronounced EVENING PEAK, when lighting and cooking coincide, and a deep overnight trough.**

| Period | Demand | Value of energy |
|---|---|---|
| **Evening PEAK (roughly 6-10 pm)** | **HIGHEST** | **HIGHEST — this is when supply is short and load-shedding occurs** ← |
| **Daytime** | Moderate | Moderate |
| **Overnight trough** | **LOWEST** | **LOWEST — the system may have surplus** ← |

> **A simple ROR plant generates at the same rate around the clock, so much of its output arrives at night when it is least needed and worth least.**

> **A PROR plant of the SAME AVERAGE FLOW holds back the overnight water and releases it in the evening — producing the SAME TOTAL ENERGY but far MORE VALUABLE energy.**

> **This is why PPAs commonly pay a higher tariff for peak-hour energy, and why the modest cost of a pondage and a larger installed capacity is usually recovered several times over.**

> **The essential point: PONDAGE DOES NOT CREATE ENERGY; IT MOVES IT TO WHEN IT IS WORTH MORE.**

**A worked illustration of the capacity difference:**

> **A river offers a steady 10 m³/s at a net head of 100 m, with an overall efficiency of 85 per cent.**

| Scheme | Design discharge | Installed capacity | Operating hours | Daily energy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Simple ROR** | **10 m³/s continuously** | **9.81 × 10 × 100 × 0.85 = 8.34 MW** | **24 h** | **200 MWh** ← |
| **PROR, 6-hour peaking** | **40 m³/s for 6 hours** | **9.81 × 40 × 100 × 0.85 = 33.4 MW** ← | **6 h** | **200 MWh — the SAME** ← |

> **The PROR plant has FOUR TIMES the installed capacity and produces the SAME energy, delivered in a quarter of the time.**

> **That is the trade the developer evaluates: four times the turbine, penstock and powerhouse capacity, plus a pondage, against a much higher tariff for every unit sold.**

> **In practice the peaking ratio chosen is more modest, because the penstock and turbines must be sized for the peak discharge and the cost rises steeply — but the principle drives the design.**

**Why Nepal has so few STORAGE projects, despite needing them most:**

| Obstacle | Note |
|---|---|
| **Very high CAPITAL cost** | A large dam dominates the project cost |
| **SUBMERGENCE and RESETTLEMENT** | **A reservoir in a settled Himalayan valley displaces communities and inundates the limited flat, fertile land** ← |
| **SEDIMENTATION** | **Himalayan rivers carry enormous sediment loads; a reservoir's useful life can be far shorter than the dam's** ← |
| **Seismic risk and geology** | A large dam in an active mountain belt |
| **Long construction period and financing difficulty** | ← |
| **Downstream and transboundary considerations** | — |

> **THE SEDIMENTATION PROBLEM IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE MOST SPECIFIC TO THE HIMALAYA, and it deserves a plain statement:**

> **Himalayan rivers are among the most sediment-laden in the world, because the mountains are young, rising rapidly, steep, seismically shattered and subject to intense monsoon rainfall.**

> **A reservoir traps that sediment. Its dead storage fills first, then its live storage, and the plant's regulating capability declines year by year.**

> **Design lives assumed at 100 years have in some cases proved to be 30 or 40, and sediment once deposited is extremely difficult and expensive to remove.**

> **Mitigation — sluicing, flushing, density-current venting, catchment management, and designing the intake high above the dead storage — must be built into the scheme from the start, because it cannot be retrofitted.**

> **This is the principal technical reason why Nepal's development has concentrated on ROR and PROR schemes, and why the country's dry-season deficit persists despite its very large theoretical potential.**

**And the corresponding seasonal problem that storage would solve:**

| Season | River flow | Demand |
|---|---|---|
| **MONSOON (June-September)** | **HIGH — ROR plants run at full capacity and may SPILL** ← | Moderate |
| **DRY (December-April)** | **LOW — flows fall to a small fraction of the monsoon value** ← | **HIGH, and heating adds to it** ← |

> **So a country supplied mainly by ROR plants has SURPLUS in the monsoon and DEFICIT in the dry season — which is precisely Nepal's position, and the reason for both dry-season imports and monsoon exports.**

> **Storage would resolve the mismatch directly; in its absence, the alternatives are regional power trade, which converts the seasonal mismatch into a commercial opportunity, and complementary sources such as solar, whose output is highest in the dry, clear months when the rivers are lowest.**

examTip.trick: **Regulation PERIOD is the distinction: ROR none, PROR DAILY (pondage of 4-6 hours), STORAGE seasonal.** Option (d) describes the storage plant.
examTip.trap: **Pondage does not create energy — it MOVES it to when it is worth more.** A 6-hour PROR plant has four times the installed capacity of the equivalent ROR plant and produces the same daily energy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Himalayan SEDIMENT is why Nepal has so little storage** — reservoirs designed for 100 years have filled in 30-40. Hence ROR/PROR dominance, hence monsoon surplus and dry-season deficit.

questions.stem: The FIRM (or primary) POWER of a hydropower plant is the power:
options: Produced at the maximum recorded river discharge
That can be guaranteed to be available at ALL TIMES, corresponding to the minimum dependable flow
Equal to the installed capacity of the plant
questions.solution:
**The power that can be GUARANTEED at all times**, corresponding to the minimum dependable flow.

**The categories of power and energy:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **FIRM (primary) power** | **Available at ALL times with a stated reliability — based on the minimum dependable flow, commonly Q₉₅ or Q₁₀₀** ← |
| **SECONDARY (non-firm) power** | **Available only when the flow exceeds the minimum — the surplus above firm** ← |
| **AVERAGE power** | The mean over the period (option d) |
| **INSTALLED CAPACITY** | **The nameplate rating of the generators — the maximum the plant CAN produce** ← (option c) |
| **Peak power** | The maximum a plant delivers in a period |

> **Options (c) and (d) are real and distinct quantities from the same analysis, which makes them well-made distractors — installed capacity and average power are both routinely quoted alongside firm power and mean quite different things.**

**Why firm power matters more than the other figures:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is what a system can DEPEND on** | **A system's ability to meet its load is set by what is available in the worst season, not on average** ← |
| **It commands a HIGHER TARIFF** | **Firm energy is worth more than dumped surplus** ← |
| **It determines the plant's contribution to system CAPACITY** | **Reserve planning is based on firm, not installed, capacity** ← |
| **It is what lenders lend against** | **See project finance — the DSCR is computed from dependable revenue** ← |

> **The FIRST ROW states the essential idea: a plant that produces 100 MW for four monsoon months and 8 MW in the dry season is, from the point of view of system reliability, an 8 MW plant with a large seasonal bonus.**

> **That is why Nepal's dry-season firm capacity, rather than its installed capacity, is the number that governs whether load-shedding occurs.**

**The FLOW DURATION CURVE, which is where these quantities are read:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | **A plot of DISCHARGE against the PERCENTAGE OF TIME that discharge is EQUALLED OR EXCEEDED** ← |
| **How it is built** | **Rank all the flow records in DESCENDING order; plot each against its exceedance percentage** ← |
| **Q₄₀** | **The flow equalled or exceeded 40 % of the time — a common design discharge for ROR plants in Nepal** ← |
| **Q₉₅, Q₁₀₀** | **The dependable low flows, used for FIRM power** ← |
| **A STEEP curve** | **A flashy river — large floods, very low dry-season flow; poor for ROR** ← |
| **A FLAT curve** | **A well-regulated river, often snow- or spring-fed; excellent for ROR** ← |

> **The SHAPE of the curve is as informative as any single point on it, and the last two rows are the practical reading:**

> **A river fed by GLACIER MELT AND SNOW has a flatter duration curve, because the melt continues into the dry months when rainfall has ceased — which is why Nepal's snow-fed rivers are far more attractive for run-of-river development than purely rain-fed ones.**

> **A rain-fed river in the Middle Hills may carry fifty times its dry-season flow during the monsoon, and a plant sized for even a modest fraction of the peak will stand nearly idle for half the year.**

> **So the choice of design discharge is a direct reading of the duration curve against the tariff structure: a higher design flow captures more monsoon energy at a lower capacity factor, and a lower one gives a smaller, more consistently loaded plant.**

**The PERFORMANCE FACTORS, since they describe how a plant is actually used:**

| Factor | Definition | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD FACTOR** | **Average load ÷ PEAK load, over a period** ← | **0.4 to 0.7 for a system** |
| **CAPACITY (plant) FACTOR** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED CAPACITY** ← | **ROR in Nepal: 0.5-0.6; PROR: 0.3-0.4** ← |
| **UTILISATION factor** | Peak load ÷ installed capacity | — |
| **DIVERSITY factor** | **Sum of individual peaks ÷ the system's coincident peak — always > 1** ← | 1.2 to 2.0 |

> **The distinction between LOAD FACTOR and CAPACITY FACTOR is the one most often blurred, and it is simply the denominator: load factor divides by the PEAK LOAD ACTUALLY REACHED, capacity factor by the PLANT'S RATING.**

> **They coincide only when the plant's peak output equals its installed capacity.**

> **And a LOW capacity factor is not necessarily a fault — a peaking plant is DESIGNED to run few hours at full output, so its capacity factor is low by intention, while its value to the system is high.**

> **Judging a PROR plant by its capacity factor, or a baseload plant by its peaking ability, misreads what each was built to do.**

**And the DIVERSITY FACTOR in the last row deserves a note, since it explains why systems are smaller than the sum of their parts:**

> **Every consumer has a peak demand, and they do not all occur at the same instant. The system's peak is therefore LESS than the sum of the individual peaks, and the ratio between them is the diversity factor.**

> **This is the same statistical averaging met in the water-supply peak factor: the larger and more varied the population, the greater the diversity and the flatter the aggregate load.**

> **It is why generation capacity need not equal the sum of connected loads, and why an isolated single consumer — a factory, or a village mini-grid — needs proportionally far more capacity than a large interconnected system does.**

examTip.trick: **FIRM power = guaranteed at all times, from the minimum dependable flow (Q₉₅-Q₁₀₀). SECONDARY = the surplus above it.** Options (c) and (d) are installed capacity and average power — real, different quantities.
examTip.trap: **LOAD factor divides by the PEAK LOAD; CAPACITY factor divides by the INSTALLED CAPACITY.** A low capacity factor is by design for a peaking plant, not a fault.
examTip.mnemonic: **A flow duration curve's SHAPE is the reading: STEEP = flashy rain-fed river, poor for ROR; FLAT = snow- or spring-fed, excellent.** And a system's reliability rests on dry-season FIRM capacity, not installed capacity.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant has a design discharge of 20 m³/s, a net head of 60 m and an overall efficiency of 85 per cent. Its power output is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 10.0 MW.**

**The computation:**

> **P = ρ g Q H η**

> **P = 1000 × 9.81 × 20 × 60 × 0.85 = 10,006,200 W ≈ 10.0 MW** ←

> **Or in the convenient working form: P (kW) = 9.81 Q H η, with Q in m³/s and H in metres.**

> **P = 9.81 × 20 × 60 × 0.85 = 10,006 kW = 10.0 MW** ←

| Distractor | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **11.8 MW** | **9.81 × 20 × 60 × 1.0 = 11.77 — the efficiency OMITTED** ← |
| **14.0 MW** | Efficiency applied as a divisor, or a mis-set decimal |
| **8.5 MW** | **Efficiency applied twice (0.85²), or 9.81 taken as 8.34** ← |

> **The 11.8 MW distractor is the one to watch: forgetting the efficiency is the single commonest error in this calculation, and the answer it gives looks entirely plausible.**

> **A useful rough check: with η ≈ 0.85, P (kW) ≈ 8.34 Q H — so 8.34 × 20 × 60 = 10,008 kW, confirming 10 MW in one step.**

**The terms in the equation, each of which hides a subtlety:**

| Term | Note |
|---|---|
| **ρ = 1000 kg/m³** | Water's density |
| **g = 9.81 m/s²** | — |
| **Q — the DESIGN DISCHARGE** | **Read from the flow duration curve, LESS any environmental release and any leakage** ← |
| **H — the NET head** | **The GROSS head MINUS all hydraulic losses — see below** ← |
| **η — the OVERALL efficiency** | **The PRODUCT of the turbine, generator and transformer efficiencies** ← |

> **THE NET HEAD IS WHERE ERRORS ENTER, and the distinction from gross head must be kept:**

| Head | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS head** | **The vertical difference between the intake water level and the tailwater level** ← |
| **Losses** | **Trashrack, intake, tunnel friction, bends, valves, penstock friction, and the exit loss** ← |
| **NET (effective) head** | **Gross MINUS all those losses — and this is what the turbine actually sees** ← |

> **The head loss is commonly designed to be 5 to 10 per cent of the gross head, and that figure is itself an optimisation:**

> **A LARGER tunnel and penstock cost more but lose less head; a smaller one is cheaper but wastes energy for the whole life of the plant.**

> **The economic diameter is found by minimising the sum of the capital cost and the capitalised value of the lost energy — which is a classic engineering-economics application of exactly the kind met in project appraisal.**

**The overall efficiency and its components:**

| Component | Typical efficiency |
|---|---|
| **TURBINE at its design point** | **0.90 to 0.94** ← |
| **GENERATOR** | **0.95 to 0.98** ← |
| **Transformer** | 0.98 to 0.99 |
| **Mechanical / bearing losses** | Included in the turbine figure |
| **OVERALL (product)** | **0.83 to 0.90** ← |

> **So 0.85 is a normal overall figure, and it is the PRODUCT of the chain rather than any one machine's rating — which is why quoting "efficiency" without saying which is ambiguous.**

> **And the turbine's efficiency in the first row is its DESIGN-POINT value: at part load it falls, sometimes steeply, which is the reason a plant is often built with several smaller units rather than one large one.**

| Units | Behaviour at part flow |
|---|---|
| **ONE large unit** | **Must run at part load when the flow is low — poor efficiency, and it may not run at all below its minimum** ← |
| **TWO or THREE units** | **Shut some down and run the others near their best point — much better average efficiency, and redundancy for maintenance** ← |

> **A run-of-river plant on a river with a steep flow duration curve therefore benefits particularly from multiple units, since it spends much of the year well below its design discharge.**

> **The trade is capital cost and complexity against annual energy — and for a Nepali ROR scheme with a long low-flow season, the multiple-unit arrangement usually wins.**

**And the ENERGY that follows from the power, since revenue depends on energy rather than capacity:**

> **Annual energy (GWh) = P (MW) × 8,760 hours × capacity factor ÷ 1,000**

> **For this plant at a capacity factor of 0.55: E = 10.0 × 8,760 × 0.55 / 1,000 = 48.2 GWh per year.**

> **At an average tariff of, say, NPR 8 per kWh, that is roughly NPR 385 million of annual revenue — and it is this figure, not the 10 MW, that the project's financial viability rests on.**

> **Which is the practical reason for insisting on the distinction between capacity and energy: a plant is BUILT in megawatts and PAID in kilowatt-hours.**

examTip.trap: **11.8 MW is the answer with the EFFICIENCY OMITTED** — the commonest error in this calculation, and it looks perfectly plausible.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use NET head (gross minus 5-10 % losses), and η is the PRODUCT of turbine × generator × transformer (~0.85).** A plant is BUILT in megawatts and PAID in kilowatt-hours — energy needs the capacity factor.

questions.stem: For NO TENSION to develop at the heel of a gravity dam, the resultant of all forces at the base must pass within:
options: The upstream half of the base
A distance of b/3 from the toe
The downstream quarter of the base
The MIDDLE THIRD of the base
questions.solution:
**The MIDDLE THIRD of the base** — that is, the eccentricity e must not exceed b/6.

**The derivation, which is the same middle-third rule met in foundation design:**

> **The base is subject to a direct stress from the vertical load and a bending stress from the moment of the eccentric resultant:**

> **σ = (ΣV/b)(1 ± 6e/b)** per unit length of dam

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| **e < b/6** | **6e/b < 1, so BOTH stresses are COMPRESSIVE** ← |
| **e = b/6** | **The stress at the heel is exactly ZERO — the limiting case** ← |
| **e > b/6** | **The stress at the heel becomes NEGATIVE, i.e. TENSILE** ← |

> **Since e can be either side of the centre, the resultant must lie within b/6 on each side — a band of width b/3 centred on the base, which is the MIDDLE THIRD.**

> **Option (b), "within b/3 of the toe", is a genuine part of the answer stated incompletely: the middle third does extend from b/3 to 2b/3, so being within b/3 of the toe is necessary but not sufficient — the resultant must also be at least b/3 from the heel.**

**Why tension is unacceptable in a gravity dam:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Concrete and masonry have very little TENSILE strength** | **And it cannot be relied on** ← |
| **A crack opens at the HEEL** | ← |
| **WATER ENTERS the crack and applies FULL RESERVOIR PRESSURE inside it** ← | **This is the critical consequence** |
| **That pressure increases the UPLIFT and extends the crack further** | **A PROGRESSIVE, self-worsening failure** ← |
| **The effective base area is reduced, raising the stress on what remains** | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS DESCRIBE WHY THIS IS NOT MERELY A SERVICEABILITY MATTER: a crack at the heel is not a cosmetic defect but the beginning of a runaway mechanism.**

> **Water at full reservoir head entering the crack pushes it open, which admits more water over a larger area, which pushes harder — and the crack propagates toward the toe until the dam overturns or slides.**

> **That is why the no-tension rule is applied at the HEEL specifically, and why it is treated as a fundamental requirement rather than one criterion among several.**

**The full set of stability requirements for a gravity dam:**

| Check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Against OVERTURNING** | **Factor of safety ≥ 1.5 (ratio of resisting to overturning moments about the toe)** ← |
| **Against SLIDING** | **Sliding factor ΣH/ΣV < μ; shear friction factor ≥ 4 to 5** ← |
| **NO TENSION at the heel** | **Resultant within the middle third** ← |
| **COMPRESSIVE stress within the allowable** | **For the concrete and for the foundation rock** ← |
| **Against flotation** | Rarely governs for a gravity dam |

> **UPLIFT is the force that makes all of these harder, and it deserves its own note because it was historically underestimated:**

| Aspect of uplift | Note |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | **Water pressure acting UPWARD on the base, from seepage through the foundation and the body** ← |
| **Its effect** | **REDUCES the effective weight ΣV — which worsens sliding, overturning AND the tension check simultaneously** ← |
| **Distribution assumed** | **Full reservoir head at the heel, tailwater head at the toe, varying linearly between** ← |
| **Reduction by DRAINAGE GALLERY** | **Drainage holes near the heel relieve the pressure — the uplift diagram drops sharply at the drain line** ← |
| **Typical relief** | **The uplift at the drain can be reduced to about a third of the difference between headwater and tailwater** ← |

> **The DRAINAGE GALLERY is one of the most cost-effective features of a gravity dam: a line of holes drilled down from a gallery near the heel intercepts the seepage and relieves the uplift, and the saving in dam volume greatly exceeds the gallery's cost.**

> **Several nineteenth-century dam failures were attributable to uplift being ignored altogether, and the practice of assuming a full linear uplift diagram, relieved by drains, is the direct result of that experience.**

**And the elementary profile, which follows from the same two conditions:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Shape** | **A right-angled TRIANGLE, apex at the top water level, vertical face upstream** ← |
| **Base width for NO TENSION** | **b = H / √(G − c), with G the specific gravity of the material and c the uplift coefficient** ← |
| **With no uplift (c = 0) and G = 2.4** | **b = H / √2.4 = 0.65 H** ← |
| **With full uplift (c = 1)** | **b = H / √1.4 = 0.85 H** ← |

> **The comparison between the last two rows quantifies what uplift costs: allowing for full uplift makes the dam some 30 per cent wider, and therefore 30 per cent more expensive in material.**

> **That is exactly the saving the drainage gallery buys back — which is why every modern gravity dam has one, and why the assumed uplift diagram is one of the most consequential assumptions in the whole design.**

examTip.trick: **Resultant within the MIDDLE THIRD, i.e. e ≤ b/6** — from σ = (ΣV/b)(1 ± 6e/b), which goes tensile once 6e/b exceeds 1.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is half the answer** — within b/3 of the toe is necessary but not sufficient; the resultant must also be b/3 from the HEEL.
examTip.mnemonic: **A heel crack is a RUNAWAY: water enters at full reservoir head, pushes it open, admits more water, pushes harder.** And UPLIFT worsens sliding, overturning and tension all at once — the DRAINAGE GALLERY relieves it and saves ~30 % of the dam's width.

questions.stem: The SETTLING BASIN of a run-of-river hydropower plant in Nepal is designed principally to remove particles larger than about:
questions.solution:
**About 0.2 mm** (commonly 0.15 to 0.2 mm for high-head plants; a coarser limit of 0.3 to 0.5 mm may be accepted for low-head Francis and Kaplan installations).

**Why that size, and why it matters so much in Nepal:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Particles LARGER than about 0.2 mm cause severe ABRASION of turbine runners, needles and nozzles** ← | **Especially at high head, where the velocity is greatest** |
| **Himalayan sediment is rich in QUARTZ and FELDSPAR** ← | **Hardness 6-7 on Mohs — HARDER than the turbine steel** ← |
| **Removing finer particles requires a very large basin** | **Settling velocity falls as the SQUARE of the diameter, so halving the size quadruples the basin** ← |
| **So 0.2 mm is an ECONOMIC compromise** ← | **Between abrasion damage and basin cost** |

> **THE QUARTZ CONTENT IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE FACT THAT MAKES NEPALI HYDROPOWER DISTINCTIVE, and it deserves plain statement:**

> **The abrasiveness of sediment depends on the HARDNESS of its minerals, not merely on its quantity. Himalayan rivers carry sediment derived from granites and gneisses, with quartz contents commonly of 30 to 60 per cent.**

> **Quartz at Mohs 6-7 is harder than the martensitic stainless steels used for runners, so the particles cut the metal rather than being deflected by it.**

> **The result is that Nepali high-head plants have suffered runner erosion severe enough to require overhaul or replacement within a few YEARS of commissioning, and in the worst monsoon conditions within a single season.**

> **That is why the settling basin is not a peripheral structure on a Himalayan scheme but one of its most important, and why it is often the largest civil structure after the tunnel.**

**How the basin works, and the design criterion:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **The flow is SLOWED by widening and deepening the channel** | **Typical through velocity 0.2 to 0.4 m/s** ← |
| **The particle must SETTLE to the floor before the flow carries it out** | **The basic criterion** ← |
| **Condition** | **(Length / horizontal velocity) ≥ (Depth / settling velocity)** ← |
| **Rearranged** | **L ≥ V·D / w, with w the settling velocity of the target particle** ← |
| **A settled particle must then be REMOVED** | **By flushing — see below** ← |

> **A worked feel for the numbers: a 0.2 mm sand grain settles at roughly 0.02 m/s. With a basin 3 m deep and a through velocity of 0.3 m/s:**

> **L ≥ 0.3 × 3 / 0.02 = 45 m**

> **So a basin of the order of 45 to 60 m long (with allowances for turbulence and inlet transition) is required — which is why settling basins are such large structures.**

> **And the SQUARE-LAW in the third row of the first table is what forbids going finer: a 0.1 mm particle settles four times more slowly, so the basin would need to be about 180 m long.**

**FLUSHING — the part that is most often the weak point:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Settled sediment must be removed, or the basin fills and stops working** ← | ← |
| **INTERMITTENT flushing** | **The basin (or one of two bays) is taken out of service, drained and flushed** ← |
| **CONTINUOUS flushing** | **Hoppers and flushing ducts remove sediment while the basin remains in operation** ← |
| **Water used in flushing is LOST to generation** | **Typically 5-10 per cent of the flow — a real production cost** ← |
| **Two or more BAYS are usual** | **So one can be flushed while the others operate — otherwise the plant must shut down** ← |

> **The TWO-BAY arrangement in the last row is the standard solution and it is worth understanding why: during the monsoon, when the sediment load is highest, the plant also has the most water and the greatest value in running.**

> **A single-bay basin must be shut down to be flushed, precisely when shutting down is most costly — so the second bay pays for itself in avoided outage during the very season the basin is most needed.**

**The other sediment defences on a run-of-river scheme, since the basin is only one:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Intake location and orientation** | **On the OUTER bank of a bend, drawing from above the bed layer** ← |
| **Trashrack** | Floating debris and coarse material |
| **GRAVEL TRAP immediately after the intake** | **Removes the coarsest fraction before the settling basin** ← |
| **SETTLING BASIN** | **The main defence** ← |
| **Sediment-resistant runner materials and COATINGS** | **Hard facings, tungsten carbide or ceramic coatings** ← |
| **Operating rules** | **Shutting down or reducing load during the highest sediment events** ← |
| **Catchment management** | Long-term, and largely outside the developer's control |

> **The OPERATING RULES entry in the sixth row is the pragmatic last line of defence and it involves a genuine commercial judgement:**

> **The sediment concentration in a Himalayan river peaks sharply during and just after intense rainfall, and much of the annual sediment load passes in a few days.**

> **Shutting the plant down during those events avoids a large fraction of the annual abrasion at the cost of a small fraction of the annual energy — provided the concentration is actually MEASURED, which requires monitoring instruments and a rule for acting on them.**

> **Plants that generate through the peak sediment events to capture the monsoon energy pay for it in runner wear, and the trade-off between the two is one of the recurring operating decisions in Nepali hydropower.**

examTip.trick: **About 0.2 mm for high-head plants** (0.15-0.2 typical; 0.3-0.5 tolerable for low-head Francis/Kaplan). Criterion: L ≥ V·D/w — length ≥ velocity × depth ÷ settling velocity.
examTip.trap: **Settling velocity falls as the SQUARE of the diameter** — targeting 0.1 mm instead of 0.2 mm would quadruple the basin length, from about 45 m to 180 m. That square law is why 0.2 mm is the economic limit.
examTip.mnemonic: **Himalayan sediment is 30-60 % QUARTZ at Mohs 6-7 — HARDER than turbine steel**, so it cuts rather than glances off. Runners have needed replacement within a few years. Always TWO bays, so one can flush while the other runs.

questions.stem: The principal function of a SURGE TANK in a hydropower conveyance system is to:
options: Relieve WATER HAMMER pressure in the tunnel and supply or absorb water during load changes
Settle out the sediment carried by the headrace tunnel
Increase the gross head available to the turbine
Serve as the intake structure at the reservoir
questions.solution:
**To relieve WATER HAMMER pressure in the tunnel, and to supply or absorb water during changes of load.**

**Where it sits and why:**

> **A surge tank is placed at the junction of the LOW-PRESSURE headrace tunnel and the HIGH-PRESSURE penstock — as close to the powerhouse as the topography allows.**

> **Its position is the whole point: it provides a FREE WATER SURFACE at the end of the long tunnel, so that pressure waves travelling up the penstock are reflected there instead of continuing into the tunnel.**

**The two functions in detail:**

| Function | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1 — Relieving WATER HAMMER** | **When the turbine gates close suddenly, a pressure wave travels UP the penstock. At the surge tank it meets a free surface and is REFLECTED, so the long headrace tunnel is protected and only the short penstock carries the surge** ← |
| **2 — Supplying water on LOAD INCREASE** | **When the gates open, the turbine demands more water at once. The long tunnel's water column cannot accelerate instantly, so the surge tank SUPPLIES the deficit from its own storage until the tunnel flow builds up** ← |
| **3 — Absorbing water on LOAD REJECTION** | **Conversely the tunnel's flow cannot stop instantly, and the surplus rises into the tank rather than over-pressurising the system** ← |
| **4 — Improving GOVERNING stability** | **By decoupling the tunnel from the penstock, it makes the turbine governor's task manageable** ← |

> **THE INERTIA OF THE TUNNEL'S WATER COLUMN IS THE UNDERLYING PROBLEM, and it is worth appreciating the scale: a headrace tunnel may be several kilometres long and carry many thousands of tonnes of water moving at 2 m/s.**

> **Stopping or starting that mass takes time. Without a surge tank, the attempt to do so instantly would generate pressures capable of bursting the tunnel lining — and the governor would be unable to regulate the machine at all.**

> **The surge tank converts an impossible problem into a manageable oscillation.**

**The resulting SURGE OSCILLATION:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **On load rejection, the level in the tank RISES above the reservoir level** | **UPSURGE — the tank must be high enough not to overflow** ← |
| **It then falls BELOW, and oscillates** | **DOWNSURGE — the tank must be deep enough not to draw air into the penstock** ← |
| **The oscillation DAMPS out through friction** | **Over several minutes, with a period of minutes rather than seconds** ← |
| **Governing the surge is a slow oscillation; water hammer is a fast wave** ← | **The two phenomena are quite distinct in period** |

> **THE DISTINCTION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE TO CARRY: water hammer is an ELASTIC pressure wave travelling at the speed of sound in water (about 1,000-1,400 m/s), completing its cycle in a fraction of a second.**

> **Surge is a RIGID-COLUMN mass oscillation, with a period of one to several minutes.**

> **They are governed by different equations and require different remedies — the surge tank addresses the surge and protects the tunnel from the hammer, while the penstock itself must be designed to withstand the hammer directly.**

**The types of surge tank:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE (cylindrical)** | **A plain shaft; simplest; slow damping, so it must be large** ← |
| **RESTRICTED ORIFICE (throttled)** | **A constriction at the base dissipates energy, damping the oscillation faster and reducing the tank's size** ← |
| **DIFFERENTIAL (Johnson)** | **An inner riser plus an outer chamber — rapid initial response with strong damping; the most efficient** ← |
| **Gallery / expansion chamber** | Upper and lower chambers limit the extreme levels economically |
| **Air cushion chamber** | **A sealed chamber with compressed air — used where a shaft to the surface is impractical, as in deep underground schemes** ← |
| **Inclined** | Follows the hillside; increases the effective surface area |

> **The RESTRICTED ORIFICE and DIFFERENTIAL types both exist for the same reason: a simple tank must be very large to keep the surge within acceptable limits, and adding a throttle converts some of the surge energy into head loss so the oscillation dies away faster.**

> **The trade-off is that the throttle also transmits some of the water-hammer pressure into the tunnel — so it must be sized to damp the surge without defeating the tank's primary protective purpose.**

**When a surge tank is NOT required:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A SHORT penstock direct from the reservoir, with no long tunnel** | **Nothing to protect; the reservoir itself is the free surface** ← |
| **A very low-head plant** | Surge pressures are small |
| **Where the ratio of tunnel LENGTH to HEAD is small** | **A common rule of thumb: a surge tank is needed if L/H exceeds about 5** ← |
| **Where a pressure relief valve or a synchronous bypass can do the job** | **On smaller plants, cheaper than a shaft** ← |

> **The L/H RULE in the third row is the practical screening test: it is the tunnel's length relative to the head that determines whether the water column's inertia is a problem, since the head sets the force available to decelerate the column.**

> **A 3 km tunnel on a 500 m head (L/H = 6) needs a surge tank; the same tunnel on a 50 m head (L/H = 60) needs one urgently; a 200 m tunnel on a 400 m head (L/H = 0.5) does not.**

> **And in Nepal's high-head schemes, where tunnels of several kilometres serve heads of several hundred metres, the surge tank is almost invariably required — usually as a vertical shaft driven from the hillside above the penstock, which is itself a significant piece of construction in steep terrain.**

examTip.trick: **At the junction of the low-pressure TUNNEL and the high-pressure PENSTOCK.** It reflects the water-hammer wave (protecting the tunnel) and supplies or absorbs water while the tunnel's flow catches up with a load change.
examTip.trap: **Water hammer and surge are DIFFERENT phenomena: hammer is an ELASTIC wave at ~1,000-1,400 m/s completing in a fraction of a second; surge is a RIGID-COLUMN oscillation with a period of MINUTES.** The tank handles the surge; the penstock must withstand the hammer.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rule of thumb: a surge tank is needed when L/H exceeds about 5.** Types: simple, restricted-orifice (throttled, damps faster), differential (most efficient), and air-cushion where no shaft to the surface is possible.

questions.stem: In a hydropower scheme, the FOREBAY differs from a surge tank in that a forebay is provided:
options: Only in schemes with an underground powerhouse
At the downstream end of the penstock, next to the turbine
Inside the settling basin, to trap fine sediment
At the end of an OPEN CHANNEL (canal) headrace, serving as a small reservoir and the transition to the penstock
questions.solution:
**At the end of an OPEN CHANNEL headrace**, serving as a small reservoir and the transition from the free-surface canal to the pressurised penstock.

**The two structures compared:**

| | FOREBAY | SURGE TANK |
|---|---|---|
| **Used when the headrace is** | **An OPEN CHANNEL (canal or flume) with a free surface** ← | **A pressurised TUNNEL or pipe** ← |
| **Position** | **At the end of the canal, immediately before the penstock** | **At the junction of the tunnel and penstock** |
| **Free surface** | **YES — it is simply an enlargement of the open channel** ← | **YES — deliberately created, since the tunnel has none** ← |
| **Primary purpose** | **Storage for load changes; final sediment and trash removal; transition to the penstock** ← | **Water hammer relief and mass-oscillation control** ← |
| **Water hammer in the conveyance upstream** | **Not an issue — the canal already has a free surface throughout** ← | **The problem the tank exists to solve** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL DISTINCTION: an open canal cannot transmit water hammer, because it has a free surface along its whole length.**

> **So a canal-fed scheme needs no surge tank — it needs a forebay, which performs the STORAGE and TRANSITION functions without needing to solve a pressure problem that does not arise.**

> **A tunnel-fed scheme needs a surge tank, which provides the free surface that the tunnel lacks.**

> **In effect the forebay and the surge tank are the same idea applied to two different conveyance systems, which is why their functions overlap and their names are confused.**

**What the forebay does:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provides STORAGE for short-term load fluctuations** | **The canal's flow cannot change quickly; the forebay buffers the difference** ← |
| **Acts as the final SETTLING and TRASH removal point** | **Trashracks, and a last chance to drop sediment before the turbine** ← |
| **Provides the TRANSITION from free surface to pressure flow** | **The penstock intake is submerged below the forebay's water level** ← |
| **Ensures adequate SUBMERGENCE, preventing air entrainment** | **A vortex drawing air into the penstock is damaging and must be prevented** ← |
| **Provides a SPILLWAY for surplus water** | **Essential — see below** ← |
| **Houses the penstock intake gate and its controls** | For isolating the penstock |

> **THE SPILLWAY IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE FOREBAY'S MOST IMPORTANT SAFETY FEATURE, and its necessity follows directly from the canal's inertia:**

> **When the turbine shuts down suddenly, the canal continues to deliver its full flow for some minutes. That water must go somewhere.**

> **Without an adequate spillway the forebay overtops, and the resulting flow down the hillside can wash out the penstock's foundations, the access track and whatever lies below.**

> **The spillway must therefore be sized for the FULL canal discharge, not for some fraction of it, and it must discharge to a properly protected channel — because it will be used at every load rejection, not merely in emergencies.**

**The SUBMERGENCE requirement, since air entrainment is the other characteristic failure:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The problem** | **Insufficient depth over the penstock intake lets a VORTEX form and draw AIR into the penstock** ← |
| **Consequences** | **Loss of efficiency; violent pressure fluctuations; vibration; and in severe cases damage to the turbine and the penstock** ← |
| **Remedy** | **Adequate submergence depth; anti-vortex devices; a bellmouth intake; approach flow free of swirl** ← |
| **Rule of thumb** | **Submergence of at least 1.5 to 2 times the penstock diameter above the intake soffit** ← |

> **An air pocket travelling down a long penstock and reaching the turbine can produce a pressure transient comparable with a valve closure — so this is a real structural concern and not merely an efficiency matter.**

**The PENSTOCK itself, since the forebay feeds it:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Materials** | **Mild steel (most common), HDPE for small low-head schemes, GRP, ductile iron** ← |
| **Thickness governed by** | **The design pressure = static head PLUS water hammer surge** ← |
| **Water hammer allowance** | **Commonly 25-50 % above the static head for a well-governed machine** ← |
| **Anchor blocks** | **At every bend and at intervals on straights — resist the unbalanced thrust** ← |
| **Expansion joints** | **Between anchor blocks, to absorb thermal movement** ← |
| **Support piers / saddles** | Carry the weight between anchors |
| **Economic diameter** | **Balances capital cost against the capitalised value of the head lost to friction** ← |

> **The ANCHOR BLOCK and EXPANSION JOINT pair in the fourth and fifth rows work together and their logic is worth noting: an exposed steel penstock on a hillside expands and contracts appreciably with temperature — a 500 m run can move over 100 mm between a cold night and a sunny afternoon.**

> **Anchor blocks hold the pipe rigidly at fixed points and take the thrust from bends; expansion joints between them allow the intervening lengths to move freely.**

> **Omitting the joints, or letting one seize, transfers enormous thermal forces into the anchors and the pipe itself — and buckled penstocks from precisely this cause are not rare.**

> **The ECONOMIC DIAMETER in the last row closes the loop with the project economics discussed earlier: a larger penstock costs more steel and loses less head, and the optimum is where the marginal capital cost equals the capitalised value of the marginal energy gained over the plant's life.**

examTip.trick: **FOREBAY = end of an OPEN CHANNEL headrace; SURGE TANK = on a pressurised TUNNEL.** An open canal cannot transmit water hammer, so a canal-fed scheme needs no surge tank.
examTip.trap: **The forebay SPILLWAY must be sized for the FULL canal discharge** — on load rejection the canal keeps delivering for minutes, and an undersized spillway washes out the hillside below. It is used at every shutdown, not just in emergencies.
examTip.mnemonic: **Submergence ≥ 1.5-2 × penstock diameter, or a vortex draws AIR into the penstock** — which causes pressure transients comparable with a valve closure. And penstocks need ANCHOR BLOCKS at bends with EXPANSION JOINTS between: 500 m of steel moves over 100 mm.

questions.stem: For a hydropower plant operating under a net head of 400 m, the most suitable type of turbine is:
questions.solution:
**A PELTON turbine.**

**Turbine selection by head:**

| Turbine | Head range | Type | Flow |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PELTON** | **Above about 250-300 m, up to 1,800 m** ← | **IMPULSE** ← | **LOW** |
| **Turgo** | **50 to 250 m** | Impulse | Low to medium |
| **CROSSFLOW (Banki-Michell)** | **5 to 200 m** | **Impulse** | **Low to medium — favoured for small and micro schemes** ← |
| **FRANCIS** | **25 to 350 m** ← | **REACTION** ← | **Medium** |
| **KAPLAN / propeller** | **Below about 60 m, typically 2-40 m** ← | **Reaction** | **HIGH** |
| **BULB / tubular** | **Below 15 m** ← | Reaction | Very high — run-of-river on large rivers |

> **At 400 m the choice is clearly Pelton; a Francis machine at that head would be at the extreme upper end of its range and would suffer cavitation and erosion problems.**

> **Every distractor — Kaplan, propeller and bulb — is a LOW-HEAD reaction machine, so the option set tests the head-to-machine association directly.**

**IMPULSE against REACTION, which is the fundamental division:**

| | IMPULSE (Pelton, Turgo, crossflow) | REACTION (Francis, Kaplan, bulb) |
|---|---|---|
| **Energy at the runner inlet** | **ALL KINETIC — the pressure has already been converted in the nozzle** ← | **Both PRESSURE and kinetic — the pressure drops THROUGH the runner** ← |
| **Runner** | **Runs in AIR, at atmospheric pressure** ← | **Runs FULLY SUBMERGED in the flowing water** ← |
| **Water contact** | **Only some buckets are struck at any instant** | **All passages flow continuously** |
| **Casing** | **Merely a housing to contain splash** ← | **A pressure casing — a working part of the machine** ← |
| **DRAFT TUBE** | **NOT used — there is nothing to recover** ← | **ESSENTIAL — recovers the exit kinetic energy and the head below the runner** ← |
| **Flow control** | **Nozzle needle (spear valve), plus deflector** | **Adjustable GUIDE VANES (wicket gates), and on Kaplan the BLADES too** ← |
| **Suits** | **HIGH head, LOW flow** | **LOW-to-medium head, HIGH flow** |

> **THE DRAFT TUBE ROW IS THE ONE THAT MOST CLEARLY SEPARATES THEM, and it is worth understanding:**

> **A reaction turbine's runner sits ABOVE the tailwater, and without a draft tube the head between the runner and the tailwater would be lost entirely.**

> **The draft tube — a gradually expanding passage from the runner to below the tailwater surface — recovers that head by creating a partial vacuum beneath the runner, and it also decelerates the exit flow so its kinetic energy is recovered rather than dissipated.**

> **On a low-head machine the draft tube may recover a substantial fraction of the total head, which is why it is a designed hydraulic component rather than a mere discharge pipe.**

> **A Pelton has nothing to recover: its water leaves the buckets at atmospheric pressure with little velocity, and it simply falls to the tailrace — so the Pelton runner must be set ABOVE the maximum tailwater level, and any head below that is lost.**

**SPECIFIC SPEED, which formalises the selection:**

> **Nₛ = N √P / H^(5/4), with N in rpm, P in kW and H in metres.**

| Turbine | Specific speed range |
|---|---|
| **Pelton, single jet** | **8 to 30** ← |
| **Pelton, multi-jet** | **30 to 70** |
| **Francis, slow to fast** | **60 to 400** ← |
| **Kaplan / propeller** | **300 to 1,000** ← |

> **The pattern: HIGH head goes with LOW specific speed, and low head with high specific speed.**

> **The MULTI-JET row shows how the parameter is used in design: adding jets to a Pelton increases its specific speed, allowing a smaller, faster runner for the same power — which is why large Pelton machines commonly have four to six jets.**

**CAVITATION, since it limits the reaction machines:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cause** | **Local pressure falls BELOW the vapour pressure; vapour bubbles form and then COLLAPSE violently as pressure recovers** ← |
| **Damage** | **Pitting of the runner and draft tube; noise; vibration; loss of efficiency** ← |
| **Where** | **On the low-pressure side of reaction runner blades, and at the draft tube inlet** ← |
| **Thoma's cavitation factor** | **σ = (H_atm − H_vapour − H_s)/H, with H_s the setting above tailwater** ← |
| **Requirement** | **σ ≥ σ_critical, which INCREASES with specific speed** ← |
| **Remedy** | **Lower the SETTING — place the runner nearer to, or below, the tailwater level** ← |

> **THE CONSEQUENCE OF THE LAST TWO ROWS IS AN IMPORTANT PRACTICAL ONE: high-specific-speed machines (Kaplan, fast Francis) are the MOST prone to cavitation, and they must therefore be set LOW — frequently BELOW the tailwater level.**

> **That means excavating the powerhouse below river level, which is expensive and complicates construction and dewatering.**

> **So the cavitation requirement has a direct and substantial civil cost, and the turbine setting is one of the points where the mechanical and civil designs are most tightly coupled.**

> **A Pelton, by contrast, cannot cavitate — its runner is in air at atmospheric pressure — which is one more reason it suits the high-head Himalayan schemes where the powerhouse must often be perched on a steep valley side with no possibility of deep excavation.**

examTip.trick: **Pelton above ~250-300 m; Francis 25-350 m; Kaplan/propeller below ~60 m; bulb below 15 m.** All three distractors are LOW-head reaction machines.
examTip.trap: **A DRAFT TUBE is essential on a REACTION turbine and absent on an IMPULSE one** — the Pelton runs in air at atmospheric pressure with nothing to recover, so it must be set ABOVE maximum tailwater and that head is lost.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nₛ = N√P/H^(5/4): Pelton 8-30, Francis 60-400, Kaplan 300-1,000 — high head, LOW specific speed.** High-Nₛ machines cavitate most and must be set LOW, sometimes below tailwater — an expensive civil consequence. A Pelton cannot cavitate at all.

questions.stem: The function of a DRAFT TUBE in a reaction turbine installation is to:
options: Supply water to the runner at high velocity
Prevent sediment from reaching the runner
Recover the head between the runner and the tailwater, and convert the exit kinetic energy into pressure
Support the weight of the generator
questions.solution:
**To recover the head between the runner and the tailwater, and to convert the water's EXIT KINETIC ENERGY into pressure by gradual expansion.**

**The two recoveries it achieves:**

| Recovery | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **1 — The STATIC head between the runner and the tailwater** | **By sealing the runner outlet to the tailwater, a partial VACUUM is created beneath the runner, so the machine effectively uses the head down to the tailwater level rather than only to its own elevation** ← |
| **2 — The EXIT KINETIC energy** | **The tube EXPANDS gradually, so the velocity falls and the kinetic energy is converted to pressure (a diffuser) rather than being dumped as turbulence** ← |

> **Without a draft tube, a reaction turbine set above the tailwater would lose BOTH: the water would discharge to atmosphere at the runner's level, and its exit velocity head would be thrown away.**

> **The efficiency gain is substantial, and it is greatest for LOW-HEAD machines — precisely because a fixed loss is a larger proportion of a small head.**

| Head | Exit velocity head as a proportion of the total | Draft tube's importance |
|---|---|---|
| **A high-head Francis (300 m)** | **A fraction of 1 per cent** | Modest |
| **A medium-head Francis (50 m)** | **2 to 4 per cent** | Significant |
| **A KAPLAN at low head (5 m)** | **Can exceed 40 per cent** ← | **Absolutely essential — the machine would be unworkable without it** ← |

> **THAT LAST ROW EXPLAINS WHY THE DRAFT TUBE IS A DESIGNED HYDRAULIC COMPONENT AND NOT A DISCHARGE PIPE: on a very low-head machine, the water leaves the runner still carrying a large share of the available energy, and recovering it is the difference between a viable machine and an unviable one.**

**The types of draft tube:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Conical (straight divergent)** | **Simplest and most efficient — up to about 90 per cent recovery; needs vertical depth below the runner** ← |
| **Moody spreading (hydraucone)** | A bell-mouth with a central core; reduces whirl |
| **Simple ELBOW** | Where depth is restricted; lower efficiency |
| **ELBOW with varying rectangular section** | **The standard for large Kaplan installations — turns the flow horizontally within limited depth** ← |

> **The ELBOW forms exist for a purely practical reason: a straight conical tube of adequate length requires deep excavation below the powerhouse, and on a large low-head plant that depth becomes prohibitive.**

> **The elbow turns the flow to horizontal within a shallower excavation, at some cost in efficiency — so the choice is a direct trade between civil cost and hydraulic performance.**

**The design constraints, which come back to cavitation:**

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **The CONE ANGLE must be small — about 4 to 8 degrees total** | **A wider angle causes the flow to SEPARATE from the walls, destroying the diffuser action** ← |
| **Hence the tube must be LONG** | Which is why depth is needed |
| **The outlet must remain SUBMERGED at all tailwater levels** | **If it draws air, the vacuum is broken and the recovery is lost** ← |
| **The vacuum must not fall below the vapour pressure** | **Or CAVITATION occurs at the runner exit and in the tube** ← |
| **The runner SETTING is limited accordingly** | **By Thoma's criterion — see below** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND FOURTH ROWS ARE IN DIRECT TENSION, and that tension is the heart of draft tube design:**

> **Setting the runner HIGHER above the tailwater recovers MORE head — but it also deepens the vacuum beneath the runner, and beyond a limit the pressure reaches the vapour pressure and the machine cavitates.**

> **So there is a maximum permissible setting, given by Thoma's criterion:**

> **σ = (H_atm − H_vapour − H_s) / H ≥ σ_critical**

> **where H_s is the runner's height above the tailwater. Rearranged, the maximum setting is:**

> **H_s ≤ H_atm − H_vapour − σ_critical × H**

| Factor | Effect on the permissible setting |
|---|---|
| **A HIGHER head H** | **LOWERS the permissible setting** ← |
| **A HIGHER specific speed (Kaplan)** | **σ_critical is larger, so the setting is LOWER — often NEGATIVE, i.e. below tailwater** ← |
| **HIGH ALTITUDE — lower atmospheric pressure** | **LOWERS the permissible setting** ← |
| **Warm water — higher vapour pressure** | Lowers it slightly |

> **THE ALTITUDE TERM IN THE THIRD ROW IS DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO NEPAL and is easily overlooked:**

> **Atmospheric pressure falls with elevation — about 10.3 m of water at sea level, but only about 9.0 m at 1,200 m and around 8.0 m at 2,500 m.**

> **So a turbine installed at a high-altitude powerhouse has 1 to 2 metres LESS atmospheric head available to suppress cavitation, and its permissible setting is correspondingly lower.**

> **A machine specified for a sea-level installation and installed in the Nepali hills without recalculating the setting will cavitate — which is a genuine and avoidable design error, and one that appears only after commissioning.**

> **The correction is straightforward once recognised: use the local atmospheric pressure, not the standard value, in Thoma's criterion, and set the runner accordingly.**

examTip.trick: **Two recoveries: the STATIC head between runner and tailwater (by creating a partial vacuum), and the EXIT KINETIC energy (by gradual expansion — a diffuser).**
examTip.trap: **Its importance grows as the head FALLS** — on a 5 m Kaplan the exit velocity head can exceed 40 % of the total, so the machine is unworkable without one. Cone angle must stay at 4-8° or the flow SEPARATES and the diffuser fails.
examTip.mnemonic: **Raising the setting recovers more head but deepens the vacuum — Thoma's σ sets the limit.** And ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE FALLS WITH ALTITUDE (10.3 m at sea level, ~8.0 m at 2,500 m), so a machine set by sea-level figures will cavitate in the Nepali hills.

questions.stem: In the alignment survey of a hill road, the ZERO LINE (grade contour) is:
options: A line traced on the ground at a CONSTANT RULING GRADIENT, along which the earthwork would be nearly balanced
The line joining the lowest points of the valley
The centre line of the finally adopted alignment
The boundary line of the land to be acquired
questions.solution:
**A line traced on the ground at a CONSTANT (ruling) GRADIENT** — so called because along it the road would be at ground level and the earthwork would be nearly zero.

**How it is set out:**

| Method | Procedure |
|---|---|
| **On the MAP** | **Set a pair of dividers to the horizontal distance corresponding to one contour interval at the ruling gradient, and step from contour to contour** ← |
| **On the GROUND** | **Use an ABNEY LEVEL or clinometer set to the ruling gradient, and mark successive points; the chain of points is the zero line** ← |

> **The horizontal distance per contour interval is simply the interval divided by the gradient:**

| Contour interval | Ruling gradient | Horizontal step |
|---|---|---|
| **5 m** | **5 % (1 in 20)** | **100 m** ← |
| **5 m** | **6 % (1 in 16.7)** | **83 m** |
| **10 m** | **5 %** | **200 m** ← |
| **20 m** | **6 %** | **333 m** |

> **The resulting line is extremely sinuous, following every re-entrant and spur, and it is NOT the alignment — it is the STARTING POINT for one.**

**Why it is called the ZERO line, and what it is used for:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Along it, the formation is at ground level** | **So CUT and FILL are both nearly zero — hence "zero line"** ← |
| **It represents the LONGEST possible route at that gradient** | **Because it never cuts across a contour** ← |
| **It shows what gradient the terrain will actually permit** | **If no zero line can be traced at the ruling gradient, the gradient must be relaxed or the route abandoned** ← |
| **It is then SMOOTHED into a practicable alignment** | **By cutting across the sharper re-entrants and spurs, accepting cut and fill in exchange for a shorter, straighter road** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHERE THE ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT LIES, and it is worth setting out because it is the essence of hill road location:**

> **Following the zero line exactly gives no earthwork and an absurdly long, twisting road with innumerable curves.**

> **Straightening it completely gives the shortest road and enormous cut and fill.**

> **The chosen alignment lies between: it departs from the zero line where the saving in length and curvature is worth the earthwork, and follows it where it is not.**

> **Balancing CUT against FILL along the route is the other objective, since haulage on a hill road is very expensive and surplus spoil is an environmental liability.**

**The stages of a highway location survey, within which this sits:**

| Stage | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **MAP study** | **Identify possible routes, obligatory points, and the general corridor from topographic maps** ← |
| **RECONNAISSANCE** | **A rapid ground inspection of the corridors identified; no instruments, or simple ones** ← |
| **PRELIMINARY survey** | **Instrument survey of the selected corridors; the ZERO LINE is traced at this stage; comparison of alternatives** ← |
| **FINAL LOCATION and detailed survey** | **The chosen alignment is pegged on the ground and surveyed in detail for design** ← |

> **The zero line belongs to the PRELIMINARY survey, and its purpose is comparative: two candidate routes are each given a zero line, and their lengths, curvature and difficulty are compared before either is surveyed in detail.**

**OBLIGATORY POINTS, which constrain the alignment before any gradient is considered:**

| Points the alignment MUST pass through | Points it must AVOID |
|---|---|
| **A bridge site — a narrow, stable, straight reach of river** ← | **Unstable slopes, active landslides and slip zones** ← |
| **A mountain PASS or saddle** ← | **Marshy and poor ground** |
| **Intermediate towns and settlements to be served** | **Religious, cultural and archaeological sites** ← |
| **An existing road or bridge to be connected to** | **Forest and protected areas** |
| **A ridge or a stable bench** | **Expensive land and built-up property** |
| **Sources of construction material** | **Steep rock faces requiring heavy cutting** |

> **THE BRIDGE SITE IN THE FIRST ROW IS USUALLY THE STRONGEST CONSTRAINT ON A HILL ROAD, and the reason is economic:**

> **A bridge costs far more per metre than road, and a good crossing — narrow, with firm banks, a stable channel and a straight approach — may occur at only one or two places along a river.**

> **So the practice is to FIX THE BRIDGE SITES FIRST and then align the road to reach them, rather than aligning the road and crossing wherever it happens to arrive.**

> **That is a genuine reversal of the intuitive order, and it is one of the more useful practical principles in route location.**

**And the specific hazards that govern alignment in Nepal:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **SLOPE STABILITY** | **The dominant factor — an alignment through an unstable slope will never be maintainable** ← |
| **Geology — dip of the strata relative to the slope** | **A cut into DIP SLOPE strata removes the support of the beds above and invites failure; cutting against the dip is far safer** ← |
| **Drainage crossings** | Every stream needs a culvert or bridge, and each is a maintenance point |
| **RIDGE versus VALLEY alignment** | **Ridge routes are drier, more stable and need fewer crossings; valley routes are shorter and serve settlements but are exposed to floods and debris flows** ← |
| **Avoiding the river's active floodplain and debris fans** | ← |
| **Spoil DISPOSAL sites must be identified along the route** | **Not left to the contractor to improvise** ← |

> **The DIP OF THE STRATA in the second row is the piece of geological judgement that most often distinguishes a durable hill road from a failing one, and it is straightforward to apply: where the rock beds dip INTO the hillside, a cut is stable; where they dip OUT of it, toward the road, cutting the toe removes the support and the beds above slide down the bedding planes.**

> **Aligning the road so that cuttings are made against the dip wherever there is a choice costs nothing at the design stage and saves a great deal of maintenance for the road's whole life.**

examTip.trick: **The ZERO LINE is traced at the RULING GRADIENT — step dividers set to (contour interval ÷ gradient).** At 5 m intervals and 5 %, that is a 100 m step. It is called "zero" because cut and fill along it are nearly zero.
examTip.trap: **It is NOT the alignment** — it is the longest possible route at that gradient, and is then SMOOTHED by cutting across re-entrants and spurs, trading earthwork for length and curvature.
examTip.mnemonic: **FIX THE BRIDGE SITES FIRST, then align the road to reach them** — a bridge costs far more per metre than road, and good crossings are few. And cut AGAINST the dip of the strata: cutting a dip slope removes the support of the beds above.

questions.stem: SUPERELEVATION is provided on a horizontal curve principally to:
options: Improve the drainage of the carriageway
Increase the sight distance around the curve
Counteract the CENTRIFUGAL force acting on a vehicle
Reduce the wear on the outer wheels
questions.solution:
**To counteract the CENTRIFUGAL force acting on a vehicle** negotiating the curve.

**The mechanics:**

> **A vehicle travelling at speed v round a curve of radius R experiences a centrifugal force of Wv²/(gR) acting OUTWARD through its centre of gravity.**

> **That force must be resisted, and there are only two sources:**

| Resisting force | Note |
|---|---|
| **The component of the vehicle's WEIGHT along the tilted surface — SUPERELEVATION** | **Reliable; independent of the surface condition** ← |
| **SIDE FRICTION between the tyres and the road** | **Unreliable — it collapses when the road is WET, icy or dusty** ← |

> **The design equation, for a superelevation rate e and a side friction factor f:**

> **e + f = v²/(gR)**

> **with v in m/s, or in the convenient form: e + f = V²/(127R) with V in km/h and R in metres.**

**Why superelevation is preferred to friction — the safety argument:**

> **The equation shows that e and f are interchangeable in the arithmetic, and they are NOT interchangeable in reality:**

| Condition | Available f |
|---|---|
| **Dry bituminous surface, good tyres** | **0.4 to 0.6** |
| **Wet surface** | **0.25 to 0.35** ← |
| **Wet and polished, or with a thin film of oil** | **0.1 to 0.2** ← |
| **Icy** | **0.05 to 0.1** ← |
| **DESIGN value used by IRC** | **0.15 — deliberately conservative** ← |

> **The design f of 0.15 is far below even the wet value, which is intentional: the curve must be safe in the worst reasonable condition and for the worst reasonable driver.**

> **SUPERELEVATION, by contrast, is a geometric property that does not change with the weather — which is why the design procedure provides as much of the resistance as possible through e and calls on f only for the remainder.**

**The IRC design procedure, which has a specific and often-misremembered sequence:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Calculate e for 75 per cent of the design speed, IGNORING friction entirely: e = (0.75V)²/(127R) = V²/(225R)** ← |
| **2** | **If that e ≤ 7 per cent, ADOPT it** |
| **3** | **If it exceeds 7 per cent, LIMIT e to 7 per cent and CHECK the friction required at the full design speed: f = V²/(127R) − 0.07** |
| **4** | **If that f ≤ 0.15, the curve is acceptable at the design speed** |
| **5** | **If f > 0.15, calculate the SAFE ALLOWABLE SPEED and either restrict the speed or increase the radius** ← |

> **THE 75 PER CENT IN STEP 1 IS THE FEATURE MOST OFTEN MISSED, and its reason is important:**

> **If the superelevation were designed for the FULL design speed with no friction, then a vehicle travelling SLOWLY — a loaded truck grinding up a hill, or any vehicle in congestion — would have too much tilt for its speed.**

> **It would tend to SLIDE DOWN the slope toward the inside of the curve, and friction would have to act OUTWARD to hold it, which is the reverse of the intended condition.**

> **On a wet or icy surface it would actually slide, and a high-sided loaded vehicle standing on an over-superelevated curve can OVERTURN inward.**

> **Designing for 75 per cent of the design speed is the compromise: a moderate tilt that suits the range of speeds actually used rather than only the fastest.**

> **This is the reason that superelevation is limited to 7 per cent (and 10 per cent on hill roads without snow, 4 per cent in urban areas with frequent stopping) rather than being increased indefinitely to eliminate the friction requirement.**

**Maximum superelevation by situation:**

| Situation | Maximum e |
|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling terrain** | **7 %** ← |
| **Hill roads NOT bound by snow** | **10 %** ← |
| **Snow-bound hill roads** | **7 %** ← |
| **URBAN roads with frequent intersections** | **4 %** ← |

> **The SNOW limit and the URBAN limit both exist because of SLOW or STOPPED vehicles: on ice a stationary vehicle on a 10 per cent cross-slope will slide sideways, and in a town vehicles stop on curves constantly.**

**How the superelevation is ATTAINED, since it cannot appear instantly:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Elimination of the crown (camber)** | **The outer half of the carriageway is rotated to a flat plane** ← |
| **Rotation of the whole section to the full superelevation** | Attained over the TRANSITION curve |
| **Axis of rotation** | **Usually the CENTRE LINE (keeps the earthwork balanced); sometimes the inner edge (better drainage in flat country)** ← |
| **Rate of change** | **Not steeper than 1 in 150 for plain terrain, 1 in 60 for hills** ← |

> **The TRANSITION CURVE is what makes the attainment possible and it has three purposes together:**

| Purpose of a transition curve | Note |
|---|---|
| **To introduce the CENTRIFUGAL force gradually** | **Rather than as a sudden jerk at the tangent point** ← |
| **To permit the SUPERELEVATION to be attained gradually** | ← this question's connection |
| **To permit the extra WIDENING to be introduced gradually** | — |
| **To improve the road's APPEARANCE** | A sudden change of curvature looks wrong |

> **The curve used is the SPIRAL (clothoid), whose radius decreases uniformly with its length — LR = constant — which exactly matches the path a driver naturally steers while turning the wheel at a steady rate.**

> **That correspondence is the deep justification for the spiral: it is not merely a convenient mathematical curve but the curve that vehicles actually follow.**

> **A curve without a transition is driven with a transition anyway, the driver improvising one by wandering within the lane — which is why the absence of a transition shows up as encroachment on the adjacent lane, and why it matters on a two-lane hill road where the adjacent lane carries oncoming traffic.**

examTip.trick: **e + f = V²/(127R)** with V in km/h and R in m. Superelevation is preferred to friction because it is a GEOMETRIC property that does not change with the weather.
examTip.trap: **Design e for 75 % of the design speed, ignoring friction: e = V²/(225R).** Designing for the full speed would over-tilt the curve for SLOW vehicles, which would then slide inward — and a loaded high-sided vehicle can overturn inward.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum e: 7 % plain, 10 % hills without snow, 7 % snow-bound, 4 % urban.** The snow and urban limits both exist because of STOPPED vehicles. And the design f of 0.15 is far below even the wet value of 0.25-0.35.

questions.stem: The STOPPING SIGHT DISTANCE (SSD) of a vehicle is the sum of:
options: The braking distance and the overtaking distance
The LAG (perception-reaction) distance and the BRAKING distance
The braking distance and the length of the vehicle
questions.solution:
**The LAG (perception-reaction) distance plus the BRAKING distance.**

**The formula:**

> **SSD = vt + v²/(2gf)**

> **or, with V in km/h: SSD = 0.278Vt + V²/(254f)**

| Term | Meaning | Design value |
|---|---|---|
| **vt or 0.278Vt** | **LAG distance — travelled during the perception-reaction time, at UNDIMINISHED speed** ← | **t = 2.5 seconds (IRC)** |
| **v²/(2gf)** | **BRAKING distance — travelled while decelerating** | **f = 0.35 to 0.40 (longitudinal friction)** ← |

> **On a GRADIENT, the braking term becomes v²/(2g(f ± 0.01n)) with n the gradient in per cent: PLUS for an ascending grade (gravity helps to stop) and MINUS for a descending one (gravity opposes).**

**Worked values, since the growth with speed is the point:**

> **Taking t = 2.5 s and f = 0.35 on the level:**

| Speed V (km/h) | Lag distance (m) | Braking distance (m) | SSD (m) | IRC design SSD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **20** | **13.9** | **4.5** | **18.4** | **20** |
| **40** | **27.8** | **18.0** | **45.8** | **45** |
| **60** | **41.7** | **40.5** | **82.2** | **80** ← |
| **80** | **55.6** | **72.0** | **127.6** | **120** |
| **100** | **69.5** | **112.5** | **182.0** | **180** ← |

> **Two observations from the table are worth drawing out.**

> **First, the LAG distance is LINEAR in speed while the BRAKING distance is QUADRATIC — so at low speed the reaction distance dominates and at high speed the braking distance does.**

> **At 40 km/h the lag distance is more than half the total; at 100 km/h it is under 40 per cent.**

> **Second, the SSD roughly QUADRUPLES when the speed DOUBLES — from 45 m at 40 km/h to 182 m at 100 — which is why speed limits have so large an effect on stopping and why high-speed roads need such generous geometry.**

**The 2.5-second reaction time, which is generous and deliberately so:**

| Component of the reaction | Time |
|---|---|
| **PERCEPTION — seeing the hazard** | **About 0.5 s** |
| **INTELLECTION — recognising what it is** | 0.4 s |
| **EMOTION — deciding what to do** | 0.5 s |
| **VOLITION — acting; moving the foot to the brake** | **0.6 s** |
| **Total for an alert driver** | **About 0.5 to 1.5 s** ← |
| **IRC DESIGN value** | **2.5 s** ← |

> **The design value is well above the alert driver's time because the geometry must be safe for the TIRED, DISTRACTED, ELDERLY or UNFAMILIAR driver, not only the attentive one — and for the driver who is looking at the wrong part of the scene when the hazard appears.**

> **This is the same conservatism seen in the side friction factor of 0.15 for superelevation, and it reflects the same principle: highway geometry is designed for the worst reasonable user rather than the average one, because the geometry cannot be adjusted to suit each driver.**

**The other sight distances, since SSD is only one of several:**

| Sight distance | Definition | Typical value at 80 km/h |
|---|---|---|
| **STOPPING (SSD)** | **To stop before an obstruction** | **120 m** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE (ISD)** | **TWICE the SSD — a partial overtaking provision** | **240 m** ← |
| **OVERTAKING (OSD)** | **To complete an overtaking manoeuvre safely against oncoming traffic** | **470 m** ← |
| **Safe sight distance at an uncontrolled intersection** | To see and yield | — |
| **Head-light sight distance** | **At night, from the headlight beam** | **Should equal the SSD** ← |

> **The OVERTAKING sight distance is FOUR TIMES the stopping distance, and that ratio explains a great deal about two-lane road design:**

> **OSD = d₁ + d₂ + d₃, being the distance travelled during the driver's reaction, the distance of the overtaking manoeuvre itself, and the distance covered by the ONCOMING vehicle during the manoeuvre.**

> **Providing 470 m of clear sight on a two-lane road is expensive in hilly country and often impossible — which is why OVERTAKING ZONES are provided intermittently rather than continuously, marked by a broken centre line, with the remainder marked as no-overtaking.**

> **And it is why the SSD, not the OSD, is the absolute minimum that must be provided EVERYWHERE: a driver must always be able to stop, even where they may not overtake.**

**Where the sight distance is measured, since the geometry follows from it:**

| Parameter | Value (IRC) |
|---|---|
| **Driver's EYE height** | **1.2 m above the carriageway** ← |
| **OBJECT height for SSD** | **0.15 m** ← |
| **Object height for OSD (an oncoming vehicle)** | **1.2 m** ← |

> **These heights determine the vertical curve lengths and the setback required at horizontal curves — a summit curve must be long enough for a 1.2 m eye to see a 0.15 m object at the SSD, and a horizontal curve must have its inside cleared of obstructions to the same effect.**

> **The 0.15 m OBJECT HEIGHT is the conservative element here and it is worth appreciating: it represents a low obstruction such as a rock, a pothole edge or a piece of fallen load — not another vehicle.**

> **On a Nepali hill road the relevant object is very often a FALLEN ROCK, which makes the 0.15 m assumption directly appropriate rather than theoretical, and it is one reason why sight distance provision on hill roads deserves the attention it is given.**

examTip.trick: **SSD = 0.278Vt + V²/(254f)**, with t = 2.5 s and f = 0.35-0.40. On a grade the friction term becomes (f ± 0.01n): PLUS uphill, MINUS downhill.
examTip.trap: **The lag distance is LINEAR in speed, the braking distance QUADRATIC** — so SSD roughly QUADRUPLES when speed doubles (45 m at 40 km/h to 180 m at 100).
examTip.mnemonic: **OSD is about FOUR TIMES the SSD** — which is why overtaking zones are intermittent while SSD must be provided everywhere. Eye height 1.2 m; object 0.15 m for SSD (a fallen rock), 1.2 m for OSD (an oncoming vehicle).

questions.stem: EXTRA WIDENING is provided on a horizontal curve of a highway to allow for:
options: The increase in superelevation around the curve
The additional drainage required on the curve
The reduction in sight distance on the curve
The MECHANICAL widening caused by the vehicle's rigid wheelbase, plus a PSYCHOLOGICAL allowance for the driver
questions.solution:
**MECHANICAL widening, from the rigid wheelbase of the vehicle, PLUS a PSYCHOLOGICAL allowance for the driver.**

**The two components:**

| Component | Cause | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **MECHANICAL (off-tracking)** | **A vehicle's rear wheels do not follow its front wheels around a curve — they track on a SHORTER radius, so the vehicle sweeps a wider path than its own width** ← | **W_m = n l² / (2R)** ← |
| **PSYCHOLOGICAL** | **Drivers keep further from the edge and from one another on a curve; and steering is less precise at speed** ← | **W_p = V / (9.5 √R)** ← |
| **TOTAL** | — | **W_e = n l²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)** ← |

> **where n is the number of traffic lanes, l the wheelbase (taken as 6.1 m for a commercial vehicle in IRC practice), R the radius in metres and V the design speed in km/h.**

**A worked example, since both terms matter:**

> **A two-lane road, design speed 50 km/h, curve radius 100 m:**

| Component | Working | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanical** | **2 × 6.1² / (2 × 100) = 2 × 37.21/200** | **0.372 m** ← |
| **Psychological** | **50 / (9.5 × √100) = 50/95** | **0.526 m** ← |
| **TOTAL extra widening** | 0.372 + 0.526 | **0.898 ≈ 0.9 m** ← |

> **Note that at this radius the PSYCHOLOGICAL term is the LARGER of the two — which is often the case at moderate radii and higher speeds, and is a good reason not to dismiss it as a minor allowance.**

> **The two terms behave differently with radius: the mechanical term falls as 1/R and the psychological as 1/√R, so on very sharp curves the mechanical term dominates and on gentle ones the psychological does.**

**Why OFF-TRACKING occurs — the mechanical term explained:**

> **A vehicle's front wheels are steered along the curve; its rear wheels are fixed to the chassis and simply follow.**

> **The rear axle therefore cuts the corner, tracking inside the front wheels' path — and the longer the wheelbase, the greater the difference.**

| Vehicle | Wheelbase | Off-tracking on a 100 m radius (per lane) |
|---|---|---|
| **Car** | **2.7 m** | **0.036 m — negligible** |
| **Truck / bus** | **6.1 m** | **0.186 m** ← |
| **Articulated vehicle (tractor-trailer)** | **Effectively 10 m or more** | **0.5 m and above** ← |

> **So the design is governed by the COMMERCIAL vehicle, not the car — and IRC's l = 6.1 m is chosen accordingly.**

> **On very sharp curves — a hairpin bend on a hill road — off-tracking becomes severe, which is why hairpins require such generous widening that the carriageway may be nearly double its normal width.**

**How the widening is APPLIED, since the detail matters:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Introduced GRADUALLY over the TRANSITION curve** | **Attaining its full value at the start of the circular curve, in step with the superelevation** ← |
| **Where there is no transition curve** | **Applied over a length of 30 to 60 m before the curve** |
| **On which side?** | **On a two-lane road, HALF on each side is usual; on a hill road with sharp curves, the FULL widening on the INNER side** ← |
| **Why the inner side on hill roads** | **Off-tracking throws the rear wheels toward the INSIDE of the curve, which is where the extra space is actually needed** ← |
| **Not required on curves of large radius** | **IRC: no extra widening for radii above about 300 m** ← |

> **The INNER-SIDE rule in the third and fourth rows is the practically important one on a hill road: the space is needed where the vehicle actually goes, and on the outside of a hill curve it would frequently mean building out on fill over a drop, which is both expensive and less useful.**

**And the associated provisions on a horizontal curve, since they are introduced together:**

| Provision | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **SUPERELEVATION** | **Counteracts centrifugal force** |
| **EXTRA WIDENING** | **This question** ← |
| **TRANSITION curve** | **Introduces the curvature, the superelevation and the widening gradually** ← |
| **SET-BACK distance (clearance on the inside)** | **Obstructions on the inside of the curve must be cleared so the sight distance is available** ← |
| **Grade COMPENSATION** | **Reduces the gradient through a sharp curve, since curve resistance adds to grade resistance** ← |

> **THE SET-BACK DISTANCE deserves a note because it is frequently forgotten and is a genuine safety matter on hill roads:**

> **On a curve, the driver's line of sight cuts across the inside of the bend. A cut face, a parapet, a building or vegetation on the inside will block it, and the available sight distance can fall far below the stopping sight distance even though the road itself is perfectly adequate.**

> **The required clearance from the centre line of the inner lane is m = R − (R − d) cos(θ/2), where θ = S/(R − d) radians — but the practical point is simply that the inside of every curve must be CLEARED and KEPT clear.**

> **On Nepali hill roads the obstruction is usually the cut slope itself, and the remedy is to widen the cut on the inside of curves — an item that is easy to omit from the estimate and expensive to add later.**

examTip.trick: **W_e = n l²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)** — mechanical (off-tracking, l = 6.1 m for a commercial vehicle) plus psychological. At R = 100 m and V = 50 km/h the PSYCHOLOGICAL term is the larger.
