examTip.trap: **Off-tracking sends the rear wheels toward the INSIDE of the curve** — so on hill roads the full widening goes on the INNER side, not split evenly. No extra widening is needed above about R = 300 m.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mechanical falls as 1/R, psychological as 1/√R** — so sharp curves are dominated by off-tracking and gentle ones by the driver allowance. And don't forget SET-BACK: the cut face on the inside of a curve destroys sight distance.

questions.stem: The CALIFORNIA BEARING RATIO (CBR) test result is expressed as the ratio of:
options: The load carried by the specimen to the load carried by standard crushed stone, at the same penetration
The specimen's cohesion to its angle of friction
The dry density achieved to the maximum dry density
The specimen's shear strength to its unconfined compressive strength
questions.solution:
**The load carried by the specimen to the load carried by STANDARD CRUSHED STONE at the same penetration**, expressed as a percentage.

**The test in outline:**

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Plunger** | **50 mm diameter, driven at 1.25 mm/minute** ← |
| **Penetrations at which the load is read** | **2.5 mm and 5.0 mm** ← |
| **Standard loads (crushed stone)** | **1,370 kg at 2.5 mm; 2,055 kg at 5.0 mm** ← |
| **CBR** | **(test load / standard load) × 100** |
| **Which value is reported** | **Normally the 2.5 mm value; but if the 5 mm value is HIGHER, the test is repeated, and if it repeats, the 5 mm value is taken** ← |
| **Soaking** | **4 days (96 hours) under a surcharge, for the worst-case condition** ← |
| **Surcharge** | **Simulates the weight of the pavement above — 2.5 kg minimum** |

> **The rule in the fifth row is the procedural point most often forgotten: normally the 2.5 mm ratio is greater, and where it is not, the test is repeated and the 5 mm value used if the anomaly persists.**

**The SOAKING requirement, which is the test's most important feature:**

> **The specimen is soaked for four days before testing, and this is not a formality — it changes the result profoundly:**

| Soil | Unsoaked CBR | Soaked CBR |
|---|---|---|
| **A clayey subgrade** | **Perhaps 10-15** | **2 to 4** ← |
| **A well-graded gravel** | 60 | 50 |
| **Silty sand** | 20 | 8 to 10 |

> **A clay's CBR can fall by three quarters on soaking, and the design must be based on the SOAKED value because the pavement will experience the wettest condition at some point in its life.**

> **The one situation where an unsoaked CBR may be used is an arid region where the subgrade demonstrably never becomes saturated — and that judgement must be made deliberately, not by default.**

> **For Nepal, with a monsoon delivering most of the year's rain in four months, the soaked value is unquestionably the design value.**

**Typical CBR values, for calibration:**

| Material | CBR (%) |
|---|---|
| **Very poor subgrade — soft clay, organic soil** | **2 to 3** ← |
| **Poor subgrade** | 3 to 5 |
| **Fair subgrade** | 5 to 8 |
| **Good subgrade** | **8 to 20** ← |
| **Sub-base material (granular)** | **20 to 50** ← |
| **Base course — well-graded crushed stone** | **80 to 100** ← |
| **The standard crushed stone by definition** | **100** ← |

> **CBR values above 100 are possible for exceptionally good material and are simply reported as such.**

**How CBR is used in pavement design:**

> **The IRC method (IRC:37) uses the subgrade CBR together with the design traffic in MILLION STANDARD AXLES (msa) to read the required pavement thickness from design charts.**

| Subgrade CBR | Total pavement thickness for a given traffic |
|---|---|
| **2 %** | **Very thick — perhaps 750 mm** ← |
| **5 %** | **About 550 mm** |
| **10 %** | **About 450 mm** |
| **15 %** | **About 400 mm** ← |

> **The relationship is strongly NON-LINEAR: improving a subgrade from 2 to 5 per cent saves far more thickness than improving it from 10 to 15.**

> **That is the practically decisive observation, because it identifies where money should be spent:**

| Action on a very poor subgrade | Note |
|---|---|
| **REMOVE and REPLACE the top 300-500 mm with better material** | **Often cheaper than the extra pavement thickness it saves** ← |
| **STABILISE with lime (for clays) or cement (for granular soils)** | **Lime stabilisation can raise a clay's CBR from 2 to 15** ← |
| **Provide a CAPPING LAYER of granular material** | Standard practice |
| **Improve the DRAINAGE so the subgrade never saturates** | **The cheapest measure of all, and the most neglected** ← |

> **The DRAINAGE entry deserves the emphasis it is given: a subgrade's CBR is largely a function of its MOISTURE CONTENT, and keeping water out of it is far cheaper than building a thicker pavement to compensate for its being wet.**

> **Most premature pavement failure in South Asia is a drainage failure rather than a structural one — blocked side drains, a road built below the surrounding land, no cross-drainage, a shoulder that traps water against the pavement edge.**

> **The classical statement of the point is worth remembering: the three most important things in pavement design are DRAINAGE, DRAINAGE and DRAINAGE.**

**The test's limitations, since it is an empirical index and not a fundamental property:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is EMPIRICAL — it measures no fundamental soil property** | **It correlates with performance; it does not explain it** ← |
| **It is a PENETRATION test at one rate, not a strength or stiffness test** | — |
| **It cannot represent the REPEATED LOADING a pavement receives** ← | **A pavement fails by fatigue and rutting under millions of cycles, which a single penetration cannot capture** |
| **Results are sensitive to compaction, moisture and preparation** | Poor reproducibility between laboratories |
| **It is not suited to stabilised or bound materials** | Their behaviour is quite different |

> **The THIRD row is why modern mechanistic-empirical design has moved to the RESILIENT MODULUS (M_R), measured under repeated loading, which does represent the pavement's actual loading.**

> **A common correlation is M_R (MPa) ≈ 10 × CBR for fine-grained soils with CBR below about 5, and IRC:37 in its later revisions uses M_R directly.**

> **CBR nevertheless survives everywhere because it is CHEAP, SIMPLE and BACKED BY EIGHTY YEARS OF CORRELATED PERFORMANCE — which for routine road design is worth more than theoretical purity.**

examTip.trick: **CBR = (test load / standard crushed stone load) × 100** at the same penetration. Standard loads 1,370 kg at 2.5 mm and 2,055 kg at 5.0 mm; report the 2.5 mm value unless the 5 mm value is higher on repeat.
examTip.trap: **The 4-day SOAKED value is the design value** — a clay's CBR can fall from 12 to 3 on soaking. Using an unsoaked value is a fourfold overestimate of the subgrade.
examTip.mnemonic: **The CBR-to-thickness relation is strongly NON-LINEAR** — lifting a subgrade from 2 to 5 % saves far more thickness than 10 to 15 %. And since CBR is largely a function of MOISTURE, drainage is cheaper than thickness every time.

questions.stem: The PENETRATION test on a bitumen sample measures its:
options: Consistency or hardness, as the depth a standard needle penetrates in 5 seconds
Resistance to stripping in the presence of water
questions.solution:
**Its CONSISTENCY or hardness — the depth, in tenths of a millimetre, that a standard needle penetrates the sample in 5 seconds.**

**The test conditions, all of which are part of the definition:**

| Condition | Value |
|---|---|
| **Needle load** | **100 grams** ← |
| **Time** | **5 seconds** ← |
| **Temperature** | **25 °C** ← |
| **Result unit** | **Tenths of a millimetre (0.1 mm)** ← |

> **So a penetration of 60 means the needle sank 6.0 mm — and the grade written as "60/70" means the penetration lies between 60 and 70.**

> **A HIGHER penetration means a SOFTER bitumen, which is the relation most often inverted under exam pressure.**

**The bitumen grades and where each is used:**

| Grade (penetration) | Consistency | Application |
|---|---|---|
| **30/40** | **HARDEST** | **Very hot climates; heavy traffic** ← |
| **60/70** | Medium | **The most widely used in India and Nepal; hot climates, moderate to heavy traffic** ← |
| **80/100** | Softer | **Cooler regions; lighter traffic; hill roads** ← |
| **180/200** | **SOFTEST** | Very cold regions; surface dressing in cold weather |

> **The selection principle: HOTTER climate and HEAVIER traffic call for a HARDER (lower penetration) grade.**

> **The reason is that bitumen SOFTENS with temperature, so a hot-climate pavement needs a bitumen that is still stiff at 50 or 60 °C surface temperature — otherwise it flows and RUTS.**

> **And conversely a cold-climate pavement needs a bitumen that is not brittle at low temperature, or it cracks — so the choice is a compromise between rutting in summer and cracking in winter.**

> **For Nepal that choice varies with altitude: 60/70 for the Terai and 80/100 for the hills is the usual practice, which is a sensible response to the same compromise resolved differently in different places.**

**The other bitumen tests, since they characterise different properties:**

| Test | Measures | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PENETRATION** | **Consistency at 25 °C** ← | The grading test in the penetration system |
| **SOFTENING POINT (ring and ball)** | **The temperature at which the bitumen becomes fluid enough to flow** ← | **35 to 70 °C typically; a higher value means less temperature susceptibility** |
| **DUCTILITY** | **The distance a briquette stretches before breaking, at 27 °C** ← | **Minimum 50 cm for paving grades; measures the ability to deform without cracking** |
| **VISCOSITY** | Resistance to flow, at 60 °C and 135 °C | **The basis of the modern VG grading system** ← |
| **FLASH and FIRE POINT** | **The temperature at which vapours ignite** ← | **A SAFETY test — flash point minimum 175 °C for paving bitumen** |
| **SPECIFIC GRAVITY** | About 0.97 to 1.02 | For volume-weight conversion |
| **LOSS ON HEATING / thin film oven** | **Ageing during mixing and laying** ← | Simulates the hardening in the plant |
| **SOLUBILITY in trichloroethylene** | **Purity — minimum 99 per cent** | Detects adulteration |
| **STRIPPING value** | **Resistance to displacement of bitumen from aggregate by WATER** ← | (option d) |
| **Float test** | Consistency of very soft bitumens | Where penetration is unsuitable |

> **PENETRATION and SOFTENING POINT together characterise the TEMPERATURE SUSCEPTIBILITY, which is the property that actually matters in service:**

> **Two bitumens with the same penetration at 25 °C may behave quite differently at 60 °C — and the one with the HIGHER softening point is less susceptible, hence better.**

> **This is quantified by the PENETRATION INDEX, computed from the two, running from about −3 (highly susceptible) to +7 (blown bitumens, very stable). A PI between −1 and +1 is normal for paving grades.**

> **The limitation of the penetration grading system is exactly here: it grades on a single temperature, so it cannot distinguish two bitumens of different susceptibility — which is why the VISCOSITY GRADING (VG) system has replaced it in IS 73, grading on viscosity at 60 °C (the pavement's hot service temperature) with additional requirements at 135 °C (the mixing temperature).**

**STRIPPING, since option (d) names it and it is the commonest bitumen-related failure:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What it is** | **Water displaces the bitumen film from the aggregate surface, destroying the bond** ← |
| **Which aggregates are susceptible** | **ACIDIC (siliceous) — quartzite, granite, sandstone — because they are HYDROPHILIC** ← |
| **Which resist** | **BASIC — limestone, basalt, dolomite — which bond well with the acidic bitumen** ← |
| **The visible result** | **Ravelling, potholes, loss of the surface — beginning where water stands** ← |
| **Remedies** | **ANTI-STRIPPING agents (amines); hydrated lime 1-2 % as a filler; ensuring aggregates are DRY at mixing; good drainage** ← |

> **The chemistry is simple and worth knowing: bitumen is weakly ACIDIC, so it bonds strongly with BASIC aggregates and poorly with acidic ones.**

> **Water, being more polar than bitumen, wins the competition for a hydrophilic silica surface, and the bitumen film peels away.**

> **HYDRATED LIME as a filler is the most effective and cheapest remedy: it coats the aggregate with a basic layer and gives the bitumen a surface it can bond to — so 1 to 2 per cent of lime addresses a problem that would otherwise require the aggregate source to be changed.**

> **And the DRY AGGREGATE requirement is the one most often violated on site: an aggregate that is even slightly damp when it meets the bitumen will never bond properly, which is why the mixing plant's drier temperature is a controlled parameter and not a matter of convenience.**

examTip.trick: **100 g needle, 5 seconds, 25 °C, result in TENTHS of a millimetre.** A penetration of 60 means 6.0 mm. HIGHER penetration = SOFTER bitumen — the relation most often inverted.
examTip.trap: **Hotter climate and heavier traffic need a HARDER (lower penetration) grade** — 60/70 for the Terai, 80/100 for the hills. The choice is a compromise between summer rutting and winter cracking.
examTip.mnemonic: **Penetration alone cannot show temperature SUSCEPTIBILITY** — two bitumens equal at 25 °C may differ at 60 °C, which is why VG grading (viscosity at 60 °C) replaced it. And STRIPPING: bitumen is acidic, so it bonds to BASIC aggregates; hydrated lime at 1-2 % is the cheap cure.

questions.stem: In the MARSHALL method of bituminous mix design, the two quantities measured on the compacted specimen are:
questions.solution:
**STABILITY and FLOW.**

**The two measured quantities:**

| Quantity | Definition | Requirement (IRC, heavy traffic) |
|---|---|---|
| **STABILITY** | **The MAXIMUM LOAD the specimen carries before failure, in a lateral-loading head at 60 °C** ← | **Minimum 9 kN** |
| **FLOW** | **The DEFORMATION, in units of 0.25 mm, at that maximum load** ← | **2 to 4 mm (8 to 16 units)** |

> **The test conditions: the specimen is 101.6 mm diameter and about 63.5 mm high, compacted with 75 blows on each face for heavy traffic, immersed at 60 °C for 30-40 minutes, and loaded at 50 mm/minute.**

> **The 60 °C is the significant condition — it represents the hottest pavement temperature in service, at which the mix is weakest and most prone to rutting.**

**What each quantity signifies:**

| Result | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **LOW stability** | **The mix will RUT and shove under traffic — insufficient strength** ← |
| **HIGH stability with LOW flow** | **A BRITTLE mix — it will crack rather than deform** ← |
| **HIGH flow** | **The mix is too PLASTIC — excess bitumen or too little coarse aggregate; it will rut** ← |
| **Stability and flow both within limits** | **The mix has both strength and the ability to deform without cracking** ← |

> **So the two together express the fundamental requirement of a bituminous mix: STRONG ENOUGH NOT TO RUT, FLEXIBLE ENOUGH NOT TO CRACK.**

> **That is a genuine tension — increasing the bitumen content improves flexibility and durability while reducing stability — and the Marshall method is a procedure for finding the content that satisfies both.**

**The volumetric properties, which are computed rather than measured directly:**

| Property | Meaning | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Va — AIR VOIDS** | **Voids in the compacted mix** | **3 to 5 per cent** ← |
| **VMA — voids in the MINERAL AGGREGATE** | **Voids between the aggregate particles, including those filled with bitumen** | **Minimum 11-15 %, depending on the nominal size** ← |
| **VFB — voids FILLED WITH BITUMEN** | **The percentage of the VMA occupied by bitumen** | **65 to 75 per cent** ← |
| **Unit weight** | Bulk density of the compacted specimen | — |

> **THE AIR VOID REQUIREMENT OF 3 TO 5 PER CENT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SINGLE CRITERION, and the reason it is a band rather than a minimum or a maximum is worth setting out:**

| Air voids | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Below 3 %** | **BLEEDING and RUTTING. The mix has no room to compact further under traffic, so the bitumen is squeezed to the surface — losing skid resistance and forming ruts** ← |
| **3 to 5 %** | **The design range** ← |
| **Above 5 %** | **PERMEABLE to water and air. Water causes stripping; air causes OXIDATION and hardening of the bitumen, hence cracking and ravelling** ← |

> **The lower bound exists because traffic COMPACTS the pavement further after construction — typically by about 2 per cent of voids over the first few years.**

> **So a mix laid at 4 per cent voids ends at about 2, which is acceptable; a mix laid at 2 ends at zero and bleeds.**

> **That is why the field compaction requirement is expressed as a percentage of the Marshall density and is checked by coring — undercompaction leaves excessive voids, and overcompaction is equally a defect, which surprises those who assume more compaction is always better.**

**Determining the OPTIMUM BITUMEN CONTENT — the method's purpose:**

> **Specimens are made at a range of bitumen contents (say 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0 per cent), and five curves are plotted against bitumen content:**

| Curve | Typical shape |
|---|---|
| **Stability** | **Rises to a PEAK, then falls** ← |
| **Unit weight** | **Rises to a peak (at a slightly higher content), then falls** ← |
| **Air voids** | **Falls steadily** ← |
| **VFB** | Rises steadily |
| **Flow** | Rises steadily |

> **The OBC is then taken as the AVERAGE of the bitumen contents at: maximum stability, maximum unit weight, and the mid-point of the air-void range (4 per cent).**

> **All the other properties are then CHECKED at that content, and if any fails, the AGGREGATE GRADATION must be changed — not the bitumen content, since that has already been fixed by the procedure.**

> **That last point is the one most often mishandled: the Marshall method determines the bitumen content for a GIVEN gradation, and if the resulting mix fails a criterion, the gradation is the variable to adjust.**

**The method's limitations, since it is old and has been superseded elsewhere:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The IMPACT compaction does not resemble the kneading action of a roller** ← | **The specimen's particle orientation differs from the field's** |
| **It does not measure any FUNDAMENTAL property** | Stability is not a strength in any engineering sense |
| **It cannot predict RUTTING or FATIGUE directly** | Only correlate with them |
| **It gives no measure of the mix's STIFFNESS** | Needed for mechanistic design |

> **The SUPERPAVE system developed in the United States addresses these by using a GYRATORY compactor (which kneads, as a roller does), by selecting the binder according to the site's actual temperature range (a performance-graded binder such as PG 64-10), and by adding performance tests.**

> **The Marshall method nevertheless remains the standard in India, Nepal and much of the world, and the reason is the familiar one: it is CHEAP, the equipment is everywhere, and eighty years of experience relate its results to pavements that have performed.**

> **That is a legitimate basis for a design method even without theoretical elegance — and the pragmatic judgement it represents recurs throughout this subject, in the CBR test and the penetration grade as much as here.**

examTip.trick: **STABILITY (maximum load, minimum 9 kN) and FLOW (deformation at that load, 2-4 mm), tested at 60 °C** — the hottest pavement service temperature, at which the mix is weakest.
examTip.trap: **AIR VOIDS must be 3 to 5 % — a BAND, not a maximum.** Below 3 % the mix BLEEDS and RUTS (traffic compacts it a further ~2 % in service); above 5 % it is permeable, so water strips it and air oxidises the binder.
examTip.mnemonic: **OBC = the average of the contents at maximum stability, maximum unit weight, and 4 % air voids.** If a property then fails, change the GRADATION, not the bitumen content — that has already been fixed.

questions.stem: In a SPOT SPEED study, the speed generally adopted for fixing the SPEED LIMIT on a road is the:
questions.solution:
**The 85th PERCENTILE speed** — the speed below which 85 per cent of vehicles travel.

**The percentile speeds and what each is used for:**

| Percentile | Meaning | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **15th** | **Only 15 % travel slower** | **The LOWER speed limit, where one is imposed, to remove very slow vehicles from a fast road** ← |
| **50th (MEDIAN)** | **Half travel slower** | **The AVERAGE speed; used in traffic flow and travel-time studies** ← |
| **85th** | **85 % travel slower; only 15 % exceed it** | **The SPEED LIMIT, and the SAFE SPEED for design purposes** ← |
| **98th** | **Almost all travel slower** | **The DESIGN SPEED for geometric elements — the road must be safe even for the fastest** ← |

> **Options (a) and (d) are both real and important percentiles from the same curve, which makes them well-made distractors.**

**Why the 85th percentile is chosen for the speed limit — the reasoning:**

| Argument | Note |
|---|---|
| **Most drivers choose a REASONABLE speed for the conditions** | **The road, visibility and traffic inform their judgement more reliably than a posted number** ← |
| **A limit set at the 85th percentile makes 85 % of drivers COMPLIANT without changing behaviour** | **So enforcement targets the genuinely fast minority** ← |
| **A limit set too LOW is widely ignored** | **Which breeds disrespect for limits generally, and makes enforcement arbitrary** ← |
| **SPEED VARIANCE, not speed alone, drives crash risk** | **See below — this is the strongest argument** ← |

> **THE SPEED VARIANCE ARGUMENT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE WORTH UNDERSTANDING, because it is counter-intuitive:**

> **Crash risk correlates strongly with the DIFFERENCE between a vehicle's speed and the prevailing traffic speed — in both directions.**

> **A vehicle travelling much SLOWER than the traffic around it is nearly as hazardous as one travelling much faster, because it generates overtaking manoeuvres, sudden braking and conflicts.**

> **Setting the limit unrealistically low splits the traffic into a compliant slow group and a non-compliant fast group, INCREASING the variance and therefore the risk.**

> **Setting it at the 85th percentile keeps the stream homogeneous, which is the safest condition.**

> **The important qualification: this reasoning assumes the road's existing speeds are themselves reasonable. Where the 85th percentile is plainly unsafe — a school frontage, a village bazaar, a hazardous bend — the limit must be set on SAFETY grounds and supported by physical measures, because a sign alone will not change behaviour.**

**How a spot speed study is conducted:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What is measured** | **The INSTANTANEOUS speed of vehicles at a specific point** ← |
| **Methods** | **Enoscope, stopwatch over a measured base, pneumatic tubes, RADAR/LIDAR gun, inductive loops, video analysis** ← |
| **Sample size** | **Typically 150 to 200 vehicles minimum, by vehicle class** ← |
| **Essential precaution** | **The observation must be CONCEALED — a visible observer or a radar gun changes the speeds being measured** ← |
| **Presentation** | **A frequency distribution histogram, and a CUMULATIVE frequency curve from which the percentiles are read** ← |

> **The CONCEALMENT requirement in the fourth row is not a nicety: drivers who see a person with a radar gun slow down, and the measured 85th percentile is then a measure of the observer's visibility rather than of the road.**

**The uses of spot speed data beyond the speed limit:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Fixing speed limits and their zones** | ← |
| **Establishing the DESIGN SPEED for improvements** | **The 98th percentile** |
| **Locating and timing traffic signals** | Progression speed for a co-ordinated system |
| **Justifying overtaking zones and no-overtaking markings** | Through the sight distance required |
| **Accident analysis at a site** | **Comparing speeds before and after a treatment** ← |
| **Assessing the effect of a countermeasure** | **A before-and-after study is the only sound way to judge whether a treatment worked** ← |

> **The BEFORE-AND-AFTER study in the last row is the discipline that separates traffic engineering from guesswork, and it carries a well-known statistical trap worth naming:**

> **REGRESSION TO THE MEAN. Sites are chosen for treatment BECAUSE they have had an unusually bad recent record — and an unusually bad year is likely to be followed by a better one regardless of any treatment.**

> **So a simple before-and-after comparison will credit the treatment with an improvement that would have occurred anyway, and countermeasures routinely appear more effective than they are.**

> **The remedy is to use a CONTROL group of similar untreated sites, or a longer baseline period, so that the general trend can be separated from the treatment's actual effect.**

> **This matters in practice because limited road-safety budgets are allocated on exactly this evidence, and an overstated benefit diverts money from measures that would save more lives.**

examTip.trick: **15th = lower limit; 50th = average; 85th = SPEED LIMIT and safe speed; 98th = DESIGN speed for geometry.** All four are real percentiles from the same cumulative curve.
examTip.trap: **Crash risk tracks SPEED VARIANCE, not speed alone** — a vehicle much slower than the stream is nearly as hazardous as one much faster. A limit set too low splits the traffic and INCREASES the variance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Conceal the observer** — a visible radar gun measures its own visibility, not the road. And beware REGRESSION TO THE MEAN in before-and-after studies: sites are chosen after a bad year, which was likely to improve anyway.

questions.stem: In a cement concrete (rigid) pavement, DOWEL BARS are provided at transverse joints principally to:
options: Hold the two slabs tightly together and prevent the joint opening
Reinforce the slab against flexural stresses
Provide a key for the sealing compound
TRANSFER the wheel load across the joint while permitting the slabs to move LONGITUDINALLY
questions.solution:
**To TRANSFER the wheel load across the joint while allowing the slabs to move longitudinally** relative to one another.

**DOWEL BARS against TIE BARS — the distinction that this question turns on:**

| | DOWEL BARS | TIE BARS |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | **LOAD TRANSFER across the joint** ← | **To HOLD the slabs TOGETHER and prevent the joint opening** ← (option a) |
| **Placed at** | **TRANSVERSE (expansion and contraction) joints** ← | **LONGITUDINAL joints** ← |
| **Bar type** | **PLAIN round, SMOOTH** ← | **DEFORMED (ribbed)** ← |
| **Bonded?** | **Bonded on ONE side only; the other half is greased or sleeved so it can SLIDE** ← | **BONDED at both ends — it must NOT slide** ← |
| **Movement permitted** | **YES — longitudinal expansion and contraction** ← | **NO — that is the point** ← |
| **Does it carry load across?** | **YES — its primary function** | **Incidentally; not its purpose** |

> **THE SMOOTH-VERSUS-DEFORMED DISTINCTION IS THE KEY AND IT FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM THE PURPOSE:**

> **A dowel must let the slabs move apart and together as the temperature changes, so it must be able to SLIDE — hence a plain round bar, greased or fitted with a cap on one half.**

> **A tie bar must PREVENT movement, so it must grip — hence a deformed bar bonded at both ends.**

> **Using a deformed bar as a dowel locks the joint and the slab cracks; using a plain bar as a tie lets the longitudinal joint open. Both errors are made, and both are visible in the pavement within a few years.**

**Why load transfer matters:**

> **A concrete slab is strongest when a load is applied at its INTERIOR and weakest at a free EDGE or CORNER, because the slab there is supported on fewer sides.**

| Load position | Relative critical stress |
|---|---|
| **INTERIOR** | **Lowest** ← |
| **EDGE** | **About 1.5 times the interior stress** ← |
| **CORNER** | **The most critical for deflection and for pumping** ← |

> **Every transverse joint creates two free edges. Without load transfer, a wheel approaching the joint loads a free edge, then drops onto the next slab's free edge — producing high stresses, large deflections and a rough ride.**

> **A dowel makes the two slabs act together at the joint: the load is shared between them, the edge stress falls toward the interior value, and the differential deflection ("faulting") is prevented.**

> **Typical dowels are 25 to 32 mm diameter, 450 to 500 mm long, at 250 to 300 mm centres — half the length bonded, half free to slide.**

**The joints in a rigid pavement, since dowels belong to one class of them:**

| Joint | Purpose | Spacing |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTRACTION joint** | **Relieves SHRINKAGE and thermal contraction; a groove cut to about ¼ of the slab depth induces the crack at a chosen line** ← | **4.5 m typically** |
| **EXPANSION joint** | **Allows the slab to EXPAND; a full-depth gap of 20-25 mm with a compressible filler** ← | **Formerly 50-60 m; now often omitted entirely** ← |
| **CONSTRUCTION joint** | Where a day's work ends | As required |
| **LONGITUDINAL joint** | **Controls longitudinal cracking and separates paving lanes; TIE BARS here** ← | At lane lines |
| **Warping joint** | Relieves warping stresses | — |

> **The EXPANSION JOINT entry carries an interesting change of practice worth noting: modern rigid pavement design frequently OMITS expansion joints altogether.**

> **The reason is that contraction joints, once open, provide ample room for the slab to expand back into — and expansion joints proved to be the pavement's weak points, collecting incompressible debris, spalling at their edges, and causing more trouble than they prevented.**

> **So a provision that was once considered essential has largely been abandoned on the evidence of performance, which is a good example of a design rule being corrected by observation.**

**And PUMPING, the failure that load transfer chiefly prevents:**

| Stage | Process |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Water enters through the joint and collects beneath the slab** ← |
| **2** | **A wheel load deflects the slab and EJECTS the water at high velocity through the joint** ← |
| **3** | **The water carries FINE SUBGRADE MATERIAL out with it — visible as a fan of fines on the surface** ← |
| **4** | **A VOID forms under the slab corner** ← |
| **5** | **The unsupported corner cracks and the joint FAULTS (steps)** ← |

> **The requirements for pumping are three, and removing any one prevents it: WATER, FINE-GRAINED SUBGRADE, and REPEATED HEAVY LOADS with slab deflection.**

> **So the defences are correspondingly three: SEAL the joints and drain the pavement; provide a GRANULAR or stabilised sub-base so there are no fines to pump; and provide LOAD TRANSFER so the deflection at the joint is small.**

> **The dowel bar addresses the third, which is why a doweled joint is so much more durable than a plain butt joint — and why the fan of grey fines beside a joint is the diagnostic sign that the load transfer has failed.**

examTip.trick: **DOWEL: transverse joint, PLAIN round bar, bonded one side only, TRANSFERS LOAD and lets the slab slide. TIE BAR: longitudinal joint, DEFORMED bar, bonded both ends, PREVENTS movement.** Option (a) describes the tie bar.
examTip.trap: **Smooth versus deformed follows from the purpose** — a deformed bar used as a dowel locks the joint and cracks the slab; a plain bar used as a tie lets the longitudinal joint open.
examTip.mnemonic: **PUMPING needs three things — water, fine subgrade, and deflection under load — so removing any ONE stops it:** seal and drain, use a granular sub-base, and provide dowels. A fan of grey fines beside a joint means the load transfer has failed.

questions.stem: For the stabilisation of a highly PLASTIC CLAY subgrade, the most appropriate stabilising agent is:
questions.solution:
**LIME.**

**Matching the stabiliser to the soil — the essential table:**

| Stabiliser | Suits | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **LIME** | **CLAYS and plastic soils (PI above about 10)** ← | **CATION EXCHANGE and pozzolanic reaction — see below** ← |
| **CEMENT** | **GRANULAR soils, sands and gravels; low-plasticity soils** ← | **Hydration — it cements the particles together** |
| **BITUMEN** | **SANDY and granular soils** ← | **Binds and WATERPROOFS; useless in wet clay, which it cannot coat** ← |
| **Lime + fly ash, or lime + cement** | Marginal soils | Combined |
| **Chemical (chlorides, lignin)** | **Dust control and moisture retention, not structural stabilisation** ← | Hygroscopic |
| **Mechanical (granular) stabilisation** | Any — by blending grading | Improves the particle skeleton |
| **Geosynthetics** | Soft subgrades | Separation and reinforcement |

> **The rule that organises the whole subject: LIME FOR CLAY, CEMENT FOR GRANULAR SOIL, BITUMEN FOR SAND.**

> **Option (b), cement alone in a highly plastic clay, is the well-made distractor: cement is an excellent stabiliser and a poor choice HERE, because it cannot be mixed uniformly into a plastic clay — the clay forms lumps that the cement coats without penetrating.**

> **Where a plastic clay must be cement-stabilised, LIME IS APPLIED FIRST to reduce the plasticity and make the soil friable, and cement is added afterwards — a two-stage treatment that is standard practice.**

**How lime works on a clay — two reactions on very different timescales:**

| Reaction | Timescale | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — CATION EXCHANGE (modification)** | **HOURS to a few days** ← | **Ca²⁺ replaces Na⁺ and K⁺ on the clay particles; the particles FLOCCULATE into crumbs** ← |
| **2 — POZZOLANIC reaction (stabilisation)** | **WEEKS to MONTHS, continuing for years** ← | **Lime reacts with the clay's own SILICA and ALUMINA to form calcium silicate and aluminate hydrates — the same cementing compounds as in Portland cement** ← |

> **The immediate effects of the first reaction are dramatic and are what make the soil workable at all:**

| Property | Change on adding lime |
|---|---|
| **PLASTICITY INDEX** | **Falls SHARPLY — a PI of 40 may drop to 10-15** ← |
| **Plastic limit** | **RISES** |
| **Liquid limit** | Falls slightly |
| **Optimum moisture content** | **RISES** ← |
| **Maximum dry density** | **FALLS** ← |
| **Workability** | **Transformed — a sticky clay becomes a friable, granular material that can be mixed and compacted** ← |
| **Volume change / swelling** | **Greatly REDUCED** ← |
| **Immediate bearing capacity** | Rises at once |

> **THE DENSITY ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE ONE AND IT MATTERS FOR SITE CONTROL: lime-stabilised soil compacts to a LOWER maximum dry density than the untreated soil, at a HIGHER optimum moisture content.**

> **An inspector comparing the achieved density against the UNTREATED soil's Proctor value will wrongly conclude that compaction has failed.**

> **The compaction standard must be set against a Proctor test on the LIME-TREATED material, and that test must be run at the same delay after mixing as the field work — because the values shift as the reaction proceeds.**

**The practical requirements:**

| Aspect | Typical value or requirement |
|---|---|
| **Lime content** | **2 to 8 per cent by dry weight; found by the Eades and Grim pH test or by strength trials** ← |
| **Lime type** | **Quicklime (CaO) or hydrated lime (Ca(OH)₂)** |
| **MELLOWING period between mixing and compaction** | **A few hours to 48 hours — lets the modification reaction proceed and the clods break down** ← |
| **Compaction** | **After mellowing and remixing; DELAY beyond this loses strength** ← |
| **CURING** | **Moist curing, and warmth — the pozzolanic reaction is strongly TEMPERATURE dependent and nearly stops below about 5 °C** ← |
| **Strength gain** | **Continues for months and even years** ← |

> **The two entries about DELAY appear to contradict and do not: a mellowing period BEFORE compaction is beneficial, while delay AFTER the mix is ready to compact is harmful.**

> **The reason is that the pozzolanic reaction begins to cement the material where it lies; compacting after it has started breaks the bonds already formed and the final strength is permanently reduced.**

> **So the sequence is mix, mellow, remix, then compact promptly — and "compact promptly" means within the same working day.**

**And the CARBONATION hazard, which is the characteristic failure of lime stabilisation:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **What happens** | **Lime reacts with CO₂ from the air to form calcium carbonate instead of reacting with the clay** ← |
| **Consequence** | **The lime is consumed without producing any cementing compounds — the stabilisation simply does not develop** ← |
| **When it occurs** | **When the mixed material is left loose and exposed for too long before compaction** ← |
| **Prevention** | **Keep the mellowing period within limits, keep the surface moist, and compact and seal the layer promptly** ← |

> **This is the reverse of the lime cycle being a virtue: in mortar, carbonation is the setting mechanism and is wanted; in soil stabilisation it is a competing reaction that wastes the lime.**

> **The same chemistry serves in one application and defeats the other, which is a useful reminder that a reaction is neither good nor bad in itself — only in relation to what is being asked of it.**

examTip.trick: **LIME for CLAY, CEMENT for GRANULAR soil, BITUMEN for SAND.** Option (b) is the good distractor: cement is excellent, but it cannot be mixed uniformly into a plastic clay — lime must go in first to make it friable.
examTip.trap: **Lime-treated soil has a LOWER maximum dry density at a HIGHER optimum moisture** — so compaction must be checked against a Proctor test on the TREATED material, or it will appear to have failed when it has not.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two reactions: CATION EXCHANGE in hours (plasticity collapses, soil becomes friable) and POZZOLANIC over months (the strength).** Mix, MELLOW, remix, compact PROMPTLY — and beware CARBONATION, which consumes the lime and produces no cementing at all.

questions.stem: In FIRST ANGLE projection, the view of an object as seen from the LEFT is placed:
options: To the RIGHT of the front view
To the LEFT of the front view
questions.solution:
**To the RIGHT of the front view.**

**The rule that generates every answer in this topic:**

> **In FIRST ANGLE projection, the object lies BETWEEN the observer and the plane of projection. The observer looks THROUGH the object and the view is PUSHED onto the plane BEYOND it.**

> **So each view appears on the side OPPOSITE to the direction from which it was taken.**

> **In THIRD ANGLE projection, the PLANE lies between the observer and the object — the plane behaves like a sheet of glass on which the view is traced — so each view appears on the SAME side as the direction from which it was taken.**

| View taken from the | FIRST angle — placed | THIRD angle — placed |
|---|---|---|
| **LEFT** | **RIGHT of the front view** ← | **LEFT of the front view** |
| **RIGHT** | **LEFT of the front view** | **RIGHT of the front view** |
| **ABOVE (the top view / plan)** | **BELOW the front view** ← | **ABOVE the front view** ← |
| **BELOW** | **ABOVE the front view** | Below the front view |
| **BEHIND (the rear view)** | Far right or far left | Far right or far left |

> **The single sentence that settles any question of this kind: FIRST ANGLE PUTS THE VIEW ON THE OPPOSITE SIDE; THIRD ANGLE PUTS IT ON THE SAME SIDE.**

> **And the most-used consequence, worth memorising directly because it is the quickest test of which system a drawing uses: in FIRST angle the PLAN (top view) is BELOW the front elevation, and in THIRD angle the plan is ABOVE it.**

**Why there is no second or fourth angle:**

| Quadrant | Why it is not used |
|---|---|
| **FIRST (above HP, in front of VP)** | **USED** ← |
| **SECOND (above HP, behind VP)** | **On rotating the planes flat, the two views OVERLAP each other** ← |
| **THIRD (below HP, behind VP)** | **USED** ← |
| **FOURTH (below HP, in front of VP)** | **The views overlap, as in the second** ← |

> **So the choice is not arbitrary: the second and fourth quadrants are geometrically unusable because the horizontal and vertical planes, when rotated into a single sheet, carry their views onto the same region of the paper.**

**Which system is used where:**

| Region / standard | System |
|---|---|
| **INDIA, NEPAL and most of Europe (ISO, IS)** | **FIRST angle** ← |
| **United States, Canada, Australia, Japan** | **THIRD angle** ← |
| **The symbol placed in the title block** | **A truncated CONE, drawn in the system used** ← |

> **The TRUNCATED CONE symbol is the practical safeguard and every drawing must carry it, because a drawing read in the wrong system is not merely confusing — it is a MIRROR IMAGE of the intended object, and it will be built backwards.**

| Symbol appearance | System |
|---|---|
| **The cone's small end (the apex) faces the LEFT-hand view position, i.e. the circle appears to the LEFT of the cone's side view** | **THIRD angle** |
| **The cone's small end faces the opposite way — the circle appears to the RIGHT** | **FIRST angle** ← |

> **The symbol is simply the projection rule applied to a cone, so it need not be memorised separately: draw the cone's side view, then ask where its end view would go under each system, and the symbol follows.**

**The other projections named in the syllabus, since they answer a different need:**

| Projection | Character | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **ORTHOGRAPHIC (multi-view)** | **Several 2-D views, each TRUE to scale and undistorted** ← | **WORKING drawings — every dimension can be read directly** |
| **ISOMETRIC** | **A single pictorial view; the three axes at 120° to one another; scale EQUAL along all three axes** ← | **Showing the object's shape at a glance** |
| **Oblique (cavalier / cabinet)** | One face true, the depth axis at 45° | Quick sketching |
| **PERSPECTIVE** | **Converging lines to vanishing points — how the eye actually sees** ← | **Architectural presentation; NOT for working drawings** |

> **The essential trade-off between the first two is worth stating: an ORTHOGRAPHIC drawing is hard to visualise and easy to measure, while an ISOMETRIC view is easy to visualise and misleading to measure.**

> **A working drawing must be measurable, so it is orthographic; a presentation drawing must be understood, so it is pictorial — and the two are produced from the same model for different readers.**

> **The ISOMETRIC SCALE deserves a note because it is a classic point of confusion: a TRUE isometric projection foreshortens all three axes to about 0.816 of their real length, but in practice an ISOMETRIC DRAWING is made with the FULL length along each axis.**

> **The result is a figure about 22 per cent larger than the true projection and identical in shape — so it is drawn full size for convenience, and "isometric drawing" and "isometric projection" are not quite the same thing.**

**And the SECTIONAL views the syllabus also names:**

| Convention | Rule |
|---|---|
| **The cutting plane** | **Shown on another view by a chain line thickened at its ends, with arrows giving the direction of sight** ← |
| **HATCHING (section lining)** | **Thin lines at 45°, spaced 1-3 mm; ADJACENT parts hatched in OPPOSITE directions or at different spacings** ← |
| **Parts NOT sectioned even when the plane passes through them** | **Ribs, webs, shafts, bolts, nuts, rivets, keys, spokes — shown UNCUT** ← |
| **Hidden detail in a sectional view** | **Normally OMITTED — the section exists to remove the need for it** ← |

> **The third row is the convention most often violated in student work, and its reason is legibility rather than geometry: hatching a rib along its length makes the object look solid where it is not, and gives a false impression of its bulk.**

> **So the rule is a deliberate departure from strict truth in the interest of clear communication — which is what a drawing convention is for.**

examTip.trick: **FIRST angle puts the view on the OPPOSITE side; THIRD angle on the SAME side.** So a left-side view goes to the RIGHT in first angle. Quickest test of a drawing: in FIRST angle the PLAN is BELOW the elevation; in THIRD angle, above it.
examTip.trap: **There is no second or fourth angle** — on rotating the planes flat, the views would OVERLAP. That is a geometric fact, not a convention.
examTip.mnemonic: **India and Nepal use FIRST angle; the USA uses THIRD** — and the truncated-cone symbol in the title block declares which, because a drawing read in the wrong system is a MIRROR IMAGE and will be built backwards. Also: isometric DRAWING is full size; isometric PROJECTION foreshortens to 0.816.

questions.stem: On a drawing prepared to a scale of 1:200, a wall measures 45 mm. The actual length of the wall is:
questions.solution:
**9.0 m.**

**The computation:**

> **A scale of 1:200 means ONE unit on the drawing represents TWO HUNDRED of the same units on the ground.**

> **Actual length = drawing length × scale factor = 45 mm × 200 = 9,000 mm = 9.0 m**

> **The distractors are the characteristic slips: 0.9 m and 90 m are the answer displaced by one decimal place, and 4.5 m is the result of dividing by 10 rather than multiplying by 200 — each a plausible error rather than an arbitrary number.**

> **The safeguard against all three is a SENSE CHECK: a wall 45 mm long at 1:200 is a room-sized element, so an answer of 0.9 m (a doorway) or 90 m (a football pitch) should be rejected on sight.**

**The standard scales and where each is used:**

| Scale | Ratio | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **FULL size** | **1:1** | Details, templates |
| **Enlarged** | **2:1, 5:1, 10:1** | **Small components — the only case where the drawing is LARGER than the object** ← |
| **1:5, 1:10** | Reducing | **Construction DETAILS — joints, connections, reinforcement details** ← |
| **1:20, 1:25** | — | Large-scale details, sections, stair and toilet layouts |
| **1:50** | — | **Floor plans of a house; sections; the commonest architectural scale** ← |
| **1:100** | — | **Floor plans of a larger building; general arrangement** ← |
| **1:200, 1:500** | — | **SITE plans; overall layouts** ← |
| **1:1000, 1:2500** | — | **Location and key plans; town maps** ← |

> **The two rules that govern the choice: the scale must be large enough for the smallest feature to be DRAWN and READ, and small enough for the drawing to fit the sheet.**

> **A useful check is that a line 0.5 mm wide on paper represents 100 mm at 1:200 — so a 100 mm partition wall becomes a single line thickness at that scale, which is precisely why partitions are shown on 1:50 plans and not on 1:200 site plans.**

**The REPRESENTATIVE FRACTION and the scale bar:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Representative fraction (RF)** | **The scale as a fraction — 1:200 is an RF of 1/200** ← |
| **SCALE BAR** | **A graduated bar drawn on the sheet showing the true lengths** ← |

> **THE SCALE BAR IS NOT A DECORATION and it is worth knowing why every drawing should carry one:**

> **A drawing that is PHOTOCOPIED, printed to a different sheet size, scanned or emailed as a PDF may no longer be at its stated scale — a reduction from A1 to A3 halves every dimension, so a drawing marked 1:100 is now at 1:200.**

> **The written ratio then LIES, and anyone scaling from it gets an answer that is exactly half.**

> **A SCALE BAR is drawn on the sheet and is reduced along with everything else, so it remains correct at any reproduction size — which is why it is the only reliable way to scale from a reproduced drawing.**

> **And the professional convention that accompanies it: DO NOT SCALE FROM THE DRAWING — figured dimensions govern, and where a dimension is not shown it should be asked for rather than measured.**

> **Scaling is for estimating and for understanding; it is not a source of construction dimensions.**

**The LINE TYPES, since they are the other language of the drawing sheet:**

| Line | Appearance | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous THICK** | ▬▬▬▬ | **VISIBLE outlines and edges** ← |
| **Continuous THIN** | ──── | **Dimension lines, extension lines, leaders, HATCHING, outlines of adjacent parts** ← |
| **Continuous thin FREEHAND or with zigzags** | ∿∿∿ | **Limits of a partial or interrupted view — a BREAK line** ← |
| **DASHED thin (or thick)** | ─ ─ ─ | **HIDDEN edges and outlines** ← |
| **Chain thin (long dash dot)** | ─·─·─ | **CENTRE lines, axes, lines of symmetry, pitch circles** ← |
| **Chain thin, THICKENED at the ends and at changes of direction** | ▬·─·▬ | **CUTTING PLANES** ← |
| **Chain THICK** | ▬·▬·▬ | Surfaces requiring special treatment |
| **Chain thin, double-dashed** | ─··─··─ | **Outlines of ADJACENT parts; extreme positions of a moving part; the original outline before forming** ← |

> **The essential discipline is the LINE THICKNESS HIERARCHY: the drawing should read at a glance, with the heaviest lines carrying the most important information.**

> **A drawing in which every line is the same weight is legible only by careful reading, while one with a proper hierarchy communicates its principal shape instantly — and the difference costs nothing to produce.**

> **The usual ratio is 2:1 between thick and thin, with a section outline heavier still on architectural drawings — so that a plan reads as a cut through solid material rather than as a diagram of lines.**

**And the SHEET SIZES, since they determine what scale will fit:**

| Size | Dimensions (mm) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **A0** | **841 × 1189** | **One square metre in area** ← |
| **A1** | **594 × 841** | **The common working drawing size** ← |
| **A2** | 420 × 594 | — |
| **A3** | **297 × 420** | **The common reduced/office copy** ← |
| **A4** | 210 × 297 | Schedules, letters |

> **Each size is half the previous one, cut across the longer side, and every sheet has the same ASPECT RATIO of √2 : 1 — which is exactly the property that makes the halving work.**

> **That is why an A1 drawing reduces to A3 without any part of the sheet being cropped or left blank, and it is why the A-series is used worldwide for drawings while paper sizes defined in inches are not.**

examTip.trick: **45 mm × 200 = 9,000 mm = 9.0 m.** The distractors are one decimal place either side (0.9, 90) and a division by 10 (4.5) — each a plausible slip, all three rejected by a sense check.
examTip.trap: **A photocopied or resized drawing no longer matches its written scale** — A1 reduced to A3 turns 1:100 into 1:200. Only the SCALE BAR, which reduces with the drawing, stays true. And figured dimensions always govern: DO NOT SCALE.
examTip.mnemonic: **Line types: continuous THICK = visible edges; DASHED = hidden; CHAIN thin = centre lines; chain thickened at the ends = CUTTING PLANE.** And every A-size is √2:1, which is why A1 reduces to A3 with nothing cropped.

questions.stem: The MINIMUM ATTRACTIVE RATE OF RETURN (MARR) used in engineering economic analysis is:
options: The rate of inflation prevailing in the economy
The LOWEST rate of return an organisation will accept before committing capital to a project
The rate at which the project's NPV becomes zero
The rate of interest charged by the central bank
questions.solution:
**The LOWEST rate of return an organisation will accept before committing capital to a project** — the hurdle rate.

**What the MARR is built from:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **The COST OF CAPITAL** | **The weighted cost of the organisation's debt and equity — the floor below which investing destroys value** ← |
| **A premium for RISK** | **A riskier project must promise more; the premium rises with uncertainty** ← |
| **The return available on ALTERNATIVE uses of the money** | **The OPPORTUNITY COST — the best forgone alternative** ← |
| **Capital RATIONING** | **When funds are limited, the MARR is raised until only as many projects qualify as can be funded** ← |
| **Inflation expectations** | Where the analysis is in nominal terms |

> **Option (c) defines the INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN, which is the project's own computed return — and the MARR is the standard the IRR is COMPARED AGAINST.**

> **That pairing is the substance of the topic: the IRR is what the project OFFERS; the MARR is what the organisation DEMANDS.**

| Comparison | Decision |
|---|---|
| **IRR > MARR** | **ACCEPT — the project earns more than the organisation's hurdle** ← |
| **IRR = MARR** | Indifferent |
| **IRR < MARR** | **REJECT — the capital is better used elsewhere** ← |

> **And the equivalent statement in NPV terms, which is the same test from the other side: if the cash flows are discounted AT THE MARR and the NPV is positive, then the project's return exceeds the MARR — so NPV > 0 at the MARR and IRR > MARR are the same condition.**

**The CAPITAL RATIONING row deserves expansion, because it is where the MARR is actually set in practice:**

> **A public body or a company rarely has unlimited funds. It has a budget, and more candidate projects than the budget will cover.**

> **The rational procedure is to rank the projects by return and fund downward until the budget is exhausted — and the return of the LAST project funded becomes the effective MARR.**

> **Any project below that line is rejected NOT because it is unprofitable but because a better use exists for the same money.**

> **That is why an organisation's MARR is commonly well above its cost of capital: a MARR of 15 per cent when money costs 9 per cent does not mean 12 per cent projects are bad, it means there are enough 15 per cent projects to absorb all the capital available.**

**The compound interest factors on which every one of these calculations rests:**

| Factor | Symbol | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **Single payment COMPOUND AMOUNT (F given P)** | **(F/P, i, n)** | **(1 + i)^n** ← |
| **Single payment PRESENT WORTH (P given F)** | **(P/F, i, n)** | **1/(1 + i)^n** ← |
| **Uniform series COMPOUND AMOUNT (F given A)** | **(F/A, i, n)** | **((1+i)^n − 1)/i** |
| **SINKING FUND (A given F)** | **(A/F, i, n)** | **i/((1+i)^n − 1)** ← |
| **Uniform series PRESENT WORTH (P given A)** | **(P/A, i, n)** | **((1+i)^n − 1)/(i(1+i)^n)** ← |
| **CAPITAL RECOVERY (A given P)** | **(A/P, i, n)** | **i(1+i)^n/((1+i)^n − 1)** ← |

> **The six factors are three PAIRS of reciprocals — P↔F, A↔F, A↔P — so only three need to be remembered and the others are their inverses.**

> **The CAPITAL RECOVERY factor in the last row is the most useful of them for engineering work, because it converts a capital sum into an EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST, which is what makes alternatives comparable.**

**COMPARING ALTERNATIVES, since that is what the syllabus asks for:**

| Situation | Correct method |
|---|---|
| **Alternatives with the SAME life** | **Compare NPV (or present worth of costs) directly** ← |
| **Alternatives with DIFFERENT lives** | **Compare EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST (EAC); or use a common study period equal to the LEAST COMMON MULTIPLE of the lives** ← |
| **Choosing among many independent projects with a budget limit** | **Rank by benefit-cost ratio or by IRR and fund downward** ← |
| **Mutually exclusive projects of different size** | **NPV, not IRR — see below** ← |
| **A cost-only comparison (no revenue difference)** | **Least present worth of cost, or least EAC** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENT-LIVES CASE IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG, and the error is straightforward: comparing the NPV of a 10-year asset with the NPV of a 25-year asset is meaningless, because the two do not deliver the same thing.**

> **Either the shorter asset must be assumed to be replaced until the horizons match, or both must be reduced to an annual figure — and the EAC does exactly that.**

> **A worked illustration: a steel bridge costing Rs 200 lakh with a 30-year life and a timber bridge costing Rs 60 lakh with a 10-year life, at 10 per cent.**

| Option | Capital recovery factor | EAC of capital |
|---|---|---|
| **Steel, n = 30** | **(A/P, 10 %, 30) = 0.1061** | **200 × 0.1061 = Rs 21.2 lakh/year** ← |
| **Timber, n = 10** | **(A/P, 10 %, 10) = 0.1627** | **60 × 0.1627 = Rs 9.8 lakh/year** ← |

> **The timber bridge is cheaper on this measure despite needing replacement three times — and the comparison is only valid once both are expressed annually.**

> **The raw capital figures (200 against 60) would have suggested the same conclusion here by accident; with a steel bridge at Rs 120 lakh the raw figures and the annual figures would point in opposite directions, which is exactly when the method earns its keep.**

> **Maintenance, operating cost and salvage value are then added to each EAC before the decision is made — and for infrastructure they frequently reverse it, since the cheap option to build is often the expensive one to keep.**

examTip.trick: **MARR is what the organisation DEMANDS; IRR is what the project OFFERS.** Accept when IRR > MARR — which is the same condition as NPV > 0 when discounted at the MARR. Option (c) defines the IRR.
examTip.trap: **MARR is usually well ABOVE the cost of capital** — under capital rationing it is set by the return of the LAST project the budget will fund, so a rejected project may be perfectly profitable and merely outranked.
examTip.mnemonic: **Different lives ⇒ compare EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST, never raw NPV.** The six interest factors are three pairs of reciprocals (P↔F, A↔F, A↔P), and CAPITAL RECOVERY i(1+i)ⁿ/((1+i)ⁿ−1) is the one that turns capital into an annual figure.

questions.stem: A sum P is invested at an interest rate i per annum, compounded annually. The amount accumulated after n years is:
questions.solution:
**P(1 + i)ⁿ.**

**Why, and what each distractor is:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **P(1 + ni)** | **SIMPLE interest — interest paid only on the original principal** ← |
| **P/(1 + i)ⁿ** | **The PRESENT WORTH of a future sum P — the inverse operation** ← |
| **P × i/((1+i)ⁿ − 1)** | **The SINKING FUND factor applied to P — the annual deposit needed to accumulate P** ← |
| **P(1 + i)ⁿ** | **The COMPOUND AMOUNT — correct** ← |

> **Every distractor is a genuine and commonly used expression, so the option set requires the operation to be identified rather than a formula to be recognised.**

**Simple against compound interest, since the first distractor is the classic confusion:**

> **SIMPLE interest pays i × P every year on the ORIGINAL principal. COMPOUND interest pays interest on the accumulated amount, so the interest itself earns interest.**

> **Rs 100,000 at 10 per cent:**

| Year | SIMPLE: P(1 + ni) | COMPOUND: P(1+i)ⁿ | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **1,10,000** | **1,10,000** | **0** |
| **5** | **1,50,000** | **1,61,051** | **11,051** |
| **10** | **2,00,000** | **2,59,374** | **59,374** ← |
| **20** | **3,00,000** | **6,72,750** | **3,72,750** ← |
| **30** | 4,00,000 | **17,44,940** | **13,44,940** ← |

> **At 30 years the compound figure is more than FOUR TIMES the simple one — from the same rate on the same principal.**

> **That divergence is the whole reason the time value of money matters in infrastructure appraisal, where the horizons are decades rather than years.**

**The RULE OF 72, which is the useful mental tool:**

> **The time for a sum to DOUBLE at compound interest is approximately 72/i, with i in per cent.**

| Rate | Rule of 72 estimate | Exact |
|---|---|---|
| **6 %** | **12.0 years** | **11.9** |
| **8 %** | **9.0 years** | **9.0** ← |
| **10 %** | **7.2 years** | **7.3** |
| **12 %** | **6.0 years** | **6.1** ← |
| **18 %** | **4.0 years** | 4.2 |

> **The approximation is excellent between about 5 and 15 per cent, which covers nearly every practical rate — and it is worth having, because it converts an abstract percentage into a period a person can reason about.**

> **Its use in appraisal is immediate: at a 12 per cent discount rate, a benefit is HALVED every six years, so a benefit arriving in 30 years is worth about one thirty-second of its face value.**

> **That single observation explains why high discount rates make long-lived infrastructure look unattractive, which was raised in the appraisal discussion and is worth being able to demonstrate arithmetically.**

**COMPOUNDING FREQUENCY, since "per annum" alone is not a complete specification:**

| Compounding | Effective annual rate on a NOMINAL 12 % |
|---|---|
| **ANNUAL** | **12.00 %** |
| **Half-yearly** | **(1 + 0.12/2)² − 1 = 12.36 %** |
| **QUARTERLY** | **(1 + 0.12/4)⁴ − 1 = 12.55 %** ← |
| **Monthly** | **(1 + 0.12/12)¹² − 1 = 12.68 %** ← |
| **Daily** | 12.747 % |
| **CONTINUOUS** | **e^0.12 − 1 = 12.75 %** ← |

> **The general expression: effective rate = (1 + r/m)^m − 1, where r is the nominal annual rate and m the number of compounding periods.**

> **The two things worth noticing: more frequent compounding always gives a HIGHER effective rate, and the increase CONVERGES rapidly — the gap between monthly and continuous compounding is under a hundredth of a per cent.**

> **So the distinction between annual and monthly compounding matters and the distinction between daily and continuous does not, which is a useful sense of proportion when reading a loan offer.**

> **And the practical warning that follows: a rate quoted as "1 per cent per month" is NOT 12 per cent a year — it is (1.01)¹² − 1 = 12.68 per cent, and the difference on a large borrowing is real.**

**NOMINAL against REAL rates, which is the other necessary distinction:**

| Rate | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **NOMINAL (money) rate** | **The rate as quoted, including inflation** ← |
| **REAL rate** | **The rate net of inflation — the true increase in purchasing power** ← |
| **The relation** | **(1 + nominal) = (1 + real)(1 + inflation)** ← |
| **Approximation** | **real ≈ nominal − inflation, good for small rates** |

> **The rule that must be observed in any appraisal is CONSISTENCY: discount REAL cash flows at a REAL rate, and NOMINAL cash flows at a NOMINAL rate.**

> **Mixing them is a common and serious error — discounting constant-price cost estimates at a nominal rate that includes 7 per cent inflation understates the present value of future costs by a large margin, and makes a project look far better than it is.**

> **For most infrastructure appraisal, working entirely in CONSTANT PRICES with a REAL discount rate is the simpler and safer choice, because it avoids having to forecast inflation at all — and a forecast that is not needed is a forecast that cannot be wrong.**

examTip.trick: **P(1+i)ⁿ.** Every distractor is real: P(1+ni) is SIMPLE interest, P/(1+i)ⁿ is PRESENT WORTH, and Pi/((1+i)ⁿ−1) is the SINKING FUND factor.
examTip.trap: **"1 per cent per month" is NOT 12 % a year** — it is (1.01)¹² − 1 = 12.68 %. Effective rate = (1 + r/m)^m − 1, and more frequent compounding always raises it.
examTip.mnemonic: **RULE OF 72: doubling time ≈ 72/i.** At 12 %, money doubles in 6 years — so a benefit 30 years out is worth about a thirty-second of its face value, which is why high discount rates make long-lived infrastructure look worthless. And always match REAL flows to REAL rates.

questions.stem: During which phase of the project life cycle is the ability to INFLUENCE the final outcome greatest and the COST of making a change lowest?
options: The INITIATION and PLANNING (conception and definition) phase
questions.solution:
**The INITIATION and PLANNING phase** — conception and definition, at the very beginning.

**The two opposing curves that define project management's central problem:**

| Phase | Ability to INFLUENCE the outcome | COST of making a change |
|---|---|---|
| **Initiation / conception** | **HIGHEST — everything is still open** ← | **LOWEST — a change is an eraser mark** ← |
| **Planning / design** | High, and falling | Low, and rising |
| **Execution / construction** | **LOW — the design is fixed and work is in place** ← | **HIGH — demolition, rework, delay, claims** ← |
| **Commissioning / handover** | Very low | Very high |
| **Operation** | **Effectively nil for the design** | **Prohibitive — it is a new project** ← |

> **The two curves CROSS early, and the region to the left of the crossing is where a project is actually decided.**

> **A change to a wall's position costs nothing on a drawing, a few thousand rupees before it is built, and a great deal once it is standing — and the same ratio applies to every decision from the site chosen to the structural system adopted.**

> **The conclusion that follows is the most useful single idea in project management: SPEND TIME AND EFFORT AT THE FRONT END, because that is where the leverage is.**

> **And it runs against the ordinary institutional instinct, which is to hurry through planning in order to "get started on site" — a hurry that buys a few weeks at the beginning and costs months later.**

**What each phase contains:**

| Phase | Principal activities | Key output |
|---|---|---|
| **INITIATION / conception** | **Need identification, pre-feasibility, options, stakeholder identification** | **A project brief and the decision to proceed** ← |
| **PLANNING / definition** | **Feasibility, surveys, design, estimates, programme, procurement strategy, approvals** | **Drawings, specifications, contract documents, baseline programme and budget** ← |
| **EXECUTION / implementation** | **Procurement, construction, supervision, quality control, payments, variations** | **The completed works** |
| **MONITORING and CONTROL** | **Runs THROUGHOUT execution, not after it — measuring against the baseline and correcting** ← | Progress and cost reports |
| **CLOSING / commissioning** | **Testing, commissioning, as-built drawings, O&M manuals, handover, defects period, final account, LESSONS LEARNED** ← | A functioning asset |

> **MONITORING AND CONTROL is shown deliberately as running throughout rather than as a separate stage, because that is what distinguishes control from reporting: a monthly report that records what happened is not control, and control requires the variance to be acted upon while it can still be corrected.**

> **And the LESSONS LEARNED item in the closing phase is the one omitted almost universally: the project ends, the team disperses, and the organisation repeats the same mistakes on the next one because nothing was written down while the memory was fresh.**

**The RESOURCE and EXPENDITURE profile, which is the other characteristic curve:**

| Phase | Share of total cost | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Initiation** | **Under 1 %** ← | Almost free, and it decides everything |
| **Planning and design** | **3 to 8 %** ← | **Where the leverage is, and where budgets are cut first** |
| **Execution** | **85 to 95 %** ← | The money |
| **Closing** | 1 to 2 % | — |

> **The comparison between the second and third rows is the argument for adequate design fees, and it is worth putting plainly: DESIGN COSTS ABOUT 5 PER CENT OF THE PROJECT AND DETERMINES THE OTHER 95.**

> **Reducing a design fee by a fifth saves 1 per cent of the project cost and risks a far larger sum through buildability problems, variations, delays and an inefficient design.**

> **And it becomes still clearer over the whole life: for a building, the CONSTRUCTION cost is typically a fraction of the OPERATING cost over sixty years, so design decisions about orientation, insulation, daylight, servicing and maintainability govern a sum many times the construction budget.**

> **A rough ratio often quoted for a commercial building over its life is 1 : 5 : 200 — design fees to construction cost to the cost of operating the business inside it — and while the exact figures are arguable, the order of magnitude makes the point.**

**The S-CURVE, which is how expenditure is tracked against time:**

| Stage of the works | Rate of expenditure |
|---|---|
| **Early** | **SLOW — mobilisation, setting out, foundations below ground** ← |
| **Middle** | **RAPID — the bulk of the structure and finishes; the steep part** ← |
| **Late** | **SLOW again — testing, snagging, small residual items that take disproportionate time** ← |

> **The resulting cumulative curve is S-shaped, and its value is as a BASELINE: the planned S-curve is drawn from the programme, actual expenditure is plotted against it, and the divergence is the warning signal.**

> **Reading it requires care, because a single curve confuses two different things — a project may be spending to plan while producing less work than planned.**

> **That is why EARNED VALUE analysis separates them:**

| Measure | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PV (planned value)** | **The budgeted cost of the work SCHEDULED by now** |
| **EV (earned value)** | **The budgeted cost of the work ACTUALLY DONE** ← |
| **AC (actual cost)** | **What has actually been SPENT** |
| **Schedule variance** | **EV − PV: negative means BEHIND schedule** ← |
| **Cost variance** | **EV − AC: negative means OVER budget** ← |
| **CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV** | **Below 1.0 is unfavourable in each case** ← |

> **The distinction earned value draws is the one a simple S-curve cannot: spending less than planned may mean commendable economy or it may mean nothing is happening, and only comparing the WORK DONE against both the plan and the spend separates the two.**

> **A project at CPI 0.85 and SPI 1.05 is ahead of programme and overspending to achieve it; one at CPI 1.10 and SPI 0.80 is underspending because it is not progressing — and the two demand opposite responses.**

examTip.trick: **Influence is HIGHEST and the cost of change LOWEST at the very start** — the two curves cross early, and everything to the left of the crossing is where the project is really decided.
examTip.trap: **Design is 3-8 % of the cost and determines the other 92-97 %** — which is why cutting design time or fees to "get started on site" is the most expensive economy in project management.
examTip.mnemonic: **EARNED VALUE separates what a plain S-curve confuses: SV = EV − PV (schedule), CV = EV − AC (cost).** Underspending may be economy or paralysis, and only comparing WORK DONE against both plan and spend tells you which.

questions.stem: Resource SMOOTHING differs from resource LEVELLING in that smoothing:
options: Is applied only to materials, never to labour or plant
Adjusts activities only within their available FLOAT, so the project duration is NOT changed
Removes the critical path from the network
questions.solution:
**Smoothing adjusts activities only within their available FLOAT, so the project duration is NOT changed.**

**The two techniques compared:**

| Aspect | Resource SMOOTHING | Resource LEVELLING |
|---|---|---|
| **Constraint respected** | **The project's COMPLETION DATE is fixed** ← | **The resource LIMIT is fixed** ← |
| **What is adjusted** | **Non-critical activities, WITHIN their float** ← | **Any activity, including critical ones if necessary** |
| **Effect on project duration** | **UNCHANGED** ← | **May be EXTENDED** ← |
| **Objective** | **Reduce the PEAKS and TROUGHS of resource demand** ← | **Keep demand within an available maximum** ← |
| **Used when** | **The date matters most and the resources are obtainable** | **The resource is genuinely limited — a single crane, a scarce trade** ← |

> **The distinction is one of WHICH CONSTRAINT IS TREATED AS FIXED, and that is the cleanest way to keep them apart:**

> **SMOOTHING fixes the TIME and improves the resource profile as far as the float allows.**

> **LEVELLING fixes the RESOURCE and lets the time extend as far as necessary.**

> **The mnemonic that follows is short: SMOOTHING keeps the DATE; LEVELLING keeps the LIMIT.**

**Why an uneven resource profile is a problem at all:**

| Consequence of peaks and troughs | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hiring and firing, or idle time between peaks** | **Both expensive; and a workforce dismissed is not available when needed again** ← |
| **Plant hired for a short peak** | **Mobilisation and demobilisation costs are incurred for a brief use** ← |
| **Accommodation, transport and welfare sized for the peak** | **Facilities stand largely empty for the rest of the project** ← |
| **Supervision stretched at the peak** | **Quality and safety suffer exactly when most is happening** ← |
| **Learning is lost** | A gang that disperses and reassembles loses its productivity |

> **The FOURTH row is the one with the most serious consequences and it is the least often quantified: accidents and defects cluster at periods of peak activity, because the same supervisors are spread across more work.**

> **So smoothing the resource profile is a safety and quality measure as well as a cost one, which strengthens the case for it considerably.**

**How smoothing is done, since the procedure is simple in principle:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Draw the network and compute the float of every activity** |
| **2** | **Plot the RESOURCE HISTOGRAM assuming every activity starts at its EARLIEST start** ← |
| **3** | **Identify the peaks** |
| **4** | **DELAY non-critical activities within their float to move work out of the peaks into the troughs** ← |
| **5** | **Re-plot and iterate** |

> **The rule of thumb used in step 4 is to delay the activity with the GREATEST float first, since it has the most room to move and disturbs the plan least — and to prefer moving activities of long duration and low resource intensity into the troughs.**

> **A useful check on the result: the AREA of the histogram is unchanged by smoothing, because the same total work is being done. Only its DISTRIBUTION over time changes.**

> **So smoothing cannot reduce the total resource requirement — it can only stop the project from needing forty carpenters in week 12 and six in week 13.**

**When LEVELLING is unavoidable, and its consequence:**

> **Where a resource is genuinely capped — one tower crane, one tunnel face, a limited number of qualified welders, a single access road on a hill site — the float may not be sufficient and the project must simply take longer.**

| Symptom | Note |
|---|---|
| **The levelled programme is longer than the critical path** | **The constraint is now the RESOURCE, not the logic** ← |
| **A new "CRITICAL CHAIN" appears** | **The sequence of activities constrained by the shared resource rather than by dependency** ← |
| **The classical critical path may cease to be the binding constraint** | ← |

> **The CRITICAL CHAIN concept in the second row is the important extension and it is worth stating: when a resource is limited, the longest path through the project is determined by both the LOGICAL dependencies AND the RESOURCE contentions.**

> **Two activities with no logical relationship whatever may be effectively sequential because they need the same crane — and a critical path analysis that ignores resources will not show it.**

> **That is why a programme produced without a resource check is frequently undeliverable: it is logically valid and physically impossible.**

> **The practical consequence for a hill road or a tunnel in Nepal, where access is the limiting resource, is that the programme must be built around the ACCESS constraint from the beginning rather than levelled against it afterward.**

**And the related idea of the RESOURCE HISTOGRAM's use in procurement:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Labour histogram** | **Recruitment plan; camp and welfare sizing; wage budget by month** ← |
| **Plant histogram** | **Hire periods; deciding whether to BUY or HIRE an item** ← |
| **Material schedule** | **Delivery programme; storage requirement; cash flow for purchases** ← |
| **Cash flow forecast** | **Derived from the same data — the S-curve** ← |

> **The BUY-OR-HIRE decision in the second row is a direct application: if the histogram shows a piece of plant is needed for eighteen months out of a twenty-four month project, buying is likely cheaper; if it shows three separate two-week peaks, hiring plainly is.**

> **So the histogram is not merely a planning diagram but the input to several genuine commercial decisions — which is a good reason to produce it properly rather than as an afterthought to the programme.**

examTip.trick: **SMOOTHING keeps the DATE (works within float); LEVELLING keeps the LIMIT (may extend the project).** The difference is simply which constraint is treated as fixed.
examTip.trap: **Smoothing cannot reduce the TOTAL resource requirement** — the histogram's AREA is unchanged, only its distribution. It stops the peaks; it does not do less work.
examTip.mnemonic: **When a resource is capped, the binding constraint becomes the CRITICAL CHAIN — logic PLUS resource contention.** Two unrelated activities can be effectively sequential because they share one crane, and a plain critical path analysis will never show it.

questions.stem: Taking out an insurance policy against a project risk is an example of which risk RESPONSE strategy?
questions.solution:
**Risk TRANSFER** — the risk is moved to another party better able or more willing to carry it.

**The four responses to a NEGATIVE risk (a threat):**

| Strategy | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **AVOID** | **Eliminate the risk by changing the plan so it cannot occur** ← | **Reroute the alignment away from the unstable slope entirely** |
| **TRANSFER** | **Move the FINANCIAL consequence to another party** ← | **INSURANCE; a fixed-price contract; a performance bond; a warranty** ← |
| **MITIGATE (reduce)** | **Reduce the PROBABILITY or the IMPACT** ← | **Ground investigation to reduce uncertainty; slope stabilisation; a pilot trial** |
| **ACCEPT** | **Take no action; carry the consequence if it occurs** ← | **Set aside a CONTINGENCY (active acceptance) or simply bear it (passive)** |

> **All four options are real strategies, so the question turns on matching the action to the name — and insurance is the textbook instance of transfer.**

> **The point most often missed about TRANSFER is that IT DOES NOT REMOVE THE RISK. The slope still fails, the fire still happens, the project is still delayed.**

> **What transfers is the FINANCIAL consequence — and only the part the policy or the contract actually covers.**

| What transfer does NOT cover | Note |
|---|---|
| **The DELAY, and the loss of use** | **Unless delay-in-start-up cover is bought specifically** ← |
| **The REPUTATIONAL damage** | Not insurable |
| **The management time consumed** | — |
| **Anything beyond the policy limit, or within the excess** | **The deductible is retained risk** ← |
| **Excluded perils** | **Read the exclusions — they define the cover more than the inclusions do** ← |

> **And transfer carries a price: an insurer charges the expected loss PLUS its own costs and profit, and a contractor asked to accept a risk prices it the same way — usually more conservatively, because they know less about it than the employer does.**

> **So the principle in contract drafting is to ALLOCATE EACH RISK TO THE PARTY BEST ABLE TO CONTROL IT, not to the party easiest to push it onto.**

> **Transferring a risk the contractor cannot control — unforeseen ground conditions, for instance — does not make it go away; it produces a higher price, a weaker contractor, and a dispute when it materialises.**

**The strategies for POSITIVE risks (opportunities), which mirror them:**

| Strategy | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **EXPLOIT** | **Ensure the opportunity is realised — the mirror of AVOID** ← |
| **SHARE** | **Bring in a partner better placed to capture it — the mirror of TRANSFER** ← |
| **ENHANCE** | **Increase the probability or the benefit — the mirror of MITIGATE** |
| **ACCEPT** | Take it if it comes |
