> **The symmetry is exact and it is a reminder that risk management is about UNCERTAINTY in both directions, not only about things going wrong — though in construction the downside dominates in practice.**

**The risk management PROCESS these strategies sit within:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1 — IDENTIFICATION** | **Brainstorming, checklists, lessons from previous projects, expert judgement, site inspection** ← |
| **2 — QUALITATIVE analysis** | **Score PROBABILITY × IMPACT and rank; a risk matrix** ← |
| **3 — QUANTITATIVE analysis** | **Expected monetary value; sensitivity analysis; Monte Carlo simulation of cost and programme** ← |
| **4 — RESPONSE PLANNING** | **The four strategies above, with an OWNER and a date for each action** ← |
| **5 — MONITORING and review** | **The RISK REGISTER, reviewed at every project meeting** ← |

> **STEP 1 IS BY FAR THE MOST IMPORTANT, and it is a plain but easily forgotten proposition: A RISK THAT IS NOT IDENTIFIED CANNOT BE MANAGED BY ANY STRATEGY WHATEVER.**

> **No amount of quantitative sophistication compensates for having missed the risk that actually occurs, and effort spent on elaborate simulation of a well-understood risk is worth less than effort spent finding the ones nobody has thought of.**

> **The RISK REGISTER in step 5 is the working document: each risk with its description, cause, probability, impact, score, chosen response, the action, the OWNER by name, the date, and the residual risk after the response.**

> **The two entries that make it a live document rather than a filed one are the NAMED OWNER and the REVIEW DATE — a register with unassigned risks is a list, not a management tool.**

**EXPECTED MONETARY VALUE, since it is how responses are justified:**

> **EMV = probability × impact, and the response is worth taking when its cost is less than the reduction in EMV it achieves.**

| Risk on a hill road contract | P | Impact | EMV |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Slope failure at a known unstable section** | **0.30** | **Rs 80 lakh** | **Rs 24 lakh** ← |
| **Cost of investigation and stabilisation up front** | — | **Rs 12 lakh** | — |
| **Residual risk after stabilisation** | **0.05** | Rs 80 lakh | **Rs 4 lakh** |
| **Net benefit of mitigating** | **24 − (12 + 4)** | — | **Rs 8 lakh** ← |

> **So the mitigation is worth doing on this arithmetic, and the calculation makes the case in terms a budget holder can act on.**

> **Its limitation deserves acknowledgement: EMV is a LONG-RUN AVERAGE, and it is the right basis for an organisation running many projects.**

> **For a single project facing a risk that would be fatal to it, the average is the wrong criterion — a 5 per cent chance of a loss that bankrupts the contractor is not adequately described by its expected value, and such risks justify spending more than EMV suggests.**

> **That is precisely why insurance exists and why people buy it despite its expected value being negative: the buyer is not maximising the average, but avoiding the ruinous tail.**

examTip.trick: **AVOID (change the plan), TRANSFER (insurance, bonds, fixed price), MITIGATE (reduce P or I), ACCEPT (contingency).** All four are real — insurance is the textbook TRANSFER.
examTip.trap: **Transfer does not remove the risk — only the financial consequence, and only what the policy covers.** Delay, reputation, the excess and the exclusions all stay with you.
examTip.mnemonic: **Allocate each risk to the party best able to CONTROL it, not the one easiest to push it onto** — a risk the contractor cannot control comes back as a higher price and a dispute. And a risk not IDENTIFIED cannot be managed by any strategy at all.

questions.stem: In infrastructure PROJECT FINANCE, the term NON-RECOURSE financing means that:
options: The loan carries no interest until the project is commissioned
The lenders may recover their money from any asset of the sponsoring companies
The government guarantees repayment of the entire loan
The lenders' security is limited to the PROJECT's own assets and cash flows, and they have no claim on the sponsors' other assets
questions.solution:
**The lenders' security is limited to the PROJECT's own assets and cash flows**, with no claim on the sponsors' other assets.

**What distinguishes project finance from ordinary corporate borrowing:**

| Aspect | CORPORATE finance | PROJECT finance |
|---|---|---|
| **Who borrows** | **The company, on its own balance sheet** | **A SPECIAL PURPOSE VEHICLE (SPV) created for the project alone** ← |
| **Security** | **All the company's assets** ← (option b) | **ONLY the project's assets and cash flows** ← |
| **Basis of the lending decision** | **The borrower's overall creditworthiness and history** | **The PROJECT's forecast cash flow** ← |
| **If the project fails** | The company repays from its other business | **The lenders lose; the sponsors lose only their equity** ← |
| **Gearing** | Moderate | **HIGH — commonly 70:30 or 80:20 debt to equity** ← |
| **Documentation** | Simple | **Extremely complex — the contracts ARE the security** ← |

> **Option (b) describes FULL RECOURSE, which is ordinary corporate borrowing and the exact opposite of the term asked about.**

> **In practice, pure non-recourse finance is rare; most infrastructure deals are LIMITED RECOURSE, with sponsor support during construction (the riskiest period) falling away once the project is complete and operating reliably.**

**Why the structure is used, since it is expensive and elaborate:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **It RING-FENCES the risk** | **A failed project cannot bring down the sponsor** ← |
| **It permits very HIGH GEARING** | **Which raises the return on the sponsor's equity substantially** ← |
| **It keeps the debt OFF the sponsor's balance sheet** | Preserving their capacity to borrow elsewhere |
| **It allows a project too large for any one sponsor** | **Several sponsors share the equity** ← |
| **It imposes DISCIPLINE** | **Lenders scrutinise the project intensely because they have nothing else to fall back on** ← |

> **The LAST ROW is the one with the most value for an engineer, and it is a genuine and under-appreciated benefit:**

> **Because the lenders' only security is the project itself, they employ their own independent engineer to examine the design, the geology, the hydrology, the contracts, the cost estimate and the programme — and they do so with real rigour, because they cannot recover their money any other way.**

> **That scrutiny is frequently the most searching technical review a project receives, and it has stopped many bad projects that had passed their own promoters' appraisal.**

> **A civil engineer will meet this role as the LENDERS' TECHNICAL ADVISER, and it is a substantial area of professional practice.**

**The contract structure that makes non-recourse lending possible:**

> **If the lenders can look only to the project's cash flow, then that cash flow must be made as certain as contracts can make it — so every major risk is passed to a party by an agreement:**

| Agreement | Risk it addresses |
|---|---|
| **CONCESSION agreement with the government** | **The right to build and operate; tariff; term; termination payments** ← |
| **EPC contract, fixed price and date-certain** | **CONSTRUCTION cost and time risk, passed to the contractor** ← |
| **O&M contract** | Operating cost and performance risk |
| **OFFTAKE agreement — a power purchase agreement (PPA), or a take-or-pay contract** | **REVENUE risk — the single most important document for a hydropower project** ← |
| **Fuel or input supply agreement** | Input availability and price |
| **Insurance package** | Physical damage, delay in start-up, third-party liability |
| **Government support / guarantees** | **Political, currency convertibility, change in law** ← |

> **THE OFFTAKE AGREEMENT is the heart of the structure for a Nepali hydropower project, and it is worth understanding why:**

> **A hydropower scheme has an enormous capital cost and almost no operating cost, so its entire economics rest on the price and certainty of its revenue over twenty or thirty years.**

> **A signed power purchase agreement with a creditworthy buyer at a defined tariff converts an uncertain venture into a predictable cash flow that lenders can lend against — and without one, no amount of engineering merit will raise the debt.**

> **That is why the PPA, rather than the design or the geology, is usually the critical path item in developing a hydropower project, and why so many licensed schemes never reach financial closure.**

**FINANCIAL CLOSURE and the debt service metrics:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **FINANCIAL CLOSURE** | **The point at which all financing agreements are signed and conditions precedent met, so funds can be drawn** ← |
| **DEBT SERVICE COVERAGE RATIO (DSCR)** | **Cash available for debt service ÷ debt service due in that period** ← |
| **Minimum DSCR required** | **Typically 1.2 to 1.5 for infrastructure — a margin of safety on the cash flow** ← |
| **Debt tenor** | **Must be shorter than the concession and the asset's life** ← |
| **Moratorium / grace period** | **No principal repaid during construction, when there is no revenue** ← |

> **The DSCR is the covenant that governs the project's whole financial design: if the forecast DSCR falls below the required minimum in any year, the lenders will not lend, and the structure must change — less debt, a longer tenor, a higher tariff, or a lower cost.**

> **So an engineer's cost estimate and generation forecast feed directly into a financial test that can stop the project — which is a good reason for those estimates to be honest rather than optimistic.**

> **An overstated generation forecast does not merely embarrass the forecaster: it produces a project that cannot service its debt, and the consequences fall on the operator, the lenders and eventually the public.**

**And the BOT family of structures in which this financing sits:**

| Structure | Note |
|---|---|
| **BOT — Build, Operate, Transfer** | **The concessionaire builds, operates for the concession period, then hands over** ← |
| **BOOT — Build, Own, Operate, Transfer** | Ownership during the term as well |
| **BOO — Build, Own, Operate** | No transfer |
| **DBFO — Design, Build, Finance, Operate** | Common for roads |
| **Annuity / availability payment model** | **The government pays for AVAILABILITY, not usage — the concessionaire bears no traffic risk** ← |
| **Hybrid annuity** | Part capital grant, part annuity |

> **The ANNUITY row identifies the crucial variable in any PPP: WHO BEARS THE DEMAND RISK.**

> **In a toll-based BOT the concessionaire bears it, and if the traffic forecast proves optimistic — as toll road traffic forecasts very often are — the project fails financially even though the road is built and functioning perfectly.**

> **Under an annuity model the government bears it, pays a fixed sum for keeping the road available, and consequently pays a lower price because the concessionaire is carrying less risk.**

> **Neither is automatically right; but the choice must be made deliberately, since a demand risk allocated to a party that cannot forecast or influence demand is the commonest cause of PPP failure worldwide.**

examTip.trick: **Non-recourse: the lenders can look ONLY to the project's own assets and cash flows.** Option (b) describes FULL recourse — ordinary corporate borrowing, the exact opposite.
examTip.trap: **Pure non-recourse is rare; most deals are LIMITED recourse** — sponsor support during construction, the riskiest phase, falling away once the project operates reliably.
examTip.mnemonic: **The OFFTAKE agreement (the PPA) is the heart of a hydropower financing** — it converts an uncertain venture into a lendable cash flow, and is usually the critical path item, not the engineering. And DSCR of 1.2-1.5 is the covenant that can stop the project.

questions.stem: Under virtually every engineering code of ethics, the engineer's FIRST and PARAMOUNT obligation is to:
options: Hold PARAMOUNT the safety, health and welfare of the PUBLIC
Serve the interests of the client who is paying the fee
Protect the commercial interests of the employer
Uphold the reputation and standing of the engineering profession
questions.solution:
**Hold PARAMOUNT the safety, health and welfare of the PUBLIC.**

**Why this obligation ranks first:**

> **Every one of the four options names a genuine duty, and the codes are explicit that they are NOT of equal rank:**

| Rank | Duty | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **The PUBLIC — safety, health, welfare, and the environment** ← | **Described as PARAMOUNT, meaning it overrides the others** |
| **2** | **The CLIENT and EMPLOYER — faithful service, confidentiality, diligence** | **Owed fully, but subordinate to the first** ← |
| **3** | **The PROFESSION — its integrity, standing and standards** | |
| **4** | **Fellow engineers — fairness, credit where due, no malicious criticism** | |

> **The word PARAMOUNT is chosen deliberately in these codes and carries a precise meaning: where the duties CONFLICT, the public's safety wins, and no instruction from a client or employer can displace it.**

> **That is the entire content of professional, as distinct from merely competent, practice — and it is why engineering is licensed by statute at all.**

**Why the ranking exists — the reasoning behind it:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The public cannot assess the risk themselves** | **A person crossing a bridge cannot evaluate its design; they rely entirely on the engineer** ← |
| **The public did not choose the engineer and cannot dismiss them** | **Unlike the client, they have no leverage at all** ← |
| **The consequences fall on people who took no part in the decision** | **And who receive none of the profit** ← |
| **The engineer holds a MONOPOLY of the necessary knowledge** | **A monopoly granted by the state, on the condition it is used responsibly** ← |

> **The FOURTH row expresses the bargain that underlies every licensed profession, and it is worth stating in full because it explains why a license carries duties and not only privileges:**

> **The state grants engineers the exclusive right to practise, which restricts competition and protects their livelihood.**

> **In exchange, the profession undertakes to maintain standards, to police its own members, and to place the public's safety above its members' commercial interests.**

> **A profession that fails to keep that side of the bargain forfeits the justification for its privileges — which is why a regulator's disciplinary function is not incidental to it but central.**

**Where the conflict actually arises in practice:**

| Situation | The ethical requirement |
|---|---|
| **A client instructs a reduction in specification that compromises safety** | **REFUSE; record the advice in writing; resign if it is persisted in** ← |
| **An employer conceals a defect from the owner** | **Report through the proper channel; the duty to the public overrides confidentiality here** ← |
| **Pressure to certify work that has not been properly inspected** | **NEVER certify what has not been verified — the signature is the whole point of it** ← |
| **Being asked to work beyond your competence** | **Decline, or obtain competent assistance — competence is itself an ethical duty** ← |
| **A gift or facility from a supplier or contractor** | **Refuse anything that could reasonably appear to influence judgement** ← |
| **Discovering a danger in another engineer's work** | **Raise it — properly and factually, with the engineer concerned and the responsible authority** ← |

> **THE CERTIFICATION ROW deserves emphasis because it is the commonest and most consequential lapse, and it is the one an engineer is most likely to meet early in their career:**

> **A certificate or a signature on a test result, a pour card, a measurement sheet or a completion certificate is a professional statement that the engineer has personally satisfied themselves of the fact.**

> **Signing because the work is probably fine, because the programme is pressing, because a senior person has asked, or because everyone signs, is a false statement — and it is the mechanism by which unsafe work enters a structure.**

> **The practical protection is straightforward and worth adopting as a habit: never sign for what you have not seen, and put every instruction you disagree with in writing.**

> **A written record of advice given and overruled protects the public (it forces the decision to be made consciously by someone accountable) and it protects the engineer.**

**The other elements of professional practice the syllabus names:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **COMPETENCE** | **Practise only within your field and level of competence; keep it current** ← |
| **CONTINUING professional development** | **An ethical duty, not merely a licensing formality — knowledge decays** ← |
| **INTEGRITY and honesty in statements** | **Objective and truthful reports; distinguish fact from opinion; disclose all relevant information** ← |
| **CONFLICT OF INTEREST** | **DISCLOSE it; do not accept payment from more than one party for the same service without the knowledge of all** ← |
| **CONFIDENTIALITY** | **Owed to the client — but it does NOT extend to concealing a danger to the public** ← |
| **SUSTAINABILITY and the environment** | **Now written into most modern codes alongside public safety** ← |
| **No discrimination or harassment** | — |
| **Responsibility for work done under your supervision** | **Delegation does not transfer accountability** ← |

> **The CONFIDENTIALITY row contains the limit that matters: client confidentiality is a real and serious duty, and it is not a license to keep quiet about a hazard.**

> **Where the two conflict, the ranking above applies — which is exactly the situation in which whistle-blowing arises, and why codes of ethics provide for it explicitly.**

**And the distinction between the two Nepali bodies, since both appear in this syllabus:**

| Body | Character | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **NEPAL ENGINEERING COUNCIL (NEC)** | **A STATUTORY regulator, created by the Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055** ← | **REGISTRATION and licensing; recognition of qualifications; the code of ethics; DISCIPLINE** ← |
| **NEPAL ENGINEERS' ASSOCIATION (NEA)** | **A VOLUNTARY professional association** ← | **Representing engineers' interests; professional development; conferences and publications; advocacy** ← |

> **The distinction is the same as that between a licensing board and a professional society everywhere: the COUNCIL protects the PUBLIC from engineers, and the ASSOCIATION advances the interests OF engineers.**

> **Membership of the association is optional; registration with the council is a legal requirement to practise.**

> **Keeping the two apart is worth doing, because their purposes genuinely differ and can occasionally point in different directions — and it is the council's obligation to the public, not the association's obligation to its members, that governs when they do.**

examTip.trick: **All four options are genuine duties — but the codes rank them, and the PUBLIC comes first.** "Paramount" is chosen deliberately: where duties conflict, public safety overrides the client, the employer and the profession.
examTip.trap: **Confidentiality to the client is real, and it does NOT extend to concealing a danger to the public.** That conflict is exactly where the ranking is meant to be applied.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never sign for what you have not seen, and put every disputed instruction in writing.** And keep the two bodies apart: the COUNCIL (NEC, statutory) protects the public FROM engineers; the ASSOCIATION (NEA, voluntary) advances the interests OF engineers.

questions.stem: The statutory body that registers engineers and grants the license to practise engineering in Nepal is the:
options: Council for Technical Education and Vocational Training (CTEVT)
questions.solution:
**The NEPAL ENGINEERING COUNCIL (NEC)**, established under the **Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055 (1998)**.

**Why each of the other bodies is not the answer:**

| Body | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)** | **A VOLUNTARY professional association representing engineers — it does not license anyone** ← |
| **CTEVT** | **The body for TECHNICAL and VOCATIONAL education — diploma and certificate level technical training, not degree-level engineering licensing** ← |
| **Institute of Engineering (IOE)** | **An academic institution — a constituent of Tribhuvan University that TEACHES engineering and awards DEGREES** ← |
| **NEPAL ENGINEERING COUNCIL (NEC)** | **The STATUTORY REGULATOR — registration, licensing, ethics, discipline** ← |

> **Each distractor is a real and important institution in Nepali engineering, so the question tests whether the REGULATORY function is correctly located — and the essential distinction is between EDUCATING an engineer, REPRESENTING an engineer, and LICENSING an engineer.**

> **A university awards the degree; the association represents the interests; the COUNCIL alone confers the legal right to practise.**

**The Council's principal functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **REGISTRATION of engineers and the issue of the license** | **The core function — no person may practise as an engineer in Nepal without it** ← |
| **Maintaining the REGISTER** | A public record of who is entitled to practise |
| **RECOGNITION of academic qualifications and institutions** | **Determining which degrees, Nepali and foreign, qualify for registration** ← |
| **Prescribing the CODE OF ETHICS and professional conduct** | ← |
| **DISCIPLINARY action** | **Investigating complaints; suspending or REMOVING a name from the register** ← |
| **Advising the Government on engineering education and practice** | |
| **Setting the scope of practice for different categories** | **What each class of registrant may do** ← |

> **The DISCIPLINARY power in the fifth row is what makes registration meaningful, and it is the point worth grasping about any licensing regime:**

> **A license has force only because it can be TAKEN AWAY. Without the power to remove a name from the register, a code of ethics is advice.**

> **The sanction is severe — removal ends the person's ability to practise the profession lawfully — which is why the disciplinary process must be, and is, a formal one with investigation, a hearing and a right of appeal.**

**The registration requirement and its consequences:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **No person may practise as an engineer, or use the title, without registration** | **The central prohibition of the Act** ← |
| **Registration requires a recognised qualification** | **From an institution the Council recognises** ← |
| **The certificate must be RENEWED periodically** | **Registration is not permanent — it lapses if not renewed** ← |
| **Registered engineers are bound by the code of conduct** | Enforceable by the Council |
| **Practising without registration, or after removal, is an offence** | ← |
| **Signing or certifying drawings and designs** | **Reserved to appropriately registered engineers — which is how the license bites in daily practice** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHERE REGISTRATION MATTERS MOST IN ORDINARY WORK, and it is worth being clear about:**

> **A municipality will not accept building drawings, nor a client a structural design, unless they are signed by an engineer whose registration is current — so the license is not a certificate to hang on a wall but the operative requirement for doing the work at all.**

> **And the RENEWAL requirement in the third row catches people out: an engineer whose registration has lapsed is, for legal purposes, not registered, and anything they certify in that period is open to challenge.**

> **The practical discipline is simply to treat the renewal date as a fixed professional obligation, in the same class as an insurance renewal.**

**Why a statutory regulator exists for engineering at all:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The public cannot judge an engineer's competence** | **Registration is the state's assurance that a minimum standard has been met** ← |
| **The consequences of incompetence fall on THIRD PARTIES** | **Not on the person who chose the engineer** ← |
| **The failures are catastrophic and irreversible** | **A collapsed building kills; the remedy comes too late** ← |
| **There is a strong commercial incentive to cut corners** | **A regulator supplies the counterweight** ← |

> **The SECOND row is the decisive one and it is what distinguishes engineering from most trades: if a tailor makes a poor suit, the customer bears it and can go elsewhere.**

> **If an engineer designs a poor building, the people who live in it bear it, and they never chose the engineer, never saw the drawings and cannot assess the risk.**

> **Regulation exists precisely because the market cannot protect people who are not party to the transaction — and in a country as seismically exposed as Nepal, that argument carries unusual force.**

**And the connection to the 2015 earthquake, which is the reason this matters here rather than being an administrative footnote:**

| Observation | Consequence for regulation |
|---|---|
| **Engineered buildings largely performed well; NON-ENGINEERED construction did not** | **The gap is not in the codes but in whether a competent engineer was involved at all** ← |
| **Much construction proceeds without any engineer, or with a nominal signature** | **"Rubber-stamping" a drawing an engineer has not designed is precisely the ethical failure the register exists to punish** ← |
| **Building permit systems exist and are unevenly enforced** | **Enforcement, not the absence of rules, is the binding constraint** ← |
| **Post-earthquake reconstruction required a large registered workforce** | **And exposed how thin the supervision capacity was outside the main cities** ← |

> **The second row names a practice every Nepali engineer will encounter: being asked to sign drawings prepared by someone else, for a fee, without designing or checking them.**

> **It is a straightforward breach of the code — a certificate is a statement of personal professional judgement — and it is also the mechanism by which the entire regulatory system is hollowed out from within.**

> **A register whose members will sign anything provides no protection whatever, and the buildings that fall down in the next earthquake will have been signed for.**

> **That is the clearest possible statement of why the ethical obligation and the statutory registration are the same subject rather than two, and it is a fitting note on which to close this chapter.**

examTip.trick: **NEC — statutory, under the Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055 (1998).** Distinguish the three roles: IOE/universities EDUCATE, NEA REPRESENTS, and only the COUNCIL LICENSES.
examTip.trap: **CTEVT covers technical and vocational (diploma/certificate) training, not degree-level engineering licensing** — a real and important body, but not the regulator of engineers.
examTip.mnemonic: **A license has force only because it can be TAKEN AWAY** — the disciplinary power is what makes the code of ethics more than advice. And registration must be RENEWED: a lapsed engineer is, legally, not registered, and anything certified meanwhile is open to challenge.
